units.la: AD ANTONIVM RANZOVIVM, HOLSATVM, NOBILISSIMI ET magnifici Herois, DN. ANTONII RANZOVII, filium, non solùm stemmatis & prosapia, sed etiam uirtute & ingenio nobilem, IOANNIS IACOBI GRYNAEI Proœmium.
units.tr: TO ANTONIUS RANZOVIUS OF HOLSTEIN, SON OF THE MOST NOBLE AND DISTINGUISHED LORD ANTONIUS RANZOVIUS, A MAN NOBLE NOT ONLY IN LINEAGE AND ANCESTRY BUT ALSO IN VIRTUE AND TALENT: A PREFACE BY JOHANN JAKOB GRYNAEUS.

units.la: Nfirmitatis mea quotidianus sensus, & mortalitatis meditatio, cũi non parum seruit morbus Θπιδήμιος, faciunt, ut nulla alia de re cogitare.
units.tr: The daily sense of my weakness and the meditation on mortality, while the epidemic disease [ἐπιδήμιος] weighs on me no little, make me think of nothing else.

units.la: & tecum, nobilissime RANZOVI, paucis συμφιλολογεῖν malim, quàm de ea re quæ nobis omnium est gratissima, uidelicet de Vita: deq; eius contrario, uidelicet de Morte, quam qui nimiũ timet, sententia Ioan. Chrysostomi, non sperat uiuere post mortẽ.
units.tr: With you, most noble Ranzau, I would rather talk together [συμφιλολογεῖν] briefly than about any other matter, namely about life, which is the most welcome of all things to us, and about its opposite, death. Whoever fears death too much, as John Chrysostom says, does not hope to live after death.

units.la: Oro autem Filium Dei Dominum nostrum strum IESVM CHRISTVM, ut mihi aliisq; seruis suis, pro immensa sua bonitate & φιλανθρωπίᾳ, det, ut secundum intentam expectationem & spem nostram, nulla in re pudefiamus, & ut semper in corpore cuiusq; nostrum magnificetur Christus, sive per vitam, sive per mortem: ut cum Apostolo nostro loquar.
units.tr: I pray that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, for his immense goodness and love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία], grant to me and to his other servants that, according to our earnest expectation and hope, we may be put to shame in nothing, and that in each of our bodies Christ may always be magnified, whether by life or by death, as I would say in the words of our Apostle.

units.la: Constitui autem, σὺν Χριστῷ[?], nobile dictum Pauli: Mihi autem est Christus & in vita & in morte lucrum: hypothesi ad the sin per ἀνάλυσιν[?] reducta, interpretari: ut sermo noster sale conditus non careat amabili & salutari gratia, & alienus sit ab omni vanitate.
units.tr: I have resolved, with Christ, to interpret the noble saying of Paul: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain," the hypothesis being brought back by analysis, so that our discourse may be seasoned with salt, not lacking a pleasing and wholesome grace, and may be free from all vanity.

units.la: Existimo sane pulcerrima & consolationis plenissima Enunciationis illius, hanc esse sententiam: Iesus Christus fidelium suorum seruorum lucrum est, non solum in eorum vita, sed etiam in eorundem morte. Lucrum vocat, gloriam Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qua cum inaestimabili nostro com-modo coniuncta est. Pietas enim, qua nobis in vita & morte reipsa declaranda est, ad omnia utilis est, ut qua promissionem ha[?] habeat uitæ præsentis et futuræ. Immò magnus est quæstus Pietas cum animo sua sor te contento, ut diuinus ille Apostolus alibi docuit.
units.tr: Certainly I think the meaning of that most beautiful and most consoling statement is this: Jesus Christ is the gain of his faithful servants, not only in their life but also in their death. He calls it gain, the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is joined with our inestimable advantage. For piety, which in life and in death must be shown in deed, is useful for all things, since it holds the promise of the present and the future life. Indeed piety together with a mind content with its lot is a great gain, as the divine Apostle teaches elsewhere.

units.la: Is demum rectissimè dicitur fidelium lucrũ, qui solus hoc illis præstat, ut citra fanaticã intemperiem & temeritatem, optimo consilio perinde illis sit, sive diutius viuant in carne, sive moriantur: cum æterna vitæ donum ἀμεταμέλητον καὶ μὴ παλινάγγενετον, sibi collatum esse rectè statuant. Reipsa enim declarat, vitæ animalis benedictionem ea lege se illis contulisse, ut tamen vitæ spiritualis & æterna donum, modis omnibus præstantius, anteponi uelit. Rursum, primæ mortis necessitatem sic temperat & mitigat, ut iam non sit maledictionis horribile specimen, sed mortificationis carnis nostræ necessarium complementum, & initium quietis optatissimæ. Sensit hoc Babylas Martyr, cũ spectator fuisset & hortator Martyrij casta sanctaq; ac grandæua coniugis, & dulcissimorũ optimorumq; filiorũ: & iam uenerandus senex et Christi Iesu hieromartyr, ubi cathenas ferreas sibi non detrahi petiuisset, ut ijs ornatus in resurrectione iustorum coram Domino Iesu comparere posset: & iam ceruicem feriendam carnifici praeberet, Dauidico epiphonemate usus est: Reuertere anima mea ad requiem tuam, quia Dominus benefecit tibi. Enimuero gratulari sibi requiem & aeterna uita consuetudinem, uir sanctus in illo suo agone nunquam potuisset, si non in morte lucrum maximum sibi repositum esse, persuasum habuisset.
units.tr: He is rightly called the gain of the faithful who alone grants them this, that, without fanatical intemperance and rashness, they should have the best judgement whether they live longer in the flesh or die; since they rightly judge that the gift of eternal life, which is irrevocable and not to be reversed [ἀμεταμέλητον καὶ μὴ παλινάγγενετον], has been bestowed upon them. For he shows in fact that he has bestowed on them the blessing of animal life on the condition that the gift of spiritual and eternal life, far more excellent in every way, be preferred to it. Again, he so tempers and softens the necessity of the first death that it is no longer a horrible token of the curse, but the necessary completion of the mortification of our flesh and the beginning of the most desired rest. Babylas the martyr felt this, when he was a spectator and encourager of martyrdom, as was his chaste and holy and aged wife, and his most sweet and excellent sons; and when the now venerable old man, the hieromartyr of Christ Jesus, asked that his iron chains not be taken from him, so that adorned with them he might appear before the Lord Jesus at the resurrection of the just, and was now offering his neck to the executioner to be struck, he used the Davidic exclamation: "Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you." Indeed the holy man could never have rejoiced in his rest and in the eternal life that follows, in that struggle of his, unless he had been persuaded that the greatest gain was laid up for him in death.

units.la: Sedenim Dominus & Seruator noster Iesus Christus, id nobis praestat, ut indifferens nobis, quibus datum est in eum credere, esse possit, siue diuturna sit uita huius nostra usura, siue ea breui periodo terminetur.
units.tr: But our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ grants us this, that for us, to whom it has been given to believe in him, it may be a matter of indifference whether the enjoyment of this our life be long or whether it be ended in a short span.

units.la: Vt enim eorum qui alieni sunt a Christo, ea est maledictio, ut non iniuria quaeri possit: Praestetne eos nunquam natos esse, an uero in hanc lucem editos? & Morine illos satius sit, an uero uiuere? Ita quoq; e contrario, ea est illorum, qui Christo cocorporesfacti, ut membra uiua a capite uiuificantur, benedictio, ut beatissimi sint, tam in morte (prima inquam: nam secunda mormorti, seu aterno exitio, obnoxij non sunt) quam in vita sua.
units.tr: For just as the curse on those who are estranged from Christ is such that it may fairly be asked: would it be better for them never to have been born than to have been brought into this light? And would it be better for them to die than to live? So too, conversely, the blessing of those who are made co-bodied with Christ is such, as living members are quickened by the head, that they are most blessed both in death (the first death, I mean, for they are not subject to the second death, that is, eternal destruction) and in their life.

units.la: Enimuero, quis homo pius & rerum diuinarum intelligens dubitet, beatos esse eos, vitamq; animalem ac primam mortem eis veluti quaedam ἀδιάφορα esse, qui finis ultimi & proximi tam in morte quam in vita sua participes sunt? Constat autem, fideles homines, illos fines & cum viuunt in carne, & cum moriuntur, obtinere. Etenim in cuiusque illorum corpore, magnificatur Christus: & tam cum decedunt, quam cum viuunt, Christus ipsis lucrum est. Nouimus ijs qui diligunt Deum, omnia simul conferre ad bonum, ijs uidelicet qui ex proposito ipsius uocati sunt. Editi enim in hanc lucem, non ideo renascuntur in Christo, per aquam & Spiritum, ut terrenis bonis inhient, ut delicijs affluant, ut φιλήδονοι μᾶλ-λον ἢ φιλόθεοι sint: sed ut per eos Christus glorificetur, & ab hoc tanquam capite, iustitia vitaq; aeternae donu in illos, qui membra κῇ[?] σύμφυτοι illius sunt, redudet. Nullum maius emolumentum ab eo ad nos redire potest, de quo dicitur: Et ex plenitudine ipsius omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia.
units.tr: Indeed, what pious man who understands divine things could doubt that those are blessed, and that animal life and the first death are for them as things indifferent [ἀδιάφορα], who share in the ultimate and proximate end both in death and in their life? It is certain that faithful men obtain that end both when they live in the flesh and when they die. For in the body of each of them Christ is magnified, and both when they depart and when they live, Christ is their gain. We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, namely for those who are called according to his purpose. For having been brought into this light, they are not reborn in Christ through water and the Spirit so that they may gape after earthly goods, abound in delights, and be lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God [φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι]; but so that through them Christ may be glorified, and from him as the head, righteousness and the gift of eternal life may flow back upon those who are grafted together with him as members [σύμφυτοι]. No greater advantage can come back to us from him, of whom it is said: "And of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace."

units.la: Facit Christus Iesus Dominus noster, ut dum hic in Mundo uiuimus, ipsius nomen, fidei per charitatem agentis affectu, professione, factis, gestibus & totius uitae specie, citra simulationis fucum, magnificare studeamus: facit, ut morte glorificemus Deum: facit, ut cum ipsius gloria beatitudo nostra coniungatur: facit deniq;, ut nec uita huius dulcedo desiderium aeternae uitae minuat, nec mortis horror gustum uitae beatae diluat.
units.tr: Jesus Christ our Lord brings it about that, while we live here in the world, we strive to magnify his name by our affection of faith working through love, by our profession, deeds, gestures, and the whole character of our life, without the paint of pretence. He brings it about that we glorify God in death. He brings it about that our blessedness is joined with his glory. Finally, he brings it about that neither the sweetness of this life diminishes the desire for eternal life, nor the horror of death dilutes the taste of the blessed life.

units.la: Quare in Domino persuasum habemus, nobis Iesum Christum & in uita & in morte, sanctissimum & praecipuum esse emolumentum: eoq; nomine supplices eum oramus, ut nobis det, ad ipsius laudem, uita benedictione uti: ut accedat foveatq;, in nobis uitae aeternae desiderium, efficiatq;, ne carnis intemperiem sic acuat mortis horror, ut sancta professione, fide & spe indignos gestus & sermones unquam proferamus.
units.tr: Therefore we are persuaded in the Lord that Jesus Christ, both in life and in death, is for us the most holy and chief advantage; and for that reason we pray to him as suppliants, that he would grant us to use the blessing of life to his praise, that he would cherish and increase in us the desire for eternal life, and that the horror of death would not so sharpen the intemperance of the flesh that we ever utter unworthy gestures and words against our holy profession, faith and hope.

units.la: Intueamur autem, magna cum gratulatione, & uetera & recentia exempla sanctorum storum Martyrum, quibus diuinitus datum est, αὐτῷ τῷ ἔργῳ ostendere, Christum Iesum esse seruorum suorum lucrum & in vita & in morte: & imitemur eorum fidem, considerantes qui fuerit exitus conversationis ipsorum: memores grauissimi dicti: At nos non ij sumus qui nos subducamus ad exitium, sed qui credamus ad animæ salutem.
units.tr: Let us look upon, with great rejoicing, both the old and the recent examples of the holy martyrs, to whom it has been granted by God to show, by the very deed [αὐτῷ τῷ ἔργῳ], that Christ Jesus is the gain of his servants both in life and in death. Let us imitate their faith, considering what the outcome of their conduct was, mindful of the most weighty saying: "But we are not of those who draw back to destruction, but of those who believe to the saving of the soul."

units.la: Iustinus philosophus & martyr, de conversione sua, transituq; ab Ethnicismo ad Christianismum, verba faciens, ingenuè fatetur, se Platonica secta addictum, cum Christianos velut de plaustro omni conuiciorum genere proscindi, & tamen impauidos omnium ætatum dignitatumq; homines ad mortem accedere, animaduerteret: cogitare cœpisse, fieri non posse, ut eiusmodi homines improbi, voluptatibus dediti, vitæ huius amantes iure habeantur, qui etiam cū dignitate viuendi conditione sibi oblata, mori malint, quàm Christū abnegare? Nullū enim tale præsidiū e Platonis philosophia, morti opponi posse, vir prudens & ingeniosus facilè colligebat.
units.tr: Justin the philosopher and martyr, speaking of his own conversion and passage from heathenism to Christianity, frankly confesses that he was attached to the Platonic sect; when he observed that the Christians were torn apart like a cart by every kind of abuse, and yet that men of every age and rank went to death fearlessly, he began to think that it could not be that such men were rightly held to be wicked, given over to pleasures, lovers of this life, when they preferred to die rather than deny Christ, even though a condition of living with dignity was offered to them. For the wise and clever man easily concluded that no such defence against death could be set up from the philosophy of Plato.

units.la: PROOEMIVM.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Polycarpus, Smyrnæorum Episcopus, cui hæc eximia laus tribuitur, quòd pro Ecclesiarū pace dies noctesq; precari solitus sit, cum ei auctor esset Proconsul, ut canicie ætatisq; suæ ac dignitatis et vitæ rationem haberet, iuraret per Cæsaris fortunam, ac Domino Iesu Christo maleddiceret, grauissimè respondit: Octoginta & sex annos servo ei, nec ille unquam me læsit: quomodo igitur possem maledicere Regi meo, qui salutem mihi dedit? Hæc sanè vox eius viri erat, qui verè persuasum habebat, sive viveret, sive moreretur, Domini Iesu esse: & nil Christo triste recepto sibi unquā me-tuendum esse.
units.tr: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, to whom this outstanding praise is given, that he was accustomed to pray day and night for the peace of the churches, when the proconsul urged him, out of regard for his grey hair, his age, his dignity and his way of life, to swear by the fortune of Caesar and to curse the Lord Jesus Christ, answered most gravely: "For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has never wronged me. How then could I blaspheme my King, who gave me salvation?" This was indeed the voice of a man who truly was persuaded that, whether he lived or died, he belonged to the Lord Jesus, and that once Christ was received he had nothing dreadful to fear.

units.la: Ignatius, ⌣Antiochena Ecclesia Episcopus, nisi persuasum habuisset, Christum Iesum lucrum sibi esse & in vita & in mor-te, non erupisset, iam ad bestias damnatus, in hæc voces: Frumentum ego sum Dei: bestiarum dentibus molor & subigor, ut panis mundus efficiar Christo.
units.tr: Ignatius, bishop of the Antiochene church, would not have burst out, already condemned to the beasts, into these words, had he not been persuaded that Christ Jesus was gain to him both in life and in death: "I am God's wheat. I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be made clean bread for Christ."

units.la: Addam & ex Victoris de Persecutione Vandalica lib.3. commemorabile exemplum, generosa ⌣Matrona Dionysia Afri-cana, tanæ, quæ habitu mundo matronali spoliata, flagrisq; excruciata, non solum intrepide crudelitatis administros reprehendit, dicens: Ministri diaboli, ea quæ ad contumeliam facitis, laudi mihi sunt: sed etiâ unici, nobilissimi, & adhuc tenera ætate filij Maiorici, cruciatuum spectatrix, ei dixit: Memento fili, nos in nomine sacrosanctæ Trinitatis baptizatos: ne igitur pudamus [?] indumentum nostræ salutis, ne veniens inuitator uestem non inueniat nuptialem. Illa pœna timenda est, quæ nunquam finitur. Illud autem in illa historia mirè patheticum est, quòd cum generosæ Matri, optimi Adolescentis, qui in confessionis certamine spiritum Christo tradiderat, corpus traditum esset terræ mandandum, Mater heroica corpus exanime amplexans, Deoq; gratias immortales agens, ad gaudium spei futuræ, in sua domo citra superstitionem maluit sepelire, ut quoties supra sepulcrum eius ad sacrosanctam Trinitatem preces funderet, alienam à filio eiusq; fide & spe, quæ in illo Martyre fulserant, sese neutiquam esse, testaretur.
units.tr: I will add also a memorable example from the third book of Victor's account of the Vandal persecution: the noble matron Dionysia of Africa, stripped of her respectable matronly dress and tortured with whips, not only fearlessly rebuked the agents of cruelty, saying, "Ministers of the devil, the things you do to insult me are my praise," but also, when she was watching the torments of her only son Maioricus, a most noble youth still of tender age, she said to him: "Remember, son, that we were baptized in the name of the most holy Trinity. Let us therefore not be ashamed [?] of the garment of our salvation, lest the guest who is invited, when he comes, find no wedding garment. That punishment is to be feared which never ends." In that story there is a particularly moving point: when the body of the excellent young man, who had given up his spirit to Christ in the contest of confession, was handed over to be committed to the earth, the heroic mother, embracing the lifeless body and giving immortal thanks to God, chose, for the joy of future hope, to bury him in her own house without superstition. Thus, whenever she poured out prayers to the most holy Trinity above his tomb, she would bear witness that she was in no way estranged from her son, nor from the faith and hope that had shone in that martyr.

units.la: PROOEMIVM.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Meminit Ioannes Balæus, Anglus, in historia Martyrum, Adolescētis cuiusdam, qui ob pietatem & professionem doctrinæ Euangelicæ, Mariana persecutione in Angliæ Regno ardente, à Pseudepiscopo damnatus, inq; patriam reductus, ut in solo natali exustus, terrori nostris esset, obuios habuit parentes, qui etiam non modò gratulabundi filium ad Martyrium euntem exceperunt, & ad constantiam hortati sunt: uerumetiam è carcere ad rogum comitati, & iam ardente pyra, semianimem consolati sunt.
units.tr: John Bale, the Englishman, records in his History of the Martyrs a certain young man who, during the Marian persecution raging in the kingdom of England, was condemned by the pseudo-bishop for his piety and his profession of the Evangelical doctrine. He was brought back to his homeland so that, being burned on his native soil, he might serve as a terror to our people. His parents met him on the way as he was going to his martyrdom. They not only received their son with joy and encouraged him to constancy, but also accompanied him from the prison to the stake, and when the pyre was already burning, they comforted him while he was half-dead.

units.la: O commemorabile & omnibus piis obseruandum, fidei, mundi & naturæ uictricis, exemplum. O nos nimium de-licatos Christi testes, qui etiam ad popula-ris morbi mentionem, inter media & con-solationum & remediorum præsidia, ex-horrescimus, perinde ac si nunquam nobis innotuissent fidei Articuli: Credo carnis resurrectionem: Credo æternam uitam.
units.tr: O memorable example of faith, victorious over the world and over nature, which all the godly ought to observe! O we Christ's witnesses, far too delicate, who shudder even at the mention of a plague, amid the means of consolation and the remedies at hand, as though the articles of faith had never become known to us: "I believe the resurrection of the flesh"; "I believe everlasting life."

units.la: Anna Burgao, celeberrimo Hieromar-tyri Christi, hac in ultimo agone Martyrij nox, O Domine Deus ne me deseras, ne i-pse te deseram: apud omnem posteritatem testimonio erit, Christum Iesum ei lucrum & solatium fuisse & in uita & in morte.
units.tr: Anna Burgh, the most famous holy martyr of Christ, in the last agony of her martyrdom, said: "O Lord God, do not forsake me, lest I forsake you." This will be a testimony to all posterity that Christ Jesus was her gain and her comfort, both in life and in death.

units.la: Nihil iam de ijs Iesu Christi Confessoribus dicam, qui incruento quidem, sed tamen difficilimo defunguntur Martyrio, dum aduersus manifestos & clandestinos hostes Ecclesiae, pro ueritate tuenda illis est pugnandum. Ne hi quidem periculosa & laboriosa sua militia possent defungi, nisi θεοδίδακτοι[?] intelligerent, magnificari nomen Christi in sua uita & morte: eoq; nomine breuia uitae huius incommoda magno ferenda animo, & immortalitatis fiducia leniendos esse dolores, nec uentris, reditum annuorum, aut gratiae potentum hominum caussa, quicquam contra conscientiam esse uel uoce, uel manu, uel deniq; praepostero factionis alicuius studio, committendum.
units.tr: I will say nothing now of those confessors of Jesus Christ who undergo a martyrdom that is bloodless but nonetheless most difficult, while they must fight for the truth against the open and secret enemies of the Church. Not even they could complete their dangerous and laborious warfare unless they understood, being taught by God [θεοδίδακτοι], that the name of Christ is magnified in their life and death; and that for this reason the brief troubles of this life are to be borne with a great spirit, and the pains eased by confidence in immortality; and that nothing contrary to conscience is to be committed, whether by voice or by hand, nor, finally, by any perverse zeal for a faction, for the sake of the belly, the return of the years, or the favour of powerful men.

units.la: Visum autem mihi est, ANTONI RANZOVI, Iuvenis nobilissime, haec mea in Habacucum Prophetam Hypomnemata tuo potissimum nomini inscribere: ut & laudatissimae tuae familiae & tuum nomen, genium gratiamq; etiam apud incly-ta tua Gentis Holsatica homines pios, ijs con- ciliaret. Nihil illa habent quod non respon- deat proportioni fidei: etsi non ignoro ser- monis nitorem ijs deesse, non eam solum ob causam, quòd in florido illo nitidoq; dicen- di scribendiq; genere exercitatus non sum, sed etiam quia in tanta laborum Academi- corum turba, ocio destitutus, informes fœ- tus lambendo elegantiores reddere nopos- sum: saepè repetens uersum ueterem, ut me exhilarem: Ornari res ipsa nequit, contenta doceri.
units.tr: It seemed best to me, Anton Ranzau, most noble young man, to inscribe these my Notes on the Prophet Habakkuk chiefly to your name, so that they might also win for your most praiseworthy family and your name, and for yourself, the favour and goodwill of the godly even among your distinguished Holstein nation. They contain nothing that does not correspond to the proportion of faith. Yet I am not unaware that they lack polish of style, not only because I have not been trained in that flowery and elegant manner of speaking and writing, but also because, in such a great crowd of academic labours and lacking leisure, I cannot make my shapeless offspring more elegant by licking them into shape. Often, to cheer myself, I repeat the old line: "The thing itself cannot be adorned; it is content to be taught."

units.la: Fortassis hoc postremum erit ingenij mei ἐχτςωμία: quod si argumento fuerit pijs & modestis, me, aliis quibusdam classicum bel- li ciuilis in Ecclesia canentibus, aliis tubis intestinorum motuum applaudentibus: pro meo modulo, utilia & necessaria docetem, à Συμομαχία alienum fuisse, Iuuentutem ad pietatis & seueriores Theologiae studium pro uirili hortatum esse, & Iosephi contri- tionem lugentem, hæc ὑπομνήματα con- scripsisse, me id quod uolo obtinuisse sta- tuam. Si me Deus superstitem esse uolet, Malachiæ ἐξήγησιν paulo post, ingeniosa piaq̃ {φιλ[?]} Iuventuti gratificandi causa, σω[?] δήμου Habacuco adiungam.
units.tr: Perhaps this will be the last miscarriage [ἐκτρώμα] of my talent. If it proves acceptable to the pious and modest, I shall be satisfied that I have achieved what I want: that, while others sound the trumpet call of civil war in the Church and others applaud with the trumpets of internal strife, I have kept clear of any alliance (συμμαχία), have taught what is useful and necessary according to my small measure, have urged the young, as far as I could, toward the study of piety and of a more serious theology, and have written these notes while mourning the breaking of Joseph. If God wills that I survive, I shall add to Habakkuk, a little later, an exposition of Malachi, to gratify the young, for whose benefit it is clever and pious.

units.la: Fateor autem me, toto hoc anno, quo mea domi vixisti, documētis pietatis erga Deū, iusticiæ erga homines, candoris in interpretandis aliorū dictis factisq;, singularis diligentiæ in studio Ciuilis sapientiæ, sic esse delectatum, ut Deo inprimis donorum istorum auctori benignissimo sæpè gratias agerem, & ea tibi & præstantissimis tuis Parentibus & Propinquis tacitus ex animo gratularer.
units.tr: I confess, moreover, that during this whole year in which you lived at my house, I was so delighted by your proofs of piety toward God, of justice toward men, of candour in interpreting the words and deeds of others, and of singular diligence in the study of civil wisdom, that I often thanked God, the most kind giver of these gifts, above all, and silently rejoiced with you and your most distinguished parents and relatives.

units.la: Renocasti mihi in memoriam nobile exemplum singularis diligentiæ in studio lingua Latina & Historia, Iuuenis nobilissimi, & optatissimi quondam hospitis mei, affinis tui, IOANNIS ADOLPHI À BOCKVVOLD, qui dum apud nos Basilea uiueret, assiduitate in studio optimarum literarum, expeētationem: egregio successu, iudicium meum, longè felicissimé uicit.
units.tr: You have brought back to my memory a noble example of singular diligence in the study of the Latin language and history, in the person of the most noble young man and my former dear guest, your kinsman John Adolph von Bockwold, who, while he lived with us at Basel, by his constant devotion to the study of the best literature, far surpassed my expectation, and, by his outstanding success, my judgment, by a very great margin.

units.la: Erit autem uirtutis humanitatisq; tuæ, Hypomnemata ista tuo inscripta nomini, uelut μνημόσυνον nostri contubernij, quod tibi cum lectissimis et nobilibus Iuuenibus ueruersanti, iucundum fuisse existimo, tueri aduersus sinistrum fatum: erit & pietatis, meditatione diuinæ Prouidentiæ (cuius quasi Commentarium scholasticum tibi offero) animum præmunire non solùm aduersus casus tristes, quibus hæc nostra vita obnoxia est: sed etiam aduersus illecebras blandientis fortunæ seu rerum secundarum, quæ fere maius, quàm aduersa, periculum creare solent.
units.tr: These Notes, inscribed to your name, will be, as it were, a memorial [μνημόσυνον] of our companionship, which I think was pleasant for you while you lived with the most select and noble young men; and they will serve to guard that companionship against an unfavourable fate. They will also serve piety: by meditating on divine Providence, of which I offer you a kind of scholarly commentary, the mind is to be fortified not only against the sad chances to which this our life is subject, but also against the allurements of fortune when it flatters, that is, of prosperity, which usually creates a greater danger than adversity.

units.la: Quod superest, Deum Patrem, per sanctum nomen Iesu Christi filij ipsius unigeniti, toto pectore oro, vt ad suam laudem, & Reipub. utilitatem, laudatissimorum̄ Parentum tuorum sanctam & liberalem voluptatem, id quod in te cœpit, perficiat, vt per omnem vitam pie, iuste, temperanter & studiose viuas, sisq; Patria & tibi-ipsi præsidio & ornamento. Amen. Per-scriptum Basileæ Calendis Septemb, Anno Christi 1582.
units.tr: For the rest, I pray with all my heart to God the Father, through the holy name of Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, that for his own praise and the benefit of the commonwealth, and for the holy and generous delight of your most praiseworthy parents, he may bring to completion what he has begun in you, so that you may live piously, justly, temperately and diligently all your life, and be a protection and an ornament to your country and to yourself. Amen. Written at Basel on the Kalends of September, in the year of Christ 1582.

units.la: HYPOMNEMATA IN HABACVC PROPHETAM.
units.tr: HYPOMNEMATA IN HABACUC PROPHETAM.

units.la: CUM in hac tanta Ecclesiæ mi-litantis, & laboribus senió-que iam confectæ afflictio-ne & mœsticia, Pijs omnib: capita attollenda, & iam in-stans redemptio expectanda sit: plurimum nostra interest, habere in conspectu aliquot grauissima selectissimaq; Patrū dicta, quæ monent, fatalem esse Ecclesiæ Christi crucem, & eam maximum habe-re usum, ac proinde nemini pio defugi-endam.
units.tr: Since in this great affliction and sorrow of the Church, which is still militant and already worn down by its labours, all the godly must lift up their heads and await the redemption that is now at hand, it is very much in our interest to keep before our eyes some of the most weighty and carefully chosen sayings of the Fathers, which warn that the cross of Christ's Church is bound to come, that it serves a great purpose, and that therefore no godly person should shrink from it.

units.la: Ecclesia, ut inquit Augustinus, velut li-lium inter spinas, malis & bonis est per-mixta. Quis igitur miretur se pungi rerum molestisimarum sensu?
units.tr: The Church, as Augustine says, is like a lily among thorns, mixed together with bad and good alike. Who then should be surprised that she is pricked by the feeling of the most painful troubles?

units.la: Gregorius, Ecclesiam, inquit, Christus crucis suæ hæredem constituit. Quis nostrum igitur eam detrectet defugiatq;?
units.tr: Gregory says: Christ has made the Church the heir of his cross. Which of us then should refuse it or flee from it?

units.la: Sed & hoc memoria dignisimum est, quod coronidis vice ex diui Hilarij li.7. de Trinitate, ideo adducemus, quia mo-net; veram Ecclesiam propter veritatis
units.tr: But this also is most worth remembering, and we shall cite it by way of conclusion, from the seventh book of Saint Hilary's On the Trinity, because it warns us:

units.la: profesionem exosam quidem esse, sed tamen proprium eius esse, uincere cū lę-ditur, emergere cum premitur, exaltari cum humiliatur. Magna uis est ueritatis: quæ cum per se intelligi non possit, per ea tamè ipsa quæ ei aduersantur, elucet, ut in natura sua immobilis manens, fir-mitatem naturæ suæ quotidie, dum atte-tatur, acquirat. Hoc enim Ecclesiæ proprium est, ut tum uincat cum læditur, tum intelligat cum arguitur, tum obtineat cum deseritur. O utinam, fratres optimi, istud nobis tam sit gratum, quàm esse debet persuasum.
units.tr: that the true Church, on account of its profession of the truth, is indeed hated, but that it is its own nature to conquer when it is struck, to rise up when it is pressed down, and to be exalted when it is humbled. Great is the power of truth: though it cannot be understood through itself, it nevertheless shines through the very things that oppose it, so that, remaining unmoved in its own nature, it gains the firmness of its nature every day as it is attacked. For this is the proper character of the Church: that it conquers when it is wounded, understands when it is accused, and holds on when it is forsaken. O that, best of brothers, this were as welcome to us as it ought to be believed by us.

units.la: Enimuero, ut hac quoque tempestate, in media Ecclesiæ perturbatione ἡ τῇ τα-χῇ [?], Dei providentiam lucere, & multis ac illustribus iudiciorum, clementiæ & misericordiæ Dei documentis demonstrari, ostenderem, ad mutuam consolationem, Habacucum prophetam enarrandum σὺν θεῷ [?] suscepi. Vt enim ille deplorat tristissima fata populi Iudaici, ob instantem Babylonicam captiuitatem & excidium urbis sanctæ: & tamen agnoscit, iusto Dei iudicio omnia illa esse eventura, ac Deum in sua ira misericordiæ me-morem morem fore:ac,tandem vincit fide & spe grauissimam illam tetationem: Ita nũc quoque pij omnes lugent super contritione Josephi: & non solum Antichristia-norum sæuitiam, sed etiam intestina dis-sidia, & conciuium certamina, maximo cum dolore intuentur: & luctantur cum graui illa tentatione, de Ecclesiæ & singulorum fidelium abiectione.
units.tr: Indeed, in order that I might show that God's providence shines forth even in this present storm, in the midst of the Church's disturbance, and that it is demonstrated by many clear proofs of God's judgments, clemency and mercy, I have undertaken, with God's help, to expound the prophet Habakkuk for our mutual consolation. For as he laments the most sorrowful fate of the Jewish people, on account of the impending Babylonian captivity and the destruction of the holy city, yet acknowledges that all these things will happen by the just judgment of God, and that God in his wrath will be mindful of mercy; and at last overcomes that most grievous temptation by faith and hope: so now too all the godly mourn over the affliction of Joseph, and look with great sorrow not only on the savagery of the Antichrists but also on the internal dissensions and the quarrels of fellow citizens; and they wrestle with that heavy temptation concerning the rejection of the Church and of each of the faithful.

units.la: Itaque magnum erit operæpreciũ, videre, qui dolores, & quæ consolationes, nobis cum tanto Propheta communes sint: ut discamus nos summittere sub potenti manu Dei, eius judicia adorare: & non solum bona, sed etiam mala, seu aduersa, de manu eius, cum gratiarum actione seria, suscipere.
units.tr: It will therefore be well worth our effort to see what sorrows and what consolations we share with so great a prophet, so that we may learn to submit ourselves under the mighty hand of God, to adore his judgments, and to receive from his hand, with sincere thanksgiving, not only good things but also evil or adverse things.

units.la: Sedenim cũm ea sit caligo mentium nostrarum, ut nobis consulere: ea voluntatis aversio, ut salutaria eligere: ea denique infirmitas sit, ut illa factis prosequi, non possimus: te Domine Jesu Christe, qui es doctor noster unicus, toto pectore oro, ut nos ista & alia ad salutem nostrā utilia, per Spiritum tuũ sanctum, doceas: ad gloriam nominis tui, & nostram salu-tem. Amen.
units.tr: But since there is such darkness in our minds that we cannot consult our own good, such aversion of will that we cannot choose what is wholesome, and such weakness that we cannot follow such things in our deeds, I pray with my whole heart to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who alone are our teacher, that through your Holy Spirit you would teach us these things and others useful for our salvation, to the glory of your name and our salvation. Amen.

units.la: Accedo iam, optimi auditores, ad Pro-legomena, docendi gratia ἀμαθ[?] dicturus, primùm, de Nomine Habacuc Pro-phetæ: secundò, de eius Officio: tertiò, de Tempore quo is docuit & vaticinatus est: quartò, de genere Gaussæ, quod in hac Providentiæ, Iustitiæ & Misericordiæ Dei defensione dominatur: quintò, de Statu: postremò, de eius Confirmatione: deque totius istius libelli Oeconomia, quæ interrogatione & responsione constat.
units.tr: Now, best hearers, I come to the Prolegomena, intending to speak for the sake of teaching: first, about the name of the prophet Habakkuk; second, about his office; third, about the time in which he taught and prophesied; fourth, about the kind of cause that governs in this defence of God's providence, justice and mercy; fifth, about his condition; last, about his confirmation; and about the arrangement of this whole little book, which consists of question and answer.

units.la: De canonica vero Prophetiæ istius auctoritate, illud ὑπόληψιν[?] oportet, sacrosanctam & inuiolabilem semper fuisse & esse. Neque vero Habacuci συμφωνία solum cum Prophetis & Apostolis, in doctrina cœlesti, eius rei argumentum est: sed etiam grauissimi Apostoli Pauli iudicium, quod secutus, in ardua illa de Iustificatione fidei disputatione, nobile dictum: Iustus aut ex fide sua vivet (Rom.i. 17.) ex hoc Propheta depromsit: nequaquam id facturus, si de Prophetiæ istius auctoritate pij homines dubitauissent.
units.tr: Concerning the canonical authority of this prophecy, it must be taken as established that it has always been and still is holy and inviolable. Nor is the agreement of Habakkuk with the Prophets and Apostles in heavenly doctrine the only proof of this; the judgment of the most weighty Apostle Paul also confirms it, for in his difficult disputation on the justification of faith he followed this prophet and drew from him the noble saying: "The just shall live by his faith" (Rom. 1:17). He would never have done this if godly people had doubted the authority of this prophecy.

units.la: I. NOMEN.
units.tr: I. NAME.

units.la: Habacuc, Luctatorem amplexu stringengentem,significat. Egregiè verò Prophetæ ingenio sublimi,ardenti & vehementi,& disputationi acerrimæ de fato populi Iudaici,ab ipso cū Domino habitæ,nomen istud convenit. Ardenti enim spiritu, populi sui miserias & hostium immanitatem deplorat,& de providentia cum Deo disceptat: sictamen,ut tandem luto non esse cum figulo contendendum persuasus,Deo gloriam det, nequaquam de miranda coseruatione Ecclesiæ,& de poenis quibus afficiendi essent eius hostes, dubitans. Utinam verò eadem sit nostra quoque, quę sancti huius Prophetæ fuit, modestia & ταπεινοφροσύνη[?] erga Deū, quoties de Ecclesia,& de pijs doctoribus & discipulis, Dei sanctuarium ingredietes, serió & solicitè cogitamus & preces concipimus.
units.tr: Habakkuk signifies one who grapples with and embraces a wrestler. This name fits the prophet well, with his lofty, ardent and vehement nature, and with the most fierce disputation about the fate of the Jewish people which he held with the Lord himself. For with a burning spirit he laments the miseries of his people and the savagery of their enemies, and he contends with God about providence; yet he does so in such a way that, at last, persuaded that the clay must not contend with the potter, he gives glory to God, never doubting the wonderful preservation of the Church and the punishments with which its enemies were to be afflicted. Would that our own attitude toward God might be the same as that of this holy prophet, in modesty and humility [ταπεινοφροσύνη], whenever we, entering the sanctuary of God, seriously and anxiously think about the Church, about godly teachers and disciples, and offer our prayers.

units.la: 2. OFFICIVM.
units.tr: 2. The Office.

units.la: Prophetam sese esse Habacuc noster profitetur, cap.1.v.1. Nos de prophetico munere,cui apostolicū successit,dulcissimam Christi Iesu παραβολὴν[?] adducemus. Alius est qui seminat, & alius qui metit. Ego misi vos ad id metendum,in quo vos non laborastis: alij laborauerunt, & vos in labores eorum introiftis. Ioan.4.37.38.
units.tr: Our Habakkuk professes that he is a prophet, chap. 1, verse 1. Concerning the prophetic office, to which the apostolic office succeeded, let us bring forward the sweetest parable of Christ Jesus: "One sows, and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour; others laboured, and you have entered into their labours." John 4:37-38.

units.la: Det nobis Deus, ut quemadmodū in Prophetarum labores ingresi sunt Apo-stoli: fuitque miranda ἁρμονία[?] doctrinæ, quam utriusq; Testamenti Ministri magno consensu tradiderunt: ita quoque nos primum illorum, deinde & Præceptorum orthodoxorum vestigijs insiste-tes, dulcissima συμφωνίαν[?] doctrinæ diu nitus revelatæ, pro eo dono, quod nobis Deus dedit, ad Dei gloriam & Sanctorum instaurationē, studiosè & constanter profiteamur.
units.tr: May God grant us that, just as the apostles entered into the labours of the prophets, and just as there is a wonderful harmony of doctrine, which the ministers of both Testaments handed down with great agreement, so we too, following first their footsteps and then those of the orthodox teachers, may with zeal and constancy profess the sweetest agreement of the doctrine revealed from heaven of old, for the gift that God has given us, to the glory of God and the building up of the saints.

units.la: 3. HABACUC.
units.tr: 3. HABACUC.

units.la: Non præcisè cōstat, quo anno prophe-tare cœperit Habacuc, cùm nulla ullius Regis Iudæ mentio ab eo facta sit.
units.tr: It is not precisely established in what year Habakkuk began to prophesy, since he makes no mention of any king of Judah.

units.la: D. Hieronymus in Prologo ad Chromatium Episcopum, Danieli Habacucu[?] σύγχρονον[?] facit, mentione facta historiæ de illo in leonum lacum misso, ut tamen certò non pronunciet: & alibi nō obscu-re, παραλληλόμενα[?] Danieli aspersa, neget historicam habere fidem.
units.tr: Jerome, in his preface to Bishop Chromatius, makes Habakkuk a contemporary of Daniel, citing the story of his being sent into the lions' den, though he does not pronounce on this with certainty. Elsewhere he says plainly that the story is a parallel addition [παραλληλόμενα] attached to Daniel and denies that it has historical credibility.

units.la: In libro Seder Olam, cap.20. hæc verba exstant: Ioël, Nahum & Habacuc vaticinabantur tempestate Manassis. At quoniam improbus erat Manasses, subticue-runt eius nomen. Huius libri auctorem secutus Leonhardus Crentzemius, uir multae lectionis, & edita Chronologia bene de Ecclesia meritus, statuit Habacu cum docuisse circa annum ab Orbe condito 3272. ante Christum natum an. 699.
units.tr: In the book Seder Olam, chapter 20, these words occur: "Joel, Nahum and Habakkuk prophesied in the time of Manasseh. But because Manasseh was wicked, they kept silent about his name." Following the author of this book, Leonhard Crentzemius, a man of wide reading who has deserved well of the Church by his published chronology, concluded that Habakkuk taught around the year 3272 from the creation of the world, which is 699 years before the birth of Christ.

units.la: Istud extra controuersiam est, docui-sse Prophetam ante excidium urbis Hie-rosolymorum & Babylonicam captiuitatem: cum diuinitus edoctus praenuncia-uerit Chaldaeorum expeditionem in Iu-daeam.
units.tr: It is beyond dispute that the prophet taught before the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian captivity, since, taught by God, he foretold the Chaldean expedition into Judea.

units.la: 4. GENVS CAVSSAE.
units.tr: 4. THE KIND OF CAUSE.

units.la: Nihil dubium est, totam hanc Prophetiam referendam nobis esse ad iudiciale genus causae. Etenim qualitem de Prouidentia erga genus humanum, praecipue uero erga Ecclesiam, etiam Pij (cum eos aduersa premunt, & successus improborum male habent) Deo moueat: & quomodo is prouidentiam, iusticiam & misericordiam suam, aduersus sinistra hominum iudicia, tueatur & demonstret, euidenter ostendit. Facit autem eo, ut discamus non sapere supra quam oportet, sed ad sobrietatem, Rom.12.3. & ut Dei potius, quàm nostro, iudicio stemus & cadą mus.
units.tr: There is no doubt that this whole prophecy must be referred to the judicial kind of cause. For it plainly shows what kind of feeling about God's providence towards the human race, and especially towards the Church, is stirred even in the godly, when adversity presses them and the success of the wicked troubles them; and how God defends and demonstrates his providence, justice and mercy against the perverse judgments of men. It also teaches us not to be wise above what we ought, but to be sober, Rom. 12.3, and to stand and fall by God's judgment rather than our own.

units.la: 5. STATVS.
units.tr: 5. THE STATUS.

units.la: In hac prophetia Conieșturalis status obtinet: quem ut declaremus, de ὑποθέσεως & de θέσεως agemus.
units.tr: In this prophecy the conjectural status holds. To explain it, we shall treat of the hypothesis and the thesis.

units.la: Hypothesis: Si est Prouidentia, cur pa-titur Deus populum Iudaicum, quem si-bi in peculium segregauit, à sceleratis il-lis idololatris, Chaldaeis inquâ, tam cru-deliter traʃtari? Vt enim facilè dem, Iu-daeos non esse ἀναμαρτησίας: tamen quis dubitet, longè ipsis deteriores esse Baby-lonios hostes? Quo autem quisq; peior est, tanto uidetur peiore fortuna dignus.
units.tr: Hypothesis: If there is providence, why does God allow the Jewish people, whom he has set apart for himself as his own possession, to be treated so cruelly by those wicked idolaters, the Chaldeans? For although I readily grant that the Jews are not without sin, who could doubt that the Babylonian enemies are far worse than they? Indeed, the worse someone is, the worse the fortune he seems to deserve.

units.la: Thesis: An ne in tantis afflictionibus & calamitatibus Ecclesiae & singulorum fidelium, ac in tanta saevitia impiorum, velut in medijs tenebris confusionū ge-neris humani, lucet aliqua Dei providen-tia, iustitia, misericordia?
units.tr: Thesis: Does some providence, justice and mercy of God shine forth amid such great afflictions and calamities of the Church and of individual believers, and amid such great savagery of the impious, as if in the midst of the darkness of the confusions of the human race?

units.la: Iehouah Dominus Deus noster (qui in terrogatus respondet) aietem sententiam demonstrat: & Habacucum eò adducit, ut Dei iudicia sibi adoranda & approbā-da esse, conuictus tandem statuat. Est au-tem, in disceptatione de prouidentia & prædeſtinatione diuina, felicisſimi profeſtus argumetum, altitudinem & abysſum iudiciorum Dei admirari, diuinámque uoluntatem, ut supremam cauſam, adorare, & in ea suauiter acquieſcere.
units.tr: Jehovah the Lord our God, who answers when questioned, sets out the affirmative verdict, and he leads Habakkuk to the point where, overcome at last, he concludes that God's judgments are to be adored and approved by him. Indeed, in a dispute about divine providence and predestination, the most happy outcome of the argument is to marvel at the height and abyss of God's judgments, to adore the divine will as the supreme cause, and to rest sweetly in it.

units.la: ¶ Nos, ut tota hæc doctrina tanto magis illuſtretur, Paralogiſmū maximè ſpe-ciosum, quiq̄ etiam Pijs (intuentibus tetrum & horribile ſpectaculum multiplicium confusionum in genere humano, in imperijs, in religione) magnos tumultus excitare solet, ἀτοπαλιμῳδῶς[?] proponemus, & quomodo is nobis ſit confutandus, indicabimus.
units.tr: ¶ So that this whole doctrine may be illuminated all the more, we shall set out, in inverted form, the very specious paralogism which is wont to stir great tumults even among the godly, who look upon the foul and horrible spectacle of many confusions in the human race, in empires and in religion. We shall also indicate how it is to be refuted.

units.la: Maior.
units.tr: Major.

units.la: Certiſsima & maximè illuſtria ſunt, præſentiæ Dei in humano genere, argumenta & teſtimonia inter alia multa, hęc quæ ſubijciemus.
units.tr: Among many others, the most certain and most illustrious proofs and testimonies of God's presence in the human race are the following, which we shall set out.

units.la: 1. Cum formæ diuinitùs institutì ordinis inuiolatæ manet. Vt, manet diſtinctio ſpecierum in metallis, in plantis, in animantibus.
units.tr: 1. The forms of the order divinely instituted remain unviolated; for example, the distinction of kinds remains in metals, in plants and in animals.

units.la: 2. Cū omnes euetus accuratè reſpōdēt diuinis promiſsionibus & cōminationi-bus: ſic ut bonis bene ſit, malis malè.
units.tr: 2. All events correspond accurately to the divine promises and threats, so that it goes well for the good and badly for the wicked.

units.la: 3. Cū Ecclesiæ bene est: malè uerò omnibus ijs, qui extra Ecclesiam versantur.
units.tr: 3. It goes well for the Church, but badly for all those who live outside the Church.

units.la: 4. Cum veritas Solis instar emergens, mendaciorum caliginosas nebulas fulgo-re radiorum suorum egregie discutit.
units.tr: 4. The truth, rising like the sun, dispels with the brightness of its rays the misty clouds of lies.

units.la: 5. Cum ea solum quae Deus fieri vult, fiunt; non autem ea quae hostis Dei diabolus, & improbi homines, qui sunt purgamenta & seces generis humani, effice-re conantur.
units.tr: 5. Only those things which God wills to be done are done, and not those things which God's enemy the devil and wicked men, who are the filth and dregs of the human race, try to bring about.

units.la: 6. Cum deniq; bonorum & malorum dispensatio, pulcre respondet divinae iusticiae & beneficentiae.
units.tr: 6. Finally, the distribution of good and evil fittingly corresponds to divine justice and beneficence.

units.la: Minor.
units.tr: Minor.

units.la: Atqui si propius & penitius intueare mundi huius theatrum, generis humani fata, Ecclesiae durisimam & diuturnam militiam, subitas rerum minimarum maximarumq; confusiones & coversiones, & alia vanitatis (cui tota rerum natura, post tristissimum lapsum primorum parentum, obnoxia facta est) documenta & exempla, contraria illis omnibus quae diximus, nō solum evenire, sed etiam magno ferri impetu, re ipsa experieris.
units.tr: But if you look more closely and penetratingly at the theatre of this world, at the fates of the human race, at the Church's very harsh and long-lasting warfare, at the sudden confusions and upheavals of the smallest and greatest things, and at other proofs and examples of vanity (to which all of nature became subject after the most sorrowful fall of our first parents), you will find by experience that the contrary of everything we have said not only happens but is carried forward with great force.

units.la: 1. Quae enim forma divinitus institutę τῆς ἀντιλήψεως[?], expers iam est multiplicis & perniciosae confusionis? Ecclesiasticū ordinem perturbant Sophistæ ἑτεροδιδάσκαλοι λόγιοι[?], mercenarij, indocti γαστροδούλοι[?]: Politicum, desertores publicorum munerum, ad quæ sunt vocati legitimè: contemptores & hostes magistratuum, φιλόνεικοι[?], turbulenti cives, & aliæ vomicæ civilis societatis: Oeconomicū, discordes & male conciliati coniuges, degeneres & refractarij liberi, perfidi familiares, & multæ aliæ excetræ.
units.tr: 1. What form of divinely instituted order is now free of manifold and destructive confusion? The ecclesiastical order is disturbed by sophists, teachers of other doctrines [ἑτεροδιδάσκαλοι], learned men, mercenaries, and untaught belly-slaves [γαστροδούλοι]. The political order is disturbed by deserters of the public offices to which they were lawfully called; by despisers and enemies of the magistrates; by the contentious [φιλόνεικοι], turbulent citizens, and other boils of civil society. The household order is disturbed by quarrelsome and ill-matched spouses, degenerate and unruly children, faithless servants, and many other vipers.

units.la: 2. Divinis autem promissionibus & comminationibus eventus non respondere, vel inde liquet, quòd miradi sunt improborum hominum successus etiam in pefsimis causis: & ecòtrà, pietatis, veritatis & publici boni amatissimi homines, in consiliis & actionibus optimis deseruntur & opprimutur: quòd tanta est summorū & infimorū hominum erga benemeritos, erga sapientia, doctrina & virtute excellentissimos viros, ingratitudo. Nota est Solomonis illa querela: Et conversus sum ego, & vidi omnes oppressiones quæ fiunt sub Sole: & ecce lacrymæ oppressorum, nec est eis consolator: & in manu opprimentium eos est potetia, nec est illis consolator. Ecclesiastis 4.1.
units.tr: 2. That events do not correspond to divine promises and threats is clear from this: the success of wicked men is astonishing even in the worst causes; and conversely, men most devoted to piety, truth and the public good are abandoned and oppressed in their best counsels and actions; and so great is the ingratitude of high and low alike towards those who deserve well, towards men most excellent in wisdom, learning and virtue. Solomon's well-known complaint is relevant: "And I turned, and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun; and behold the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power, but they had no comforter." Eccles. 4.1.

units.la: 3. Porrò,cur tádem in Ecclesiæ societate, è mūdo selecti,à Domino cooptamur, si ab ea potisimùm incipit Dei iudiciu,& ea est instar gregis ouium in medio luporum? Itáne ad summas & acerbissimas miserias solùm uocamur & ducimur?
units.tr: 3. Furthermore, why are we at last chosen out of the world and gathered by the Lord into the fellowship of the Church, if the judgment of God begins chiefly there, and the Church is like a flock of sheep in the midst of wolves? Are we called and led only to the greatest and most bitter miseries?

units.la: 4. Quoties autem,& quàm longo tempore ueritatis lux,mendaciorum sophismatumq; caligine & nebulis obscurata est,& prope exstincta? Nihil iam dicam de Cimmerijs illis tenebris,quas inuexit Antichristianismus Pontificius: bone Deus, quam nūc tempestatem excitant, fontes aqua carentes, & nebulæ à turbine agitatæ,ij inquam,qui uerbis quidem gloriantur se esse uindices maiestatis Filij hominis, reuera autem pernegant eū in carne uenisse? 2.Pet.2.17. 1.Ioan.4.3.
units.tr: 4. But how often, and for how long, has the light of truth been obscured, and almost extinguished, by the darkness and clouds of lies and sophisms? I will say nothing now of those Cimmerian shadows which Papist antichristianism has brought in. Good God, what a storm now stirs up springs without water and clouds driven by the whirlwind: those, I mean, who boast in words that they are the avengers of the majesty of the Son of Man, but in fact utterly deny that he has come in the flesh. 2.Pet.2.17. 1.Ioan.4.3.

units.la: 5. Iam uerò, quis non uideat, infinita fere, Deoq; summè exosa scelera, à diabolis eorumque organis & satellitibus perpetrari: nec, nisi admodum raro, ea fieri, quæ & Deo grata, & hominibus salutaria sunt?
units.tr: 5. Now, who does not see that almost infinite crimes, most hateful to God, are committed by the devils and their instruments and satellites, and that only very rarely are those things done which are both pleasing to God and salutary for men?

units.la: 6. Denique bona & mala sic obueni-unt hominibus, ut interdum communia sint probis & sceleratis: nonnunquam improimprobis & indignis bona, innoxijs & immerentibus mala eueniant.
units.tr: 6. Finally, good and evil befall men in such a way that sometimes they are shared alike by the upright and the wicked; and sometimes good things fall to the wicked and unworthy, and evils to the innocent and undeserving.

units.la: Complexio.
units.tr: Summary of the objection.

units.la: Quare non uidetur Deus aliqua rerū humanarum cura duci: & quod dolendum est maximè, Ecclesię & singulorum piorum non ita miserereri uidetur.
units.tr: Therefore God does not seem to be guided by any care for human affairs. And what is most lamentable, he does not seem to show such pity toward the Church and toward each of the godly.

units.la: Responsio ad Paralogismum.
units.tr: Response to the paralogism.

units.la: Enimuerò, ut per ἀντεναγωγὴν[?] prius re- spondeam, quàm ad illa sex capita acce- dam, nostri in iudicando errores cognoscendi prius, tum perpendendi, tum abijciendi nobis erant, quàm cum Deo liti- gādum de ipsius prouidentia & iudicijs. Cum enim cesoriam uirgulam nobis su- mimus, etsi in illa iudicioru Dei æstima- tione, multis modis ac sæpenumerò hal- lucinamur: tamen perinde nobis placemus, acsi nihil plane in nobis desiderari posset, in uera illa plenaq; rerum, actionum & eventuū cognitione & ęstimatione. Hanc uanā persuasione de nostra scientia ἡ ἀγχίνοια[?], nobis, ceu fucum quendam, detergi, maximū operæprecium est.
units.tr: Indeed, before I come to those six points, I will first answer by way of retort [ἀντεναγωγήν?]. Before we contend with God about his providence and his judgments, we must first learn to recognise our own errors in judging, then weigh them, and then cast them off. For when we take up the rod of censure, we are often mistaken in many ways in our estimation of God's judgments, yet we are so pleased with ourselves, as if nothing at all were lacking in us, in that true and complete knowledge and estimation of events, actions and outcomes. It is of the greatest benefit to wipe away this empty persuasion of our own wisdom [ἀγχίνοια?], like a kind of dye.

units.la: Inter multos autem errores, quibus mentes hominum imbutæ sunt, hi potissimùm nobis imponunt.
units.tr: Among the many errors with which people's minds are steeped, these chiefly deceive us.

units.la: 1. Non satis cogitamus, nobis imperue-stigabilem esse diuinorum iudiciorum a-byssum.
units.tr: 1. We do not sufficiently consider that the abyss of divine judgments is unsearchable by us.

units.la: 2. Nec illud semper animum subit, Deum semper bene agere, nec unquam frustrari consilij sui destinato.
units.tr: 2. Nor does it always occur to us that God always acts well, and never frustrates his purpose.

units.la: 3. Quinetiam Dei opera inter media contraria fieri, non satis uidemus. Vt, non uidemus Dei seruos, cum propter veritatis testimonium infames coram mundo fiunt, perpetuam apud Deum & eius electos ἀντ​φ & gloriam consequi.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, we do not see well enough that God's works are carried out through contrary means. For we do not see that when God's servants become infamous before the world for the sake of witnessing to the truth, they obtain a perpetual glory before God and his elect.

units.la: 4. Peccamus etiam in eo, quod oculos & metes nostras defigimus in caussas secundas & proximas publicorum & priuatorum malorum: & illis perinde irasci-mur, quemadmodum solent lapidib. isti canes, hominibus omissis, in saxa sequire.
units.tr: 4. We also sin in this, that we fix our eyes and minds upon the secondary and proximate causes of public and private evils, and are angry with these, just as dogs, when stones are thrown at them, ignore the men and run after the stones.

units.la: 5. Peccamus in eo quoq;, quod nostrarum offensarum obliuiscimur, aut certe eas leuiculas esse putamus, & nobis nimium blandimur.
units.tr: 5. We also sin in this, that we forget our own offences, or at least think them very slight, and flatter ourselves too much.

units.la: 6. Grauiter autem delinquimus, cum non in Deum respicimus, nec tristia quae eueniunt, διόπιμπη​α esse agnoscimus.
units.tr: 6. We sin gravely, moreover, when we do not look to God and do not recognise that sad events happen by his appointment [διόπιμπη?].

units.la: 7. Rebus leuiculis, eo quod illae nobis molestae sunt, mirifice offendimur: rebus autem autè maximis,& in Deũ cõtumeliosis,nõ ita afficimur: ac in iusta rerū æstimatio-ne ualde nos hallucinari,testamur inscij.[?]
units.tr: 7. We are wonderfully offended by trifling things, because they are troublesome to us; but we are not much moved by very great things, which are insults against God. And we bear witness, unwittingly, that we greatly deceive ourselves in our just estimation of things.

units.la: 8. Modestiæ aut & reuerentiæ Deo debitæ, cū de eius iudicijs argutamur, quoties, tę quæso, obliuiscimur? An'ne aut uel paterfamilias prudens seruulū uitilitiga-torem & respōsatore ferat? Et nos Deus summè bonus & iustus rixantes ferat?
units.tr: 8. How often, I ask you, do we forget the modesty and reverence owed to God when we wrangle about his judgments? Would not even a prudent householder put up with a quarrelsome servant who talks back? And will God, who is supremely good and just, put up with us when we brawl against him?

units.la: 9. Porrò, cùm aduersa sint necessarium uitæ cōdimentum, quis prudens nos ea uel uotis amolientes errare dubitet? Sci-licet gratiam aliquam & usum uita pla-nè insipida habebit?
units.tr: 9. Furthermore, since adversities are a necessary seasoning of life, what prudent person would doubt that we are wrong when we wish them away by our prayers? Surely life would have no grace or use at all, and would be utterly insipid?

units.la: 10. Iam uerò, cùm præter omne nostrū meritum, nunquam non benignè nobis-cum agi, & nos molliter ac delicatè habere uolumus, an non iniusti sumus? Scili-cet æquum fuerit, Deum nostris deside-rijs seruientem, ἐπιφθαλμός[?] esse, & iusti-ciæ suæ obliuisci?
units.tr: 10. Indeed, since we always wish to be treated kindly by God, beyond any merit of our own, and wish to be kept soft and pampered, are we not unjust? Surely it would be fair for God, who serves our desires, to be grudging, and to forget his own righteousness?

units.la: 11. Et cum ex aduersis nec utilitate, nec uoluptate percipere studemus, an'nō tyrones nos esse in schola Christiana, ipsis testamur factis? Est huius palæstræ ἀξίωμα[?]: Gloriamur in oppressionibus, scientes q[?] oppressio patientia pariat, &c.Rom.5.3.
units.tr: 11. And when we seek to gain nothing from adversity, neither profit nor pleasure, do not our very deeds testify that we are novices in the Christian school? This is the maxim of this wrestling-ground: "We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation worketh patience," etc. Rom. 5.3.

units.la: 12. Denique, cum quod ipsi uolumus; Deum ἁπλῶς facere (nulla consilij ipsius ratione habita) cupimus, an non graui-ter peccamus?
units.tr: 12. Finally, when we wish God to do simply what we ourselves want, without any regard to his counsel, do we not sin grievously?

units.la: ¶Sedenim omissis illis & similibus er-roribus, ad Sophismatis Minore, in qua τὸ ἀμφίβολον[?] latet, respondeamus.
units.tr: ¶But, leaving aside those and similar errors, let us answer the minor premise of the sophism, in which the ambiguity [τὸ ἀμφίβολον?] lies hidden.

units.la: i. Etsi uersutia dolisq; Satanæ, & homi-num multiplici errore, inuecta est multi-plex & tetra confusio operum & ordinis diuini, & ea ingentem ruinā trahens plu-rimùm obest societati hominum: tamen miranda Dei prouidentia ordo ciuilis & coniugalis seruatus est, & conseruatur e-tiam apud eas gentes, quæ fidei luce non fuerunt illustratæ. Ecclesiasticam autem ἀταξίαν[?] seruauit Deus apud eos populos, quibus sese expresso uerbo & illustribus testimonijs patefecit. Vt autem de alijs iam non dicam, an non, cum sit tanta multitudo eorum, qui sunt ἀψίνοποι[?], φιλόκακοι[?], turbulenti & seditiosi, præclarum præsentiæ & prouidentiæ Dei testimonium tibi uidetur esse, quòd non bonos solum ciues, sed etiam colluuiem illaturbulentorum hominum, unus aliquis Prin-ceps in amplissima prouincia, aut etiam paupauci Politarchae in populosissimis urbi-bus, in metu & officio continent? Quo-ties autem fit, ut unus aliquis multorum instar sit in Repub. in Ecclesia aliqua, in Academia, dum & collegas ἐπισφυγόντας[?] & imperitam multitudinem, arte tractat & flectit ad moderata consilia & actiones? Falsum itaque est quod obtenditur, omnes divinae ἀταξίας formas plane esse sublatas, & horrenda ἀταξίαν & cofusionem omnia peruasisse & corrupisse, sicut ὥσπερ ἰσχὺν[?] καὶ ὑγιὴς sit in toto humano genere.
units.tr: i. Although, by the cunning and wiles of Satan and the manifold error of men, a manifold and foul confusion of works and of divine order has been introduced, which brings great ruin and does much harm to human society, yet by the wonderful providence of God the civil and marital order has been preserved, and is preserved even among those nations which have not been illuminated by the light of faith. Moreover, God has preserved ecclesiastical order among those peoples to whom he has revealed himself through the expressed Word and by clear testimonies. But to say nothing yet of others: does it not seem to you a remarkable testimony of God's presence and providence that, since there is so great a multitude of those who are unthinking, lovers of evil, turbulent and seditious, a single prince in a very large province, or even a few magistrates [politarchae] in the most populous cities, restrain not only the good citizens but also that sewer of turbulent men, keeping them in fear and in their duty? And how often does it happen that one man in a commonwealth, or in some church, or in an academy, is the equal of many, and by skill manages and bends his colleagues, who shirk their duty, and an unskilled crowd, toward moderate counsels and actions? It is therefore false that is alleged, that all the forms of divine order have been utterly abolished, and that a dreadful disorder and confusion have pervaded and corrupted everything, as if there were such strength and health in the whole human race.

units.la: 2. Nego, non respondere divinis pro-missionibus & comminationibus euen-tus. Quid enim? An non & toti Eccle-siae, & singulis fidelibus, ubi legitime cer-taverunt, corona gloriae datur? An non aeternis bonis perfruetur in aeterna vita? Atqui nemo coronatur, nisi prius legitime certauerit: 2.Tim.2.5. Ut maxime autem infideles breui tempore floreant, piosq; premat: tamen divina voce ipsis denunciatas poenas non effugient. Iam vero, quis homo intelliges facile det, in bonorum censu ea principem habere locu, qui-bus exiguo tepore magno suo malo abu-tuntur homines ἄθεοι aut hypocritę? Rursum, quis ea [illegible, ~6 letters] mala esse dicat, quae adinmento sunt in bonum ijs qui Deum diligunt? Roman.8.28.
units.tr: 2. I deny that the outcomes do not correspond to the divine promises and threats. For what? Is not a crown of glory given to the whole Church, and to each of the faithful, where they have struggled lawfully? Do they not enjoy eternal goods in eternal life? Yet no one is crowned unless he has first struggled lawfully: 2 Tim. 2.5. And although unbelievers may flourish for a short time and oppress the pious, yet they will not escape the punishments declared to them by the divine voice. Moreover, who would not easily understand that those things should be counted among goods which people, whether godless or hypocrites, abuse for a short time to their great harm? Again, who would say that those evils are harmful which turn to good for those who love God? Rom. 8.28.

units.la: 3. Quanquam autem non uocamur ad Ecclesiae consortium ut simus miseri, sed ut Christo insiti in æternum beati simus: hæc tamen gratia non excludit nostram cū Christo capite nostro συμμόρφωσιν[?], quae afflictionū communione quoq; constat. Non sumus, ita ut est Christus, [illegible, ~8 letters] : ne ergo afflictionum cōsortium, tanquam essemus innocentes, defugiamus. Ac semper nobis in conspectu sit dictum Pauli: Si in hac solum vita speramus in Christum, miserrimi omnium hominum sumus. 1.Cor.15.19.
units.tr: 3. Although we are not called into the fellowship of the Church that we may be wretched, but that, engrafted into Christ, we may be blessed for ever, yet this grace does not exclude our conformity with Christ our head [συμμόρφωσιν?], which consists also in fellowship in afflictions. We are not as Christ is, [illegible]; therefore let us not shun fellowship in afflictions as if we were innocent. And let the saying of Paul always be before our eyes: "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable." 1 Cor. 15.19.

units.la: 4. Quasi uero veritas pressa non emergat: ut nunc ipsa experientia in Ecclesijs Germanicis aliisq; testatur? An ne aute nulla tibi videtur esse providentia, cū interim animaduertas, sic Deum ulcisci im pietatem eorum qui veritatem oderunt, mendacio fidem habent, ut interim sua septem millia eorum, qui non curuauerunt genua sua coram Baal, mirabiliter colligat & protegat? Fac habeas in numerato hæc & similia dicta: Veritati nō præ-judiiudicat antiquitas,ut Chryfostomus:Veritas magis elucet impugnata,ut Bernardus:Veritas nihil erubescit,nisi abscondi, ut Tertullianus: Contra veritatem cogni tam dimicare, idololatria superat [?], ut Augustinus pronunciavit.
units.tr: 4. As if truth, when suppressed, does not rise again! Does not present experience itself, in the German churches and elsewhere, bear witness to this? Or do you not perceive any providence here, when at the same time you see God avenging the impiety of those who hate the truth and believe lies, while he wondrously gathers and protects his seven thousand, who have not bowed their knees before Baal? Suppose you have ready these and similar sayings: "Antiquity does not prejudge truth," as Chrysostom says; "Truth shines forth the more when it is attacked," as Bernard says; "Truth is not ashamed of anything except being hidden," as Tertullian says; "To fight against a known truth is idolatry," as Augustine pronounced.

units.la: 5. Etsi magna est Satanae & satellitū illius licentia & sæuitia: nihil tamen aliud efficere poterunt, quàm quod, ut fieret, manus consiliūq; Dei decrevit. Act.4.28.
units.tr: 5. Although the licence and savagery of Satan and his henchmen are great, they will be able to accomplish nothing other than what the hand and counsel of God has decreed should happen. Acts 4.28.

units.la: Ac non modò bona à bonis fiunt, Deo dā te ut velint & perficiant: sed etiam mala improborum hominum opera, ipsis-ne-scijs, seruire Dei judicijs necesse est. Lu-cet itaq; in bonis malisq; actionibus (sed ratione diversa) admirabilis Dei prov-identia.
units.tr: And not only do good things come from good people, which God grants that they should will and accomplish; but also the works of wicked men, even though they do not know it, must serve God's judgments. Thus in good and in evil actions alike (but in different ways) the wonderful providence of God shines forth.

units.la: 6. Vera & æterna bona pis solis conferuntur: temporaria autem divinitus sic dispensantur, ut modicū quod habet ju-stus, præferri posit etiam Croesi opibus, quibus ἀθέοι [?] & improbi quidam interdū breui tempore potiuntur. Ac propitia Dei providentia interdum terrena & πρόσκαι-ρα bona nobis subducuntur, ne spinosa & noxia fiat: & ut ubertas ac plenitudo be-nedictionis spiritualis in nobis redun-det; det, ad nostram & aliorum instauratio‐nem.
units.tr: 6. True and eternal goods are bestowed only on the pious; temporal goods, however, are so dispensed by God that the little that the just man has may be preferred even to the riches of Croesus, which godless and wicked men sometimes possess for a short time. And by the gracious providence of God, earthly and passing goods are sometimes taken from us, lest they become thorny and harmful, and so that the abundance and fullness of spiritual blessing may overflow in us, for the restoration of ourselves and of others.

units.la: Ethnicorum quorundam de Prouiden‐tia præclara dicta.
units.tr: Some remarkable sayings of certain heathen writers on Providence.

units.la: Iam uerò, ut etiam Ethnici homines, e‐gregijs de Prouidentia sententijs, nobis qui de fide in Christum gloriamur, pudo‐rem incutiant, quasdam recensebimus.
units.tr: Now, so that the heathen too, by their outstanding sayings on Providence, may put us to shame, we who glory in faith in Christ, I will recount some of them.

units.la: Plato lib.4. de Legibus: Ὡς θεὸς μὲν πάν‐τα, ἀλλὰ μετὰ θεῦ τύχη καὶ καιρὸς τ' ἀνθρώπινα ἀμαυρόσυνοι ξυμπάντα. ἡμῶν τρίτον μὲν τέχνη ξυγχορήσαι, τρίτοις δὲ ἐπιδέω τέχνην. Etsi Deo quaedam iungit, uelut subordinata: Deũ tamen præcipuo loco collocat, eisque cæ‐tera subijcit.
units.tr: Plato, in book 4 of the Laws: "God indeed holds all things, but with God chance and opportunity together steer human affairs. Art is a second thing that comes to our aid, and a third is needed along with it." [Ὡς θεὸς μὲν πάντα, ἀλλὰ μετὰ θεοῦ τύχη καὶ καιρὸς τ' ἀνθρώπινα ἄμα πάντα συνωρῶσι. ἡμῶν δὲ τὸ μὲν τρίτον τέχνη συγχορηγεῖ, τρίτοις δὲ ἐπιδεῖ τέχνην] Although he joins certain other things to God, as if subordinate to him, he nonetheless places God in the chief position and subordinates the rest to him.

units.la: Aristoteles: Si, ait, Deo curæ sunt res humanæ, ut uidetur & consentaneũ est, maximè ei cordi sunt homines iusticia & alijs uirtutibus præditi.
units.tr: Aristotle: "If, he says, human affairs are a care to God, as seems likely and fitting, then men endowed with justice and the other virtues are most dear to his heart."

units.la: Cicero: Deorum (præstabat dicere, Dei) prouidentia mũdus administratur: ijdem consulunt rebus humanis: nec so‐lum uniuersis, uerum etiam singulis.
units.tr: Cicero: "The world is governed by the providence of the gods (it would be more correct to say, of God). The same gods look after human affairs, not only in general but also in particular."

units.la: Idem: Ille princeps Deus, qui omnem hunc mundum gubernat.
units.tr: The same: "That first God, who governs this whole world."

units.la: Idem: Diuina prouidentia, quocunq; se moueat, efficere potest quicquid uelit. Idem:Sit igitur,inquit,hoc persuasum omnibus, Dominos esse omnium rerum ac moderatores deos : eaq; quæ geratur, eorum geri ditione ac numine : eosdémque optimè de genere humano mereri: & qualis quisque sit,quid agat,quid in se admittat,qua mente,qua pietate religiones colat, piorum & impiorum habere ra-tionem. De Nat.Deorum.
units.tr: The same: "Divine providence, wherever it turns, can bring about whatever it wills." The same: "Let this be persuaded to everyone, he says, that the gods are lords and governors of all things, that what is done is done under their authority and will, and that they deserve best of the human race; and that they take account of the pious and the impious, of what sort each person is, what he does, what he allows himself, and with what mind and piety he worships religiously." On the Nature of the Gods.

units.la: Galenus de usu partium : Arbitror in eo esse ueram pietatem,non taurorum he-catombas Deo plures sacrificare, & ca-sias aliaq; sexcenta odorameta & ungué-ta suffumigare: sed si nouerim ipse pri-mus,deinde & aliis exposuerim,quæ'nā sitipsius sapientia,quæ uirtus,quæ boni-tas? Quód enim cultu conueniente ex-ornare omnia, nihilq; suis beneficijs pri-uatum esse uoluerit,id perfectissimæ bo-nitatis specimen esse statuo. Et hac qui-dem ratione bonitas eius hymnis est no-bis celebranda. Hoc autē inuenisse, quo pacto omnia potissimùm adornarentur, summæ sapientiæ est: effecisse autem omnia quæ uoluit,uirtutis est inuictæ atq; insuperabilis.
units.tr: Galen, On the Use of the Parts: "I think true piety consists not in sacrificing many hecatombs of bulls to God, nor in burning incense of cassia and six hundred other perfumes and ointments, but in first knowing, and then explaining to others, what his wisdom is, what his power is, what his goodness is. For I hold that it is a mark of the most perfect goodness that he willed to adorn all things with a fitting order and to leave nothing deprived of his benefits. In this way his goodness is to be celebrated by us in hymns. Moreover, to have discovered how all things might be best arranged belongs to supreme wisdom, and to have brought about all that he willed belongs to an unconquered and insuperable power."

units.la: 6. CONFIRMATIO, ET TOtius Disputationis Oeconomia breuiter adumbrata.
units.tr: 6. Confirmation, and a brief outline of the whole structure of the disputation.

units.la: Caput 1.
units.tr: Chapter 1.

units.la: Si in ἀνατομίᾳ cerebri humani, sententia Galeni, uelut in templo religiose uersandum est Medicis: multo maiore cum religione in Oraculorum Prophetiorum & Apostolicorum ὀρθοτομίᾳ, tanquam in Dei sanctuario, sacrae Theologiae Candidatis uersandum est. Adeste igitur, optimi fratres, animis attentis, & unum hoc agentibus, ut συμφωνοποιήσαιμεν[?] ueram Oraculorum in libello Habacuci instituamus dextrè, & eam ad Dei gloriā referamus. Sed iam ad ipsam διορθώσωμεν[?] accedamus.
units.tr: If, in the dissection of the human brain, as Galen holds, physicians must move about as if in a temple with due reverence, then those who are candidates for sacred theology must move about the true cutting straight of the oracles of the prophets and apostles, as in God's sanctuary, with far greater reverence. Come then, excellent brothers, with attentive minds, and intent on this one thing alone, so that we may harmonise [συμφωνοποιήσαιμεν] the true meaning of the oracles in the little book of Habakkuk properly and refer it to the glory of God. But now let us come to the setting right [διορθώσωμεν] itself.

units.la: I. Habacuc Propheta, Onus quod uiderat, orditur à tristi querela, cuius hęc summa & sententia est: Pios, etsi dies noctesque indesinenter orantes, ad Deum uociferentur: tamen grauissimam persecutionem sustinere, & atrocibus Chaldaeorum iniurijs obnoxios esse. Eo autem nomine & doctrinam diuinitus patefactam, & iudicium Dei, contemtui esse: qua in re quantum sit mali, intelligentibus non esse obscurum. versu 2.3.4.
units.tr: I. The prophet Habakkuk, in the burden that he had seen, begins with a sorrowful complaint, the sum and substance of which is this: though the godly pray without ceasing, day and night, and cry out to God, they nevertheless endure the most grievous persecution and are exposed to the savage injuries of the Chaldeans. On that account the doctrine revealed by God and the judgement of God are held in contempt; how great an evil this is, is not obscure to those who understand. Verses 2, 3, 4.

units.la: II. Ei respondens Iehovah Deus noster, primùm revocat Pios ad suorum operū διὰ μεγαλείων[?] meditationem, v.5. Exhilarant enim nos opera Dei rectè consi-derata. Psal. 92.4 Deinde Chaldaeos, à se ad vindictam capiendam de refractaria Iudaeorum gente excitatos, graphicè describit, mentione facta gentis illius nominis, crudelitatis, celeritatis, πλεονεξίας[?], quae est ξυμφυτον νόσημα τοῖς Διωγενέσιν[?], ut ait Plutarchus: item eius θηριότητος, φιλαυ-τίας[?], aduentus, rapacitatis, successuum, & ex his natae fiduciae & admirationis suarum virium. v.6.7.8.9.10.11.
units.tr: II. The Lord our God answers him. First he recalls the godly to meditation on his works through his magnificent deeds (διὰ μεγαλείων), verse 5, for the works of God, rightly considered, gladden us (Psalm 92:4). Then he vividly describes the Chaldeans, whom he has stirred up to take vengeance on the stubborn nation of the Jews. He mentions the name of that nation, its cruelty, its speed, its covetousness (πλεονεξία), which is an innate disease of the Diogenians, as Plutarch says; likewise its brutishness (θηριότης), its self-love (φιλαυτία), its coming, its rapacity, its successes, and the confidence and admiration of its own strength born from these. Verses 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.

units.la: III.
