Habacuc verò instans, ut populo Dei, sanda atq; infanda perferenti, patrocinetur: & ut doceat, durius cum illo agi quàm oportuerit: argumenta ducit, à segregatione populi huius, iam olim eo nomine facta, ut esset Dei peculiū: à destinato Dei in excitadis Chaldaeis, quod erat facere iudicium, non autem delere Iudaicū populum: verf. 12. à natura Dei munda & iusta: à comparatione Iudeorum & Chaldaeorum, in qua ostenditur, Iudaeis, etsi nō essent inculpati, multò tamen deteriores esse Chaldeos, v.13. à di-spasparatis. Non ita tractandos esse homi-nes, ac si non essent disimiles piscibus a-lijsue bestijs.v.14. à nocendi libidine & ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ[?] Chaldaeorum.v.15. à sacrile-ga eorudem persuasione de suis uiribus, quibus solis successus & uictorias acce-ptas ferant.v.16. à perpetuis Chaldaeorū molitionibus ad opprimendas & sub ser-uitutis iugum mittendas alias atq; alias gentes.v.17.
units.tr: III. Habakkuk, however, insisting that he should defend the people of God, who suffer things both right and wrong, and wishing to teach that God has dealt too harshly with them, than was fitting, brings forward arguments: from the separation of this people, made long ago for this very purpose, that they should be God's peculiar possession; from God's appointed purpose in stirring up the Chaldeans, which was to execute judgement, not to destroy the Jewish people (verse 12); from the pure and just nature of God; from the comparison of Jews and Chaldeans, in which it is shown that the Jews, though not blameless, were nevertheless far less wicked than the Chaldeans (verse 13); from the principle that men are not to be treated as if they were no different from fishes or other beasts (verse 14); from the lust for harm and the malicious joy (ἐπιχαιρεκακία) of the Chaldeans (verse 15); from their sacrilegious conviction about their own strength, to which alone they attribute their successes and the victories they have won (verse 16); and from the perpetual schemes of the Chaldeans to oppress other nations, one after another, and to put them under the yoke of slavery (verse 17).

units.la: Hæcubi ad rei indignitatem tum indi-eandam, tum amplificandam, Habacuc magno zelo dixisset,
units.tr: When Habakkuk had said these things with great zeal, both to point out and to magnify the indignity of the matter,

units.la: Caput 2.
units.tr: Chapter 2.

units.la: versu 1. modestè responsionem à Iehou-ah petit, & attentè eandem exspectat. Neque uero obscurè fatetur, se, ut alijs quoque de hisce iudiciorum diuinorum causis & circumstantijs interrogantibus satisfacere possit, oraculum diuinum religiosè expetere.
units.tr: In verse 1 he humbly asks Jehovah for an answer and waits for it attentively. He also openly admits that he piously seeks a divine oracle, so that he may be able to satisfy others too who ask about these causes and circumstances of the divine judgments.

units.la: IIII. Respodet iterum Iehouah Deus noster: ac ubi seriam attentionem requi-siuisset,v.2. & certò complendum uaticinium testatus esset,v.3. subiungit bipartitā propositione, de Iniustis breui tempore se-se attollentib. & floretibus, & de Iustis fide sua perpetuo victuris[?], v.4. Prius aut propositionis membrum, de Iniustis, ἀντ’ ὑπόθεσιν[?] de Nebucadnezare & Chaldæis, ἀλλεξοδίκως[?] tractat: & magnitudine rerum gestarum ebrium, πλεονεξίαν[?] & alienis inhiantem provincijs scitè depingit: v.5.6. Deinde, talionis pœnam à Persis infligendam, Chaldæos prædones exspectare iubet, v.7.8. ac horum peccata percenset & amplificat: auariciam, v.9. alijs nocendi, suamq; potentiam constabiliendi præposterum conatum, v.10. Postea per ἐπαναστροφὴν[?] redit ad pœnarum denunciationem, & iusti iudicij Dei declarationem, v.11.12.13.14. Talionis autem pœnam Chaldæo-rum Monarchę iterum comminatur, v.15.16.17. Ac negat, Chaldæis idololatris, in illa tanta coversione & fatali inclinatione ruentis imperij Babylonici, quicquâ profutura esse vanissima idola & eorum cultum, v.18.19. Postremò, Dominus, ut se ἀνυπεύθυνον[?] esse ostendat, sibi uni ius & auctoritatem vendicat in omnes creaturas, potissimum autem in homines: ut coram illo obmutescant, seq; sub excelsa & potenti eius manu omnes summa cum reverentia summittant, v.20.
units.tr: IV. God our Lord answers again. When he had required serious attention (v. 2) and had testified that the prophecy would certainly be fulfilled (v. 3), he adds a twofold proposition: about the unjust, who will for a short time lift themselves up and flourish, and about the just, who will live forever by their faith (v. 4). The first part of the proposition, concerning the unjust, deals by way of contrast with Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans [ἀντ’ ὑπόθεσιν], and it vividly portrays them as drunk with the greatness of their achievements, greedy [πλεονεξίαν] and coveting foreign provinces (vv. 5, 6). Then he bids the Chaldean robbers expect the penalty of retaliation to be inflicted by the Persians (vv. 7, 8), and he lists and magnifies their sins: their avarice (v. 9), their rash attempt to harm others and to strengthen their own power (v. 10). Afterwards, by way of reversal [ἐπαναστροφὴν], he returns to the announcement of punishments and the declaration of God's just judgment (vv. 11–14). He threatens the king of the Chaldeans again with the penalty of retaliation (vv. 15–17). And he denies that the idolatrous Chaldeans will gain anything from their worthless idols and their worship in that great upheaval and fatal collapse of the Babylonian empire (vv. 18, 19). Lastly, to show that he is [ἀνυπεύθυνον] answerable to no one, the Lord claims for himself alone the right and authority over all creatures, above all over human beings, so that they fall silent before him and submit themselves under his lofty and mighty hand with the greatest reverence (v. 20).

units.la: V. Habacuc, conscientia ignoratiae hominum pudefactus, erumpit in Dei laudes & θεολογίαν[?], v.1. Ac ubi supplicitèr pro populo Iudaico intercedens, precatus esset, ut Deus in ira sua misericordiae recordari uellet, v.2. magnifica Dei opera ad Auctoris laudem recenset. Memi-nit autem, 1. Νομοθέτας[?], seu promulgatae legis, & miraculorum quae tum perācta fuerunt, v.3 & 4. 2. Plagarum paulo ante eductionem Israelitarum Aegyptiis infli-ctarum, & quidem κατὰ αὐτενδοχλὼ[?], pestis mentione facta: nisi quis haec de peste, qua Cananaeos[?], tum, cum Israelitas ex Aegypto Deus educeret, exstirpare aggressus est, malitacc ipere: v.5. 3. Distributionis terrae Canaan, secundum xii. tribus Israelis, & expulsionis Gentium: v.6. 4. Defensionis Israelitarum aduersus Midianitas & alios hostes: v.7. 5. Transitus per mare rubrum, & per Iordanem fluuium: v.8. 6. Potentiae & ueracitatis Dei documentorum: v.9.10. 7. Praelij, in quo de coelo pugnauit Dominus pro Iosua & Israelitis aduersus Cananaeos, Amorrhaeos & alios populos, Sole stante:
units.tr: V. Habakkuk, put to shame by the consciousness of human ignorance, breaks out into praises of God and into theology [θεολογίαν] (v. 1). And when he has prayed earnestly, interceding for the Jewish people, that God would remember mercy in his wrath (v. 2), he recounts the magnificent works of God to the praise of the Author. He recalls: (1) the [Νομοθέτας], that is, the promulgated law, and the miracles that were then performed (vv. 3, 4); (2) the plagues inflicted on the Egyptians shortly before the Israelites were led out, and this in passing [κατὰ αὐτενδοχλὼ], with mention of the pestilence, unless someone prefers to understand these words of the pestilence with which God, when he led the Israelites out of Egypt, set about exterminating the Canaanites (v. 5); (3) the distribution of the land of Canaan among the twelve tribes of Israel, and the expulsion of the nations (v. 6); (4) the defence of the Israelites against the Midianites and other enemies (v. 7); (5) the passage through the Red Sea and through the river Jordan (v. 8); (6) the proofs of God's power and truthfulness (vv. 9, 10); (7) the battle in which the Lord fought from heaven for Joshua and the Israelites against the Canaanites, the Amorites and other peoples, with the sun standing still.
Verse 11.

units.la: v.11.12. 8.Victoriarum & succeffuü,quos aduersus uarios hostes obtinuit C h r i- s t i I e s v typus Rex Dauid: v.13. Item alij pij Principes, quibus sese adfuisse, i- pfis factis,uires humanas longe superan- tibus, testatum fecit: v.14.15.
units.tr: Verses 11, 12. (8) The victories and successes which Christ, the type of King David, won against various enemies (v. 13). Likewise he testifies that other pious princes had God present with them, by deeds that far surpass human strength (vv. 14, 15).

units.la: His omnibus ordine expositis,diuino rum iudiciorum erga Iudæos inobedien tes,& Gentes Dei expertes,consideratio- ne, mirifice sese perculsum,Propheta in- genuè fatetur: v.16.17. Dei tamen uirtu- tis & bonitatis fiducia rursus erectum & animatum, de seipso & piorum reliquiis bene sperare,eoq; nomine Deum collau dare, religioso epiphonemate gloriatur. Hæc confirmationis,& totius istius libel li ἀνταξία est. Deum precor,ut eius benefi- cio sic in eo enucleando uersemur, ut Dei nomen sanctificetur, & non modò fides in nobis confirmetur, sed etiam ui- ta emendetur, & acerbus ille malorum publice priuatimque grassantium sensus leniatur.
units.tr: Having set all these things out in order, the Prophet frankly confesses that he was greatly struck by the consideration of God's judgments against the disobedient Jews and the Gentiles who lack God (vv. 16, 17). Yet, raised up and encouraged again by confidence in God's power and goodness, he hopes well for himself and the remnant of the pious, and on that account he praises God, exulting in a devout exclamation. This is the worth [ἀνταξία] of the confirmation and of this whole little book. I pray God that, by his blessing, we may so labour in unfolding it that God's name is sanctified, and not only is faith confirmed in us but our lives are also amended, and that bitter feeling of the evils that rage publicly and privately is eased.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: CAP. I. V. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I. V. 1.

units.la: ONVS illud quod uidit Habacuc Propheta.
units.tr: The burden which Habakkuk the prophet saw.

units.la: מַשָּׂא[?], Onus hoc loco significat grauissimam denunciationem atrocium poenarum, quæ regulariter comitari solent atrocia delicta. Denunciantur autem poenæ illæ, tum Iudæis, qui inuincibili sua contumacia Deum offenderant: tum Babylonijs, qui immani erga illos aliosq; populos sq;[?] uitia, modū inculpatæ seueritatis & uindictæ excesserant.
units.tr: The Hebrew word משא [maśśāʾ], "burden", here signifies a most grave denunciation of atrocious punishments, which regularly accompany atrocious crimes. These punishments are announced both to the Jews, who had offended God by their invincible obstinacy, and to the Babylonians, who in their monstrous treatment of those and other peoples had exceeded the measure of blameless severity and vengeance.

units.la: Peccata oneribus conferuntur, Psal. 38. 4. Nam iniquitates meæ transgressæ sunt caput meum, & sicut onus graue aggrauatæ sunt supra uires meas. 2. Timoth. 3. 6. Mulierculæ onustæ peccatis, & actæ cupiditatibus uarijs.
units.tr: Sins are compared to burdens. Ps. 38. 4: "For my iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they weigh me down beyond my strength." 2 Tim. 3. 6: "Silly women laden with sins, and led away by various lusts."

units.la: Comminationes itaq; uindictæ diuinæ aduersus impietatem & iniusticiam hominum, Prophetæ Onera uocare solent, ut animadversionem diuinam culpæ respondere ostendant.
units.tr: Accordingly the prophets are accustomed to call the threats of divine vengeance against the impiety and injustice of men "burdens", to show that God's punishment corresponds to the guilt.

units.la: Nos docendi causa, ἀξιολογικῶς uersi-culum primum explicabimus: ut uideat Iuniores, quibus rationibus attentione Propheta captauerit. Syllogismi autem ueluti complexu, causas quarum hæc mē tio est facta, συλλήβδην[?] perstringemus.
units.tr: For the sake of teaching, we will explain the first verse with careful rhetorical precision, so that the younger students may see by what arguments the prophet held their attention. We will also briefly sum up, as it were in a compressed syllogism, the causes of which this mention is made.

units.la: Illud oraculum ἀξιομνημόνευτον[?] haberi, & summa cum attentione cognosci debet, quod diuinitus uero Prophetæ patefactum est, & in quo agitur de grauissimis rebus populû Dei & eius hostes attinentibus.
units.tr: This oracle ought to be held worthy of remembrance and to be known with the greatest attention, since it was revealed to the prophet by God and deals with the gravest matters concerning the people of God and its enemies.

units.la: Tale autem est istud Onus, quod in uisione oblatum est Habacuc Prophetæ. Etenim fi spectes eius causam efficientem principem, occurret Deus in cœlo, qui reuelat secreta: Dan.2.28.& 47. fi patefactionis formam, occurret uisio prophetica: de qua Num.12.6. Si fuerit Propheta uobis, ego Iehouah in uisione apparebo ei, in somnio loquar cū eo. fi materiam, occurret castigationum & poenarum diuinarum denuciatio. Amos 3.7. Quia nō facit Dominus Iehouah quicquam, nisi reuelauerit secretum suum seruis suis Prophetis. denique fi præconem, uelut organica causam spectes, occurret Habacuc Propheta fidelis, qui de impendentibus malis sic uaticinatus est, ut ab omnibus γνησιολογίας ἢ ψιθυρολογίας[?] abstineret: multū sanè dissimilis Pseudoprophetis, quì curabant contritionem filiæ populi Dei leui sermone,dicentes,Pax,pax: cum nō esset pax.Ierem.6.11.
units.tr: Such indeed is this burden, which was presented in a vision to the prophet Habakkuk. For if you look at its principal efficient cause, God in heaven presents himself, who reveals secrets (Dan. 2. 28 and 47). If you look at the form of the revelation, the prophetic vision presents itself, of which Num. 12. 6: "If there is a prophet among you, I, Jehovah, will appear to him in a vision; I will speak with him in a dream." If you look at the matter, the announcement of divine chastisements and punishments presents itself (Amos 3. 7): "Surely the Lord Jehovah does nothing unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets." Finally, if you look at the herald, as it were the instrumental cause, the faithful prophet Habakkuk presents himself, who prophesied of impending evils in such a way as to abstain from all flattering or whispered talk [γνησιολογίας ἢ ψιθυρολογίας]. He was quite unlike the false prophets, who sought to heal the hurt of the daughter of God's people with a light word, saying "Peace, peace", when there was no peace (Jer. 6. 11).

units.la: Quare hoc Onus ut ἀξιόλογον magnifa-ciendum,& accuratè perpendendum est: ac pœnitetia omnibus agenda, ad quam illud hortatur, ut effugere posimus imminentem Dei iram.
units.tr: This burden, therefore, is to be esteemed as worthy and weighed with care, and all men are to undertake repentance, to which it exhorts us, so that we may escape the impending wrath of God.

units.la: DE ONERVM VISIONE; Aphorismi.
units.tr: ON THE VISION OF THE BURDENS; Aphorisms.

units.la: ı. Onera diuinitùs nobis commonstra-ta, nemini nostrūm sunt contemnenda.
units.tr: 1. The burdens revealed to us by God are not to be despised by any of us.

units.la: Irrisorum enim, non autè piorum hominum est, in suisipsorum cupiditatibus incedere: & etiam extremi iudicij denūciationes in dubiū vocare,ac dicere: Vbi est pollicitatio aduentus tui ? 2.Pet.3.4.
units.tr: For it belongs to scoffers, not to pious people, to walk according to their own lusts, and to call into doubt the denunciations of the final judgement, saying, "Where is the promise of his coming?" (2 Pet. 3. 4).

units.la: 2. Sunt autem duūm generum, προγνω-στικὰ ἢ παθογνωμονικά. Prognostica onera voco ea, quæ Deo revelante,impenden-tia mala denunciant. Pathognomica, quæ eventuum complementis constant & cognoscuntur.
units.tr: 2. There are two kinds: prognostic and pathognomonic. I call prognostic those burdens which, by God's revelation, announce impending evils. Pathognomonic are those which consist in, and are recognised by, the fulfilment of events.

units.la: 3. Prognostica, ordinis præcipui sunt, quæ extra ordinem, diuina revelatione, innotescunt: inferioris aût, quæ ex collatione divinarum legum, promissionū & comminationum cum hominū factis totaq; vita, [illegible, ~8 letters] colliguntur.
units.tr: 3. Prognostic burdens are of the higher order, which become known outside the ordinary course through divine revelation; those of the lower order are gathered from the comparison of divine laws, promises and threats with the deeds and whole life of men.

units.la: Michaeas revelatione divina edoctus, Achabo Israelitarum Regi, bellum Syriae Regi inferenti, cladem exercitus & inte-ritum praenunciavit. 3.Reg.22.23.
units.tr: Micaiah, taught by divine revelation, announced to Ahab, king of Israel, who was waging war on the king of Syria, the defeat and destruction of his army (3 Reg. 22. 23).

units.la: At nunc multi cordati homines, impietatem & iniusticiam hominum aspicientes, & divinas comminationes perpendentes, profspicienter κατανυκτικῶς[?] colligunt, mundum poenas esse daturum. Nec difficile est Prophetas & historiam sacram veteris Testamenti legentibus, & omnia illa cum nostris temporibus moribusque conferentibus, colligere [illegible, ~6 letters], quid de genere humano sit futu-rum. Non enim nudis illi dubiisque coniecturis agunt, sed exempla vitae ad le-gum & promissionum divinarum canones exigunt, & recte facta, praemia: scelera autem, poenas secuturas, certò pronunciant.
units.tr: But now many discerning men, looking upon the impiety and injustice of men and weighing the divine threats, conclude with penetrating and compunctious insight that the world will suffer punishment. Nor is it difficult for those who read the prophets and the sacred history of the Old Testament, and who compare all those things with our times and customs, to gather what is going to happen to the human race. For they do not proceed by bare and doubtful conjectures, but measure the examples of life by the rules of the divine laws and promises, and they pronounce with certainty that right deeds will bring rewards, and crimes will bring the punishments that follow.

units.la: 4. Pathognomica, κατ' ἀνάλυσιν[?], ab eventibus ad antecedentes causas animum revocant. Ut quum videmus, quam tristis & turbulenta sit Ecclesiae ταραχὴ[?] in hac mundi fenesta: quibus bellorum & seditionum fluctibus turbetur Respub. quàm sint multiplices aerumnæ publicæ & priuatæ: quæ sit audacia fanaticorum ingeniorum, perniciosam ἐπιφοδιλαθαλίκῳ[?] in Ecclesiam inuehentium: non possumus non ἀναλυτικῶς[?] colligere, Deum nobis grauiter & optimo iure irasci: achæ mala quibus laboramus, autoramenta esse peccatorum nostrorum: & perniciosorum dogmatum auctores paulo post atrocissimis supplicijs diuinitus afficiendos.
units.tr: 4. Pathognomonic burdens, by analysis, lead the mind back from the events to their antecedent causes. When we see how sad and turbulent the disturbance of the Church is in this corner of the world, by what waves of wars and seditions the commonwealth is troubled, how manifold the public and private miseries are, and what boldness there is in fanatical minds that bring pernicious doctrines into the Church, we cannot but conclude by analysis that God is gravely and with the best right angry with us, that the evils we suffer are the wages of our sins, and that the authors of pernicious doctrines are soon to be visited by God with the most atrocious punishments.

units.la: 5. Vt autem illa fide potissimum, sic hæc etiam sensibus, & euentu, qui stultorum magister esse dicitur, percipiuntur.
units.tr: 5. But just as the former are perceived chiefly by faith, so these are perceived also by the senses and by the outcome, which is said to be the teacher of fools.

units.la: Quid uero tibi, mi frater, hoc tempore facta Ecclesiæ & Reipub. intuenti, in mentem uenire solet?
units.tr: But what, my brother, usually comes into your mind when you look at the state of the Church and the commonwealth at this time?

units.la: Cæcos esse ἡ ἀναισθησίας[?] eos omnes, qui necuident, nec sentiunt grauissimum Onus, uere iam ψευδογνωμένον[?], quo premuntur huius ætatis homines. Quid enim? An non totis uiribus, & omni Sophistica Ecclesiâ oppugnant Antichristiani? An non Diotrephes nonnulli, armati brachio seculari, nō modò dominatur clero Domini mini, multisq; in locis,pulsis apiculis,su-cos substituerunt: sed etiam in eos qui inuocant nomen Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, saeviunt, anathematismis, proscriptionibus,& satyrica dicacitate?
units.tr: That all those are blind who neither see nor feel the most grievous burden, now truly misjudged, under which the men of this age are oppressed. For what? Do not the Antichristians attack the Church with all their strength and every sophistry? Do not some Diotrephes, armed with the secular arm, not only lord it over the clergy of the Lord, but in many places, the bees having been driven out, have set up drones in their place? And do they not rage against those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ with anathemas, proscriptions and satirical bitterness?

units.la: Porrò, si Rempublicam spectes, an' ne inficias ibis, summos iuxta & inferiores gubernatores,maximis incommodis,ue luti secundae nauigationis remoris,uehe menter laborare? Siccine negabis, Dy-naftas non paucos usque adeò ebrios esse voluptatibus: ac παροξυσμοῖς [?], ut aleae,ue-nationibus, non necessarijs μεγάλης φαυ- ταολοῖς [?] negocijs, adeò immersos, ut vixil-lis vacet alienis oculis cernere,alienis au-ribus audire,alienis manibus aliquid ag-gredi? Quàm multi boni & patriae amant-issimi Politarchae,habent collegas ἐπισκόποις [?],qui etiam optimis consilijs refragatur, non aliam ob caussam, quàm quòd domi suae non esse nata uideant? Quoties & quàm multis in locis, turbuleti & uagabundi ἀλλοτριεπίσκοποι [?], qui interim nuncios pacis sese esse fingunt,ubi percuniculos irrepserunt in alienas sedes,turbas maximas dant Politicis gubernatoribus,Verbi diuini Ministris,& bene costitutis Ecclesijs: in sinu interim Antichristianis ridentibus? ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν περίττυχθ' ἱκοσμεν ἀχρύμενοι ὥσπ: ne etiam iustisimà querelam mouentes,ungues in vlcere fimus.
units.tr: Further, if you look at the commonwealth, will you deny that the rulers, both highest and lower, labour heavily under the greatest hindrances, like drags upon a favourable voyage? Will you deny that not a few dynasts are so drunk with pleasures and fits of passion, and so immersed in dice, hunting and unnecessary, great, frivolous business, that they scarcely have leisure to see with other men's eyes, hear with other men's ears, or lay hands on anything with other men's hands? How many good and most patriotic magistrates have colleagues who meddle with the affairs of others and oppose even the best counsels for no other reason than that they see things not born in their own household? How often, and in how many places, do restless and wandering men, who pretend meanwhile to be messengers of peace, when they have crept in through tunnels into other men's seats, cause very great disturbances for the civil governors, the ministers of the divine Word, and well-established churches, while the Antichristians laugh in their bosom? But we, lamenting, bear these things as we can, lest even by making a most just complaint we fling our fingers into the ulcer as if into filth.

units.la: Sed quid,quæso, tibi tetra ista & tragica spectacula intuenti solatio est?
units.tr: But what, I ask, is your consolation when you look upon these foul and tragic spectacles?

units.la: Hoc præcipuè, quòd definito Dei consilio ista fieri persuasum habeo. Nouit enim Deus,pro infinita sua sapientia & bonitate, sic istas confusionum tenebras diuidere, ut homini pio & intelligenti nequaquam difficile sit,in Ecclesiæ militātis tristicia, solidū perpetuumq; gaudiū: in veritatis contemtu & oppressione, eiusdem gloriam & emergentem fulgorem: in piorum doctorum seu incruento, seu cruento martyrio,eorum defensione: in mercenariorum successibus & fama, confusionem & infamiam: in piorū gubernatorum laboribus & ærumnis, præclara ἀνατροφὰ & lætitiam: deniq; in media ἀτα ξία, diuinam ἀντα ξίαν, Dei gloriæ,piorum usibus,& improborum confusioni mirando modo seruientem, αὐτῷ τῷ ἔργῳ demonstrare. In his ergo omnibus, cum Dei prouidentiam, misericordiam diam & iusticiam lucere experiar,cur ta-dem deiecto essem animo? Inuito Deo nihil fit eorum quae fieri uideo. Quod si ista Deo uolente fiunt, ut maxime mihi de multis operum istorum circumstatijs & finibus non constet: libenter tamen a-nimo pacato in propitia Dei prouiden-tia acquiesco. Præstat enim ea fieri, quae manus consiliumque Dei decreuit ut fie-rent, quam ea quae ipse fieri malim, mo-tus uidelicet meis quibusdam rationibus.
units.tr: Chiefly this: I am persuaded that these things happen by the settled counsel of God. For God knows, in his infinite wisdom and goodness, how to divide these shadows of confusion in such a way that it is by no means difficult for a pious and intelligent man to see, in the sadness of the militant Church, solid and perpetual joy; in the contempt and oppression of the truth, its glory and emerging brightness; in the defence of pious teachers, whether by bloodless or bloody martyrdom, their vindication; in the successes and reputation of hirelings, confusion and infamy; in the labours and distresses of pious rulers, a splendid restoration and joy; and finally, in the midst of the unworthy, a divine worthiness, serving in a wonderful way the glory of God, the use of the pious, and the confusion of the wicked, to be shown by the very fact itself. In all these things, then, since I experience God's providence, mercy and justice shining forth, why should I be cast down in spirit? Nothing happens of those things which I see happen against God's will. But if these things happen by God's will, though I am by no means clear about many of the circumstances and ends of these works, I nonetheless gladly rest with a calm mind in God's gracious providence. For it is better that those things happen which the hand and counsel of God have decreed should happen, than those which I myself would prefer, moved by certain reasons of my own.

units.la: VERSVS II:
units.tr: VERSE 2:

units.la: Vsquequo lehouah clamabo, & non ex-audies? nociferabor ad te propter uiolen-tiam, & non saluabis?
units.tr: How long, Jehovah, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out to thee because of violence, and thou wilt not save?

units.la: Propheta post difficillimum & diutur-num tentationis, in qua sibi unà cum po-pulo Iudaico à Deo desertus & neglectus uidebatur, παροξυσμὸν[?], tandem in admo-dum pathetica querimoniam erumpit: Ac initium facit Disceptationis de Iudaicae gentis & singulorum piorum miserabili fato, deq; sæuitia hostium Chaldaeo-rum. Nos θεωρητικὰ primò, deinde πρακτικὰ tractabimus.
units.tr: After a most difficult and long-lasting temptation, in which he seemed to himself, together with the Jewish people, to have been forsaken and neglected by God, the prophet at last breaks out into a most pathetic complaint [παροξυσμόν]. He begins a disputation about the miserable fate of the Jewish nation and of individual pious people, and about the savagery of the Chaldean enemies. We shall treat the theoretical matters first [θεωρητικὰ] and then the practical [πρακτικὰ].

units.la: Sic autem argumentatur ab ingenio & natura Dei summè sapientis, summè boni, summè etiam φιλανθρώπ[?]ης.
units.tr: He reasons in this way from the nature and character of God, who is supremely wise, supremely good and supremely philanthropic [φιλανθρωπίας].

units.la: Est hoc Deo solenne, se invocates exaudire, opemq; eius implorantibus succurrere. Juxta dulcissima haec oracula: Oculi Jehouae sunt super justos: & aures eius (intentae) ad clamorem eorum. Vultus autem Jehouae super facientes malu, ut exscindat e terra memoriam eorum. Clamant (afflicti) & Jehouah audit: & ex omnibus angustiis eorum liberat eos. Psal. 34.15.16.17. Item: Erit praeterea, antequam clament, ego audiam: adhuc ipsis loquentibus, ego audiam: Isa.65.24. Huc referri potest universalis experietia omnium Sanctorum, de qua dicitur: In te speraverunt patres nostri: speraverunt, & liberasti eos. Ad te clamaverunt, & liberati sunt: in te speraverunt, & non sunt pudefacti: Psal. 22.4.5. Et illud eiusdem Dauidis dictum[?], experientia comprobatum: Multa sunt adversa justis: sed tamen ex ijs omnibus liberat eos Jehouah. Psal.34.19.
units.tr: It is God's custom to hear those who call upon him and to come to the aid of those who implore his help. In keeping with these most sweet oracles: "The eyes of Jehovah are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their cry. But the face of Jehovah is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth. The afflicted cry out, and Jehovah hears, and delivers them from all their distresses." Ps. 34.15.16.17. Likewise: "Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear." Isa. 65.24. To this may be referred the universal experience of all the saints, of which it is said: "Our fathers trusted in thee; they trusted, and thou didst deliver them. They cried to thee and were delivered; they trusted in thee and were not put to shame." Ps. 22.4.5. And that saying of the same David, confirmed by experience: "Many are the adversities of the righteous, but out of them all Jehovah delivers them." Ps. 34.19.

units.la: Ego vero, inquit Habacuc, jam diu multumq; ad Jehouam clamavi, nec tamen mihi videor exauditus: ac manifestam notoriamq; vim passus, pro defen-sione sione & liberatione obtinenda uocifera-tus sum, nec tamen quod uolebam im-petraui.
units.tr: "But I," says Habakkuk, "have cried to Jehovah long and much, and yet I do not seem to myself to have been heard. Suffering manifest and notorious violence, I have cried out to obtain defence and deliverance, and yet I have not obtained what I wanted."

units.la: In hac Minore propositione obserua-bimus haec capita:
units.tr: In this minor proposition we shall observe the following heads:

units.la: 1. Crucis ueluti torculari, exprimi no-bis preces ardentes ad liberatorem Deu.
units.tr: 1. As if in a wine press, fervent prayers are pressed out of us to God, our Deliverer.

units.la: 2. Mirum in modum eandem amplifi-cari temporis & specierum ratione. Species sunt, odium quo impii fideles perse-quuntur, violentia notoria, morbi,pau-pertas, & aliae malorum formae, quae cū diu admodum durant, graviora & acer-biora fiunt.
units.tr: 2. The same complaint is wonderfully amplified by the reckoning of time and of kinds. The kinds are: the hatred with which the wicked persecute the faithful, notorious violence, sickness, poverty, and other forms of evil, which, when they last a very long time, become heavier and more bitter.

units.la: 3. Neminem nisi Deum, vere ἀλεξιφάρμακον[?], nos è tantis malis liberare posse.
units.tr: 3. No one but God, the true antidote [ἀλεξιφάρμακον], can free us from such great evils.

units.la: 4. In precibus feriis, vocem oris difer-tum esse affectus cordis (remissione peccatorum & liberationem a malo peten-tis) testem & praeconem. Certum autem est, sacrilegam Dei irrisionem esse, ina-nes sonos precum, & concepta verba sine mete & religioso voto, instar psittaci, pronunciare.
units.tr: 4. In prayers offered on working days, the voice of the mouth is the witness and herald of the affection of the heart seeking forgiveness of sins and deliverance from evil. It is certain, however, that to utter empty sounds of prayer, and words conceived without a mind and religious devotion, like a parrot, is a sacrilegious mockery of God.

units.la: Itaque quasi putaret, Deum aliter er-ga suos affici coepisse, & implacabiliter nunc irasci, concludit querula oratione: Vsquequò Iehouah clamabo, & non exaudies? uociferabor ad te uim patiens, & non saluabis?
units.tr: Therefore, as if he thought God had begun to be disposed otherwise towards his own and was now implacably angry, he concludes with a plaintive prayer: "How long, Jehovah, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out to thee suffering violence, and thou wilt not save?"

units.la: DE TENTATIONE, IN QVA Sancti sibi uidentur à Deo negligi ac deseri.
units.tr: ON THE TEMPTATION, IN WHICH the saints seem to themselves to be neglected and forsaken by God

units.la: Vt quales sint Sancti in rebus secundis & aduersis, & quàm sit Deus mirabilis in operibus suis, innotescat serui eius: subitis rerum conuersionibus & diuturnis afflictionibus eosdem exercet. Nos docendi causa, Tentationis istius Protasin, Epitasin & Catastrophen, ἐμφα-[?] λακωνικῶς[?] proponemus.
units.tr: So that his servants may come to know what the saints are like in prosperity and adversity, and how wonderful God is in his works, he exercises them with sudden reversals of fortune and lasting afflictions. For the sake of teaching, we shall set out the protasis, epitasis and catastrophe of this temptation, briefly [λακωνικῶς].

units.la: Protasis.
units.tr: Protasis.

units.la: Ita ingenium est hominum, ut animadversis animi & corporis externis dotibus & præsidijs, maiores spiritus concipiant, quàm oportebat. Hos autem alit memoria præclarè factorum, applausus hominum, & successus in consilijs & actionibus publicis & priuatis: quæ omnia faciunt, ut liberaliter nobis lætos euentus spe quasi despondeamus, immemores sanè fati fortisq; futurae. Nec hoc rerum statu æquam mentem seruamus, sed quibus uisum est impensè fauemus : caeteros uel negligimus, ut indignos nostra beneuolentia[?]: uel odio habemus, le-uicula ἀφοφμὴ[?] irritati. Nota est pijs omnibus ingenua Dauidis confessio: Ego uero dicebam in prosperitate mea: Non mouebor in æternum. Iehouah, tu pro beneplacito tuo stabiliueras monti meo robur. Psal.3o.6.7. Verùm de hac parte ista dixisse satis esto.
units.tr: Human nature is such that, having noticed the external gifts and resources of body and mind, people conceive greater spirits than they should. These are nourished by the memory of nobly done deeds, by the applause of men, and by success in counsels and in public and private affairs. All of this brings it about that we, as it were, promise ourselves happy outcomes in advance, forgetting indeed the fate and the strength of what is to come. Nor in this state of affairs do we keep an even mind; we favour lavishly those whom it pleases us to favour, and we neglect others as unworthy of our goodwill, or hate them, roused by some slight pretext. The honest confession of David is known to all the pious: "But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved. Jehovah, by thy good pleasure thou hadst made my mountain stand strong." Ps. 30.6.7. But let this much be said about this part.

units.la: Epitasis.
units.tr: Epitasis.

units.la: Vbi uero inopinatę ruinæ se proximos, aut etiam se iam cocidisse uident, cum Salomone exclamant: Vanitas uanitatū, & omnia uanitas. Ecclesiast.1.1. Hanc sententiam ferunt clara uoce recitauisse Vandalorum Regem Gilimerum, cum à Belisario acie uictus & captus, Constantinopolim in triumpho ductus, & ad pedes Iustiniani Imperatoris prostratus iaceret, anno Christi 534.
units.tr: But when they see unexpected ruin close at hand, or see that they have already fallen, they cry out with Solomon: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Eccl. 1.1. They say that Gelimer, king of the Vandals, recited this sentence in a clear voice when, defeated and captured in battle by Belisarius, he was led in triumph to Constantinople and lay prostrate at the feet of the emperor Justinian, in the year of Christ 534.

units.la: Quomodo hoc rerum statu ægerani-mus, dum sibi relinquitur, semper pauidus & attonitus erret in consilijs & conatibus suis, hæc sequentia docent.
units.tr: How the mind is affected in this state, when it is left to itself and always wanders fearful and astonished in its counsels and endeavours, the following passages teach.

units.la: Rectè quidem homo in aduersis, veluti cuiusdam labyrinthi tricis, hærens, de liberatione sibi consultandum & follicitè laborandum, statuit. In eo autem toto cœlo errat, cum ad humana præsidia pri-mùm confugit.
units.tr: Rightly indeed does a man in adversity, caught as it were in the tangles of a labyrinth, resolve to take counsel for his deliverance and to labour anxiously over it. But he errs entirely in that direction when he first flees to human aids.

units.la: Initiò autem, illud præclarum & homi-ne prudente dignum iudicat, salutis præ-sidia in seipso quærere, Consilium uideli-cet, & ea exequendi uires & facultates. Nam si sic instituta succedant ex sententia, esse cur sibi ipsis solis liberationem è malis acceptâ ferant. Quasi verò tam fit homini facile & expeditum è malis elu-ctari, quàm proclive est peccatis & temeritate sua calamitates accersere.
units.tr: At the outset, however, he judges it an excellent thing, and worthy of a prudent man, to seek the means of salvation in himself, that is, counsel, and the strength and resources to carry it out. For if matters so undertaken succeed as he wished, he has reason to credit his deliverance from evils to himself alone. As if it were as easy and simple for a man to struggle out of evils as it is natural for him to bring calamities upon himself by sin and rashness.

units.la: Ponit itaque homo sibi relictus, consilia in anima sua: sed experitur illa nihil aliud esse, quàm anxietatem cordis quotidianam & infructuosam. Psal.13,2. Lu-ctatur cum rebus aduersis totis suis uiribus: sed eo successu, quo aduerso Rheno natates, rapidissimi fluminis cursum multa ui brachiorum contrà nitendo, (si Deo placet) uincunt, ad superiora nequicquam contendentes.
units.tr: Therefore the man left to himself places his counsels in his own soul, but he finds them to be nothing other than a daily and fruitless anxiety of heart. Ps. 13.2. He struggles against adversities with all his strength, but with the success of swimmers who, swimming against the Rhine, struggle against the course of that most rapid river by the great force of their arms, straining in vain to make headway upstream.

units.la: Etsi autem ægrè deponit homo fiduciam de suis uiribus: tamen, ne sæpius tur-piter se det, tardiusculè & timidè ad alio-rum hominum, auctoritate (ut uidetur,) pruprudentia & potentia excellentium patrocinium & opem sese recipit. Hic uero, dum in aliis iudiciū, in aliis fidem, in aliis facultatem iuuandi desiderat: dum unumquenq; sua potius quàm aliena animo uersare & studiosè tractare, & non nisi perfunctoriè sibi adesse animaduertit, [illegible, ~12 letters] deplorat, & cum Dauide exclamat: Ego dixi in trepidatione mea, Omnis homo mendax: Psal.116.11. Item: Certè uanitas sunt filij Adam: falsitas sunt filij Potentum, adeò ut in statera ascendant ipsi omnes præ uanitate. Psal.62.9. Item: Amici mei & sodales mei ex aduerso plagæ meæ stant, & propinqui mei procul abstiterunt: Psal.38.11.
units.tr: Although a man reluctantly gives up his trust in his own powers, nevertheless, lest he disgrace himself too often, he more slowly and timidly betakes himself to the patronage and help of other men who excel, as it seems, in authority, prudence and power. But here, while he looks for judgement in some, faith in others, and the ability to help in others, and while he perceives that each man attends to his own affairs rather than to those of others, and treats them diligently, and that they are present to him only perfunctorily, [illegible] he laments, and with David he cries out: "I said in my alarm, every man is a liar." Ps. 116.11. Likewise: "Surely the sons of Adam are vanity, and the sons of the mighty are falsehood; laid in the balance, they all go up together, lighter than vanity." Ps. 62.9. Likewise: "My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my kinsmen have stood afar off." Ps. 38.11.

units.la: Malis itaque nonnihil doctus & dominus, de humanis uiribus desperans, ab errore in uiam tandem aliquando redit, & diuinum auxilium anxiè implorat. Et cum Deum omnipotentem & omniscium esse audiat, statim sibi laborati opem fer-ri uult.
units.tr: Thus somewhat taught by his misfortunes, and despairing of human strength, he at last returns from error to the right way and anxiously implores divine help. And since he hears that God is omnipotent and omniscient, he at once wishes that help be brought to him in his distress.

units.la: Etsi autem rectè facit, cum ad Deum confugit: in eo tamen peccat, quòd liberationis tempus modumq; Deo præscribit. Vt si captiuus ob malefactum, misericordia magistratus sicimploret,ut etiam quam primùm & qua lege è carcere dimitti uelit,liberius moneat.
units.tr: Although he does rightly in fleeing to God, he sins in this, that he prescribes to God the time and manner of his deliverance. It is as when a captive, guilty of some crime, implores the mercy of the magistrate and, more presumptuously, advises him as to how soon and under what conditions he wishes to be released from prison.

units.la: Clamat tum afflictus cum Dauide: Ad te, Iehouah, clamaui: & Iehouam sum his uerbis deprecatus: Quæ utilitas prodibit ex sanguine meo, descendente me in foueam ? num celebrabit te puluis? num prædicabit ueritatem tuam ? Psal-mo 30.8.9.
units.tr: Then the afflicted man cries out with David: "To thee, Jehovah, I cried, and I besought Jehovah with these words: What profit will come from my blood, if I go down into the pit? Will the dust praise thee? Will it proclaim thy truth?" Ps. 30.8.9.

units.la: Queritur etiam, uim iniustam sibi in-ferri, quam propulsare Deo admodum dignum & gloriosum sit futurum: ut est uidere in hac Habacuci querimonia.
units.tr: He also complains that unjust violence is being done to him, which it would be most worthy and glorious for God to repel, as may be seen in this complaint of Habakkuk.

units.la: Vbi liberationem differri sentit, suos dolores magis respicit, quàm Dei omnia suo tempore facientis iudicium : ac cum Dauide uociferatur: Quare Iehouah stas procul ? quare abscondis te opportuno tempore, in tribulatione? In elatione impij persecutionem patitur oppressus. Psal.10.1.2.
units.tr: When he feels that deliverance is delayed, he looks more to his own pains than to God's judgement, who does all things in his own time; and with David he cries out: "Why, Jehovah, do you stand so far off? Why do you hide yourself in the time of trouble? In the pride of the wicked the oppressed suffer persecution." Ps. 10.1.2.

units.la: Vbi uero nec suarum miseriarum, nec insolentiæ hostium, eam quâ homo perturbatus uellet, rationem à Deo haberi opinatur, [illegible, ~8 letters] repetit: An oblitus est miseri Deus? nunquid contraxit in ira miserationes suas? Et dixi, Caedes mea haec: sed mutationes sunt dexterę excel-si. Psalmo 77.9.10.
units.tr: But where he thinks that God does not take account of his troubles or the insolence of his enemies in the way a troubled man would wish, [illegible] he repeats: "Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassions?" And "I said, This is my wound: but the years of the right hand of the Most High are changed." Psalm 77.9, 10.

units.la: Catastrophe.
units.tr: Catastrophe.

units.la: Quibus gradibus Catastrophę tentationis constet, iam videamus. Occurrūt[?] autē inter alios hi, qui abnegationis no-stri proprij sunt.
units.tr: Let us now see by what steps the catastrophe of temptation proceeds. Among others, these occur, which concern the renunciation of our own self.

units.la: 1. Adprobatio iudicij diuini, de qua Ps. 119.67. Priusquàm humiliarer, ego errabam: sed nunc sermonem tuum custodio. 71. Bonum est mihi quòd afflictus sum, ut discam edicta tua.
units.tr: (1) Approval of the divine judgement, of which Ps. 119.67: "Before I was humbled I went astray, but now I keep your word." 71: "It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes."

units.la: 2. Patientia & Confesio. Mich.7.9. Irâ Iehouæ ferâ, quoniâ peccavi ei: donec iudicet causam meā, & faciat iudicium meum: educet me in lucē, videbo iusticiam eius.
units.tr: (2) Patience and confession. Mic. 7.9: "I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgement for me. He will bring me forth to the light, and I shall see his righteousness."

units.la: 3. Spes immota. Psal.23.4. Etiamsi ambulavero in valle umbrę mortis, nō timebo malum: quia tu mecum es: virga tua & pedum tuum me consolantur. Cæterùm spes non confundit. Rom.5.5.
units.tr: (3) Unshaken hope. Ps. 23.4: "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff comfort me." Moreover, hope does not disappoint. Rom. 5.5.

units.la: 4. Exspectatio æternæ vitæ, in qua abstergentur lacrymæ ab oculis nostris, & erit æterna nostra læticia: quia Deo fruemur, qui erit omnia in omnibus. 1. Corinth.15.
units.tr: (4) The expectation of eternal life, in which our tears will be wiped from our eyes, and our joy will be eternal, because we shall enjoy God, who will be all in all. 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: DE STRATAGEMATE DIABO-li Tentatoris, nobis persuadere cupientis, Deum non exaudire beneficiarios suos, cum eum invocant: & negligere eosdem opem Domini implorantes.
units.tr: On the stratagem of the devil the tempter, who wishes to persuade us that God does not hear his beneficiaries when they call upon him, and neglects those who implore the help of the Lord.

units.la: Initiò Paralogismum, quem cruci infesta caro, à diabolo inculcatum, ceu Cram-bem identidem recoquit, & quem urgēdo miras tragœdias excitat, recitabimus: deinde, quàtum in eodem impietatis sit, ostendemus.
units.tr: First I shall set out the fallacy, which the flesh hostile to the cross, having been instilled by the devil, keeps reheating like a stale crust, and which, by pressing it, he stirs up wonderful tragedies; then I shall show how great the impiety in it is.

units.la: Paralogismus.
units.tr: The fallacy.

units.la: Quicunque sibi addictissimos, si quando eius opem implorant, non euestigiò, malis omnibus (quæ & molestiam & pe-riculū creant) depulsis, liberat, is nec au-dit clamantes, nec etiam curat.
units.tr: Whoever does not at once free from all evils (which both cause trouble and bring danger) those who most devotedly cling to him, when at any time they implore his help, neither hears those who cry out nor even cares for them.

units.la: Hæc propositio falsa est: quia <bl>τὸ μὴ αἰ-</bl>τίου ὡς αἴτιον[?] allegat. Non enim uel mitigationem malorum, uel plenam ab eis liberationem, ideo differt Deus, quòd uel surda[?] aure preces prætereat, uel non curet suos beneficiarios: sed ut eos ob peccata castiget: ut eorum fidem & spem, uelut aurum, in tribulationis igne exploret: ut docedoceat eos in tribulationibus gloriari: ut denique in ijsdem superabundet consolatio CHRISTI: ideo, inquam, illos affligit & exercet: præstituta interim afflictionibus istis certa periodo, quam pios in silentio & spe præstolari æquum est.
units.tr: This proposition is false, because it takes [τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον] what is not the cause as the cause. For God does not delay either the easing of evils or their full deliverance because he passes over prayers with a deaf ear, or because he does not care for his beneficiaries; but he chastises them for their sins, so that he may test their faith and hope, as gold, in the fire of tribulation; so that he may teach them to glory in tribulations; so that, finally, the consolation of Christ may abound in those same trials. Therefore, I say, he afflicts and exercises them, a certain limit to these afflictions having been set in the meantime, which it is right that the godly await in silence and hope.

units.la: Deus autem se invocantes non audit, nec liberat: ut hoc loco Habacuc gravissime conqueritur.
units.tr: But God does not hear and deliver those who call upon him, as Habakkuk complains most bitterly in this place.

units.la: In hac Minore est petitio principij. Eã κατὰ βίαιον retundere licebit: Immò uerò Deus omni tepore & loco exaudit se invocantes, & cum est optimum, uel mitigat, uel tollit mala quibus premuntur. Psal.99. Et erit Iehouah exaltatio oppressio, exaltatio opportunis temporibus in tribulatione.
units.tr: In this minor premise there is a begging of the question. It may be refuted [κατὰ βίαιον] by force: indeed God hears those who call upon him at every time and place, and when it is best, either eases or removes the evils by which they are oppressed. Ps. 99: "And the LORD will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble."

units.la: Quare Deus suos fideles auersari, nullamq; eorundē ratione habere uidetur.
units.tr: Hence God seems to turn away from his faithful ones and to have no regard for any of them.

units.la: Hæc Conclusio nō caret blasphemia: quo nomine pijs sollicitè cauendum est, ne impatientiæ spiritu uicti, eam perinco gitantia uel effutiant, nedum seriò propugnent. Huc enim πανοῦργος ille Satan, fraudibus dolisq; suis, à se circumuentos pellicere conatur, ut infidelibus συμφωνεῖν, ad Dei contumeliam, discant.
units.tr: This conclusion is not free from blasphemy; for which reason the godly must take careful heed not to utter or seriously defend such things, overcome by a spirit of impatience. For that crafty [πανοῦργος] Satan strives by his deceits and tricks to entice those whom he has ensnared, so that they learn to agree [συμφωνεῖν] with unbelievers to the dishonour of God.

units.la: Iam & illud secundo loco paucis attin-gamus, quantum uidelicet mali hac in re sit, ut tanto magis ab ea abhorrentes, ceu pestem quandam, fugiamus.
units.tr: Next, let us touch briefly on the second point, namely how much evil there is in this matter, so that, the more we abhor it, the more we may flee from it as from a kind of plague.

units.la: Scopus illius quem adduximus Parali-logismi est, fidei lucem & ardorem ex-stinguere, nec in Deum respiciat, & in eo uno acquiescat.
units.tr: The aim of the fallacy we have cited is to extinguish the light and fervour of faith, not to look to God, and to rest in him alone.

units.la: Cur enim, horrendum inclamat Ca-codaemon, in eum credas, quem re ipsa experiaris ad tua uota surdum: & ad ma-la seu leuanda, seu tollenda, neutiquam promptum: nedum ἀλεξικακον[?], seu malo-rum quibus opprimeris, depulsorem?
units.tr: For why, the Cacodaemon cries out horribly, should you believe in him whom in fact you experience as deaf to your prayers, and by no means ready either to ease or remove evils, let alone a repeller [ἀλεξίκακον] of evils, or of the evils by which you are oppressed?

units.la: Si is nouit, quibus hoc tempore malis labores, cur non etiam non rogatus bene-ficiario laboranti opem fert? Sin uero illa ignorat, cur pro Deo habes non omniscium?
units.tr: If he knows by what evils you labour at this time, why does he not also bring help to his labouring beneficiary without being asked? But if he is ignorant of them, why do you hold him not to be omniscient?

units.la: Si bonus, misericors & omnipotens est, cur se non praestat φιλανθρωπον[?], miseri-cordem, opitulatorem? Rursum, si talem se, etiam diu multumq; rogatus, nō prae-stat, cur talis habeatur?
units.tr: If he is good, merciful and omnipotent, why does he not show himself humane [φιλάνθρωπον], merciful and a helper? Again, if he does not show himself such, even when asked for a long time and much, why is he regarded as such?

units.la: Si is ferre potest, ut ex fidelissimis ipsi-us clientibus alij diuturno moerore, alij morbis conficiantur, alij miserabili morte intereant: denique ut calamitosissimi per omnem suam vitam sint, qui ei uni adhaerent veluti summo bono: cur non statuas, eum non solùm illam quam o-portuit suorum seruorum rationem non habere: sed etiam ἐπιχαιρέκακον[?], delecta-ri eorum miseriis?
units.tr: If he can bear that some of his most faithful clients are worn out by long grief, others by sickness, others perish by a miserable death, and finally that those who cling to him alone as the highest good are most calamitous throughout their whole life: why should you not conclude that he not only does not take account of the due treatment of his servants, but is even one who rejoices [ἐπιχαιρέκακον] in evil, delighting in their miseries?

units.la: Huiusmodi strophis Satan audacia sa-crilega Deo eripere conatur laudem providentiae, bonitatis & misericordiae: ut si qua fieri queat, ipso è corde hominis submoto, succedat proq; numine habea-tur. Et carni quidem facilè imponit: spiritum autem aduersarium habet: qui fidei τῇ πληροφορίᾳ[?] instructus, ignita illius tela hebetat & exstinguit: ac firmiter stat-tuit, & Deum exaudire gemitus seruorum suorum, & eisdem succurrere cū est opportunum.
units.tr: By such twists Satan, with sacrilegious audacity, tries to snatch from God the praise of providence, goodness and mercy, so that, if it can be managed, God being removed from the heart of man, he may take his place and be regarded as a god. And indeed he easily deceives the flesh; but he has an adversary in the Spirit, who, armed with [τῇ πληροφορίᾳ] full assurance of faith, blunts and quenches his fiery darts, and firmly establishes that God hears the groanings of his servants and helps them when it is fitting.

units.la: Sed quid causæ esse censes, quòd ista λεπτολογίαι[?] μάταια[?] Satanæ, etiam Pijs ad tempus imponunt?
units.tr: But what do you think is the cause why those subtle and vain quibbles [λεπτολογίαι ματαῖαι] of Satan impose even on the godly for a time?

units.la: 1. Quia fidei lux & ardor interdum obscuratur & restinguitur tempestate caliginosa rerum aduersarum: quam tamen, ut Sol nubes, ita ipsa radijs suis tandem discutit.
units.tr: (1) Because the light and fervour of faith are sometimes obscured and quenched by a dark tempest of adverse circumstances; yet, as the sun does with clouds, faith at last dispels that tempest with its own rays.

units.la: 1. Quia errat, cum res aduersas, quibus ipsi laborant, in malorum: res autem secundas, quibus breui tempore potiuntur infideles, in bonorum numerum, ἀπλῶς [?] tantisper referunt, dum Spiritus sanctus, ἀγγελικῶς [?] & utilitatem rerum tristium, & temporariorum bonorum τὴν ἀλλότητα [?] commostret. Atqui uel Cicero malis doctus fatetur, res suas, in secundis fluxas & euanidas, in aduersis bonas fuisse: quòd hæ fere moderatos efficiat, & fatorum suorum conscios. Quantò magis nos, quib. omnia aduersa adiumento sunt in bonū, eleganter, prudenter & constanter ea (cū ineuitabilia sunt) adire, sustinere & vincere par est?
units.tr: (2) Because they err when they count adverse circumstances, by which they themselves are troubled, among evils, but simply count among goods the prosperous circumstances which the unbelievers enjoy for a short time, while the Holy Spirit, in angelic fashion [ἀγγελικῶς], shows both the usefulness of sad things and the otherness [τὴν ἀλλότητα] of temporal goods. Indeed even Cicero, taught by misfortunes, confesses that his own goods were fleeting and vanishing in prosperity but good in adversity, because the latter usually makes men moderate and conscious of their destiny. How much more ought we, for whom all adversity turns to good, to approach, bear and overcome these things elegantly, wisely and steadfastly, since they are unavoidable?

units.la: 2. Quia falsò sibi persuadent, Crucis & fidei in Christum optabile quoddam diuortium introduci posse. Somniant florentem Ecclesiam, imperij cuiusdam instar, gloria, legibus, ordine, præsidijs instructam. Atqui nisi Christo capiti conformes fiant per afflictiones, ne quidem eidem in gloria similes erunt. Hæc de secundo uersu dixisse satis sit. Christus Iesus
units.tr: (3) Because they falsely persuade themselves that a certain desirable divorce between the cross and faith in Christ can be introduced. They dream of a flourishing Church, furnished with glory, laws, order and protection, like some empire. Yet unless they are made conformable to Christ their head through afflictions, they will not even be made like him in glory. Let what I have said about the second verse suffice.

units.la: [?] Iesus det nobis, istiusmodi tentationes fide & spe inuicta superare: Amen.
units.tr: May Jesus Christ grant us to overcome such temptations with unconquered faith and hope. Amen.

units.la: VERSUS III.
units.tr: Verse 3.

units.la: Ut quid ostendis mihi molestiam, & per-versitatem aspicis: & est vastitas & vio-lentia coram me? estq; qui litem & con-tentionem (contra me) suscipiat?
units.tr: "Why do you show me iniquity, and look upon perverseness? For spoiling and violence are before me; and there are those who raise up strife and contention." (Hab. 1:3)

units.la: Propheta rei indignitatem amplificat, enumeratione rerum non solum inhonestarum, sed etiam perniciosarum.
units.tr: The prophet heightens the outrageousness of the matter by listing things that are not only dishonourable but also ruinous.

units.la: Cui bono non ex animo doleat, impune grassari atrocia delicta, quae turbant societatem & tranquillitatem generis humani?
units.tr: Who would not grieve in his heart that atrocious crimes, which disturb society and the tranquillity of the human race, run riot with impunity?

units.la: Atqui hoc tempore molestia, perversi-tas, vastitas, violentia, lis, contentio, & a-liae pestes mirum in modum grassantur. Pellitur e medio sapientia, vi geritur res.
units.tr: Indeed at this time trouble, perversity, devastation, violence, strife, contention and other plagues rage in a remarkable way. Wisdom is driven from the midst, and affairs are conducted by force.

units.la: Quare in summo moerore esse bonos omnes, nihil dubiū est: ut qui, quae'nam scelerum auctoramenta secutura sint, nō obscure videant.
units.tr: There is no doubt, then, that all good people are in the deepest mourning, since they can plainly see what outrages of crime are to follow.

units.la: Cum vocabula quae in Minore occur-runt, saepe cōfundantur, nō laborabimus in ijsdem scrupulose distinguendis.
units.tr: Since the words that occur in the Minor Prophets are often confused, we will not labour to distinguish them scrupulously.

units.la: Est sanè triste & lugendum spectaculum, intuenti œconomiarum fata, videre disipationes honestarum familiarum, piorum parentum & liberorum exilia, distractiones: incommoda quæ adferre solent orbitas, paupertas, contemtus & iniuriæ inhospitalium Læstrigonum, & alia mala. Ad vitam enim honestè & commodè transigendam opus nobis est variis præsidijs & humanitatis officijs: quæ si desint, reuera ἀβίωτος ἐστὶ ὁ βίος. de qua vita senarius ἀλλ' [illegible, ~8 letters] ἐν ἑαυτῷ βίος exstat: βίος ἕλις ἀλέ[?] ἐν ἐμοὶ βίος.
units.tr: It is indeed a sad and lamentable spectacle, for one who looks on, to see the fortunes of households: the breaking up of honourable families, the exile and separation of pious parents and children, and the troubles that bereavement, poverty, contempt and the wrongs of inhospitable Laestrygonians usually bring, with other evils. For to live honourably and comfortably we need various aids and the offices of humanity; if these are lacking, life is indeed unlivable [ἀβίωτος ἐστὶ ὁ βίος]. And concerning this life there is the verse, garbled in the scan: [ἀλλ' ... ἐν ἑαυτῷ βίος ... βίος ἕλις ... ἐν ἐμοὶ βίος].

units.la: Sed tamen, si Rempub. spectes, multò est tristius magisque lugendum, spectatorem agere horribilium confusionum in Imperijs, in regnis, in prouincijs & in ciuitatibus, & in societate hominum: quam legibus, ordine & præsidijs florere oportebat. Neque enim tranquillam & pacatam vitam agere licet, nisi cum mediocris ἀνομία & πολιτικὴ λειτουργία obtinet. Ac pacis publicæ tuendæ fouendæque gratia, [illegible, ~25 letters]; & promtè ac libeter officijs publicis & priuatis bonos ciues defungi decet. Immò verò nō solum mansuetudine, tolerantia, iniuriarū obliuione, φιλανθρωπίᾳ[?], lacrymis: sed etiam, si fit opus, sudore & sanguine, pax ciuilis bonis ciuibus est redimeda. Tantum enim generis humani interest, si non ab omni parte felicem & florentem, mediocrem aut saltem tolerabilem esse eius statum & tranquillitatem. Ac vere Solon censuit, mala publica priuatorum aedes invadere, nec excludi posse à vestibularibus.
units.tr: But if you look at the commonwealth, it is much sadder and more lamentable to be a witness of dreadful confusions in empires, kingdoms, provinces, cities and human society, which ought to flourish by laws, order and protection. For one cannot lead a calm and peaceful life unless a moderate [ἀνομία] and civic service [πολιτικὴ λειτουργία] prevail. And for the sake of preserving and fostering public peace, [illegible in the scan]; and good citizens ought to discharge public and private duties promptly and willingly. Indeed, not only by gentleness, patience, forgetting of injuries, love of mankind [φιλανθρωπία] and tears, but also, if need be, by sweat and blood, civil peace must be bought back by good citizens. For it matters so much to the human race that its state and tranquillity should not be wholly happy and flourishing, but at least moderate and tolerable. And truly Solon judged that public evils enter private houses and cannot be kept out of the forecourts.

units.la: στω ἀληθίου λαχὼν ἐρχ[illegible, ~8 letters] ἐπὶ[?] ἑκάστῳ[?],
units.tr: [Greek verse, garbled in the scan: each man, having obtained his share of the evil ...]

units.la: ἄλλοι δὲ τ' ἔχειν ἐν ἰδίαι θύρᾳ[?].
units.tr: [Greek verse: "but others have it at their own door."]

units.la: Istud autem omnium est tristissimum, si quis animaduertat, Ecclesiae, quae communis omnium nostrum mater, eaque summe φιλόγοφος[?] & officiosa est, unitate factionibus scindi in contraria studia: ministerium verbi vilipendi: loco motis fidelibus pastoribus & doctoribus, mercenarios, sophistas aut indoctos homines (ad stiuam potius, quàm ad cathedrâ natos factosq;) substitui: doctrinae coelestis ἀληθείας[?] & sinceritatem seu palàm sine frôte & fuco, seu subdolè, veteratoria [illegible, ~3 letters] corrumpi & depravari: Ecclesiasticâ disciplinam nullo haberi loco, immo ἐωὶ λοιπασίας [illegible, ~8 letters] eorum praepediri, qui eius ἔργο- [illegible, ~9 letters] esse debebant: refrigescere zelum pro gloria Dei, pro tuenda veritate: [illegible, ~7 letters] charitatis exstinguis magistratus colludere cum laruatis praesulibus, cum idololatris: denique civitatem non ita multo ante fidelem, fieri meretricem. Intelligunt enim piae mentes, hac rerū Ecclesiasticarum ἀνατάραξις [?] & perturbatione in discrimen adduci, non tam corpora, ut fit politijs turbatis, quàm animas: & perniciosum hoc exemplum noxium esse huic aetati & toti posteritati.
units.tr: Worst of all is this, if one notices that the Church, the common mother of us all, and most devoted to learning and to duty, is torn by factions into opposing aims: the ministry of the Word is despised; faithful ministers and teachers have been removed and mercenaries, sophists or unlearned men, born and made for the stable rather than the chair, have been put in their place; the sincerity and purity of heavenly doctrine is corrupted and depraved, whether openly and without pretence or deceitfully by crafty tricks; ecclesiastical discipline is held in no regard, and indeed those who ought to be its ministers are hindered from their work; zeal for the glory of God and for defending the truth grows cold; the bond of charity is extinguished; the magistrate colludes with masked prelates and with idolaters; and finally a city not long ago faithful becomes a harlot. For pious minds understand that by this upheaval and disturbance of ecclesiastical affairs not so much bodies as souls are brought into peril, as happens when civil polities are thrown into turmoil; and that this pernicious example is harmful to this age and to all posterity.

units.la: Enimuerò qui istis omnibus non afficitur, is profectò cor habet durius Caucasi rupibus.
units.tr: Indeed, whoever is not moved by all these things has a heart harder than the rocks of Caucasus.

units.la: Quid igitur Dei seruus tantorumq; malorum [illegible, ~8 letters] faciat, cum nec iam natis malis sese mederi, nec etiam nascituris occurrere posse uidet?
units.tr: What then should the servant of God do in the face of such great evils, when he sees that he can neither remedy the evils already born nor meet those yet to be born?

units.la: Primum cogitet, hoc funestum spectaculum sibi esse commune cum Patribus, Prophetis, sanctis Iudicibus & Regibus, denique cum Christo, Apostolis & Martyribus: quibus omnibus cū is se meliorem non esse intelligat, ne meliorem in huius uitæ militia conditionem expetat, quàm olim fuit illorum luminum & columnarum Ecclesiæ. Magna enim impatientia foret, ea ferre nolle, quæ æquis animis & longo tempore tulerunt Adam, Henoch, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Iesaias, Paulus, &c innumeri alij.
units.tr: First, let him reflect that this deadly spectacle is shared by him with the Fathers, Prophets, holy Judges and Kings, and finally with Christ, the Apostles and Martyrs. Since he understands that he is no better than all of these, let him not seek in the warfare of this life a better condition than that of those lights and pillars of the Church of old. For it would be great impatience to be unwilling to bear what Adam, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Isaiah, Paul, and countless others bore with calm minds and for a long time.

units.la: Secundò, statuat diuinitus & singulari consilio sibi obijci tetra illa spectacula, nō ut de prouidentia dubitet, ut desperet, ut ad iniquitatem mittat manus suas. Psal. 125.3. sed potius ut obseruet, admiretur & adoret Dei longanimitatem in ferendis improbis: eiusdem præsentiam, quâ conseruatione politici, Ecclesiastici & œconomici ordinis declarat: potentiam inuictam, quam Satanæ & satellitum eius rabiem & conatus infringedo testatur: sapientiam, quam suos instruendo necessa-rijs & salutaribus consilijs, hostes autem infatuando & confundendo & comprehedendo multiuariam exercet. Cum intuetur serpentes, leones, lupos, & alias immanes bestias, etsi earum τλὼ θηριότητα[?] & squitiam[?] admiratur: tamen non sine numine conditas esse & conseruari, facilè sibi persuadet. Curuerò nō idem cogitat, cū
units.tr: Second, let him hold that these foul sights are set before him by God's will and by a singular counsel: not so that he should doubt providence, despair, or put his hand to iniquity (Ps. 125.3), but rather so that he may observe, marvel at and adore God's long-suffering in bearing with the wicked. He declares his presence by preserving political, ecclesiastical and domestic order; he attests his invincible power by breaking the rage and attempts of Satan and his henchmen; and he exercises his wisdom manifold, by instructing his own with necessary and salutary counsels, and by making the enemies foolish, confounding and catching them. When he looks at serpents, lions, wolves and other savage beasts, then, although he marvels at their brutality and foulness, he readily persuades himself that they were created and are preserved not without the divine will. But he does not think the same when he sees tyrants, hypocrites, mercenaries, ἀθέως ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, who are the vomit and scum of the human race? Aristotle rightly said: ἀδικωτέρους οἱ ἐπιβουλότεροι [the more crafty are the more unjust]. Greater danger therefore threatens from a Sinon, with honey in his mouth and gall in his heart, than from a wolf at evening or a snake coiling through the grass.

units.la: uidet tyrannos, hypocritas, mercenarios, ἀθίως ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, qui sunt uomicæ & ἀλλά-γοροι humani generis? Rectè Aristoteles, ἀδικωτέρους, inquit, οἱ ἐπιβουλότεροι. Maius itaque periculum imminet à Sinone, mel in ore, fel autem in corde habente, quàm à lupo uespertino, aut ab angue sinuosa uolumina uersante.
units.tr: Do we not see tyrants, hypocrites and mercenaries, atheists in the world [ἀθέως ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ], who are the sores and outcasts [ἀλλάγοροι] of the human race? Aristotle rightly says: the more treacherous are the more unjust [ἀδικωτέρους οἱ ἐπιβουλότεροι]. Therefore the danger is greater from a Sinon, who has honey in his mouth and gall in his heart, than from a wolf prowling at evening or a snake coiling through its winding folds.

units.la: Tertiò, discat Dei exemplo τροπoφορεῖν. Act.13.18. Deus circiter 40. annorum tempus mores Israelitarū tulit in deserto. Ferat igitur & Dei seruus mores alienos: secundum illud Græcorū dictum : τὸν φρό-νιμον ἀεὶ τάδε ἢ τάδε φέρειν.
units.tr: Thirdly, let him learn from God's example to bear with others' ways [τροποφορεῖν] (Acts 13:18). God bore the conduct of the Israelites in the wilderness for about forty years. So let the servant of God also bear with the faults of others, according to the Greek saying: the wise man must always bear this or that [τὸν φρόνιμον ἀεὶ τάδε ἢ τάδε φέρειν].

units.la: Quartò, ne sibi unquam per errorem persuadeat, furias & excetras illas, quæ turbant Ecclesiasticum, ciuilem & domesticū ordinem, minus torqueri, q̈ discruciantur animi eorū qui Iosephi contritio-nem lugent. Etenim dum uident, nequaquam omnia pro scelerato eorum uoto succedere: dum inculpatæ uitæ eorum quos insectantur præiudicio sese laborare sentiunt: deniq;, dum uiolatæ religionis & pacis conscientia excarnificantur, & tamen istos dolores dissimulare conātur, horribiliter excruciantur. Ac multò sunt sæuiores illi dolores, qui cum cæco ἀλλ' ἀνιάτῳ conscientiæ vulnere sunt coniuncti: quàm illi, quos mens conscia recti eo nomine sustinet, quòd ab aliis multa impudenter & sceleratè admitti uidet. Ut autem pius dolorem suum, culpæ uidelicet expertem, æque zelo pro gloria Dei tanquam è fonte promanantem, ingenuè profitetur: sic ediuersò impius, quoad eius fieri potest, premit alto corde dolorem, & Thrasonis instar mirà quandam confidentiam præ se fert, ne sibi malè conscius esse & uehementer terreri, uideatur.
units.tr: Fourthly, let him never persuade himself, through error, that those furies and vipers which trouble the ecclesiastical, civil and domestic order are tormented less than the minds of those who mourn the ruin of Joseph. For while they see that everything does not turn out according to their wicked wish, while they feel that they are harmed by the prejudice against the blameless lives of those they harass, and finally, while their conscience of violated religion and peace tears them apart, yet they try to hide these pains, they are horribly tormented. The pains are far more severe for those who carry an incurable wound of conscience than for those whom a mind aware of what is right sustains under the sense that they see many things done shamelessly and wickedly by others. The godly man frankly confesses his sorrow, which is free of guilt and springs equally from zeal for the glory of God as from a fountain; but the ungodly man, on the contrary, as far as he can, buries his pain deep in his heart and, like Thrasos, puts on a strange show of confidence, so that he may not appear conscious of wrongdoing and greatly terrified.

units.la: Quintò, firmiter statuat, Deum non solum uiolentiæ & iniuriarum, aliorumq; malorum nebulas fulgore iudicij sui discutere: uerumetiam ex malis istis mirâ do modo bona efficere, sic ut Dei seruis adiumento sint in bonum.
units.tr: Fifthly, let him firmly settle in his mind that God not only dispels with the brightness of his judgment the clouds of violence, injuries and other evils, but also, in a wonderful way, brings good out of these very evils, so that they serve the servants of God for their good.

units.la: Ut enim ignis auru[?] liquefacit & à scoriis perpurgat, non autem illud absumit: sic iniusta uis qua ille premitur, calumniæ & conuicia quibus proscinditur, ad eum explorandum, & ad sinceritatem integri tatemq; eius in lucem producedam[?], plurimum conducunt.
units.tr: For as fire melts gold and purges it of dross, without consuming it, so the unjust force by which he is oppressed, and the slanders and reproaches with which he is torn, greatly help to test him and to bring his sincerity and integrity to light.

units.la: Postremò, ad πολίτευμα[?] suum in cœlis respicies, spe vitæ æternæ, dolores leniat. Scitè enim dixit Augustinus: Vita vitæ mortalis, spes est vitæ immortalis.
units.tr: Lastly, let him look to his citizenship in heaven and let hope of eternal life soothe his pains. For Augustine rightly said: the life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life.

units.la: VERSVS IIII.
units.tr: VERSE 4.

units.la: Propterea debilitatur Lex, & (dicunt homines) Non egredietur in seculum judicium: nam impius quivis circumdat ju-stum: propterea (aiunt) egredietur judi-cium perversum.
units.tr: Therefore the law is weakened, and (men say) judgement will never go forth for ever: for the wicked man surrounds the righteous; therefore (they say) perverse judgement goes forth.

units.la: PHRASIUM QUARUNDAM declaratio.
units.tr: A declaration of certain phrases.

units.la: 1. Lex debilitari dicitur, cum eo nomine in despectum abit, quod non videtur habere ullum ὑφηγοδιώντλω[?], qui ei obedientes tueatur & ornet: prævaricatores aut & transgressores pro malis suis meritis puniat. Notum est Æschinis oratoris dictum: ἰδὼν ὄφελος πολιτείας μὴ ἔχοντας νόμους λα- τὰ τῶν ἀδικούντων[?]. Legi divinæ duæ comites junguntur, Promissio & Commi-natio. Cum harum fides & certitudo in dubium vocatur, concidit etiam legis totius autoritas & existimatio. Porrò, legum divinarum contemtus conjunctus est cum Dei legislatoris contumelia.
units.tr: 1. The law is said to be weakened when it falls into contempt on this account, that it seems to have no one to defend and honour those who obey it, or to punish transgressors and violators according to their evil deserts. The saying of the orator Aeschines is well known, that a commonwealth without laws offers no advantage, and that the laws are ruined by wrongdoers. Two companions are joined to the divine law, Promise and Threat. When the trust and certainty of these are called into doubt, the authority and esteem of the whole law also collapses. Moreover, contempt for the divine laws is bound up with insult to God, the lawgiver.

units.la: 2. Non egredietur iudiciū in seculum. Querela est etiam piorum, Iustos saepe in bona causa opprimi ab iis de quibus dicitur: Cui vis[?] est, ius non metuit: ius op-primitur vi. Dauid hominū praeiudicijs se premi sentiēs, ad Deū vniuersorū iudi-ce iustū clamat: A' facie tua iudiciū meū prodeat: Psal.17.2. Idem Dei iudicia in suis hostibus animaduertens: Immò, inquit, Iehouah in aeternum sedebit, parās ad iudicium sedem suam. Et ipse iudicabit orbem in iusticia, & iudicabit populos rectissimè. Item: Innotuit Iehouah iudicio quod fecit: opere manuū suarū illaqueatus est malus. Psal.9.7.8. & 16.
units.tr: 2. "Judgement will not go forth for ever." This is also the complaint of the godly, that the just are often oppressed in a good cause by those of whom it is said: "Whoever has power does not fear right; right is oppressed by force." David, feeling himself pressed down by the prejudices of men, cries out to God, the just judge of all: "Let my judgement go forth from your presence" (Ps. 17:2). The same man, observing God's judgements on his enemies, says: "Indeed, Jehovah will sit for ever, preparing his seat for judgement. And he himself will judge the world in righteousness, and will judge the peoples most uprightly." Again: "Jehovah has made known the judgement he executed; the wicked man is ensnared by the work of his own hands" (Ps. 9:7–8, 16).

units.la: Maximè autem ad phrasin illam intelligendam facit versus 15.Psal.94. Quia ad iusticiam reuertetur iudicium: & posti-psum ibunt omnes recti corde. Sic autē fideles, spe bona erecti, pronunciare solent, cum durandum esse, & ut maximè iniusticia grassetur mundiq; statum perturbet, tandem tamen iusticia & iudiciū quasi postliminiò revocanda, monent.
units.tr: Verse 15 of Psalm 94 contributes most to understanding this phrase: "For judgement will return to righteousness, and all the upright in heart will follow it." Thus the faithful, raised up by good hope, are accustomed to declare that, though one must endure, and though injustice rages as much as it will and disturbs the state of the world, justice and judgement must at length be recalled, as if by postliminy.

units.la: 3. Impius quiuis circumdat iustum. Intelligatur non solum de dolis, sed etiam de aperta vi. Iuxta hæc dicta: Laqueos etiam mihi tendunt, qui quaerunt uitam meam: & qui quaerunt quomodo nocent mihi, loquuntur praua, & dolos quotidie meditantur: Pfal.38.12. Item: Miserere mei Deus: nam iste me absorbet, & quotidie me uorans coarctat me. Sorbet me obseruatores mei quotidie: certe multi belligerantes aduersus me, o Deus excelse. Quotidie uerba mea torquent: aduersus me sunt omnes cogitationes eorum ad nocendum. Congregantur, occultant se, calcaneos meos obseruant, exspectantes animam meam: Pfal.56.1.2.5.6. In his & similibus dictis imaginem uitae piorum, qui sunt uelut agni in medio luporum, nobis proponi, meminerimus.
units.tr: 3. "Every wicked man surrounds the just." This is to be understood not only of deceits but also of open violence. In accordance with these words: "They also lay snares for me, who seek my life; and those who seek how to harm me speak perverse things and plot deceits every day" (Ps. 38:12). Again: "Have mercy on me, O God, for this man swallows me up; crushing me every day, he devours me. My watchers devour me daily; surely many fight against me, O God most high. Every day they twist my words; all their thoughts are directed against me to harm. They gather together, they hide themselves, they watch my heels, waiting for my soul" (Ps. 56:1, 2, 5, 6). Let us remember that in these and similar sayings the image of the life of the godly, who are like lambs in the midst of wolves, is set before us.

units.la: 4. Egredietur iudicium peruersum. Hoc est: Patroni malarū causarū, superiores euadet, & quod uolunt obtinebunt. Pfal.10.
units.tr: 4. "Perverse judgement goes forth." That is: the advocates of bad causes will prevail over the better ones, and will obtain what they want (Ps. 10).

units.la: 2. In elatione impij persecutione patitur oppressus: comprehenditur in consilijs suis quae cogitat. 3. Quonia gloriatur impius super desiderio animae suae: & auaro benedicit: insultat Iehouae. 4. Impius in altitudine naris suae nō inquirit: omnes cogitationes eius sunt, quod Deus nō sit. 5. Succedunt viae eius omni tempore.
units.tr: 2. In the pride of the wicked the oppressed suffers persecution; he is caught in the schemes he devises. 3. For the wicked man boasts of the desire of his soul, and blesses the greedy; he insults Jehovah. 4. In the haughtiness of his nose the wicked man does not seek; all his thoughts are that there is no God. 5. His ways prosper at all times.

units.la: Actū est nō modò de piorū salute & incolumitate, sed etiā de gloria Dei, cū lex, seu etiā tota doctrina diuinitus inspirata & tradita, debilitatur, id est, ut nihili fit: & tam promissiones diuinae, quàm comminationes, uidentur esse λόγοι [?] λῆροι.
units.tr: Not only the salvation and safety of the godly, but also the glory of God, is at stake when the law, or indeed the whole doctrine divinely inspired and handed down, is weakened, that is, is made as nothing; and both the divine promises and the threats seem to be empty tales [λῆροι].

units.la: Atqui hoc tempore Lex debilitatur.
