Nam piij quidem querūtur, nō patefieri Dei iudiciū de sontibus & insontibus, immò pios deteriore loco uersari, & ab impijs opprimi: improbi uerò illusores, fureter cotendunt[?], nūnquā eiusmodi iudiciū instituendū & exequedū[?]: nec dubitāt, etiā scelerātos conatus ex uoto sibi successuros esse: eoq; nomine iustos circundat, hoc est, & per cuniculos, & aperto Marte oppugnāt.
units.tr: Yet at this time the law is weakened. For the godly indeed complain that God's judgement concerning the guilty and the innocent is not made manifest, and that the pious are, on the contrary, placed in a worse position and oppressed by the wicked. The wicked, however, mockers that they are, argue vehemently that such a judgement is never to be instituted or carried out; nor do they doubt that even their wicked attempts will succeed for them as they wish. On this account they surround the just, that is, they attack them both by underhand means and in open war.

units.la: Itaque non pij solùm, secundum uetus Prouerbium, in cuspide nouaculæ cõstituti, sed etiam Dei auctoritas & gloria in periculum adducta uidetur.
units.tr: Therefore, according to the old proverb, not only the godly stand on the edge of a razor, but the authority and glory of God also seem to be brought into danger.

units.la: Maior sic probatur ἐπιλογισμῷ: Non po-test sacrosancta manere & uigere eius auctoritas & gloria, cuius leges & edicta pro fulgure è pelui, & cuius promissiones pro fumo euanido, comminationes aut pro fulmine bruto habentur: nec etiā extra te-lorum iactum positi uideri possunt, qui frustra talium editorū studiosi sunt: immō qui eorum causa in discrimen adducunt uitam,familias,facultates opum, & alia uitæ præsidia. Dei autem leges debilitantur, & earum studiosi opprimuntur. Quare & illius auctoritas, & horū salus, summè periclitatur.
units.tr: The major premise is proved by a syllogism. The most holy authority and glory of that one cannot remain and flourish whose laws and edicts are held as mere flashes, whose promises are held as vanishing smoke, and whose threats are held as a harmless thunderbolt. Nor can those who are zealous for such edicts seem to be placed beyond the range of missiles; rather, those who for their sake put life, families, wealth and the other safeguards of life in peril. But God's laws are weakened, and their zealous adherents are oppressed. Therefore both his authority and their safety are in the greatest danger.

units.la: Minor probatur ab uniuersali piorum & aliorum experientia,quam lugubri o-ratione Propheta allegat.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved from the universal experience of the godly and of others, which the Prophet recounts in a mournful speech.

units.la: Grauissima Chori apud Euripidem in Iphigenia Aulidensi querela,mihi nō in-digna relatu uisa est, quia etiam de legū contemtu agit:
units.tr: The very grave lament of the Chorus in Euripides' Iphigenia at Aulis seems to me not unworthy of being related, since it too deals with contempt for the laws:

units.la: ἦ [?] τὸ [?] τᾶς [?] αἰδῶς [?] — ἃ [?] τὸ [?] τᾶς [?] ἀρετᾶς [?] δύνα- [?] μιν [?] ἔχει [?] δέμας [?] τε [?] πρόσωπον [?] — ὅπῃ [?] τὸ [?] μὲν [?] ἀσφαλὲς [?] ἐ-δυνάμιν [?], ἃ [?] δ᾽ [?] ἀρετὰ [?] λαλόπιδεν [?] (χ [?] θνατοῖς [?] ἀμιλλᾶται [?], — ἀνομία [?] δὲ [?] νόμων [?] λεγάτα [?]. ξὺν [?] λοιγὸς [?] ἀγὼν [?] βροτοῖς [?], — μῆτις [?] θεῶν [?] φθόνος [?] ἔλθῃ [?].
units.tr: Where is the form of modesty, and where the power of virtue? For safety has no power, while virtue is contested among mortals, and lawlessness is proclaimed in place of laws. Struggle and ruin come upon mortals, unless the wisdom of the gods or their envy intervenes.

units.la: Quòd si uel maximè ad ulcisenda hominum scelera,Deus peccata peccatis puniens, tantam ἀταξίαν [?], confusionem,& iniuriarum congeriem inualescere sinat: gloriæ tamen ipsius intererat,tantum legis suæ contemtum, tantam θεομαχωαν insolentiam, non ferre: cùm non tantùm quid improbi homines mereatur, sed etiam quid maiestati diuinæ coueniat, spe standum sit.
units.tr: But even if God, punishing sins by sins, lets such great disorder, confusion and heap of injuries prevail, chiefly to avenge men's crimes, it was nonetheless in the interest of his glory not to bear such contempt for his law and such insolent defiance of God [θεομαχίαν]. For one must hold to hope, not only regarding what wicked men deserve, but also regarding what befits the divine majesty.

units.la: Dicitur etiam Lex Dei debilitari, cùm eo nomine uilescit, quòd propemodum melior esse uideatur conditio transgressorum eius, quàm eorum qui diligenter eam custodiunt.
units.tr: The law of God is also said to be weakened when it is cheapened on this account: the condition of its transgressors seems almost better than that of those who keep it diligently.

units.la: DE SCANDALO, QVO AFFICIVNTUR ET VRUNTUR pij, cum impios florere, et sibi uim inferre uident.
units.tr: On the scandal by which the godly are wounded and shaken when they see the wicked flourish and themselves suffer violence.

units.la: Hoc mirificè etiam pias mentes afficit, quòd Canonem diuinum intuentes, & ad eum omnia tum sua, tum aliena facta exigentes, circa ista tamè grauiter impingunt.
units.tr: This especially troubles pious minds: while they look to the divine canon and measure by it all their own deeds and those of others, they nonetheless stumble badly over these points.

units.la: 1. Pios semper florere cupiunt, nunquam premi aduersis.
units.tr: 1. They always want the godly to flourish and never to be oppressed by adversity.

units.la: 2. Impios ne quidem τοῖς βιωτικοῖς bonis frui uolunt.
units.tr: 2. They do not want the wicked to enjoy even the good things of this life [τοῖς βιωτικοῖς].

units.la: 3. Nolunt rectè aut secus factorum remunerationem aut poenas differri à Domino, sed accelerari.
units.tr: 3. They are unwilling for the Lord to defer the reward of good deeds or the punishment of evil ones, but want both hastened.

units.la: 4. Non illud semper cogitant, pijs omnia in bonum cedere. Rom. 8.28.
units.tr: 4. They do not always reflect that all things work together for good for the godly. Rom. 8.28.

units.la: 5. Non satis perpendunt, bona temporaria & successus improbis in malum cedere. Psal.69.22. Sit mensa eorum ipsis pro laqueo, & illorum prospera pro reti.
units.tr: 5. They do not sufficiently weigh that temporal goods and success turn to evil for the wicked. Ps. 69.22: Let their table become a snare before them, and their prosperity a net.

units.la: 6. Verisimum esse Nazianzeni dictu: Nemo vires suas in pace cognoscit: si enim bella desunt, virtutum experimenta non prosunt. non satis perpendunt. Alioquin virtutem in fide & caritate per adversa illustrari, animaduerterent.
units.tr: 6. Nazianzen's saying is true: no one knows his own strength in peace, for if there are no wars, the proofs of virtue do not help. They do not sufficiently weigh this. Otherwise they would notice that virtue in faith and love is made more brilliant through adversity.

units.la: Etsi autè dulcisimè dicitur: Pietas ad omnia utilis est, ut quæ promissiones habeat vitæ prꝗsentis & futuræ: 1. Tim. 4.8. Item: Timete Iehova Sancti eius: quia nihil deest timetibus eum: Psal. 34.9. acualde jucunda sunt exempla Iosephi & Dauidis & Danielis, e gurgitibus malorum emergētium, & ad summos honorum & gloriæ gradus eue&torum: tamen nunquā crux a pietate & veritate separanda erat, tantisper donec fideles in hoc mundo militat. Nam & ista verè dicitur: Omnes qui volent piè viuere in Christo Iesu, persecutionem patientur: 2. Tim. 3.12. Item: Multa sunt adversa iustis, sed ex ijs omnibus liberat unusquisq; eorum Iehovah: Psal. 34.19. Et experti sunt Sancti illi viri, quorum memimeminimus, esse quandam διαδοχῇ[?] adversarum & secundatum rerum; quam Deus mirandis modis temperat.
units.tr: Although it is sweetly said, "Godliness is useful for all things, since it holds promise for the life that now is and for that which is to come," 1 Tim. 4.8; and likewise, "Fear Jehovah, you his saints, for nothing is lacking to those who fear him," Ps. 34.9; and although the examples of Joseph, David and Daniel, drawn out of the whirlpools of evils and raised to the highest degrees of honour and glory, are very pleasing, yet the cross was never to be separated from godliness and truth while the faithful are fighting in this world. For this too is truly said: "All who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution," 2 Tim. 3.12. Likewise: "Many are the adversities of the righteous, but Jehovah delivers each one of them from all of them," Ps. 34.19. And those holy men whom we remember experienced a certain succession [διαδοχή] of adversities and prosperous things, which God tempers in wonderful ways.

units.la: Primùm itaq; in eo peccát, quòd ante-quā certamen ritè absolverint, coronari: præterq; suum meritum, molliter tracta-ri volùt. Notum est illud Pauli: Tu igitur feras laborem, ut bonus miles Iesu Christi. Nemo qui militat, implicatur vitæ negocijs, ut ei placeat, à quo delectus est mi les. Quòd si certet etiā aliquis, nō coronatur, nisi legitimè certaverit. 2.Tim.1.3.4.5.
units.tr: First, then, they sin in this: before they have properly finished the contest, they want to be crowned, and they want to be treated gently beyond their own merit. Paul's saying is well known: "Therefore endure hardship, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ." No one who serves as a soldier is entangled in the affairs of life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him. But even if someone competes, he is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. 2 Tim. 1.3.4.5.

units.la: Secundò, nimium sunt morosi, cum etiam πρόσκαιρα[?] bona improbis adimunt: non satis cogitantes, sibi quoq; dictum: Diligite inimicos vestros, benedicite ijs qui devovet vos, benefacite ijs qui oderunt vos, & precamini pro ijs qui vos infestant, & persequuntur vos: ut sitis filij Patris vestri, qui est in coelis. facit enim ut Sol suus exoriatur super malos ac bonos, & pluit super iustos & iniustos: Mat-thæi 5.44.45. Si Deus vult divitem Epulonem bona sua in hac vita accipere, Lu-cæ 16.25. non fuerit Servorum Dei diversum quiddam expetere.
units.tr: Second, they are too peevish when the wicked are deprived even of temporal goods, not sufficiently considering that this was said to them too: "Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat and persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous," Matt. 5.44-45. If God wills that the rich man Dives receive his good things in this life, Luke 16.25, it is not for the servants of God to desire something different.

units.la: 3. Sapienter autè dijudicat tertiù scandali illius scopulum Augustinus, cum mo-net, ideo quorundam pœnas in alterum feculû differri, ut restare pœnas æternas, quibus afficiendi sint reprobi, intelliga-mus. Rursus, Sanctorum gratuita premia itidem differri, ut statuamus, æternam ui tam & læticiam illis esse expectandam.
units.tr: 3. Augustine judges wisely the rock of this third scandal, when he warns that the punishments of some are deferred to another age so that we may understand that the eternal punishments with which the reprobate are to be afflicted remain. Likewise, the free rewards of the saints are deferred, so that we may consider that eternal power and joy are to be awaited by them.

units.la: Verum enimuerò, ut se iudicem mundi esse Deus ipsis factis testetur, tempora-les pœnas interdum accelerat. Psal.139.19. Si occideris Deus impium: tunc uiri san-guinû declinate à me. Vt Ahitophel, Saul, Absalom & alij citò dederunt pœnas. in-terdû eo consilio differt, de quo dicitur: Ne interficias eos, ne forte obliuiscatur populus meus: sed uagari fac eos uirtute tua, & deijce eos tu clypeus noster Domi-ne: Psal.59.11. Testatiora enim fiunt Dei iudicia, cum sensim hostes piorum è me-dio tollit. Chosroes Persarum Rex potë-tissimus, Heraclij Imperatoris ἰσόχρονος, multis bellis ex sententia confectis, ac suc-cessuû magnitudine ebrius, Romanis pa-cem petentibus, superbè respondit: Non parcam uobis donec Crucifixum, quem Deum esse creditis, adoraueritis: & non unà nobiscum Soli cultum diuinû detu-leritis. leritis.[?] Secuta est diuina νέμεσις[?], cùm magna rerum illius μεταβολὴ[?] & inclinatione facta, tandem à Siroë filio captus, numellis & compedibus constrictus, in carcere diu detentus, & à satrapis filij mandatu conspurus, & horribili genere supplicij, sagittis cõfixus, interijt. Dignum est memoratu Valerij Maximi dictum: Lento gradu ad sui uindictam diuina procedit ira, tarditatemq; supplicij grauitate pœ-næ compensat. Et exstat Plutarchi Com-mentarius de sera Numinis uindicta:
units.tr: But indeed, so that God may attest by the very facts that he is judge of the world, he sometimes hastens temporal punishments. Ps. 139.19: "If you slay the wicked, O God, depart from me, men of blood." So Ahithophel, Saul, Absalom and others quickly paid their penalties. At other times he defers them, with the intention spoken of in the words: "Do not slay them, lest my people forget; but scatter them by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our shield," Ps. 59.11. For God's judgments become more evident when he removes the enemies of the godly little by little from the midst. Chosroes, the most powerful king of the Persians, contemporary of the emperor Heraclius, after many wars had been brought to a successful end, drunk with the greatness of his successes, answered the Romans who sought peace haughtily: "I will not spare you until you have worshipped the Crucified One whom you believe to be God, and have given no divine worship to the Sun along with us." Divine nemesis followed, when a great change and reversal of his affairs occurred. At last captured by his son Siroes, bound with fetters and chains, long held in prison, and by the son's command treated with contempt by the satraps, he died, pierced through with arrows, by a horrible kind of punishment. The saying of Valerius Maximus is worth recalling: "Divine wrath proceeds with slow step to take vengeance, and compensates for the tardiness of punishment by its severity." And there exists Plutarch's treatise on the delayed vengeance of the deity.

units.la: Iam uerò, quòd præmia rectè factorū attinet, cùm non ex merito, sed ex gratia conferantur, quis non uideat, nequaquam nobis ante tempus diuinitus præstitutū esse exigenda? Ergo cùm citò conferun-tur, gratiæ Deo, sua dona coronanti, agē-dæ: cùm differuntur, æquis animis exspe standa sunt.
units.tr: Indeed, as far as the rewards of right deeds are concerned, since they are conferred not according to merit but according to grace, who does not see that they must by no means be demanded from us before the time divinely appointed? Therefore, when they are conferred quickly, God, who crowns his own gifts, is to be thanked; when they are deferred, they are to be awaited with calm minds.

units.la: 4. Ex ignorantia autem finium bonorum & malorum, nascitur opinio negās, ex malis ἀγνωσίαν[?] quandam ad nos redire. Quid boni secuturum esset ex scelere Patriarcharum fratrem Iosephū uendentium, nemo hominum potuit conijcere. Et tamen Deus id Iosepho mirabili quadam rationein bonum couertit.Gen.50. 20. Quàm multis & eximijs Dei feruis, qui nunc carcerum,exilij,paupertatis,ini quisimorū præiudiciorū & anathema-tismorum incommodis laborat, propter ueritatis amorem & profesionem, hæc tristia mala non multo pòst erunt utilia & honorifica coram Deo & electis angelis & hominibus?
units.tr: 4. From ignorance of the limits of good and evil arises the opinion that denies that some unknown good returns to us from evils. No man could have guessed what good would follow from the crime of the patriarchs' brothers in selling Joseph. Yet God, by a wonderful design, turned it to good. Gen. 50.20. How many of God's excellent servants, who now suffer the discomforts of prisons, exile, poverty, and unjust prejudices and anathemas for the love and profession of the truth, will these sad evils soon make useful and honourable before God, the elect angels and men?

units.la: 5. An non autem magna est incogitantia & in iudicando hebetudo, non uidere, quòd improborum hominum, (quos Deus in lubrico posuit,Psal.73.18.)successus rectà eos ad horribile præcipitium deducant? Et quòd eorum opes & delitiæ ipsis sint pro reti,quo miserè intricati dét poenas?
units.tr: 5. Is it not great thoughtlessness and dullness of judgment not to see that the success of wicked men, whom God has set on slippery ground (Ps. 73.18), leads them straight to a horrible precipice? And that their wealth and delights, which are a net for them, entangle them wretchedly so that they pay the penalty?

units.la: 6. Quò autem maiora certamina, Dei caussa Pijs adeunda & superanda sunt, tanto magis elucet fidei, quæ mundum vincit,decus: & tanto erit illustrior victoria. Fidus est hic sermo,ut ait Paulus Apostolus.Nam si cum Christo mortui sumus,cum eo etiam uiuemus:si toleramus,etiam cum eo regnabimus: Tim.2.11.12. Item : Qui uicerit,amicietur uestimentis albis: neq; delebo nomè eius ex libro uitæ,sed pro-fitefitebor nomen eius coram Patre meo, & coram angelis eius. Apoc.3.5.
units.tr: 6. But the greater the struggles that the godly must undertake and overcome for God's sake, the more the glory of faith, which overcomes the world, shines forth, and the more illustrious the victory will be. "This is a faithful saying," as the apostle Paul says: "For if we have died with Christ, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him," 2 Tim. 2.11-12. Likewise: "He who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments; and I will not blot his name out of the book of life, but will confess his name before my Father and before his angels," Rev. 3.5.

units.la: Quid causæ est, quòd etiàm sanctos sic offen-dunt secundæ res improborum, & eorum sceleris[?] & iniuriæ?
units.tr: What is the cause that even the saints are offended when the wicked prosper, and when their crimes and injuries succeed?

units.la: Quòd ἐτρῴωσιν[?] quādam affectuum admittūt, quæ facit ut sibi ipsis nonnunquā dissimiles sint. Rectè sanè faciunt, si quādo cum Nazianzeno dicunt:
units.tr: Because they admit certain emotions, which at times make them unlike themselves. They rightly do so when, with Nazianzen, they say:

units.la: [illegible, ~38 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~26 letters] [illegible, ~26 letters]
units.tr: [illegible in the scan]

units.la: Idem verò sanctis accidere solet, quod ingeniōso & solerti viatori, qui cœlo admodum sereno, in amœnissima cultisi-maq; regione, summa suā cum voluptate iter facit, & oculis huc illuc versis lustrat, alias quidem prata cōsita gramine, variisq; pulcerrimisq; floribus, ac frugiferis arboribus: alias lætas segetes, copiosæ messis spem facientes: alias vineas egregiè excultas, & naturæ parturientis miraculis ornatas. Quid enim homini sano, ista Dei opera aspicienti, aliud in me-te veniat, quàm illud ἐπιφώνημα Dauidis: Sit gloria Iehouæ in seculum: lætetur Iehouah in operibus suis? Pfal.104.31. Neque etiam pia mens, intuens humani generis διατροφήν, & perpendens eius originem, propagationem & conseruationem: institutionem ordinis Ecclesiastici, politici & œconomici: leges & uitæ præsidia: Gentium colonias, incrementa, mores, gesta, fata: Ecclesiæ collectionem & conseruationem, & alia prope innumera rite considerans, sese continebit, quo minus erumpat in λογολογίαν: Magnus est Dominus Deus noster in omnibus operib. suis.
units.tr: But it usually happens to the saints as it does to a clever and skilful traveller who, under a very clear sky and in a most pleasant and well-cultivated region, makes his journey with great delight, and with his eyes turned here and there surveys now meadows planted with grass and with various most beautiful flowers and fruit-bearing trees, now cheerful crops promising an abundant harvest, now vineyards excellently tended and adorned with the wonders of a fertile nature. For what else would come to the mind of a sound man looking at these works of God than that exclamation of David: "May the glory of Jehovah endure for ever; may Jehovah rejoice in his works," Ps. 104.31? Nor will a godly mind, considering the sustenance of the human race, weighing its origin, propagation and preservation, the establishment of ecclesiastical, political and domestic order, the laws and safeguards of life, the colonies, growth, customs, deeds and fates of the nations, the gathering and preservation of the Church, and many other things almost countless, rightly consider them and restrain itself from breaking out into praise: "Great is the Lord our God in all his works."

units.la: At si idem ille uiator, prata paulo ante uernatia eluuione uastari: regiones quæ iam ad messem albæ erant, grādine prosterni & conteri: uites pluuijs & frigore corrumpi: deniq; omne decus agrorum solui, admodum attonitus & stupefactus uideat: quid ei in res destructas oculos defigenti, tristissima earum facies aliud suggerat, quàm modis omnibus dolendum esse, quòd bonæ Dei creaturæ breui tempore uastatæ, hominumq; usibus ereptæ sint, sic ut non impijs solum (ista nimirum calamitate dignis) sed etiam pijs, istorum uitæ adminiculorum indigis, eis sit carendum?
units.tr: But if that same traveller saw the meadows, just beginning to turn green, laid waste by a flood, the fields that were already white for harvest beaten down and crushed by hail, the vines ruined by rain and cold, and at last all the beauty of the countryside stripped away, he would be astonished and stunned. As he fixed his eyes on the ruined land, what could its saddest appearance suggest to him, other than that it is grievous in every way that good creatures of God should in a short time be laid waste and snatched from human use, so that not only the wicked, who deserve such calamity, but also the godly, who need these aids to life, must go without them?

units.la: Et tamen si idem ille αὐτότῃς in Deum respiciat, ac diuinitùs ista omnia facta sibi persuadeat, quid aliud, te quæso, dicat, quàm id quod Iobum, tristi nuncio prope exanimatum, fides serena docuit: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit?
units.tr: And yet if that same man looked to God as the cause of all things, and was persuaded that all these things were done by divine action, what else, I ask you, would he say than what steadfast faith taught Job, when he was almost overcome by the sad news: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away"?

units.la: Ita quoque Sancti, crucis molestia breui tempore nonihil liberati, hilares & alacres Dei conditoris & conseruatoris laudes concelebrant: sic propemodum animati, quemadmodum solent esse ἀσκηταὶ scholastici, si quando eis feriæ & relaxationes à discendi intentione & studio concedantur, ac præclarè secum agi putant, cum non adiguntur ad utilia proficiendi exercitia.
units.tr: So too the saints, briefly freed from some of the burden of the cross, celebrate with cheerful and eager hearts the praises of God, their creator and preserver. They are roused in much the same way as scholars are wont to be when holidays and relaxation from the strain and effort of study are granted them, and they think they have been treated very well, since they are not driven on to the profitable exercises of advancement.

units.la: Sed cum ijdem intuentur tetra & tristia spectacula confusionum in imperijs, in religione & Ecclesia, in œconomijs & Academijs, & deniq; in omnibus gradibus uitæ & societatis humanæ: consternati mœstique stant, & illa quæ diximus, cū doctrina de Prouidentia, de promissionibus diuinis, è diametro pugnare, suspicantur. Adeò magnum quiddā est in aduersis, Deū agnoscere & amare ut Patrem, ut ὑποφυγὴ: & sub paterna eius ferula proficere: nos'percutientem & mortificantem diligere: & sese sub potenti eius manu summittere.
units.tr: But when these same saints look upon the foul and sad spectacles of disorder in the commonwealths, in religion and the Church, in households and academies, and finally in every rank of human life and society, they stand dismayed and sorrowful, and they suspect that the things we have mentioned are flatly at odds with the doctrine of providence and the divine promises. So great a thing it is, in adversity, to acknowledge and love God as Father, and to make progress under his fatherly rod, to love him even as he strikes and mortifies us, and to submit ourselves beneath his mighty hand.

units.la: Nos, memores nostrae stulticiae & infir-mitatis, quotiescunq; carnis intelligentia & impatientia transuersos rapere conatur, Dauidis dictum repetamus: Obmu-tui, non aperiam os meum: nam tu fecisti: Psal.39.9. Statim enim atque diuinitus aliquid factum nobis persuadere coepimus, illud quoq; animum subibit, Re-cte factum. Quid enim? An ne melius erat id fieri quod nobis, quam quod Deo summe iusto,bono,sapienti est visum?
units.tr: Let us, mindful of our folly and weakness, whenever our fleshly understanding and impatience try to drag us off course, repeat the saying of David: "I was dumb, I did not open my mouth, because you have done it" (Ps. 39.9). For as soon as we begin to be persuaded that something has been done to us by God, there immediately comes into our minds the thought, "It was done rightly." For what? Was it not better that what happened to us should be done otherwise, than that it should be done as seemed good to God, who is supremely just, good and wise?

units.la: Sed tu Domine Iesv, da nobis miseris, ut nos ipsos abnegantes, & πᾶν νόημα αἰχμαλωτίζοντες[?] tua adoremus iudicia: uel hac in parte felices & prudentes, quod tuo iudicio stare nobis sit iucundum.
units.tr: But you, Lord Jesus, grant us wretched creatures that, denying ourselves and bringing every thought into captivity [πᾶν νόημα αἰχμαλωτίζοντες], we may worship your judgements; and in this respect at least may we be happy and wise, in that it is pleasing to us to stand by your judgement.

units.la: VERSVS V.
units.tr: VERSE V.

units.la: II. Responsio Iehouae ad querimoniam Habacuci Prophetae.
units.tr: II. The response of Jehovah to the complaint of the prophet Habakkuk.

units.la: Videte in Gentibus, & aspicite, & admiramini, admiramini: (Deus) enim operaturus est opus in diebus vestris, non credetis detis cum narrabitur: seu cum vobis prae-dicetur.
units.tr: Look among the nations, and observe, and wonder, wonder: for God is going to work a work in your days, which you will not believe when it is told you, or when it is declared to you.

units.la: Iehovah Deus noster orditur Responsionem suam à παραινέσεως[?], qua non solùm attentionem summam flagitat, sed etiā accuratam iudiciorum & præstantiū fuorū factorum considerationem. Iuxta illud: Videant recti, & lætentur; & omnes iniqui claudant ora sua. Quis est sapiens, ut hæc obseruet, ut (homines) intelligât bonitates Iehovæ? Psal.107.42.43.
units.tr: Jehovah our God begins his reply with an exhortation [παραινέσεως], which demands not only the closest attention but also a careful consideration of his judgements and excellent deeds, in keeping with that saying: "Let the upright see it and rejoice, and let all the wicked stop their mouths." Who is wise enough to observe these things, so that men may understand the goodness of Jehovah? (Ps. 107.42-43).

units.la: I. ARGUMENTUM, AB AD-iunctis hominum.
units.tr: I. ARGUMENT, DRAWN FROM THE ATTRIBUTES OF MEN.

units.la: Homines intelligentia præditos longè aliter aspicere decet opera Dei, quàm bruta animantia. Ideò Deus per Prophetam ędicit: Ne sitis sicut equus, & sicut mulus, quibus non est intelligentia. Psal-mo 32.9.
units.tr: Men endowed with understanding ought to regard the works of God in a far different way from brute animals. Therefore God says through the prophet: "Do not be like the horse or the mule, which have no understanding" (Ps. 32.9).

units.la: Bruta uerò oculis solùm externis aliquid cernunt: & ea tantùm obseruant, quæ externi sensus utcunq; percipiunt: secundum illud Isaiæ: Cognouit bos pos-fessorem suum, & asinus præsepe domini sui. Cap.1.3.
units.tr: Brute beasts, however, perceive only with their outward eyes, and they take note only of those things which the outward senses somehow perceive, according to that saying of Isaiah: "The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's crib" (Isa. 1.3).

units.la: Homines uerò intelligentes, non solùm τὰ ἀκουστά, sed etiam τὰ νοητά, admirabili sagacitate ἡ ἀγχινοΐα mentis, aliud ex alio rite colligentis, percipiunt. Ac non tam oculis cernūt, quàm mente uident: sicut rectè monet Aristoteles in Problematis, cū adducit peruulgatum dictum: Νῆς ὀφθαλμὸς ἡ νῦς ἀνθρώπου. Idem de Morte: Delectationes, inquit, animæ sunt, cognoscere creatorem, considerare opera cœlorum, & sapientiam illius. Plutarchus ad priu-s Aristotelis, immò uulgi dictum alludens: Mens, ait, uidet, mens audit: reliqua surda cæcaq; sunt, & rationis indiga. In Commentario de Fortuna Alexandri.
units.tr: Intelligent men, however, perceive not only things heard [τὰ ἀκουστά] but also things grasped by the mind [τὰ νοητά], by the remarkable quickness [ἡ ἀγχινοΐα] of a mind that rightly draws one thing from another. And they see not so much with their eyes as with the mind; as Aristotle rightly observes in the Problems, when he cites the commonly repeated saying: "The mind is the eye of man" [Νοῦς ὀφθαλμὸς ἀνθρώπου]. He says the same in his work On Death: the delights of the soul are to know the Creator, to consider the works of heaven and his wisdom. Plutarch, alluding to Aristotle's saying, or rather to a popular saying: "The mind," he says, "sees, the mind hears; the rest are deaf and blind, and in need of reason." In his Commentary on the Fortune of Alexander.

units.la: Iam uerò, cum ij quos Iehouah alloquitur in hac oratione, etiam fidei luce illuminatos haberent mentis oculos, multo magis decebat eos opera Domini rite cō templari. Fide enim intelligimus, quid rerū Deus ille conditor & redemtor nobis-cum agat. Hebr. 11.
units.tr: Now, since those whom Jehovah addresses in this speech had the eyes of their minds enlightened even by the light of faith, it was all the more fitting that they should contemplate the works of the Lord rightly. For by faith we understand what that God, our creator and redeemer, is doing with us (Heb. 11).

units.la: Quare longè aliter Dei opera hominibus intelligentibus, quàm brutis animalibus: fidelibus hominibus, quàm ceteri, qui sunt infideles, solent, spectanda & perpendenda sunt.
units.tr: Therefore the works of God must be viewed and weighed quite differently by men who understand than by brute animals, and by believing men than by the rest, who are unbelievers.

units.la: Quomodo Dei opera intuentur homines fideles?
units.tr: How do faithful people look upon the works of God?

units.la: Primùm, fide sic ea uident, ut Dei esse opera firmiter statuant, eique uni dent gloriam.
units.tr: First, by faith they see them in such a way that they firmly hold them to be works of God, and they give the glory to him alone.

units.la: Deinde, fide persuasi Deum facere mirifica,Psal.77.14.ferio admirantur & magnificiunt ea: non autem,impiorum more, uilipendunt. Et admiratio quidem operum Dei facit, ut in ijs cognoscendis maiore studio uersentur, ut de philosophantibus dixit Aristoteles in Metaph. Propter admirari coeperunt homines nunc & iam pridem philosophari. Vtinam uero perinde ut olim αὐτοπτῶ miraculorum Christi,ita hoc tempore ipsi quoque Dei opera intuentes, ad ipsius gloriam dicamus: καλῶς πάντα ποιῶν: Bene omnia fecit.Marci 7.37.
units.tr: Second, persuaded by faith that God does wonderful things (Ps. 77.14), they wonder at them and magnify them, and they do not, as the impious do, make light of them. Indeed, wonder at the works of God leads people to study them with greater diligence, as Aristotle said of philosophers in the Metaphysics: "Through wonder, men both began to philosophise now and at first." Would that, as once [αὐτόπται] eyewitnesses of Christ's miracles, so now too we who look upon God's works would say to his glory: [καλῶς πάντα ποιῶν] "He has done all things well" (Mark 7.37).

units.la: II. ARGVMENTVM, A comparatis.
units.tr: II. The argument from comparison.

units.la: Non suae tantum gentis,sed etiam aliarum ratio habenda est pijs & amatibus societatis humanae: ac peccat, qui sic suae gentis tristia fata deplorant,ut aliorum populorum non misereantur.
units.tr: Those who are godly and who love human society must take account not only of their own nation but also of others. They sin who so lament the sad fates of their own people as to have no pity for other peoples.

units.la: Vos autem Iudaei uestra tantùm mala planplangitis: nec istud cogitatis, Gentes plu-rimas multis & magnis calamitatibus la-borare.
units.tr: But you Jews only bewail your own misfortunes, and you do not consider that very many Gentiles labour under many great calamities.

units.la: Quare iubeo vos oculos vestros ani-mosq; ad alias quoque Gentes convertere, & eis laborantibus συμπάσχειν: nam hoc caritas & Gentiū cognatio postulat.
units.tr: Therefore I bid you turn your eyes and minds also to other nations, and to [συμπάσχειν] suffer with them as they suffer; for charity and the kinship of the Gentiles require this.

units.la: In hoc secundo argumento obseruanda nobis est amplificatio in vocabulo Goijm, Gentes. Aduersos casus multò re-ctius ferre possunt fideles, qui se Dei peculium esse, ac sibi post miseram hanc vitam æterna bona parata esse, nouerunt: q;[?] Gentes ignaræ Dei veri, & alienæ à testamentis promissionis, & quæ spem nō habent. Atqui vos Iudæi gens sancta & λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν estis: cæteri autem populi, qui non minus aduersis laborant & infestum experiuntur hostem, quàm vos, ver-santur in tenebris & umbra mortis, ignari scilicet Dei & voluntatis eius. Certum itaq; est, minus vos habere de quo conqueramini, quàm cæteras Gentes: etsi ne hæ quidem Deum incusare debent, cum scelerum suorum pœnas dent.
units.tr: In this second argument we must note the amplification in the word Goyim, Gentiles. Faithful people, who know that they are God's own possession and that eternal goods are laid up for them after this wretched life, are much better able to bear adversities than the Gentiles, who are ignorant of the true God, are strangers to the covenants of promise, and have no hope. Yet you Jews are a holy nation and a people for God's own possession (1 Pet. 2.9). The other peoples, who suffer no less than you from adversities and experience a hostile enemy, dwell in darkness and the shadow of death, ignorant of God and of his will. It is certain, therefore, that you have less cause to complain than the other Gentiles; and even they ought not to accuse God, since they are paying the penalties of their own crimes.

units.la: Det Dominus Iesus fratribus nostris, qui hoc tempore propter veritate à ψαν-[?] ἀδελφοῖς[?] & ab Antichristianis affliguntur, ut hoc meminerint, non carere solatio eam persecutionem, quam φιλαληθείας[?] caussa sustinent. Præstat enim confiteri, IESVM CHRISTVM in carne venisse, & eo nomine traduci & exagitari: quàm ὑπομένειν[?] fructum aulicæ beneuolentiæ falsa docendo captare, & breui tempore percipere.
units.tr: May the Lord Jesus grant to our brothers who at this time are afflicted for the truth, by the ...  brethren and by the Antichristians, that they remember this: the persecution which they endure for the love of truth is not without consolation. For it is better to confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh and to be called names and harassed for that name, than to seek the fruit of courtly favour by teaching falsehoods and to gain it in a short time.

units.la: III. ARGUMENTUM, AB EF- ficiente principe.
units.tr: III. The argument from the efficient cause, the prince.

units.la: Nullius opera maioris nobis facienda, & proinde maiore studio cognoscenda sunt, q; eius in quo sumus, uiuimus & mouemur, & qui uniuersorum iudex est.
units.tr: No works should be more important to us, and therefore none should be studied with greater diligence, than those of him in whom we live, move and have our being, and who is the judge of all things.

units.la: In Iehouah autem sumus, uiuimus & mouemur. Actor.17.28. Ipse est iudex & moderator omnium.
units.tr: Now in Jehovah we live, move and have our being (Acts 17.28). He himself is the judge and governor of all.

units.la: Quare eius opera summo studio nobis sunt cognoscenda. Atque eo potissimum nomine temulenti grauiter reprehenduntur, quòd opus Iehouæ non respiciant, & opera manuum eius non uideant: Iesa.5.12. Utinam huius temulentiæ nulla, tum in communibus œconomijs, tum præcipuè in aulis, exempla, hoc tempore perturbatissimo, pijs occurrant.
units.tr: Therefore his works must be studied with the utmost care. And drunkards are severely rebuked on this very ground, that they do not regard the work of Jehovah nor see the operation of his hands (Isa. 5.12). Would that at this most disturbed time no examples of this drunkenness, both in ordinary households and especially in courts, might meet the godly.

units.la: Cum multa sint Dei opera, quorum alia mediatè agit, alia immediatè: illa potissimum spectanda sunt, quæ præ omnibus aliis sunt ἐξοχὰ[?] & eximia.
units.tr: Since there are many works of God, some of which he performs mediately and others immediately, those above all must be considered which are outstanding and remarkable beyond all others.

units.la: Tale autem est istud quod iam aggredior, adhibito Nebucadnezare seruo meo. Poenas enim sumam de Iudæis & Gentibus: & quidem eiusmodi pœnas, ut si quis uobis eas prænunciet, non sitis crediturí inferri unam posse.
units.tr: Such is the matter I now take up, with my servant Nebuchadnezzar brought in. For I will execute judgements upon the Jews and the Gentiles, and indeed judgements of such a kind that, were anyone to foretell them to you, you would not believe that they could be inflicted.

units.la: Itaque hoc insigne opus Dei diligen-ter spectandum & perpendendum erit.
units.tr: Therefore this remarkable work of God must be carefully observed and weighed.

units.la: De operibus Dei quæ Aliena vocantur.
units.tr: On the works of God which are called strange.

units.la: Inter alia Dei opera, quibus iusta sua judicia declarat, referri debet Reipub. & Ecclesiæ [illegible, ~12 letters] qua Deus ulcisci-tur impietatem & iniusticiam hominum, cum, seu submotis è suo loco, seu præpeditis viris cordatis, placidis, & pacis amantibus, turbulentis & seditiosis hominibus laxat habenas, & improbè agentium, suaq;, non quæ Dei sunt, quærentium ministerio optimè interim utitur. Eadem autē opera & impios punit, & & pios probat seu explorat Dominus, facitq; ut reuelentur corda multorum hominum, & manifesti fiant ij qui probati sunt in fide. Vt enim etiam heroici viri, de gradu & statione moti, tum demum, quos amicos & quos inimicos habeat, cognoscunt, cum nec illis prodesse, nec his resistere aut obesse posse videntur: ita quoque in magna rerum perturbatione, cum oppressis aut pulsis bonis, improbi rerum potiuntur, tum demum apparet, quinam ex animo boni fuerint, qui simulatè.
units.tr: Among the other works by which God declares his righteous judgements, must be reckoned the [illegible] of commonwealth and Church, by which God punishes the impiety and injustice of men when, either by removing from their place or by hindering wise, calm and peace-loving men, he loosens the reins for troublesome and seditious men, and meanwhile makes excellent use of the service of those who act wickedly and seek their own ends, not the things of God. The same works both punish the impious and test or prove the godly, and the Lord brings it about that the hearts of many men are revealed and those who are approved in the faith become manifest. For just as even heroic men, when moved from their rank and station, then at last recognise who are their friends and who their enemies, since they seem able neither to help the one nor to resist or harm the others, so too in a great upheaval of affairs, when the good are oppressed or driven out and the wicked gain power, then at last it appears who were truly good at heart and who only feigned it.

units.la: De Republica, cuius insigne exemplū Habacucus subministrat, nunc nihil dicam: sed de Ecclesia, quæ cum intestinis dissidijs concutitur, etsi discit quinam sint amantes verę doctrinæ, qui non sint: tamen tristissimo documento experitur, quàm sit vere dictū ab exoterico illo Historico: Στάσεις ἐμφύλος πολέμῳ ὁμοφρονίσονς, τοῦτο λαὸν ἐστιν, ὅσῳ πόλεμος εἰρήνης.
units.tr: I will say nothing now about the commonwealth, of which Habakkuk supplies a remarkable example; but about the Church, which is shaken by internal dissensions. Although it learns who are lovers of true doctrine and who are not, nevertheless it experiences, by a most sorrowful lesson, how truly that exoteric historian spoke: [Στάσεις ... πολέμου] civil strife, a war within one people, is the more grievous the more its harmony is lacking in peace.

units.la: Cum Eutychianorum & Acephalorū certaminibus Martianus Imperator fine, in Chalcedonensi Synodo, editis sanctissimis sententijs de veritate utriusq; naturæ in una Christi persona, impositui esse videretur: statim post eius obitū, sub Leone Magno &Zenone, Ecclesiam perturbauerūt Timotheus Ælurus, Petrus Cnaphæus, Petrus Mongus antesignani, qui, ut fit rebus turbatis, nacti suffragatores, Alexadrinam in Ægypto, Antiochenā in Syria, Ecclesias,& alias multas, pulsis piis doctoribus, occupauerūt, & in rectè sententes proscriptionibus, exilijs, cædibus sequierunt. Erant enim armati Basilisci & aliorū auctoritate & armis: ac his potius præsidijs, uerè carnalibus, quàm spiritualibus armis sibi pugnandum iudicabant: homines nimirum sibi male conscij,mente[?] corrupti, & reprobi circa fidem.
units.tr: When, at the conclusion of the contests with the Eutychians and Acephali, the Emperor Marcian seemed to have settled matters by the most holy decisions published at the Synod of Chalcedon concerning the truth of both natures in the one person of Christ, immediately after his death, under Leo the Great and Zeno, Timothy Aelurus, Peter Fuller and Peter Mongus, leaders of the movement, disturbed the Church. As happens in troubled times, they found supporters and seized the churches of Alexandria in Egypt, of Antioch in Syria and many others, driving out the godly teachers; and they pursued those who thought rightly with proscriptions, exiles and slaughter. For they were armed with the authority and arms of Basiliscus and others, and they judged that they should fight with these carnal protections, truly, rather than with spiritual weapons. These were men, to be sure, who were conscious of their own wrongdoing, corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith.

units.la: Horum sæuitiam cū experirentur Orthodoxi, agnouerunt iustum Dei iudicium erga eos, qui locum dare cœpissent idolis, cultui reliquiarum, & alijs religionis uerae dehonestametis & corruptelis: ac statuebat, iram Domini, cui peccatuissent, sibi ferendam: à veritatis autè pro-fesione nequaquam discedendum.
units.tr: When the orthodox experienced their savagery, they recognised the just judgement of God upon those who had begun to give place to idols, to the worship of relics and to other corruptions and dishonourings of the true religion. And they resolved that the wrath of the Lord, against whom they had sinned, must be borne by them; but that they must by no means depart from the profession of the truth.

units.la: Interea à quibusdam ambitiosis hominibus caussa nō ut par erat perpensa, nec auditis Orthodoxis, σοφὰ φωνήματα[?] excogitari & usurpari cœperūt, pacis (cui veritatis fulcrum deerat) plausibili prætextu.
units.tr: Meanwhile, by certain ambitious men, the cause was not weighed as it ought to be, nor were the orthodox heard, and clever-sounding phrases began to be devised and employed, under the plausible pretext of peace, from which the support of truth was lacking.

units.la: Nam ut Georgius Cedrenus memoriæ prodidit, anno imperij sui xv, Acacij Patriarchæ Constantinopolitani suasu, Zeno Imperator Orientales Episcopos coegit, tum ut subscriberent τῷ σὺν αὐτῷ, ὅπερ αὐτὸς Ἀκάκιος ἐπονομάσῃ ἐξ ἰδίας λαμβάνων αὐτάς, tum ut communicarent Petro Mongo, mostrosarum opinionum architecto. Pecunia quoq; data (habent enim & tum nulæ istæ rationes, & pollicitationū aulicarum thus, miram uim apud eos qui pietatem putant esse quæstum) Roma missos Legatos eò perduxit, ut contra mada ta quæ acceperant, Acacio, homini polypragmonico ἡ ἀλλοπροσάκτῳ, subscriberent & communicarent, &c. Cedr. pag. 290.
units.tr: For, as George Cedrenus has recorded, in the fifteenth year of his reign, at the persuasion of Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, the Emperor Zeno compelled the Eastern bishops both to subscribe to what Acacius himself had named and to communicate with Peter Mongus, the architect of monstrous opinions. Money was also given (for even then these kinds of reasons and the incense of courtly promises had a wonderful power among those who think piety is a source of profit), and it brought the legates sent from Rome to such a point that, contrary to the commands they had received, they subscribed to and communicated with Acacius, a meddlesome busybody, and so on. Cedrenus, p. 290.

units.la: Cùm eodem loco res Ecclesiæ & piorum doctorum uersantur, ne frangatur animis, sed pro tueda ueritate contra mendaciū audentiores eant, nec dubitent futurum, ut in medijs perturbationum tenebris, ipsis diuinæ lucis & ueritatis & consolationis Christi radius affulgeat. Sed de his alijs pluribus agedum erit. Dominus det, ut φιλαλήθειαν καὶ τὴν φιλαδελφίαν semper coniungamus, & ut τρόπῳ φορᾷν discamus, ad illius gloriam.
units.tr: In the same place stand the affairs of the Church and of the godly teachers: let them not be broken in spirit, but go forward more boldly to defend the truth against lies, and let them not doubt that, in the midst of the darkness of disturbances, a ray of the divine light and truth and of Christ's consolation will shine upon them. But these and many other matters will need to be treated at another time. May the Lord grant that we always join [φιλαλήθειαν καὶ φιλαδελφίαν] love of truth and love of the brethren, and that we learn [τρόπῳ φορᾷν] to bear ourselves in a manner worthy of his glory.

units.la: V. ARGV.
units.tr: V. ARGUMENT.

units.la: VI. ARGUMENTUM, A CON-nexis, seu à tempore.
units.tr: VI. ARGUMENT, from connection, or from time.

units.la: Est hoc hominis pij & cordàti, nō prę-teritorum solùm, sed etiam fui seculi fa-torum spectatorem prudetem agere: ne-que enim ulla fuit ætas, in qua Deus non perspicuè multisque modis declarauerit summam iusticiam & misericordia suā.
units.tr: It is the mark of a pious and wise person to observe carefully not only the things that have passed but also the deeds of his own age, for there has never been an age in which God has not made his supreme righteousness and mercy plain and manifest in many ways.

units.la: Atqui hoc vestro tempore operaturus est Deus opus suā maiestate, providetia, iusticia & misericordia dignisimum, & vere ἀξιομνημόνευτον[?].
units.tr: Yet in your own time God is about to work a work most worthy of his majesty, providence, justice and mercy, and truly [ἀξιομνημόνευτον] worthy of being remembered.

units.la: Quare capita attollere, & opus Domini ὑψηλῶς[?] intueri decet. Ac digna est memoria sententia Gregorij in Moral. Diui-na mirabilia semper debent considerari per studium, & nunquam discuti per intellectū: nam hunc superarant. Et illa Augustini: Dicamus aliquid Deum posse, quod nos fateamur investigare non pos-se: in rebus enim mirabilibus, tota ratio faciendi, est ipsa potestas faciendi.
units.tr: Therefore it is fitting to lift up our heads and to behold the work of the Lord [ὑψηλῶς] on high. And the saying of Gregory in the Moralia is worth remembering: divine wonders should always be considered with study and never be investigated by the intellect, for the intellect is overcome by them. And that saying of Augustine: let us say that God can do something which we confess we cannot investigate; for in wonderful things the whole reason of doing is the very power of doing.

units.la: VI. ARGUMENTUM, ab inopinato:
units.tr: VI. ARGUMENT, from the unexpected:

units.la: Non ea solùm quæ eventurà nobis persvasimus, sed etiam quæ ἀπροσδοκήτως accidunt, eo quòd, etsi illa nobis prius denunciata essent, fieri tamen non posse o-pinati fueramus, prudenter aspicieda & perpendenda sunt. Etenim, ut recte Plinius iunior censuit, sunt maxime mirabilia, quae maxime inexspectata.
units.tr: Not only those things which we have persuaded ourselves are going to happen, but also those which happen [ἀπροσδοκήτως] unexpectedly, must be prudently observed and weighed, because although they had been announced to us beforehand, we had nevertheless thought they could not come to pass. For, as Pliny the Younger rightly judged, the most wonderful things are those that are least expected.

units.la: Tale autem erit illud opus Iehouae é-xercituum, (id est, executio iudicij diui-ni aduersus Iudaeos & Gentes) quod etsi vobis nunc mandatu divino praedicitur; nemo tamen est, qui illud fieri posse in a-nimum inducat suum. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Such, moreover, will be that work of Jehovah of hosts (that is, the execution of divine judgment against the Jews and the Gentiles). Although it is now foretold to you by divine command, nobody is there who brings himself to believe that it can come to pass. Therefore, etc.

units.la: An non mitius tractandus erat Dei populus, quàm Gentes idololatræ[?]?
units.tr: Should not the people of God have been treated more mildly than the idolatrous Gentiles?

units.la: Deus cum illo mitius agit, si officium faciat. At si eius causa Dei nomen blas-phemetur inter Gentes: Rom.2.24. quid mirum, si pro suis malis meritis male quo-que tractetur? Ille enim seruus, qui novit voluntatem Domini sui, nec se comparavit, nec fecit ex voluntate eius, caedetur multis plagis. Qui vero non novit, & fecit digna plagis, caedetur plagis paucis. Porrò cuicunq; multum datum est, multum repetetur ab eo: & apud quem deposuerunt multa, amplius reposcent ab eo. Luc.12.v.47.48.
units.tr: God deals more mildly with a person when he does his duty. But if, on account of that person, the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles (Rom. 2.24), what wonder is it if he is treated harshly in return for his evil deeds? For that servant who knew the will of his lord, and neither prepared himself nor acted according to his will, shall be beaten with many blows; but he who did not know, and did things worthy of blows, shall be beaten with few. Moreover, from everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from him to whom much has been entrusted, more will be demanded. (Luke 12.47-48)

units.la: Quid uero nobis cogitandum est, cum hoc tri-stissimum onus & similia legimus?
units.tr: But what are we to think when we read this most grievous burden and similar things?

units.la: Cognoscenda nobis & admirada Dei opera, quae his nostris oculis uidemus.
units.tr: We must recognise and admire the works of God, which we see with our own eyes.

units.la: Respub. Christiana partim bellis ciui-libus, partim armis Turcicis, in summas angustias adducta est. Amisimus bonam Pannoniae partem, & iam in uestibulo Germaniae acinaces suos acuut & in nos stringunt impij Mahometistae. Parte altera rapaces Iberi Antichristo seruiunt ciui-libus motib.excitandis & fouendis. Monarchae delirantes Achiuos pleƈtut. Grassantur etiam morbi uarij, rerum uenaliū precium augetur, & alia ingentia mala. Saeuit etiam non in corpora solum, sed etiam in animas, Homo ille sceleratus, & perditionis filius: cui dolet, quòd Spiritu oris Domini sese confici, & paulo post illustri aduentu Christi abolendū uidet. Vt autem hunc exhilarant Cadmaei fratres, auctores dissidiorum & nouorum dogmatum in Ecclesia: sic ingenti dolo-re afficiunt pios omnes, quibus & doctrinae sinceritas & Ecclesiae coniunctio cordi est. Eodemne modo fideles & infideles intuentur opera Iehouæ?
units.tr: The Christian commonwealth, partly by civil wars and partly by Turkish arms, has been reduced to the greatest straits. We have lost a good part of Pannonia, and already at the threshold of Germany the impious Mahometans are sharpening their scimitars and drawing them against us. On the other side, the rapacious Spaniards serve the Antichrist by stirring up and fostering civil disturbances. Raging monarchs lash the Achaeans. Various diseases are also rampant, the prices of goods are rising, and many other great evils. That wicked man, the son of perdition, rages not only against bodies but also against souls; he grieves that he is being destroyed by the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord, and sees that he will be abolished shortly by the glorious coming of Christ. And just as the Cadmean brothers, the authors of dissensions and new doctrines in the Church, cheer him up, so they bring great grief upon all the pious, who hold dear both the purity of doctrine and the unity of the Church. Do the faithful and the unfaithful look upon the works of Jehovah in the same way?

units.la: Nequaquam. Etsi enim ἀντάξι[?] communia sunt haec duo, uidere & audire: quia tamen in operibus illis, quae media-te fiunt, fideles non hominum tantum, sed etiam Dei opus uident: infideles autem proximas tantum causas animaduertunt: fit, ut illi quidem erudiantur & proficiant: hi uero euanescant, ac poenas suae incredulitatis dent.
units.tr: Not at all. For although these two things, seeing and hearing, are common to both, nevertheless, because the faithful see in those works which are done through intermediaries not only the work of men but also the work of God, while the unfaithful notice only the proximate causes, it comes about that the former are instructed and make progress, but the latter vanish away and pay the penalty of their unbelief.

units.la: Etenim fide intelligimus, bona & mala diuinitus sic dispensari, ut improbi homines ne digitum quidem aduersus nos attollere, nedum nos miseradum[?] in modum affligere possint, sine Dei nutu & consilio: ut dum nobis obesse conantur, plurimum prosint: ut metas illorum libidini & sequitiae praestitutas nō dubitemus: ut deniq; in eadem re, uerbi gratia, in Sanctorum afflictionibus, diaboli & satellitiū eius immane odiū & saeuitia, & Dei praesentia & consilium in exploratione & de-fensione piorum, magis elucescat.
units.tr: For by faith we understand that good and evil are so dispensed by God that wicked men cannot lift so much as a finger against us, much less afflict us miserably, without the nod and counsel of God; so that while they try to harm us, they especially help us; so that we do not doubt that limits have been set for their lust and wickedness; and so that finally, in the very same matter, for instance in the afflictions of the saints, the immense hatred and cruelty of the devil and his henchmen, and the presence and counsel of God in the testing and defence of the pious, shine out all the more clearly.

units.la: Ediuerso infideles tristi malorum sensu exasperati, non ad Deum percutiente attollunt oculos, sed in homines, ut ipsi uideuidetur, iniurios defigunt, & eis infensi malo conduplicato dolori suo medetur, <bl>[?]</bl> & neutiquam memores praecepti divini: Ne dixeris, Que-admodum fecit mihi, sic faciam ei: red-dam ipsi uiro secundum opus suum. Pro-uerb. 24.29.
units.tr: On the contrary, the unfaithful, exasperated by a bitter sense of evils, do not lift their eyes to God who strikes, but fix them upon men who, as it seems to them, have wronged them, and, hostile to them, seek to relieve their sorrow by doubling the evil, and are in no way mindful of the divine precept: Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work (Prov. 24.29).

units.la: VERSVS VI.
units.tr: VERSE 6.

units.la: Quia ecce ego suscito Chaldaeos, gentem amaram & praecipitem: quae perambulabit latitudinem terrae, ut possideat habitacula non sua.
units.tr: For behold, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the earth, to possess dwelling places that are not theirs.

units.la: Initio, quo tendat haec oratio: deinde, quid ea sibi velit, seu quae eius sententia sit: postremo, quis eius usus sit, spectandum nobis erit.
units.tr: At the outset we must consider where this discourse tends, then what it means or what its sense is, and lastly what its use is.

units.la: Scopus orationis est, si hypothesin spectes, Iudaeis non esse apud Deum querimonia, de Chaldęorum iniurijs, utendum. At si <bl>[?]</bl> respicias, hic erit scopus, Ecclesiae toti, & singulis fidelibus, non esse utilitigationem de iudicio divino instituendam propter hostiū saeuitiam: sed potius iram Domini, cui peccauerunt, tantisper ferendam, donec eam, pro infinita sua clementia, mitiget: ac non dubium esse
units.tr: The aim of the passage is, if you look at the thesis, that the Jews should not make a complaint before God about the wrongs of the Chaldeans. But if you look further on, the aim here is that the whole Church and each of the faithful should not bring a lawsuit against the divine judgment because of the savagery of their enemies. Rather, they should bear for a while the wrath of the Lord, against whom they have sinned, until in his infinite mercy he softens it.

units.la: {?} Greek words in the text: <bl>[?]</bl> read as θείου[?] in the Greek ("θείου" with doubt). esse debere, diuinitus & optimo consilio suscitari hostes piorum, ut hi praeclaram militantes militiam, retineant fidem & bonam conscientiam.
units.tr: And there is no doubt that the enemies of the godly ought to be raised up by God, by divine and most wise counsel, so that they may keep their faith and good conscience while fighting a splendid warfare.

units.la: Argumentum, quo hypothesis demo-stratur, ducitur ab αἰτίῳ λογίῳ [?], ab efficiente instrumentali, & a fine proximo.
units.tr: The argument by which the thesis is demonstrated is drawn from the causal reasoning [αἰτίῳ λογίῳ], from the efficient and instrumental cause, and from the proximate end.

units.la: Quicquid fit Deo decernente, & abijs quibus hoc diuinitus delegatum est, certoq; fine, de eo non pium foret cum Deo contendere. Rationes Maioris hæ sunt:
units.tr: Whatever happens by God's decree, and by those to whom this has been divinely entrusted, and for a certain end, it would not be pious to contend with God about. These are the reasons for the major premise:

units.la: 1. Deus, cum sit omnium conditor, ius summum in omnia obtinet, est παντοκράτωρ [?] uniuersorum Dominus & Iudex.
units.tr: 1. God, since he is the creator of all things, holds supreme right over all things; he is the almighty Lord and Judge of the universe.

units.la: 2. Idem in agendo nunquam aberrat à iusto, æquo & bono.
units.tr: 2. The same God never goes astray from what is just, equitable and good in his actions.

units.la: 3. Operatus est autem uniuersa propter semetipsum: etiam impium ad diem malum: Prouerb. 16.4. Impius autem malorum quibus laborat, caussam προκατακρισιν [?] in seipso habens, non potest criminari iustum iudicem.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, he has made all things for his own sake, even the wicked for the day of evil (Prov. 16.4). But the wicked man, who has the cause of his miseries within himself, cannot accuse the just Judge.

units.la: Atqui Deus suscitat Chaldæos, iam inhiantes alienis prouinciis & urbibus.
units.tr: But God raises up the Chaldeans, who already lust after foreign provinces and cities.

units.la: In hac Minore propositione obseruabimus:
units.tr: In this minor premise we shall observe:

units.la: 1. Belli istius αὐτίος λογίος [?], uidelicet Deu, qui hoc loco diserte dicit : Ego suscito[?] Chaldæos.
units.tr: 1. The cause of this war, namely God, who here expressly says: "I raise up the Chaldeans."

units.la: Obiectio, Iunioribus notanda.
units.tr: An objection, to be noted by the younger students.

units.la: Nullum malum est à Deo. Nam hic summè est bonus. Matth.19.17. Bellum autem malum est atrocissimum. Quare non est ab auctore Deo.
units.tr: No evil comes from God, for he is supremely good (Matt. 19.17). But war is a most dreadful evil. Therefore it does not have God as its author.

units.la: Respondeo: Sunt quatuor termini in isto leptologemate. In Maiore, Malum de culpa dicitur: ut Isa.5.20. Væ dicentibus malū bonum, & bonū malum. In Minore autem de pœna agitur, quæ ordini diuinæ iusticiæ respondet. Iuxta dictum: An erit malum in ciuitate, & Iehouah illud nō fecerit? Amos 3.6. Est itaq; paralogismus æquiuocationis in illo sophismate.
units.tr: I answer: there are four terms in this sophism. In the major premise, "evil" is said of guilt, as in Isa. 5.20: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil." But in the minor premise it is a matter of punishment, which corresponds to the order of divine justice, according to the saying: "Shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD has not done it?" (Amos 3.6). So there is a paralogism of equivocation in that sophism.

units.la: Porrò Deum bellis punire hominum genus, hæc dicta testantur: Super omnia loca excelsa in deserto uenerunt uastato res: quia gladius Iehouæ deuorat ab extremo terræ usq; ad extremum eius: non est pax uniuersæ carni: Ier.12.16. Item, de hoc ipso bello prophetas Ieremias in nomine Iehouæ, inquit: Ecce mittam & assumam omnes cognationes Aquilonis, ait Iehouah, & Nebucadnezar Regem Babel seruum meum, & adducam eos ad terram istam, & ad habitatores eius, & ad o-mnes nationes istas per circuitum, & interficiam eos, ponamq; eos in stuporem & in sibilum, &c. cap.25.9.
units.tr: Moreover, that God punishes the human race with wars is attested by these words: "Upon all the high places in the wilderness the spoilers are come; for the sword of the LORD shall devour from the one end of the land even to the other end of the land; no flesh shall have peace" (Jer. 12.12). Likewise, concerning this very war, the prophet Jeremiah says in the name of the LORD: "Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the LORD, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing," etc. (Jer. 25.9).

units.la: 2. [illegible, ~9 letters] Chaldaeos & eorum Regem Nebucadnezare, quos Dominus ipse describit, gentis, ingenij & finis qui ad bellum inferendū impulerat, metione facta.
units.tr: 2. [illegible, about nine letters] the Chaldeans and their king Nebuchadnezzar, whom the Lord himself describes, with mention made of their nation, their character and the aim that drove them to wage war.

units.la: Nomen Chasdim, Chaldaeos significat, quorum crebra in S. Biblijs mentio fit.
units.tr: The name Chasdim means Chaldeans, whose mention is frequent in the Holy Bible.

units.la: Si quis vestrum aliquid aliud cognoscere volet de eorū regione, metropoli, studijs, rebus gestis, cosulat Strabonem lib. 16. Geographiae: Plinium Natural.Hist. lib.6.cap.26.27. Pomp.Melam lib.3. de situ Orbis, cap. 8. Ioachimum Vadianū in Commentario de trib.partibus orbis terrarum, in titulo, de Chaldaea: Volaterranum lib.11.Geographiae: & Peucerum in Commentarij de generib.diuinationum ea parte, in qua de Chaldęorum religione, in sapientiam philosophicā transformata, disserit, eamq; speciebus τῆς ἀστρονομίας[?] annumerat. pag.130.
units.tr: If any of you wishes to learn something else about their region, capital, learning and deeds, let him consult Strabo, Geography book 16; Pliny, Natural History book 6, chapters 26 and 27; Pomponius Mela, On the Situation of the World, book 3, chapter 8; Joachim Vadian in his commentary On the Three Parts of the World, under the heading "Chaldea"; Volaterranus, Geography book 11; and Peucer in his commentary On Kinds of Divination, in the part where he discusses the religion of the Chaldeans, transformed into a philosophical wisdom, and reckons it among the species of astronomy, p. 130.

units.la: De ingenijs Chaldaeorum infra plura dicentur. Hoc loco Gens amara & præceps uocantur. Tribuuntur illis duo, πνευπικρίᾳ[?] ὀξύτης, amarulentia & celeritas in rebus aggrediendis & conficiendis: quibus dotibus Iberos nostra ætate prædi-tos, proh dolor, experimur.
units.tr: More will be said below about the character of the Chaldeans. Here they are called a bitter and hasty nation. Two qualities are attributed to them: bitterness and swiftness in undertaking and completing their affairs. Alas, we have experience of these gifts in the Iberians of our own age.

units.la: Etsi autem anima amara, sæpe tristem & lugentem significat,ut cū tribuitur Davidis exulis socijs & συνεθλιμμοῖς[?], 1. Sam. 22.2. & 30.6. tamen & de virorum bellicosorum indignatione heroica adversus hostes prædicatur, 2. Sam. 17.8. Et ait Hu-sai: Tu nosti patrem tuum, & viros eius fortes, & amaro esse animo, velut cum ursus orbatur catulis in campo. Et Act. 8.23. Simoni Mago χολὴ πικρίας ἡ[?] συνδέσμος τῆς ἀδικίας tribuitur.
units.tr: Although a bitter soul often signifies a sad and mourning person, as when it is attributed to David's companions in exile, who were in distress (1 Sam. 22.2; 30.6), it is also said of the heroic indignation of warlike men against their enemies (2 Sam. 17.8). Hushai says: "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and they are chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps in the field." And in Acts 8.23 the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity are attributed to Simon the Magician.

units.la: Cum autem præcipitem vocat Chaldaeorum gentem, istud innuit, eam μηδὲ[?] ἀναβαλλομένῳ[?] successus suos urgere, & magna celeritate perambulare regiones, easq; subigere.
units.tr: But when he calls the Chaldeans a hasty nation, he hints that they press on their successes without delay, and sweep through regions with great speed and subdue them.

units.la: Idem sane initio superioris seculi, Ruperto Palatino Cæsare, à Tamerlane Scytharum principe (qui devicto Baiazethe Turcorum Imperatore, multas Orientis provincias cum ingentibus copiis perua-gatus, reuera Dei flagellum fuit) factum esse, notum est. Ac nostra memoria Li-vonia [?]onia tales sensit Moschos, qui etsi Christianos se esse gloriantur, non minus tamen in nostros, cum data est copia, saeviunt, quam impij Mahometistae.
units.tr: That the same thing happened at the beginning of the last century, when Rupert the Elector Palatine was Emperor, at the hands of Tamerlane, prince of the Scythians (who, after defeating Bayezid, emperor of the Turks, roamed through many provinces of the East with huge forces and was truly a scourge of God), is well known. And in our own memory Livonia has felt such Muscovites, who, though they glory that they are Christians, nevertheless rage no less against our people, whenever they have the opportunity, than the impious Mahometans.

units.la: 3. Destinatum Chaldaeorum, ut inhabitent tabernacula non sua. Hoc no de [illegible, ~8 letters] Chaldaeorum, qui sedes auitas nunquam deseruerunt: sed de possessione aliorum regnorum & prouinciarum, accipiendum est.
units.tr: 3. The Chaldeans are destined to dwell in tents not their own. This must not be understood of the original dwelling places of the Chaldeans, who never left their ancestral seats, but of the possession of other kingdoms and provinces.

units.la: Videmus autem, Chaldaeos, non ut Dei judicijs servirent, sed ut imperij sui pomoeria longe lateq; proferrent, utque ex spoliis multarum gentium ditiores fierent, ingens illud bellum mouisse. Est enim, ut ille dicebat, [?]συμφυτὸν νόσημα τὰς ἀλαζονείας, ἢ πλεονεξία: ac pleriq; Principes non quam bene, sed quam multis praesint, spectare videntur: ut ciuis quondam noster Academicus, Erasmus, dicere solebat.
units.tr: Indeed we see that the Chaldeans stirred up this vast war not in order to serve the judgments of God, but in order to extend the boundaries of their empire far and wide, and to grow richer from the spoils of many nations. For, as a certain man used to say, ambition and greed are a natural disease, and most princes seem to look not at how well they rule, but at how many they rule. So our fellow citizen, the academic Erasmus, used to say.

units.la: Jam, ut tandem concludamus, non est obscurum, causam plane nullam esse querelae Judaeorum de Babylonijs hostibus, apud Dei tribunal movendae. Diuinitus excitari hostes Ecclesiæ & singulorum piorum, sed iustis de causis & optimo consilio.
units.tr: Now, to conclude at last: it is not obscure that there is plainly no ground for the complaint of the Jews against their Babylonian enemies to be brought before the tribunal of God. Enemies of the Church and of each of the godly are raised up by divine providence, but for just causes and by the best counsel.

units.la: Digni sunt memoria uersus: Nunquam bella pijs, nunquam discrimina desunt, Et cum quo certet, mens pia semper habet.
units.tr: Worthy of remembrance are the verses: "Wars and dangers are never absent from the godly, and a pious mind always has someone to contend with."

units.la: Et illud Pauli Apostoli: Sed & omnes qui uolunt pie uiuere in Christo Iesu, per-secutionem patientur: 2.Tim.3.12.
units.tr: And the saying of the Apostle Paul: "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim. 3.12).

units.la: 1. Αἴτιος λύσιος [?] & dux ac protector Ecclesiæ est Deus, qui ut olim Gentes quasdam reliquit, ut per eas tentaret Israelem, Iudicum 3.1. ut sciret an parerent prȩceptis Iehouæ, quæ præceperat Patribus eorū, v.4. sic omnibus temporibus, & hacno-stra ætate, bonos milites Iesu Christi la-borem ferre, 2.Tim.2.3. & legitimè certa-re uult.v.5. cum sit illis lucta [?] non tam aduersus carnem & sanguinem, quàm aduersus imperia, aduersus potestates, aduersus mundi dominos, (rectores) tene-brarum seculi huius, aduersus spirituales malitias, quæ sunt in sublimi. Eph.6.12.
units.tr: 1. God is the author and the leader and protector of the Church. As once he left certain nations so that he might test Israel through them (Judges 3.1), to know whether they would obey the commandments of the LORD which he had commanded their fathers (v. 4), so in all times, and in this our age, he wills that the good soldiers of Jesus Christ endure hardship (2 Tim. 2.3) and contend lawfully (v. 5). For their struggle is not so much against flesh and blood as against principalities, against powers, against the world rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in high places (Eph. 6.12).

units.la: Dux belli aduersus Sanctos, est diabolus, qui obambulat tānquam leo rugiens, quærens quem deuoret. Ei igitur resista-mus firmi per fidem. 1.Pet.5.8.9. Sub illius signis militat Mundus, is inquam, cuius ille Deus uocatur: 2.Cor.4. 4. Huius scelerati exercitus descriptio exstat toto Psal.14. & in alijs multis Scripturae diuinae locis.
units.tr: The leader of the war against the saints is the devil, who walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Therefore resist him, steadfast in faith (1 Pet. 5.8-9). Under his standards fights the world, I mean that world whose god he is called (2 Cor. 4.4). The description of this wicked army stands out in the whole of Psalm 14 and in many other places of divine Scripture.

units.la: Tradunt autem hostibus apertis mutuas operas domestici perduelles, qui in Ecclesia quidem sunt, sed non sunt ex ea. Hi uero illis multo sunt nocetiores: quia nihil minus uideri uolunt, quàm auctores calamitatum quibus laborat Ecclesia, quàm ἑτεροδιδάσκαλοι[?] & deprauatores doctrinæ cœlestis. Tales pestes olim fuerunt, Arius, Eutyches, Neftorius, quorum uestigijs utinam nulli hac aetate insisterent. Dauid eiusmodi hominum saeuitiam expertus, eos his uerbis graphicè depinxit: Enim uerò nō inimicus probro affecit me, nam ego sustinerem: nō aduersarius aliquis meus extulit se in me, nam abscodisem me ab eo. Sed tu homo ordinis mei, dux meus, & familiaris meus: Qui simul dulce capiebamus consilium, & in aede Domini ibamus ut socij. Psal.55. v.12.13.14.
units.tr: Moreover, domestic traitors, who are indeed in the Church but not of it, lend mutual services to open enemies. These are far more harmful than the enemies themselves, because they want to appear least of all to be the authors of the calamities that afflict the Church: the teachers of other doctrines [ἑτεροδιδάσκαλοι] and the corrupters of heavenly doctrine. Such pests existed once: Arius, Eutyches and Nestorius. Would that no one in this age followed in their footsteps. David, having experienced the savagery of men of this kind, depicted them vividly in these words: "For it was not an enemy who reproached me, for then I could have borne it; nor did an adversary of mine lift himself up against me, for then I would have hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man of my rank, my leader and my familiar friend, with whom I took sweet counsel together and walked in the house of the Lord as companions." Ps. 55:12–14.

units.la: Etsi autem Diotrephes & Sinones isti interdū rerum potiri, & psychotyrânidem suam constabilire, pijs & ueritatem amā-tibus tibus oppresfsis,& clero Domini ἀλλανυμι[?] σύναν[?] uidentur: Deo tamen linguas eorū diuidente, & syncretismum in vatinianū odium vertente, ac in reprobam metem eos tradente,non procedunt amplius,& amentia eorum euidens fit omnibus. Exemplo sunt, Arianorum γραφολογία περὶ τῆς ὁμοουσίας Filij Dei & Patris æterni: κιβωτικὸν[?] Acacij: Interim, seu Sphynx Augustana, & similes Empusæ vetores & recentes.
units.tr: Although Diotrephes and these Sinons sometimes seem to gain control of affairs and to establish their own tyranny over souls, oppressing the pious and the lovers of truth, and seem to be among the clergy of the Lord, yet God divides their tongues, turns their syncretism into hatred of the Vatinian kind, and hands them over to a reprobate mind. So they go no further, and their madness becomes plain to all. Examples are the Arians' writing on the consubstantiality of the Son of God and the eternal Father [γραφολογία περὶ τῆς ὁμοουσίας], the "ark" of Acacius, the Interim, the Augsburg Sphinx, and similar Empusae, old and new.

units.la: 2. Caussa προγυμνασμένη[?] est sapientissimum Dei consilium, quo cauere solet, ne longæ pacis incommoda redeant ad Ecclesiam & singulos fideles. Cum enim diuinitus reprimūtur manifesti hostes Ecclesiæ,& quidem vel immediatè,vel mediatè opera piorum Magistratuum, tum vero plurimi remissiores in studio doctrinæ & pietatis facti, indulget opinionibus & cupiditatibus suis,& mouent non necessaria & periculosa certamina. Vt Constantino Magno imperante, cū Ecclesiæ pax & relaxatio à persecutionum æstu cōcef-sa fuisset,Arius pestilentissimum suū dogma profiteri cœpit, fuitq; incendij tanti autor, ut ne quidem aliquot seculis illud restinrestingui posset: ac ut illud maiora damna Ecclesiæ adferret, quàm ullæ persecutiones Domitiani, Traiani, Diocletiani & aliorum.
units.tr: 2. The cause [προγυμνασμένη] is God's most wise counsel, by which he is accustomed to guard against the troubles of a long peace returning to the Church and to individual believers. For when the manifest enemies of the Church are restrained by God, either immediately or mediately through the work of pious magistrates, then very many people, having grown more careless in the study of doctrine and piety, indulge their own opinions and desires and stir up unnecessary and dangerous contests. So under Constantine the Great, when peace had been granted to the Church and it had been relieved from the heat of persecution, Arius began to profess his most pestilent dogma. He was the author of such a great conflagration that it could not be quenched for several centuries, and it brought greater losses to the Church than any persecutions under Domitian, Trajan, Diocletian or others.

units.la: Eius rei tristissimum exemplum hac ætate, proh dolor, uidemus. Quid enim? An'nō eæ Ecclesiæ, quæ impijs Antichristianorum Monarcharum armis maximè impetuntur & prémuntur, sub cruce florent, & ἀδιαφθορίᾳ[?] doctrinæ cœlestis fideliter retinent? Nonnullæ autem aliæ, lögæ pacis incommoda sentientes, delicatos sanè pastores habet, quorū an'ne quidam purè fatéatur Deū in carne uenisse, & ecquid Chalcedonensis Synodi pios Canones retineat, iudicet Ecclesia. Deū sanè oro, ut illos in uiam ueritatis reducat, ut unà nobiscum & doctrina & uita inculpata, illius sanctū nomen celebret.
units.tr: We see the saddest example of this in our own age, alas. For what? Do not those churches which are most assailed and oppressed by the impious arms of the Antichristian monarchs flourish under the cross, and faithfully retain the incorruptness of heavenly doctrine? Others, however, feeling the troubles of a long peace, have ministers who are indeed delicate. Whether some of them purely confess that God came in the flesh, and whether they hold to the pious canons of the Synod of Chalcedon, let the Church judge. I earnestly pray God to lead them back into the way of truth, so that together with us, both in doctrine and in blameless life, they may celebrate his holy name.

units.la: 3. Multæ autem sunt causæ [illegible, ~12 letters] & finales, propter quas Deus seruos suos ad eum modum exercet.
units.tr: 3. There are many causes [illegible] and final causes for which God exercises his servants in this manner.

units.la: Prima est, nimius huius mundi amor, qui in animis hominum Dei odium tandem generat. Iuxta illud: Nescitis, amicitiam mundi, inimicitiam esse cum Deo? Quicunq; ergo amicus uoluerit esse mū-di, di,inimicus Dei constituitur: Iacob.4.4. Quid ita? Quia Sanctorum est, non diligere mundum, neque ea quae in mundo sunt. Si quis enim mundum diligit, non est charitas Patris in eo. Quoniam quicquid est in mundo, cupiditas carnis, & libido oculorum, & fastus vitae, non est ex Patre, sed ex mundo est. 1.Ioan.2.15.16.
units.tr: The first is excessive love of this world, which at length breeds hatred of God in the minds of men. According to that saying: "Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Whoever therefore wishes to be a friend of the world is made an enemy of God." James 4:4. Why so? Because it is characteristic of the saints not to love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For whatever is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, is not from the Father but from the world. 1 John 2:15–16.

units.la: Secunda est, fiducia humanae benevolentiae & potentiae, quae quò est maior, tantò plus pernefarium sacrilegium detrahit gratiae & virtuti divinae, qua sola fretos & contentos, uni Deo omnem gloriam dare oportebat.
units.tr: The second is confidence in human goodwill and power. The greater this confidence is, the more it detracts from the grace and divine power, on which alone we ought to rely and be content, and to give all glory to God alone.

units.la: Tertia, abusus rerum secundatum, ad delicias & voluptates humanas, ad vanę gloriae fumum: & vana perpetuae felicitatis persuasio & spes. Quid etiam summis viris eveniat, suo exemplo docuit David, cuius haec ingenua confessio exstat: Ego vero dicebam in prosperitate mea: Non movebor in aeternum. Psal.30.6.
units.tr: The third is the abuse of prosperity for human delights and pleasures, for the smoke of empty glory, and the vain persuasion and hope of perpetual happiness.
