David, whose candid confession survives, taught by his own example what even the greatest men may suffer: "But I said in my prosperity: I shall never be moved." Ps. 30:6.

units.la: Quarta, negligentia circa suscitationem & usum donorum Dei. Vult Deus nos [?]ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα: id vero multo maiore zelo a nobis fit, cum premimur cruce, quam cum in secundis rebus exultat & luxuriat caro nostra.
units.tr: The fourth is negligence concerning the stirring up and use of God's gifts. God wills us to rekindle the gift [ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα]. But we do this with far greater zeal when we are pressed by the cross than when our flesh exults and revels in prosperous circumstances.

units.la: Quinta est, agnitio nostrae infirmitatis & stulticiæ, quâ commonefacti intelligimus nobis ad Dei præsidium & gubernationem esse confugiendum. Scio Domine, dicebat Ieremias, non esse hominis uiam eius, nec uiri dirigere suos gressus. Idem nos fateamur, & à Deo nos regi petamus.
units.tr: The fifth is the acknowledgment of our weakness and folly, by which, being admonished, we understand that we must flee for refuge to God's protection and governance. "I know, O Lord," said Jeremiah, "that the way of man is not his own, nor is it for a man to direct his steps." Let us likewise confess this, and ask to be ruled by God.

units.la: Sexta est, nostra cum Christo capite nostro συμμόρφωσις[?]. Ut de cæteris afflictionum formis nunc nō dicam, si cui Anathematistarum conuicia, uellicationes & iniuriæ uehementer dolent, is secum reputet, quis ille fit qui talem sustinuit à peccatoribus aduersus sese contradictionem: Hebr.12.3. Ne ea ferre recusemus, quibus multò graviora Christus nostra caussa tulit. Non est nunc ocium ad ista accuratè disponenda: itaque uobis & hanc congeriem piarum cogitationum, logicè disponendam, commendo. Ac multa piæ & ingeniosæ iuuetutis religiosis meditationibus confultò relinquenda, uiri sapientes pronuncia-uerunt:
units.tr: The sixth is our conformity [συμμόρφωσις] with Christ our head. Not to speak now of other forms of affliction: if anyone is deeply pained by the reproaches, reviling and injuries of the Anathematists, let him consider who that was who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself. Heb. 12:3. Let us not refuse to bear what Christ bore for our sake, things far more grievous. There is no leisure now to arrange these matters carefully, and so I commend to you this heap of pious thoughts, to be arranged logically. Wise men have also pronounced that many things are to be deliberately left to the religious meditations of pious and gifted youth:

units.la: VERSVS VII ET VIII.
units.tr: Verses 7 and 8.

units.la: Horribilis & terribilis est (Chaldaeorū gens:) ex seipsa iudicium eius & dignitas eius egredietur. Leniores sunt Pardis equi eius, & acutiores lupis uespertinis: quam-plurimi sunt equites eius qui de longè ue-nient, & aduolabunt tanquam aquila fe-stinans ad comedendum.
units.tr: Terrible and dreadful is the Chaldean nation; its judgment and its dignity shall proceed from itself. Its horses are swifter than leopards and fiercer than evening wolves. Its horsemen are very many, and they come from afar and fly like an eagle hastening to devour.

units.la: Pergit Dominus in descriptione exer-citus Chaldaeorum, ac hæcilli tribuit:
units.tr: The Lord, in describing the army of the Chaldeans, attributes these things to it:

units.la: 1. Quòd sit horribilis ac terribilis: ut ingenium crudelissimæ gentis, & belli effectum indicet, de quo Pindarus rectè pronunciauit: γλυκὺ δὲ πόλεμος ἀπείροισιν· ἐμπείρων δὲ [?]ς ταχέα [?] προσιόντα νιν [?] λαχρδίας [?] πει- ραστῶς [?].
units.tr: 1. That it is dreadful and terrible, which indicates both the savage character of the people and the nature of war, about which Pindar rightly said: [γλυκὺ δὲ πόλεμος ἀπείροισιν· ἐμπείρων δὲ [?]ς ταχέα [?] προσιόντα νιν [?] λαχρδίας [?] πει- ραστῶς [?]] ("war is sweet to the inexperienced, but to those who have experience, as it draws near swiftly...").

units.la: 2. Quòd pro suo arbitrio de iure respo-deat, leges figat & refigat, euehat in altū & deijciat quos uisum est. Hoc enim existimo sibi uelle illam phrasin, Ex seipsa iudicium eius,&c.
units.tr: 2. That it answers to the law by its own judgment, makes and unmakes laws, and raises up or casts down whom it pleases. For I think that this is what the phrase "its judgment from itself" means.

units.la: 3. Quòd eius equestres copiæ, celerita-te Pardos & aquilas: rapacitate lupos uè spertinos, qui tota die fame laborauerunt, & uespere prodeunt uenatum, ut medeantur fami, referant. Addita est autem am-plifiplificatio à numero. Videtur autem alludere ad ingenium ferarum,quod Psaltes alibi sic describit: Ponit tenebras, & fit nox: in ea proreptant omnes bestiæ sylvarum, catuli leonum rugientes ad prædam,& ad quærendū à Deo cibum suum. Oritur Sol, colliguntur: & ad domicilia sua accubant. Psal.104.20.21.22.
units.tr: 3. That its cavalry is like leopards and eagles in speed, and like evening wolves in rapacity: wolves that have gone hungry all day and come out at evening to hunt, so as to relieve their hunger. Amplification is added from the number. It seems to allude to the nature of wild beasts, which the Psalmist describes elsewhere in this way: "You make darkness, and it is night; in it all the beasts of the forest creep forth. The young lions roar after their prey and seek their food from God. The sun rises, they gather together and lie down in their dens." Ps. 104:20-22.

units.la: Huc autem tendit oratio. Non debet uideri ἀνάνομον, si quis id futurum prædicat, quod legis transgressoribus diuinitus iam olim denunciatum est. Deus aut per Mosen legem uiolantibus inter alia sic comminatus est: Adducet Iehouah aduersum te gentem à longinquo,ab extremo terræ, quemadmodū uolat aquila, gentem inquam,cuius non intelliges linguam. Deut.28.49. Ergo non est cur quisquam opinetur,nihil eorum quæ nō mine Iehouæ uobis denuncio, euenire posse.
units.tr: This is the point of the passage. It ought not to seem unlawful if someone foretells what has long since been divinely declared against the transgressors of the law. Among other threats, God through Moses warned those who violate the law: "The Lord will bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as swiftly as an eagle flies, a nation whose language you will not understand." Deut. 28:49. Therefore there is no reason for anyone to think that none of those things which I announce to you in the name of Jehovah can come to pass.

units.la: De ijs, qui in hominum manus inciderunt, Aphorismi.
units.tr: Aphorisms concerning those who have fallen into the hands of men.

units.la: i. In hominum manus nemo,nisi quem Deus tradit, incidere potest. Matt.10.29. Nónne duo passerculi assario uenneunt,& unus ex eis nō cadet humi sine Patre uestro? stro ? 30. Vestri uerò etiam capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. 31. Ne igitur timete: uos multis passerculis prestatis. Deus maiorem habet rationem hominis ad imaginem ipsius conditi, quàm abiectisi[?] marum uoluctrum. Atqui ne passerculus humi cadit sine prouidentia. Igitur multo minus homo in hominum manus incidit sine consilio Dei.
units.tr: i. No one can fall into the hands of men unless God delivers him up. Matt. 10:29: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. 30. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. 31. Fear not therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows." God has greater regard for man, made in his own image, than for worthless birds. But not even a sparrow falls to the ground without providence. Therefore much less does a man fall into the hands of men without the counsel of God.

units.la: Item, Psal.66.12. Equitare fecisti unûquemq; super capita nostra: uenimus in ignem & in aquas: sed duxisti nos in locum irriguum.
units.tr: Likewise Ps. 66:12: "You have made men ride over our heads; we went through fire and water, but you brought us out into a place of abundance."

units.la: Ergo, non quàm multi, quamq; improbi aut sordidi homines nos uexent calū-nijs aut iniurijs: sed quis nos in eorum manus tradiderit, spectantes, obediamus Deo in aerumnis, & spe liberationis nos sustetemus ac leniamus dolores nostros.
units.tr: Therefore, let us not consider how many or how wicked or base men harass us with slanders or injuries, but who has handed us over into their hands. Looking to that, let us obey God in our afflictions, sustain ourselves with the hope of deliverance, and soothe our sorrows.

units.la: ɩ.[?] Tradit autem uel immediatè, ut Iobum Satanæ affligendum: uel mediatè, ut Christum per manus Iudæorum Pilato crucifigendum dedit. Ioan.19.11. Respondit D. Iesus Pilato: Non haberes potestatem aduersus me ullam, nisi tibi datum esset supernè: propterea qui me tradidit tibi, maius peccatum habet. Cæterum Deus,qui nos,cum ei uisum est,tradit in manus improborum: idem ex ijsdem eripit, cū est optimum: ut suo exemplo docet Apostolus, cum inquit: Et ereptus fui ex ore leonis.2.Tim.4.17.
units.tr: ɩ. God delivers people either directly, as he gave Job over to Satan to be afflicted, or indirectly, as he gave Christ up to be crucified by Pilate through the hands of the Jews. John 19:11: "Jesus answered Pilate: You would have no power against me unless it had been given you from above; therefore he who delivered me to you has the greater sin." But God, who when it pleases him hands us over into the hands of the wicked, also snatches us out of them when it is best. The Apostle teaches this by his own example when he says: "And I was rescued from the mouth of the lion." 2 Tim. 4:17.

units.la: 3. Porrò, Deus tradit uel castigandos, uel probandos, uel pleftendos,ad gloriā misericordiæ & iusticiæ suæ. Dauidem castigari uoluit à filio Absolomo & coniuratis. Iosephū, Danielem & alios probari uoluit per aduersa: ut ἐν τοῖς ἀντ[?]ιχ[?] ταῖς ἐλύκερε posset τὸ λ[?] fidei, spei, tolerantiæ. Iudæos autem puniendos tradidit Nebucadnezari, & seculis aliquot post Tito, Vespasiani Imperatoris filio, qui urbem Hierosolymorū deleuit, multis milibus Iudæorum trucidatis, cæteris abdu&tis & uenditis.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, God hands people over either to be chastened, or to be tested, or to be [?] for the glory of his mercy and justice. He willed David to be chastened by his son Absalom and the conspirators. He willed Joseph, Daniel and others to be tested through adversity, so that they might [ἐν τοῖς ἀντ[?]ιχ[?] ταῖς ἐλύκερε] and so that [τὸ λ[?]] of faith, hope and patience might be shown. He handed the Jews over to be punished by Nebuchadnezzar, and centuries later by Titus, son of the Emperor Vespasian, who destroyed the city of Jerusalem, many thousands of Jews being slaughtered, and the rest carried off and sold.

units.la: His autem rationibus illustrari gloriā gratiæ Dei erga uasa gratiæ, & gloriā iusticiæ Dei erga uasa iræ, nihil dubiū est: Psal.86.9. Omnes Gentes,quas fecisti,uenient, & adorabunt coram facie tua Domine: & gloriā dabunt nōmini tuo. io. Quia magnus tu: & facis mirabilia tu Deus solus.
units.tr: There is no doubt that these reasons illustrate the glory of God's grace towards the vessels of grace, and the glory of God's justice towards the vessels of wrath. Ps. 86:9-10: "All nations whom you have made shall come and worship before your face, Lord, and shall give glory to your name. For you are great, and you do wonders; you alone are God."

units.la: 4. Interdum bonos in manus bonorū tradit, ut utrique humani erroris & infirmitatis sensu admoniti, Deo gloriam dent, & iterum in Domino coalescant. Tales fuerunt συμφωνίας Pauli & Barnabæ: Act. 15.39. Augustini & Hieronymi super dicto Pauli, Gal. 2. Ioannis Chrysostomi & Epiphanii, propter Anthropomorphiticam hæresin: quam ille quidem pie refutabat, hic autem, in gratiam Theophili Alexandrini, parum prudenter tuebatur. Etsi autem hi duo eruperunt in voces manticas, cum ille quidem huic diceret, Non redibis ad tuos vivos: hic autem illi responderet, Nec tu morieris Episcopus: ac utrique dicto euentus respondit: tamen οἱ τοιοῦτοι ἡ θεη-γορεῖ ἡ θεοφιλὲς ἀνθρωποι, in gratiam repositi sunt. Ac videtur μεταμέλεια Epiphanio soluenti Constantinopoli dictasse hanc vocem: Σπάσθω ἐγώ. Ἀφήμι δὲ ὑμῖν τὰ βασιλέα ἡ τῶν πόλιν ἡ τῶν ὑπόκεισιν. quam eandem sententiam nostro tempore multi præstantes Christi serui & Ecclesiarum pastores, pulsi e suis sedibus, pronunciare possent.
units.tr: 4. Sometimes he hands good men over into the hands of good men, so that both, admonished by a sense of human error and weakness, may give glory to God and be reconciled again in the Lord. Such was the agreement [συμφωνίας] of Paul and Barnabas, Acts 15:39. Such were Augustine and Jerome over the saying of Paul, Gal. 2; and John Chrysostom and Epiphanius over the Anthropomorphite heresy. The former refuted it piously; the latter, out of regard for Theophilus of Alexandria, defended it rather imprudently. Although these two broke out into prophetic-sounding words, one saying to the other, "You will not return alive to your people," and the other replying, "Nor will you die a bishop," and the outcome answered both sayings, yet [οἱ τοιοῦτοι ἡ θεη-γορεῖ ἡ θεοφιλὲς ἀνθρωποι] they were reconciled. And it seems that Epiphanius, when he was leaving Constantinople, dictated the word μεταμέλεια [repentance] and these words: Σπάσθω ἐγώ. Ἀφήμι δὲ ὑμῖν τὰ βασιλέα ἡ τῶν πόλιν ἡ τῶν ὑπόκεισιν ("let me be drawn away; I leave to you the kings of the city and those beneath them"). This same sentiment many excellent servants of Christ and pastors of the Churches, driven from their seats, could express in our own time.

units.la: 5. Nonnunquam malos in bonorum manus tradit: ut Saulem Regem bis tradidit Deus in manus Dauidis, qui etiam ab uncto unsto[?] Domini abstinuit. 2.Samuel.24.11. &26.10.11.
units.tr: 5. Sometimes he hands evil men over into the hands of good men: as God twice delivered King Saul into the hands of David, who also refrained from touching the Lord's anointed. 2 Sam. 24:11 and 26:10-11.

units.la: Ita Haman Agagites hostis Iudæorū, traditus fuit in manus Mardochæi: & duo senes, iudices iniusti, in manus Danielis.
units.tr: So Haman the Agagite, enemy of the Jews, was delivered into the hands of Mordecai, and two old men, unjust judges, into the hands of Daniel.

units.la: 6. Actum pijs solicitè spectādum, quid priuatam personam, & quid Magistratu fungentem, deceat. Etenim Magistratū in homines facinorosos, diuinitus (id quod ex mirandis occasionibus liquet) in manus traditos, animaduertere, iustū & laudabile est. Ut rectè fecit Dauid, supplicio afficiēs nefarios illos latrones, Banam & Rechab, qui Isbosethum truci-dauerant, suæ domi quiescentem. 1. Re-gum 4.10.11.12.
units.tr: 6. Pious people must carefully consider what befits a private person and what befits one who holds the magistracy. For it is just and laudable for the magistrate to punish men guilty of crimes who have been handed over to him by God (as is clear from the remarkable occasions). Just as David rightly did, when he put to death those wicked robbers Baanah and Rechab, who had murdered Ish-bosheth while he was resting at home. 1 Kings 4:10-12.

units.la: Econtrà grauiter peccauit Saul, cui cū in manus traditus esset Agag Amelecitarum Rex plectendus, pepercit hosti impio. 1.Sam.15.9. Saulis clementiam præposteram ij imitatur, qui blasphemis hæresiarchis, cōtumeliosis[?] in filium Dei, & convictis, nec tamen Deo gloriam dantibus, sed virus suum spargentibus, & simplices ac imperitos seducentibus, parcendum esse iudicant: cotra expressum Dei edictum de blasphemis & de pseudopro-phetis ad idolorum cultum invitatibus Leuit.24.14. Deut.13.5.
units.tr: On the contrary, Saul sinned grievously when Agag, king of the Amalekites, who was to be punished, was delivered into his hands, and he spared the impious enemy. 1 Sam. 15:9. Those who judge that blasphemous heresiarchs, who insult the Son of God and are convicted, yet do not give glory to God but spread their poison and seduce simple and untaught people, should be spared, imitate Saul's misplaced clemency. This is against God's express edict concerning blasphemers and false prophets who invite people to the worship of idols: Lev. 24:14; Deut. 13:5.

units.la: 7. Omnium aut gravissimum est, cum boni in malorum manus veniunt.
units.tr: 7. The most grievous of all is when good men come into the hands of evil men.

units.la: Ideo Dauid optione belli, famis & pestis sibi data, respondit Gad Prophetae: Angustiis afficior supra modū: incidam oblecro in manus Iehouae, quia multae sunt miserationes eius: & in manum hominum ne incidam. Idem: Ne, inquit, invadant me pedes superborum: & ne manus impiorum detrudat me. Psal.36.11. Erat enim alta mente repositum, quod quaeritur Psal.129.1. Saepe afflixerunt me a iuventute mea, dicat nunc Israel. 2. Saepe afflixerunt me a iuventute mea, nec tamen quicquam potuerunt contra me. 3. Supra dorsum meum arauerunt aratores, & produxerunt sulcos suos. 4. Iehouah est iustus: concidit funes impiorum. Eadem sane voces Zelotę & Anathematistę, pijs doctoribus & pastoribus hoc tempore exprimunt. Sed spes est futurum, ut Deus funes impiorum discindat.
units.tr: Therefore David, when given the choice of war, famine and pestilence, answered the prophet Gad: "I am in great distress; let me fall, I beg you, into the hand of Jehovah, for his mercies are many, but let me not fall into the hand of men." He also said: "Let not the foot of the proud overtake me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." Ps. 36:11. For there was deeply fixed in his mind what is asked in Ps. 129:1-4: "Often have they afflicted me from my youth; let Israel now say: often have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me. The ploughmen ploughed upon my back and made their furrows long. Jehovah is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked." Indeed these same words express the zealots and anathematisers of this time, who press them upon pious teachers and pastors. But there is hope that God will cut through the cords of the wicked.

units.la: 8. Fit enim homo homini lupus, leo, serpens, chamaeleon, &c. Iuxta haec dicta: Ἀνθρώπως ἀνθρώπῳ λύκος[?]. Hoc de iis dicitur, qui sunt, luporum instar, ἀνθρωποφάγοι, ἀ-[?] [illegible, ~8 letters] : & qui tum maxime nocent, cum uel ἀγχολογίας[?] coram utuntur, uel se subducunt, ut per cuniculos emi-nus laedant, alieno ministerio interueni-ente, & Sinonio artificio: uel palam graf-fantur, cu se armatos potentia ciuili animaduertunt.
units.tr: 8. For man becomes a wolf, a lion, a serpent, a chameleon, and so on, to man. In keeping with these words: "Man is a wolf to man" [ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπῳ λύκος]. This is said of those who, like wolves, are man-eaters [ἀνθρωποφάγοι], and who do the most harm when they use throttling talk [ἀγχολογίας] face to face, or when they withdraw and wound from a distance through tunnels, with another's agency intervening and by Sinon's trickery, or when they attack openly, once they see that they are armed with civil power.

units.la: Psal.22. 12. Circumdant me tauri ualidi: tauri Basan cinguntme. 13. Aperiunt super me os suum, sicut leo rapax & rugiens. 20. Serua ex gladio animam meam: & e manu canis solitariam meam. 21. Serua me ab ore leonis: & a cornibus unicornium exaudias me.
units.tr: Ps. 22.12. Many bulls have encompassed me; strong bulls of Bashan have surrounded me. 13. They open their mouth upon me, as a ravening and roaring lion. 20. Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the power of the dog. 21. Save me from the lion's mouth, and hear me from the horns of the wild oxen.

units.la: Recte autem Seneca: Crudelitas, inquit, minime humanum malum est, indignumque regio animo: ferina ista rabies est, sanguine gaudere ac vulneribus, & abiecto homine in sylvestre animal transfire.
units.tr: Seneca rightly says: "Cruelty is the least human of evils and unworthy of a royal spirit. It is a beastly frenzy, to delight in blood and wounds, and to cast off the man and pass into a savage animal."

units.la: Quod aut Chamæleotis instar sint nō pauci homines, & alias bene tum uelint tum faciant, alias male, omnium temporum historiae testantur: quae etiam monent, ne in carne & sanguine, seu in humana beneuolentia,prudentia & potentia spem ponamus : sed in Deo uiuo, qui est φιλανθρωπος, οἰκτιρμων, omnipotens & uerax.
units.tr: That not a few men are like the chameleon, sometimes willing and doing good, sometimes doing evil, the histories of all ages bear witness. These histories also warn us not to place our hope in flesh and blood, or in human goodwill, prudence and power, but in the living God, who is loving toward mankind [φιλάνθρωπος], merciful [οἰκτίρμων], almighty and true.

units.la: Commemorabile exemplum sæuitiæ & uanitatis, qua interdum homo hominem prosequitur, exstat in historia Leonis Magni Imperatoris,cuius imperij anno 1o Ifocafius, Antiocheæ quæstor, homo literatus,per calumniam delatus est, quasi qui alienus à religione & pietate Christiana,Ethnicifmo clàm effet addictus. Imperator totius rei cognitionem Pofæo Conftantinopoleos præfecto demandat. Is collegæ quondam suo,manibus post tergum reuinctis, habituq; lugubri ad tribunal adducto, sarcasmo insultans, dixit: Videsne Ifocafi quo habitu adstes? Respondit ille: Ὁπῶ, ἀλλὰ ἡ ἐγκλίομαι[?] ἄνθρωπος γὰρ ὤν, ἀνθρωπίνοις πορίζεσθαι συμ-[?] φορὰς. ἀλλὰ ἀδίκως ἐπ᾽ ἐμοί, ὡς ἐδίκαις σύ ἐ-[?] μοί. Hoc est: Video, neque miror. homo enim in calamitatem incidi humanam. Tu uero ita mihi iius dicito, sicut me collega folebas dicere. Tandem recognita, absolutus est Ifocafius, magno cum circumstantis coronæ gaudio. Serpentinas autem sycophantarum calumnias, quibus Pij impetuntur & lacerantur, multis in locis describit Psaltes, cuius haec dicta inter alia occurrunt:
units.tr: A memorable example of the cruelty and vanity with which a man sometimes pursues another man is found in the history of the Emperor Leo the Great. In the tenth year of his reign, Isocasius, quaestor of Antioch, a learned man, was denounced through calumny, as one estranged from the Christian religion and secretly devoted to paganism. The Emperor committed the whole inquiry to Poseus, prefect of Constantinople. He brought his former colleague before the tribunal, his hands bound behind his back and in mournful dress, and mocking him with sarcasm, said: "Do you see, Isocasius, in what garb you stand?" He replied: "I see it, and I am not amazed [ὁρῶ, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θαυμάζω]; for being a man, I have fallen into human misfortune. But pronounce judgment on me in the same way that you used to speak to me when you were my colleague." Finally, after the matter was examined, Isocasius was acquitted, to the great joy of the surrounding crowd. The psalmist describes in many places the serpent-like slanders of the sycophants by which the godly are attacked and torn to pieces, and among other sayings these words occur:

units.la: Psal.140.3.Acuut linguas suas sicut serpens: uenenū aspidis sub labijs eorum.
units.tr: Ps. 140.3. They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; the venom of asps is under their lips.

units.la: Psal.58.4.Venenum ipsis secundum similitudinem ueneni serpentis: sicut aspidis surdae, quae obturat aurem suam. 5. Quae non audit uocem incantantium,& coniurantis coniurationes perite.
units.tr: Ps. 58.4. Their poison is according to the likeness of the venom of a serpent, like the deaf asp that stops its ear. 5. Which does not hear the voice of charmers, or of one who skilfully casts spells.

units.la: Etsi autem uere dixit Cicero, Verrina, si non fallit memoria, 5. Habet quendam aculeum contumelia, quem pati prudentes & boni uiri difficillime possunt: nobis tamen id cordi esse debet, quod praeclare Augustinus dixit: Iniuriae uirū fortem probant. Pudeat autem nos, quòd, ut beati Hieronymi uerbis utar, in Dei in iurijs benigni sumus, in nostris contumeliijs exercemus odia.
units.tr: Although Cicero spoke truly in the Verrines, if my memory does not fail me: "Insult has a certain sting, which wise and good men can least endure." Yet for us what Augustine said so admirably should be at heart: "Injuries prove a brave man." We ought to be ashamed, however, that, to use the words of blessed Jerome, we are gentle in the injuries done to God, yet in our own insults we indulge our hatreds.

units.la: 9. Nonnunquam tamen fit, ut praeter omnem tum agentis tum patientis opinionem, homo in hominis manus incidat.
units.tr: 9. Sometimes, however, it happens that, beyond the expectation of both the one who acts and the one who suffers, a man falls into the hands of a man.

units.la: Deut.19.5.6.de homicida inuoluntario, cui locus erat in refugij urbe.
units.tr: Deut. 19.5, 6, concerning the involuntary homicide, who had a place in a city of refuge.

units.la: Tota ipsa (gens) propter rapinam veniet: Oppositio faciei eorum (similis erit) uento Orientali: Congregabitq;[?] tanquam arenam captiuitatem.
units.tr: Habakkuk 1.9: "They shall all come for violence: their faces shall be like the east wind, and they shall gather the captivity together as the sand."

units.la: Tria hoc loco praenuntiantur, de quibus σὺν θεῷ[?] nobis agendum erit.
units.tr: Three things are foretold in this place, which with God's help we must treat.

units.la: 1. Quod sit destinatum Chaldaeorū, uidelicet, prædis agendis, & aliis spoliandis, opes suas augere.
units.tr: 1. That it is determined for the Chaldeans to increase their wealth by carrying off plunder and despoiling others.

units.la: 2. Quòd ἀνυπόστατοις[?] illis nulla ui humana resisti possit? non certè magis quàm olera uirentia resistere possunt Orientali uento, qui uehementissimus est.
units.tr: 2. That no human force can resist those invincible men, any more than tender herbs can resist the east wind, which is most violent.

units.la: 3. Quòd multa hominum millia in captiuitatem sint abducturi.
units.tr: 3. That they will lead away many thousands of men into captivity.

units.la: 1. DE CHALDAEORUM rapinis.
units.tr: 1. CONCERNING THE RAPINES OF THE CHALDEANS.

units.la: Transgressoribus legis inter alias poenas, etiam hæc uoce diuina denunciatur: Adducet Iehouah gentem robustā facie, quæ non eleuabit faciem ad senem, nec puero parcet: Et deuorabit fructum iumenti tui, & fructum terræ tuæ, donec disperdaris: quæ nō relinquet tibi frumentum, uinū nouū, & oleum, nec primogenitum boum tuorū,nec greges ouium tua-rum,donec perdat te. Deut.28.50.51.
units.tr: Among other punishments, the divine voice threatens transgressors of the law with this: "The Lord will bring against you a nation strong of countenance, which will not lift up its face for the old, nor spare the young. And it will devour the fruit of your cattle and the fruit of your land, until you are destroyed; it will leave you no grain, new wine, or oil, nor the firstborn of your herds, nor the flocks of your sheep, until it destroys you." Deut. 28.50, 51.

units.la: Vos uerò, ô Iudæi, transgressores estis legis diuinæ. Ergo ne uobis uideatur incredibile aut [illegible, ~9 letters], quod prædixi, futurum ut Chaldæi diripiant uestras & aliarum Gentium opes.
units.tr: But you, O Jews, are transgressors of the divine law. Therefore let it not seem incredible to you, or [illegible], what I have foretold: that the Chaldeans will plunder your wealth and the wealth of other nations.

units.la: 2. DE EORVNDEM SVC-cessibus.
units.tr: 2. CONCERNING THEIR SUCCESSES.

units.la: Sicut se habet uetus Orietalis seu Subsolanus ad plagas[?],arbores,frutices & suffrutices: ita se habebit hostis Chaldæus erga Iudæos. Sed uehementissimus ille & ures uentus obstatia omnia prosternit,uirentia adurit,ut arescat. Ita igitur etiā hostis Chaldæus uim omne sibi oppositam leui momento impulsam prosternet,& uigorem eius omne extinguet & auferet.
units.tr: As the old east or sunrise wind stands in relation to the regions, trees, shrubs and undershrubs, so the Chaldean enemy will stand in relation to the Jews. But that most violent and scorching wind overthrows every obstacle, and burns the green things so that they wither. So too the Chaldean enemy will, at the first impulse, overthrow every force opposed to it, and will extinguish and take away all its vigour.

units.la: 3. DE CAPTIVITATE Iudæorum.
units.tr: 3. ON THE CAPTIVITY OF THE JEWS

units.la: Leuit.26.33.Vos autem dispergā in Getes, & euaginabo post uos gladium: eritq; terra uestra desolata,& ciuitates uestræ destru-ctæ. 34.Tunc perficiet terra sabbata sua, cunctis diebus quibus desolata fuerit:uos autem eritis in terra inimicorum uestrorum. Itaq; nō dubium uobis esse debet de ἀχμαλω-σίας[?] αἰχ[?], seu captiuitate, quam multiplici legis transgressione promeriti estis.
units.tr: Leviticus 26:33: "But I will scatter you among the nations, and will draw out the sword after you; and your land shall be desolate, and your cities destroyed." 34: "Then shall the land enjoy its sabbaths, all the days that it lies desolate, while you are in the land of your enemies. Therefore there ought to be no doubt for you about the captivity [αἰχμαλωσία], or captivity, which you have deserved by your manifold transgression of the law."

units.la: ¶ Iam uerò, ut ab ὑποθέσεως[?] ad Thesin accedamus, gradus sunt malorum, Amissio facultatum, Inclinatio auctoritatis & potentiae, & Captiuitas, seu libertatis στάσεως[?]. De his ordine, ἡ διὰ βραχέων[?], agemus.
units.tr: ¶ Now, to move from the hypothesis [ὑπόθεσις] to the thesis, there are degrees of evils: the loss of property, the decline of authority and power, and captivity, or the loss of liberty [στάσις]. We shall treat these in order, briefly [ἡ διὰ βραχέων].

units.la: I. DE AMISSIONE FACVLTA-tum, Aphorismi.
units.tr: I. CONCERNING THE LOSS OF GOODS: Aphorisms.

units.la: 1. Facultates opum dare & auferre, Dei solius est. Recte ergo Iobus, spoliatus diuitijs suis, pronunciauit: Nudus egressus sum ex utero matris meae, & nudus reuertar illuc: Iehouah dedit, & Iehouah abstulit: sit nomen Iehouae benedictum. Iob.1.2i.[?]
units.tr: 1. To give and to take away wealth belongs to God alone. Rightly therefore Job, stripped of his riches, declared: "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return there: the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Job 1.21.

units.la: 2. Aufert autem eas uel ἀμέσως[?], uel mediate. Immediate quidem, cū illud quod praesto est, exsufflado mirabiliter dispergit, sicut nemo hominum, qua ratione opes dissipatę sint, cognoscere possit. Haggaei 1.9. Mediate autem, cum uel hostiū, uel aliorum opera utitur ad facultatum diu & auarè congestarum dissipationem & direptionem.
units.tr: 2. God takes away goods either immediately or mediately. Immediately, when he disperses what is at hand, blowing upon it in a wonderful way, so that no one can know by what means the wealth was scattered (Haggai 1.9). Mediately, when he uses the work of enemies or of others to scatter and plunder wealth that was gathered long and greedily.

units.la: 3. Aliter autem ferunt facultatum suarum suarum iafturam filij Dei, aliter filij huius seculi: ut ex dicto Pauli liquet,in quo fideles Hebraeos collaudans inquit: Direptionem facultatum uestrarum cum gaudio accepistis: ut qui sciretis uos habere apud uos potiorem substantiam in coelis, & quae permaneat: Hebr.10.34. Econtrà filij huius seculi thesaurizant in terris,nō satis cogitantes illud Iacobi Apostoli: Agite nunc divites, flete, ululantes super miserijs uestris superuenturis. Divitiae uestrae putrefactae sunt, uestimenta uestra obnoxia tineis facta sunt: aurū & argentū uestrū aerugine uitiatū est, &c. Iac.5.1.2.3.
units.tr: 3. The sons of God bear the loss of their goods differently from the sons of this world, as is clear from the words of Paul, in which he praises the faithful Hebrews, saying: "You accepted the plundering of your goods with joy, knowing that you have for yourselves a better and lasting substance in heaven" (Hebrews 10.34). On the other hand, the sons of this world store up treasure on earth, not sufficiently considering that saying of the Apostle James: "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, your garments have become moth-eaten, your gold and silver are corroded by rust," etc. (James 5.1-3).

units.la: 4. Cæterum infideles omnium sunt infelicissimi, & cum aliis sua adimunt, & cum ipsi facultates suas amittunt. Etenim alios depraedantes, peccant in legem, Ne furtum facias: & accersunt sibi talionis poenam divinitus denunciatam: Vae qui praedaris, & tu non es praedationem passus: & qui praevaricaris, & non sunt praevaricati in te: cum consummaveris esse praedator, praedationem patieris: cum consummaveris praevaricati, alij praevaricabitur in te. Isa.33.1. Rursum, cum eis adimuntur externa bona, quae illis summa fuerant, non habent quo sese erigant & consolentur.
units.tr: 4. Moreover, unbelievers are the most wretched of all, both when they take away what belongs to others and when they lose their own goods. For in plundering others they sin against the law, "You shall not steal," and they bring upon themselves the penalty of retaliation divinely declared: "Woe to you who plunder, and you have not been plundered; and who deal treacherously, and they have not dealt treacherously with you. When you have finished plundering, you will be plundered; when you have finished dealing treacherously, others will deal treacherously with you" (Isaiah 33.1). Again, when external goods, which had been their highest good, are taken from them, they have nothing by which to raise and console themselves.

units.la: 2. DE INCLINATIONE POTEN-tiæ & existimationis humanæ.
units.tr: 2. CONCERNING THE DECLINE OF POWER AND HUMAN ESTEEM.

units.la: Plenæ sunt omnes historiæ, & alij de hominum vita coscripti libri, tristissimis querelis de fragilitate & incostantia humanarū rerū: quæ sane tanta est, ut pro-verbio, Homo bulla, locum dederit. Ait quidam, sua culpa miser:
units.tr: All histories, and other books written about human life, are full of the most mournful complaints about the frailty and inconstancy of human affairs; this is so great that it has given rise to the proverb, "Man is a bubble." One writer, wretched through his own fault, says:

units.la: Nos quoq; floruimus: sed erat flos ille caducus: Flammaq; de stipula nostra breuisq; fuit.
units.tr: "We too once flourished, but that flower was fleeting; our flame was like fire from stubble, and it was brief."

units.la: Psaltes inquit: Abripis homines tanquā nimbus: sunt somnium: mane sunt tanquā herba transmutanda: Quæ mane floret, & mutatur: vespere[?] exscinditur, & arescit. Psal. 90.5.6.
units.tr: The Psalmist says: "You sweep men away like a flood; they are like a dream; in the morning they are like grass that is renewed: in the morning it flourishes and is changed; in the evening it is cut down and withers" (Psalm 90.5-6).

units.la: Vt Subsolanus ventus populatur & a-refacit virentia omnia: sic hominū vigo-rem, virtutem, auctoritate, levi momento impulsam evanescere, experietia docet:
units.tr: As the east wind lays waste and withers everything green, so experience teaches that the vigour, virtue and authority of men, struck by a slight breath, vanish.

units.la: Cum aute conspectiora sint summorū Principum exempla, quàm priuatorū hominum, Valeriani Imperatoris exemplū adducam. Cum is Persis bellū intulisset, amisso exercitu, captus, coactus est quadrupes scabelli vice esse Regi Persico equum ascensuro. Tandem etiam miserrimus senex excoriatus dicitur.
units.tr: Since the examples of the greatest princes are more conspicuous than those of private men, I will adduce the example of the Emperor Valerian. When he had waged war against the Persians, he lost his army, was taken captive, and was forced to serve as a footstool for the Persian king, who was about to mount his horse. At last, the most wretched old man is said to have been flayed alive.

units.la: Gilimerus Vandalorum Rex, obsessus in monte Numidiae Pappua, cum miserrime in hibernis uiueret, a Phara succeturiato absentis Bellisarij petijt panem, ut fame laborans eum gustaret: fpogiam, qua lacrymas abstergeret: cithara, qua lugubre melos de suis miserijs cataret. Idem pstratus Con[?] statinopoli ad pedes Iustiniani Imp. Vandalica lingua prolulit Salomonis dictu: Vanitas uanitatum, & omnia uanitas. Eccl. 1.
units.tr: Gelimer, king of the Vandals, besieged on the mountain Papua in Numidia, lived most wretchedly in winter quarters. Asking Pharas, a subordinate of the absent Belisarius, for bread, he took it to eat, as one suffering from hunger; he asked for a sponge with which to wipe away his tears, and for a lyre on which to sing a mournful song about his miseries. The same man, prostrate at the feet of the Emperor Justinian in Constantinople, uttered in the Vandal tongue the words of Solomon: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1).

units.la: 3. DE CAPTIVITATE.
units.tr: 3. CONCERNING CAPTIVITY.

units.la: Grauis est uiro honesto, bonorum cessio: grauior, existimationis & uirium iactura: ad haec si seruitus & αἰχμαλωσία[?] accedat, grauissimum erit maximorum malorum complementum.
units.tr: The surrender of goods is grievous to an honourable man; more grievous is the loss of esteem and strength; if slavery and captivity are added to these, it will be the most grievous completion of the greatest evils.

units.la: Recte beatus Hieronymus in epistola quadam: Captiuitatis, inquit, nulla maior calamitas est, quàm ad alienam libidinem trahi. Recte & Chrysostomus: Captiuitatis persecutio imputatur ad martyrium.
units.tr: Rightly does Saint Jerome, in a certain letter, say: "There is no greater calamity of captivity than to be dragged into another's lust." Rightly too Chrysostom: "The persecution of captivity is reckoned as martyrdom."

units.la: Infidelium autem in seruitutem redactorum, non multo alia est conditio, quàm ferarum, quae contra naturae suae [illegible, ~8 letters] caueis ferferreis inclusae haerent inuitae & fremen-tes. Nam & illi, cum non auctoritate diuina, sed humana uiolentia sese constrictos teneri putent: uehementer & suam seruitutem deplorant, & alienae potentiae infensi sunt, ac in omnes euadendi occasiones intenti. Illud autem magnum & gloriosum ducunt, non modo iugum excutere: uerum etiam in seruitutem eos redigere, quorum non multo ante oppressi fuerant tyrannide.
units.tr: The condition of unbelievers reduced to servitude is not much different from that of wild beasts, which, shut up in iron cages against their nature, cling to them unwillingly and roar. For these men too, since they think they are bound not by divine authority but by human violence, deeply lament their servitude, are hostile to the power of another, and are intent on every opportunity of escape. They regard it as a great and glorious thing not only to throw off the yoke, but even to reduce to servitude those by whom they had not long before been oppressed by tyranny.

units.la: Vt cum Zeno, Imperator non admodum laudatus, Basiliscum affinem suum, a quo aliquandiu imperatoria dignitate priuatus fuerat, dolo circumuentum, in potestatem sua redactum, Cucufum Cappadociae relegauit, ibiq; cum uxore & liberis in una turri conclusum fame necauit: ut est auctor Cedrenus, pag.289.
units.tr: So it was when Zeno, an emperor not much praised, having craftily ensnared his kinsman Basiliscus, by whom he had for some time been deprived of imperial dignity, brought him into his power and banished him to Cucusus in Cappadocia, where he shut him up with his wife and children in a single tower and starved them to death, as the author Cedrenus relates, p. 289.

units.la: PARADOXA CHRISTIANA.
units.tr: PARADOXA CHRISTIANA.

units.la: I. DE CESSIONE bonorum:
units.tr: I. ON THE CESSION OF goods:

units.la: Pij, cum Christi causa spoliantur, ditescunt. Matth.19.29. Et quisquis reliquerit domos, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut pa-trem, trem,aut matrem,aut uxorem,aut liberos,aut agros,caussa[?] nominis mei,centuplicia accipiet,& uitam æternam hæredi tatis iure possidebit. Hoc sibi persuadeant pij & orthodoxi pastores Ecclesiarum,cum propter ueritatis professionem è suis sedibus pelluntur, nulla habita ratione fidei in docendo, nulla inculpatæ eorum uitæ, nulla deniq; lugetis Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The godly, when they are stripped of their goods for Christ's sake, grow rich. Matt. 19.29. "And everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life as an inheritance." Let godly and orthodox ministers of the Churches take this to heart when they are driven from their seats for the profession of the truth, with no regard had to the faith they teach, no regard to the blamelessness of their lives, and, finally, with no regard to the grief of the Church.

units.la: Meminerint etiam pij, pro terrenis bonis, plenitudinem spiritualium donorum, quæ æterna sunt, à Domino substitui.
units.tr: The godly should also remember that for earthly goods the Lord substitutes the fullness of spiritual gifts, which are eternal.

units.la: 2. DE EORVNDEM αὐτάρκεια[?]
units.tr: 2. ON THE SAME SELF-SUFFICIENCY [αὐτάρκεια]

units.la: Iidem præsentibus contenti sunt, qualia aut quantacunq; tandem illa sint.
units.tr: The same people are content with what they have at present, whatever and however much it may be.

units.la: Etenim illud persuasum habent, hominis uitam & opulentiam, nō in superflua abundantia: Luc.12.15. sed in animo pio & sua forte contento, esse positam. i.Timoth.6.6.
units.tr: For they are convinced that a person's life and wealth consist not in superfluous abundance but in a pious mind content with what it has. 1 Tim. 6.6.

units.la: Deinde, nōrunt, Deo æque facile esse, & parua augere benedicendo, & magna minuere maledicendo.
units.tr: Next, they know that it is equally easy for God to increase small things by blessing them and to diminish great things by cursing them.

units.la: Postremò, discunt cum Paulo, deprimi & abundare, cum sint initiati & ad saturitatem & ad esuritionem: id est, tum
units.tr: Finally, they learn with Paul both to be brought low and to abound; they are initiated both into being full and into being hungry, that is,

units.la: ad abundantiam, tum ad inopiam: Phi-lipp.4.12. Quem, inquit Gregorius, nec in abundantia superbia eleuat, nec in ne-cessitate cupiditas irritat, nouit abunda-re, nouit penuriam pati.
units.tr: both into abundance and into want. Phil. 4.12. Of whom, says Gregory, pride does not lift up in abundance, nor covetousness stir up in necessity; he knows how to abound, and knows how to suffer want.

units.la: 3. DE BONORVM EV-ΔΟΞΙΑ [?].
units.tr: 3. ON THE GLORY OF GOODS [εὐδοξία].

units.la: Ea demum uera gloria est, Christi, quæ veritas est, causa probris & contumelia affici.
units.tr: That is true glory which consists in being exposed to reproach and insult for the sake of Christ, who is the truth.

units.la: Augustinus: Laus, ait, mundi parum prodest, si conscientia criminis mordet. Itaq; à contrario, vituperium mundi parum obest, si conscientiam integritas exhilaret.
units.tr: Augustine: "The praise of the world," he says, "is of little use if conscience gnaws at a crime. And conversely, the world's censure does little harm if integrity gladdens the conscience."

units.la: Sapienter Chrysostomus: Laudes, inquit, humanæ simul apparent & euanescunt. Si laudes, multò magis iniustæ criminationes.
units.tr: Chrysostom wisely says: "Human praises appear and vanish at the same time. If praises do, much more do unjust accusations."

units.la: 4. DE BONORVM VIR-tute.
units.tr: 4. ON THE VIRTUE OF GOODS.

units.la: Et ea demum uera potentia uerumq; robur est, Christi causa infirmum fieri. 2.Cor.12.9. Et dixit mihi Dominus: Sufficit tibi gratia mea: nam potentia mea per infirmitatem perficitur. Libentissimè igitur gloriabor potius de infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me potentia Christi. 10. Propterea oblector in infirmitatibus, in contumeliis, in necessitatibus, in persecutionibus, in angustiis pro Christo: cum enim impotens sum, tunc potens sum.
units.tr: And that is finally true power and true strength: to be made weak for Christ's sake. 2 Cor. 12.9. "And the Lord said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Therefore I will most gladly boast rather of my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me. 10. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ; for when I am weak, then I am strong.

units.la: 5. DE LIBERTATE piorum.
units.tr: 5. ON THE LIBERTY OF the godly.

units.la: Seruitus carnis, libertatis spiritus initium est. Ego, inquit Paulus, contundo corpus meum, & in seruitutem redigo: ne quo modo, cum aliis praedicarim, ipse fiam reprobus. 1. Cor. 9. 27.
units.tr: The servitude of the flesh is the beginning of the liberty of the spirit. "I," says Paul, "buffet my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become a castaway." 1 Cor. 9.27.

units.la: Iam si ciuilem conditionem spectes, liber tus est Domini, qui in Domino vocatus est seruus. 1. Cor. 7. 20.
units.tr: Again, if you regard civil condition, the one who is called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman. 1 Cor. 7.20.

units.la: Quia otio ad haec prosequenda destituor, coronidis vice dico: Nil Christo tri-ste [?] recepto, cum is nobis situia [?], veritas, vita, & plenitudo benedictionis spiritualis. Caetera vestrae pietati ἀλλὰ φιλομαθείας [?] perpendenda relinquo.
units.tr: Since I lack the leisure to pursue these matters further, I say by way of a crown to my discourse: nothing is sad when Christ has been received, since he is for us wisdom, truth, life, and the fullness of spiritual blessing. The rest I leave for your piety and love of learning [φιλομαθεία] to weigh.

units.la: VERSVS X.
units.tr: VERSE 10.

units.la: Illa quoque Reges ipsos ridet: & risus sunt ei Principes, Omnem urbem munitam ridet: & congregabit terram, & capiet eam.
units.tr: "He also mocks kings, and princes are a laughingstock to him; he mocks every fortified city and heaps up earth and takes it."

units.la: Fiduciam humanorum præsidiorum hoc versu excludit Dominus, nec Reges inui-ctos, nec urbes inexpugnabiles fore ostendens, tali argumento:
units.tr: By this verse the Lord excludes confidence in human defences, showing that neither kings nor cities will be unconquerable, by the following argument:

units.la: Non est spes ponenda in ijs, quæ hostibus ridicula ὰωωωωωωωωωω sunt futura.
units.tr: Hope should not be placed in things which are going to be a laughingstock to enemies [ὰωωωωωωωωωω].

units.la: Atqui Reges & Principes πολυμαχωωωω, item arces & urbes munitæ, & late patentes ac exculteæ provinciæ, Nebucadnezari & Chaldæis erut ludicra quædam crepundia, quibus pro suo libitu potientur & utentur. Vrbes etiam aggeribus actis κατὰ κράτος facile expugnabunt.
units.tr: But kings and princes [πολυμαχωωωω], likewise citadels and fortified cities and widely spreading and cultivated provinces, will be to Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans mere playthings, which they will possess and use at their pleasure. They will also take cities by force [κατὰ κράτος] with siege mounds, and easily storm them.

units.la: Quare non est cur illis præsidijs, reuera ficulneis, quisquam fretus, sibijpsi imponat.
units.tr: Therefore there is no reason for anyone to rely on those defences, which are truly fig-leaves, and to deceive himself.

units.la: EXEMPLA SVMMORVM HOMINVM, qui facti sunt ludibrium generis humani.
units.tr: EXAMPLES OF THE HIGHEST MEN, who became a laughingstock to the human race.

units.la: Sefostris Rex Ægypti, curru aureo uehi solitus est, quē quatuor denicti Reges trahebant. Horum unus, interrogatus à superbo uictore, cur identidem respice-ret: Intuens, inquit, rotæ uolubilitatem, de sorte nostra cogito. Sefostris ea uoce motus, captiuos dimisit. Adonibezec Regibus septuaginta pollices manuum & pedum præcidit, & eos sub mensa sua micas panis colligere coegit. Sed secuta est talionis pœna, quam ipse quoque agnouit. Iudic.1.7.
units.tr: Sesostris, king of Egypt, was accustomed to be carried in a golden chariot, drawn by four conquered kings. When one of these, asked by the proud victor why he kept looking back, answered: "Watching the turning of the wheel, I am thinking of our lot." Sesostris, moved by those words, released the captives. Adonibezek cut off the thumbs and big toes of seventy kings and made them gather scraps of bread under his table. But the penalty of retaliation followed, which he himself acknowledged. Judg. 1.7.

units.la: Blasphemus ille Senacherib, qui Iudæam inuasit, & in magnas angustias piū Regem Ezechiam cum suis coniecit, tandem à filijs in delubro suo trucidatus est. Ei posita est statua, non sine commemorabili inscriptione: ὡς ἐμὲ τίς ἐφίωμ[?] σιθῆς ἐγώ.
units.tr: That blasphemous Sennacherib, who invaded Judah and brought the pious king Hezekiah and his people into great distress, was finally slain by his sons in his own temple. A statue was set up to him, with a memorable inscription: [ὡς ἐμὲ τίς ἐφίωμ...].

units.la: Perseus Rex Macedonū, impius in patrem Philippum & fratrem Demetrium, quem trucidari curauit, tandem à Paulo Æmilio victus, & in triumpho, seruili habitu & manibus vinctis, cum duobus filijs ductus Romam, in carcerem publicū detrusus fuit. In eo fame compulsus panem petijt à concaptiuis, quibus tamen homo miserrimus ludibrio erat. Tandē cum dormiendi copia illi non concederetur, miserrimè perijt, insomnia, fame, doloribusq; alijs confectus.
units.tr: Perseus, king of Macedonia, impious toward his father Philip and toward his brother Demetrius, whom he had arranged to be murdered, was at last defeated by Paulus Aemilius. In the triumph he was led to Rome in servile dress, with his hands bound, together with his two sons, and was thrust into the public prison. There, driven by hunger, he asked the fellow prisoners for bread, yet the wretched man was a figure of mockery to them. Finally, since he was not allowed the chance to sleep, he perished most miserably, worn down by sleeplessness, hunger, and other pains.

units.la: Illud autem omnium est grauissimū, si quis à suis liberis, aut à familiaribus, circumuentus, non solùm ludibrio habea-tur, sed etiam in extremas calamitates cō[illegible, ~1 letters]ijciaijciatur: ut hæc exempla ostendunt.
units.tr: But the gravest of all is when someone, circumvented by his own children or household, is not only made a laughingstock but is even cast into the worst calamities, as these examples show.

units.la: Cofroës Persarum Rex, qui Romanis pacem petentibus, superbè respondit: Non parcam vobis tantisper donec Crucifixum illum, quem Deum esse perhibetis, adoraveritis, non autem unà nobiscū Solem: à Siroë filio captus, numellis[?] detentus, à primoribus suis iussu filij cōsputus, tandem etiam telis confixus, miserabiliter perijt: ut supra quoq; dixi.
units.tr: Cofroës, king of the Persians, who, when the Romans sought peace, replied proudly: "I will not spare you until you have adored that crucified man whom you say is God, and not the Sun along with us." Captured by his son Siroes, kept in chains, spat upon at his son's command by his leading men, he was finally pierced with weapons and perished miserably, as I have also said above.

units.la: Verum enimvero, etiam bonis principibus ista nonnunquā evenisse, testantur historiæ, de Mauricio Imperatore, quem cum tota familia Phocas tyrannus occidit: de Hildericho Francorum Rege, in monasterium detruso: de Henrico IIII. Imperatore, qui Pontifice Romano procurante, opera ingrati filij Henrici V. imperatoria dignitate spoliatus, Leodij extremos dies clausit, & sepulcri honore ꝑ[?] annos aliquot caruit: & de multis alijs.
units.tr: Indeed, histories bear witness that such things have sometimes happened even to good princes: to the Emperor Maurice, whom the tyrant Phocas killed together with his whole family; to Childeric, king of the Franks, thrust into a monastery; to the Emperor Henry IV, who, through the scheming of the Roman Pontiff and the work of his ungrateful son Henry V, was stripped of the imperial dignity, closed his last days at Liège, and for some years was denied honourable burial; and to many others.

units.la: Cominęus lib.5. Historiarum testatur, Arnoldum Ducē Geldriæ, jam natu grandem, ab ingrato filio Adolpho, nocte quadam, cū iam iturus esset cubitum, captū, ac discalceatum, asperrima hyeme per quinq; milliaria abductū, inq; teterrimū carcarcerem detrusum fuisse. Cum aut[?] ille, post sex menses, Pontificis & Caesaris mandatu, ægre liberatus[?] esset a Carolo Bur-gundiae Duce, ac coram isto Principe causam ageret: infelix pater etiam duellum filio detulit. Censebat Carolus, Graviam[?] oppidum ad Mosam, cū tribus millibus florenorum, & tantundem ex annua pensione, una cum titulo Geldriae, miserrimo patri concedendum. Verum impius filius Adolphus respodit, Patrem totos 44 annos Geldriam possedisse: æquum igitur esse, ut tandem aliquando filio locum det. Malle autem se patrem in puteum præcipitem dare, ac deinde eodem safe conij-cere, quam istas conditiones acceptare.
units.tr: Commines, in book 5 of his Histories, testifies that Arnold, Duke of Guelders, already advanced in years, was seized by his ungrateful son Adolph one night, just as he was about to go to bed; he was stripped of his shoes, dragged through five miles in the harshest winter, and thrust into a most foul prison. When, after six months, he had with difficulty been freed by Charles, Duke of Burgundy, by the order of the Pontiff and the Emperor, and was pleading his case before that prince, the unhappy father also brought a duel against his son. Charles judged that the town of Grave on the Maas, with three thousand florins and as much again from an annual pension, together with the title of Guelders, should be granted to the most wretched father. But the impious son Adolph replied that his father had possessed Guelders for a full 44 years; it was therefore fair that at last he should give place to his son. He would rather, he said, throw his father headlong into a well and then cast the same well-cover over him than accept those terms.

units.la: Ferre tamen se posse, ut ille habeat tria millia florenorum, sed ea lege atq; omine[?], ut è Geldria discedat.
units.tr: Still, he said he could bear that the old man should have three thousand florins, but only on condition and under the omen that he leave Guelders.

units.la: Secundæ autem sunt pœnæ, secundum illud Herodoti: τῶν μεγάλων ἀδικημάτων, μεγάλα εἰσὶ καὶ τιμωρίαι παρὰ τῆς θεοῦ[?].
units.tr: The punishments that follow are the second kind, according to the saying of Herodotus: great wrongs bring great punishments from God [τῶν μεγάλων ἀδικημάτων, μεγάλα εἰσὶ καὶ τιμωρίαι παρὰ τῆς θεοῦ].

units.la: Adolphus enim, dissimulata persona, habituq; Gallico sumto, iter facies[?], apud Namurcum, dum persoluit naulum, agnitus & captus est, & donec vixit Carolus Burgundus, in carcere detentus. Liberatus demū à Gandauensibus, & bello ad-versus Tornacenses gesto præfectus, mi-serabiliter fuit trucidatus. Geldriæ pof-sesio, testamento patris Arnoldi, Carolo & eius posteris cessit.
units.tr: For Adolph, disguising his identity and assuming French dress, was making a journey; at Namur, while he was paying his passage, he was recognised and seized, and he was held in prison as long as Charles the Burgundian lived. Finally freed by the men of Ghent, and placed in command in a war waged against the Tournaisians, he was miserably slaughtered. The possession of Guelders, by the will of his father Arnold, passed to Charles and his successors.

units.la: Ergóne ista humanitus tantum fiunt?
units.tr: Are these things, then, done merely by human agency?

units.la: Nequaquam. Deus enim est, qui cum ei uisum est, auctoritatis, ἀξίας, gratiæ subiectorum dona subtrahit, & effundit contemtum in Principes: & errare facit eos in inanitate sine via.Psalmo 107.40. Deus est qui vindemiat spiritum Principum, & terribilis est Regibus terræ.Pfal. 76.12. Deus gubernator est: hic humiliat, & hic exaltat.Pfal.75.7. Falsum itaque erat Demetrij Regis, fortunam pro Dea habentis, apophthegma: Σύ τοι μ' ἐ-φυσας, σὺ λαλὰ λαμπαδὴ [?] ἀόνεις [?].
units.tr: By no means. For it is God who, when it pleases him, takes away from subjects their authority, their worth [ἀξίας], and the favour and grace they enjoy, and pours contempt upon the princes, and causes them to wander in emptiness where there is no way (Ps. 107.40). It is God who gathers the spirit of princes, and he is terrible to the kings of the earth (Ps. 76.12). God is the governor: he humbles one and exalts another (Ps. 75.7). So the saying of King Demetrius, who regarded Fortune as a goddess, was false: "You made me, you..." [Σύ τοι μ' ἐφυσας, σὺ λαλὰ λαμπαδὴ ἀόνεις, the text is garbled in the scan].

units.la: ¶ Quando autem extollit illos aut humiliat Dominus, utitur, cum ei libet, opera seu hostium, seu familiarium: ut histo-riæ sacræ & profanæ testantur.
units.tr: Now when the Lord raises up or humbles these men, he uses, as he pleases, the work either of enemies or of familiars, as both sacred and profane histories bear witness.

units.la: Nos, intuentes tempora nostra, diligen-ter observemus, in quorum manus nos tradiderit Deus, ut seu aperto Marte, ut aiunt, seu per cuniculos, nos oppugna-rent: quibus etiam dixerit, ut nobis ma-lediIedicerent[?]: quibus exosi,& quibus ludibrio simus.
units.tr: Let us, considering our own times, observe carefully into whose hands God has delivered us, and whether they attack us openly, as they say, in war, or by mines and secret tunnels; whom he has also allowed to curse us; by whom we are hated, and at whose mockery we are.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem illud semper cordi nobis fit, quod Dominus per Apostolum edixit: Ne uincitor ab eo quod malum est: sed uince bonitate malicia. Roman.12.21. Nocendi studium,quo ardent æmuli nostri, accendere debet & fouere in nobis etiam inimicos diligendi, bene agendi & merendi studium.
units.tr: And first of all, let this always lie close to our heart, which the Lord commanded through the Apostle: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Rom. 12.21). The eagerness to harm, with which our rivals burn, ought to kindle and foster in us an eagerness to love even our enemies, to do good and to deserve well.

units.la: Deinde, cum nemo posit dicere sibi nullum esse inimicum, qui ullum sibi amicum esse fatetur (consequuntur enim sese inuicem amicitiæ & inimicitiæ) constanter & prudenter feramus commune fatum: nec patiamur nobis excidere illud [illegible, ~12 letters]: Opus est fidis amicis, & acribus inimicis: quia utrinque sine fuco agunt.
units.tr: Next, since no one can say he has no enemy if he admits he has a friend (for friendship and enmity follow one another), let us bear our common lot steadily and wisely, and not allow ourselves to forget that saying: "We need faithful friends and sharp enemies, because both act without pretence."

units.la: Tertiò, sollicitè caueamus cõuicijs deformati, ne cum profiteamur fidem in Christum, & eius comitem charitatem, deteriores simus Ethniço illo homine, q apud Herodotū grauisime in Polymnia respondet conuiciatori: Σὺ μὲν ἀποδιξάμε-νος ὑβρίσματα, ἡ μὴ πείθεις ἀσχήμονα ἐν τῇ ἀμοι-βῇ γενέσθαι. Quartò, optimam rationem ulciscendi inimicos cũ exoterico illo statuamus, si nos probos & honestos uiros præstiterimus. Hac enim ratione nobis maximè proderimus, & coaceruabimus carbones ardentes super capita inimicorum: qui si sint ἀνίατοι[?] & inemendabiles, tanto magis discruciabuntur, quò præstantioribus animi & corporis bonis, & recte factorum laude, nos excellere animaduerterint.
units.tr: Thirdly, let us take care, lest, being disfigured by insults, while we profess faith in Christ and his companion charity, we become worse than that heathen man who, in Herodotus, in Polymnia, answered the reviler very gravely: "You, having thrown out insults, do not persuade me to become shameful in the return" [Σὺ μὲν ἀποδιξάμενος ὑβρίσματα, ἢ μὴ πείθεις ἀσχήμονα ἐν τῇ ἀμοιβῇ γενέσθαι]. Fourthly, let us settle on this, the best way of taking vengeance on our enemies, by that common saying, if we show ourselves upright and honourable men. For in this way we will benefit ourselves most, and "heap coals of fire upon the heads of our enemies"; and if they are incurable and beyond correction, they will be tormented all the more, once they perceive that we excel them in the better goods of mind and body and in the praise of right conduct.

units.la: Postremò, ut cætera iam non attingam, cùm Dei iudicia erga aduersarios nostros quotidie conspiciamus (aliàs enim signa reprobæ mentis, aliàs tragicos furores & errores in consiliis & actionibus, & interitus eorum uidemus) caueamus nobis ab ἐπιχαιρεκακίας[?]: & misericor-dia afficiamur erga errantes, maledicos, persecutores: nec ingemiscamus contra eos: quia Deus iudex pro foribus stat,o-mnia spectans & dijudicans.
units.tr: Lastly, to pass over the rest, since we see daily God's judgments against our adversaries (for we see on the one hand the signs of a reprobate mind, on the other tragic frenzies and errors in their counsels and actions, and their ruin), let us beware of rejoicing at evil; let us be moved with pity towards those who err, who curse, who persecute; and let us not groan against them, because God the judge stands before the doors, seeing and judging all things.

units.la: ¶ Verum enimuerò ut ab exemplis & commonefactionibus istis, ad rem ipsam per ἐπανόδου redeamus, tria sunt quæ animum addere solent ijs, qui in carnis præsidia respicere solent: Principum, bellica & togata fortitudine praestantium, copiae Urbium, opportunis locis sitarum, munitiones: & denique Provinciarum multitudo & amplitudo.
units.tr: But now, to return by way of recapitulation from these examples and admonitions to the matter itself, there are three things which are wont to give courage to those who look to the defences of the flesh: the military and civil valour of princes who excel, the forces of cities placed in suitable locations, their fortifications; and finally the number and extent of provinces.

units.la: 1. Vir heroicus, qui multorum instar est, ipsos exercitus vocatur. Nec sane male pronunciavit Spartiata interrogatus, quae'nam essent & ubi essent Spartanæ urbis mœnia: ostendit armatos cives. Est tamen etiam ingens & instru-ctissimus exercitus, instar excæcati Cyclopis, cum ei deest Imperator talis, qualem descripsit ille Ethnicorum propheta:
units.tr: 1. A hero, who is equal to many, is called themselves the armies. Nor did the Spartan badly answer when he was asked what and where were the walls of the city of Sparta: he pointed to its armed citizens. Yet there is also a huge and thoroughly equipped army, like the blinded Cyclops, when it lacks a commander such as that heathen prophet described:

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters]
units.tr: [illegible in the scan, about forty letters]

units.la: Recte etiam in Apophthegmatis quidam apud Plutarchum pronunciat: Eum qui bellicis rebus praeesse dux debeat, nō in fronte modo, sed etiam in tergo oculos habere. Praeclare etiam Cicero: In summo, inquit, Imperatore quatuor haec virtutes inesse debent: scientia rei militaris, virtus, auctoritas, felicitas. Item: Haec sunt virtutis Imperatoriae, labor in negotijs, fortitudo in periculis, industria in agendo, celeritas in conficiendo, consilium in providendo.
units.tr: Rightly, too, someone in the Apophthegms, reported by Plutarch, declares that the one who ought to be leader in warlike affairs must have eyes not only in front but also in the back. Cicero also says well: "In a supreme commander, four virtues ought to be present: knowledge of military affairs, courage, authority, and good fortune." Likewise: "These are the virtues of a commander: labour in business, fortitude in dangers, diligence in acting, speed in finishing, and foresight in planning."
2. [Heading, garbled in the scan; presumably "2."]

units.la: 2. Porrò, urbium & arcium munitionibus quantum deferatur, uulgo notū est. Etsi autem magnus earum usus non rarò esse uidetur: sæpe tamen plurimùm obsunt, dum earū fiducia mouentur non necessaria & tamen periculosa bella, aut in potestatem hostium redacté urbes uel arces munitæ, seruitutis ciuium compedes & uincula fiūt: ut de Munychia Athenarum arce dicitur in uita Phocionis, apud Plutarchum. Et uidit hæc nostra ætas, multa eius rei exempla in ueterum Charitinorū regione, cum Iberi superiores facti essent, in illo ciuili bello, quod memoria nostra, religionis caussa, gestū fuit in Germania.
units.tr: Next, how much is attributed to the fortifications of cities and citadels is commonly known. Although their use often seems great, yet very often they do much harm: when wars that are unnecessary yet dangerous are undertaken, moved by confidence in them, or when cities or fortified citadels fall into the power of enemies, they become the fetters and chains of the citizens' slavery. So it is said of the citadel of Munychia at Athens, in the Life of Phocion, in Plutarch. And our own age has seen many examples of this in the region of the old Charitini, when the upper Iberians had become masters in that civil war which, in our memory, was waged in Germany for the sake of religion.

units.la: 3. Quantum etiam in bellis momentū habeant prouinciæ multæ & magnæ, & quibusdam in locis inaccessæ, uel ex historia eius belli, quod Alexāder Magnus cum Dario ultimo Persarum Rege gessit, colligere licet. Auctor est Curtius, Darium in illa tanta inclinatione rerum & Monarchiæ Persicæ, suis hominibus non parum consternatis, hac ratione animum addere solitū, quòd amissis aliquot prouincijs, multæ aliæ restarent, interq; illas HircaHircania, mille urbibus clara, & ἀναρχό-δος[?].
units.tr: 3. From the history of the war which Alexander the Great waged against Darius, the last king of the Persians, one may gather how much weight in wars is carried by many large provinces, some of them hard to reach. Curtius reports that Darius, when the affairs of the Persian monarchy were so badly tilted and his men were not a little dismayed, was accustomed to encourage his spirits in this way: that though some provinces were lost, many others remained, among them Hircania, Hyrcania, famous for its thousand cities, and [ἀναρχόδος, the text is garbled].

units.la: Sed Habacucus noster, Reges & Duces bellorum ludibrio Chaldæis fore, urbes & arces facile ab eisdem occupadas, denique multas & longè lateque patentes prouincias in ditionem potestatemq; eorum redigendas, prænuncians: uanam esse humanorum præsidiorum fiduciam, sapientissimè colligit: ac ut ne hæsitationi locum relinqueret, Deum ista sibi ape[?] ruisse testatur.
units.tr: But our Habakkuk, foretelling that kings and leaders of wars would become a mockery to the Chaldeans, that cities and citadels would easily be seized by them, and finally that many provinces spread far and wide would be brought under their dominion and power, most wisely concludes that confidence in human defences is vain; and, so that he would leave no room for hesitation, he testifies that God revealed these things to him.

units.la: Dominum IESVM precor, ut nobis det egregia cum πληροφορίᾳ[?] fidei gloriari, Deum solum nobis esse Tutamen & Robur, in quo auxilium in afflictionibus inueniamus abundè: ac propterea nos nō timere, cum mouetur terra, & concidunt montes in medio mari. Psal.46.1.2.
units.tr: I pray the Lord Jesus that he grant us to glory in the faith with a notable full assurance [πληροφορίᾳ], that God alone is our shelter and strength, in whom we find abundant help in afflictions; and therefore that we need not fear when the earth is moved and the mountains fall into the midst of the sea (Ps. 46.1, 2).

units.la: VERSVS XI.
units.tr: Verse 11.

units.la: Tunc transsibit spiritus eius, ac trāsgre-dietur atq; delinquet, (dicendo) Hanc potentiam suam Dei sui esse.
units.tr: Then his spirit shall pass over, and he shall transgress and offend, saying that this power belongs to his god.

units.la: DE OFFENSA NEBVCADNEZARIS circa successus & res secundas.
units.tr: On Nebuchadnezzar's offence in regard to success and prosperity.

units.la: Initiò phrases, quæ in hoc versu occur-runt, runt, exponam: deinde, speciem offensæ & eius gradus subiungam: postremò, de usu huius doctrinæ aliquid ἀνὼ χρῆσ τῷ ἁγίῳ dicam. Dominus Iesus vt sanctus det, utipsius gloriæ & nostræ ædificationi omnia seruiant: Amen.
units.tr: First I will explain the phrases that occur in this verse; then I will set out the kind of offence and its degrees; lastly I will say something about the use of this teaching for the use of the holy [ἀνὼ χρῆσ τῷ ἁγίῳ]. May the Lord Jesus, who is holy, grant that all things serve his own glory and our edification. Amen.

units.la: 1. Spiritum mutare dicitur, qui æquam mentem in secundis rebus nō potest ser-uare, nec retinet propositū modestiæ & grauitatis ac humanitatis: sed affectus, sermonem & gestus ac mores mutat, & laxat frenum cupiditatibus: ut olim fecerūt Alexander Magnus, Nero post exactum illud à Traiano celebratum eius quinquennium, & multi alij.
units.tr: 1. A spirit is said to change when it cannot keep an even mind in prosperity, and does not hold to the purpose of moderation, seriousness and humanity, but alters its feelings, speech, bearing and manners, and gives the reins to its desires. So once did Alexander the Great, and Nero after the five-year period, so much praised, which Trajan completed, and many others.

units.la: Ei ex aduerso respondet phrasis, Spiritum seruare, id est, sibi similem manere, & retinere laudabile illud propositum & temperamentum uerae humanitatis & grauitatis & constantiæ in totius uitæ specie. Vt de Antonino Philosopho Imperatore scribit Dion: ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ πατρὶ τῶν ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐν ἀδελφῇ ἠλαύθη. ἔτως ὡς ἀλλὰ θεῖς ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ ἦν, καὶ ἐν ἀδελφῇ προσποιούμενος ἔχει. Nos in hac parte Ethnico Principe longè fumus feliciores, cum Spiritum sanctum uitæ moderatorem habeamus.
units.tr: The opposite phrase is to keep the spirit, that is, to remain like oneself, and to hold to that praiseworthy purpose and to the measure of true humanity, seriousness and constancy throughout the whole course of life. Thus Dion writes of the philosopher-emperor Antoninus: likewise he was the same as a father to him, and he wandered in a sister's house; he was in this way as a good and excellent man, and kept up the same character in his sister's [ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ πατρὶ τῶν ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐν ἀδελφῇ ἠλαύθη. ἔτως ὡς ἀλλὰ θεῖς ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ ἦν, καὶ ἐν ἀδελφῇ προσποιούμενος ἔχει.] We are far happier than that heathen prince in this respect, since we have the Holy Spirit as the governor of our life.

units.la: ¶. Transgredi atq; delinquere, hoc loco significat, uiolatis legibus diuinis, iracundiæ, inuidiæ, & aliis perturbationibus sicindulgere, ut etiam erumpant in terra facinora. Vt Alexander, cum esset ebrius, nefariè occidit Clytum, à quo in prælio ad Granicum seruatus erat. Saul sæuijt in Domini sacerdotes, uiros sanctos & innoxios. 1.Sam.22.
units.tr: ¶. To transgress and to offend here means that, when the divine laws are violated, one indulges anger, envy and other disturbances of the mind, so that crimes break out upon the earth. Thus Alexander, when he was drunk, wickedly killed Clitus, by whom he had been saved in the battle at the Granicus. Saul raged against the priests of the Lord, holy and innocent men. 1 Sam. 22.

units.la: 3. Dicere potentiam suam Dei sui esse, nihil aliud est, quàm partim uanissimis idolis, partim suis uiribus acceptam ferre potentiam, successus, res bello & pace ex animi sententia peractas. Contrarium profitetur Dauid, Psal. 18.32. Deus accinxit me robore, & complanauitui-am meam. 33. Adæquauit pedes meos pedibus ceruarum: & super arces meas statuit me. 34. Is est qui instruxit manus meas ad prælium: adeò ut conterearetur arcus æreus brachijs meis. 35. Et præbuisti mihi scutum salutis tuæ, & dextera tua fulciuit me, & benignitas tua auxit me. Psalmo 144.1. Laus sit Iehonæ Rupi meæ: qui docet manus meas ad prælium, & digitos meos ad bellum.
units.tr: 3. To say that this power belongs to one's god is nothing other than to attribute the power, the successes and the results achieved in war and peace according to one's own wish, partly to utterly vain idols and partly to one's own strength. David professes the contrary, Ps. 18.32: "God girded me with strength and made my way perfect. 33. He made my feet like hinds' feet, and set me upon my high places. 34. He is the one who trained my hands for battle, so that a bow of bronze was broken by my arms. 35. You have given me the shield of your salvation, your right hand has upheld me, and your kindness has made me great." Ps. 144.1: "Blessed be Jehovah my rock, who teaches my hands to war and my fingers to fight."

units.la: In genere autem de omnibus munerū functionibus dicitur: Sit pulcritudo le-houæ Dei nostri super nos, & opus manuum nostrarum confirma super nos: & opus manuum nostrarum cōfirma: Psal. 90.17. Item: Non quòd idonei simus ex nobisipsis ad cogitādum quicquam, uelut ex nobisipsis: sed q; idonei sumus, id ex Deo est. 2.Cor.3.5.
units.tr: In general, it is said of all the functions of our callings: "Let the beauty of Jehovah our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; and establish the work of our hands." Ps. 90.17. Likewise: "Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is of God." 2 Cor. 3.5.

units.la: De specie offensæ & eius gradibus.
units.tr: On the kind of offence and its degrees.

units.la: Ubi Nebucadnezar Reges bellicosos & præpotentes devicerit, & populos eorum in potestatem ditionemq; suam redegerit: transibit spiritus eius, hoc est, sibi ipsi dissimilis fiet, & altiores, q; mortalem oportuit, spiritus sibi sumet: grassabitur etiam in eos quos fors aspera ei obijciet: & deniq; non Deo vero, sed idolo suo acceptas feret præclaras illas victorias & alia bona.
units.tr: When Nebuchadnezzar has conquered warlike and very powerful kings, and has reduced their peoples under his power and dominion, his spirit will pass over; that is, he will become unlike himself, and will take to himself loftier spirits than a mortal ought to have. He will also rage against those whom harsh fortune throws in his way; and finally he will attribute those famous victories and other blessings not to the true God but to his idol.

units.la: Hæc offensa amplificatur:
units.tr: This offence is magnified in the following ways.

units.la: 1. A'speciebus. Mutato spiritu, affectus, sermones, gestus, mores, consilia mutantur: seu subito, ut in Alexandro Magno: seu sensim, ut in Saule videre est.
units.tr: 1. From its forms. When the spirit is changed, the feelings, speech, bearing, manners and counsels are changed too: either suddenly, as in Alexander the Great, or gradually, as may be seen in Saul.

units.la: 2. A'vana anticipatione paralogismi huius. Nequaquam eadem tibi evenire poterunt, terunt, quæ acciderunt istis[?] Regibus & populis. Versantur autem hi in magnis miserijs: tu uerò gloria, præsidijs, successibus & uictoriis[?] frueris. Tu igitur semper eris felix: isti uerò nunquam e miseriarum gurgite emergent. An non autem παραφροσύνη[?] seu dementia magna est, opinari te ideo quiam floreas & eminéas, constitutum esse ἔξω βασιλῶν ἀνθρωπίνων[?]: & obliuisci tum eius quod Menander docuit, πάντα προσδοκᾷ ἀεὶ ἀνθρώπου ἴσα[?]: tum sapientissimi dicti Xenophontis: ὅτι ὁ θεὸς γάρ, ὡς ἔοικε, πολλάκις χαίρει, τὸν μὲν μικρὸν μεγάλως ποιῶν, τὸν δὲ μεγάλον μικρός[?].
units.tr: 2. From the vain anticipation of this fallacy. "The same things cannot happen to you as happened to those kings and peoples. They live in great miseries; but you enjoy glory, protection, success and victories. Therefore you will always be happy, while they will never emerge from the whirlpool of their miseries." Is it not great madness, or dementia, to suppose that because you flourish and stand out you have been placed beyond the reach of human kings, and to forget both what Menander taught, always expect that human things are all alike [πάντα προσδοκᾷ ἀεὶ ἀνθρώπου ἴσα], and the most wise saying of Xenophon: for God, as it seems, often rejoices in making the small great and the great small [ὅτι ὁ θεὸς γάρ, ὡς ἔοικε, πολλάκις χαίρει, τὸν μὲν μικρὸν μεγάλως ποιῶν, τὸν δὲ μεγάλον μικρός]?

units.la: Sedenim huius offersæ Nebucadnezaris optimum testem & ἐξηγητὴν Danielem Prophetam audiamus. Is enim libri sui cap.4.v.26.27.historicè oraculum hoc exposuit, his quidem verbis: In fine mesiũ duodecim, in palatio regni Babel deambulabat. Locutus est Rex, & ait: Nonne hæc est Babel magna, quam ego ædificaui in domum regni, in robore fortitudinis meæ, & in gloriam decoris mei? 18.
units.tr: But let us hear Daniel the Prophet, the best witness and expounder of this offence of Nebuchadnezzar. In the fourth chapter, verses 26 and 27, of his book, he set out this oracle historically, in these words: "At the end of twelve months he was walking in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon. The king spoke and said: Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the house of the kingdom by the strength of my power, and for the glory of my majesty?" 18.

units.la: Adhuc sermo erat in ore Regis, & uox è cœlo ruit: Tibi dicunt Nebucadnezar Rex; regnum transiuit à te, &c. Quæ uero pœnæ secutæ sint, eodem capite ostendit Propheta. Ac recte Seneca dixit:
units.tr: While the word was still in the king's mouth, a voice fell from heaven: "To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has departed from you, etc." What punishments followed the Prophet shows in the same chapter. And Seneca rightly said:

units.la: Dominare tumidus, spiritus altos gere: Sequitur superbos uictor a tergo Deus.
units.tr: Rule proudly, bear lofty spirits: God the victor follows the proud from behind.

units.la: DE HOMINIS CHRISTIANI MODE-ratione in rebus secundis.
units.tr: On the moderation of the Christian man in prosperous circumstances.

units.la: Iam, ut de usu istius exempli agamus, illud nobis certò persuasum esse debet, velle Deum, & ut successu recteq; factorum laudem ipsi in solidum deferamus, & ut ne mutemus propositum pietatis & virtutum ac bonorum morum. Τετραγώ-νοι[?] ergo ἀνὰ ψόγος[?] simus, ac meminerimus non minus ad nos fatigandos facere res secundas, quæ mirificè nobis arrident & blandiuntur, quàm aduersas, quarum horrificus aspectus esse videtur. Nec nobis imponamus uana persuasione, quasi politicis hominibus solis isti scopuli magis sint metuendi, quàm nobis, qui nobis uidemur, professionis Theologicæ causa, esse ἱερὰ ἢ ἄσυλοι[?]. Videmus enim, quò iam progressi sint Diotrephes nonnulli, qui κατακυριεύειν τῷ κλήρῳ[?] conantur, quos fidei articulos obtrudant, quàm inhumanitèr tractent modestè dissentientes, quibus a-nathehathematifmis profequantur multa pio-rum hominum, IESV CHRISTI no-minen inuocantium, millia. Dominus Ec-clesiæ misertus, uel conuertat eos, uel co-fundat: ac restituat Ecclesijs sinceram do-strinam & charitatem: & cum Anastasia-na & Zenonia tempora καὶ μηχανήματα [?] ἢ ὑπογραφὰς diu iam senserimus, det, ut Iu-stinianus aliquis orthodoxus exoriatur, qui ueritatis uexillũ attollentib. adsit, & CHRISTI IESV, Principis nostri summi, succenturiatũ fidelem agat: aut si minus hoc iam facere decreuit, det ut in patien-tia animas nostras possideamus. Amen.
