units.tr: Now, to turn to the use of this example, we must be firmly persuaded that God wishes us to ascribe the whole praise of success and of rightly done deeds to him, and that we should not change our resolve toward piety, virtue and good morals. Let us therefore be square and blameless [Τετράγωνοι ἀνὰ ψόγος], and remember that prosperous things wear us out no less than adverse ones. Prosperity charms and flatters us wonderfully, while adversity seems to have a dreadful look. Nor let us fall into the vain belief that those rocks are to be feared only by political men, and not by us, who think that, because of our theological profession, we are sacred and inviolable [ἱερὰ ἢ ἄσυλοι]. We see how far some Diotrephes have already advanced, who try to lord it over the clergy [κατακυριεύειν τῷ κλήρῳ], who force upon us articles of faith, and how inhumanly they treat those who dissent modestly, pursuing with anathemas many thousands of pious people who call upon the name of Jesus Christ. May the Lord of the Church, in mercy, either convert them or confound them, and restore to the churches sincere doctrine and charity. Since we have long felt the times of Anastasius and Zeno, with their schemes and subscriptions [καὶ μηχανήματα ἢ ὑπογραφὰς], may some orthodox Justinian arise to stand by those who raise the banner of truth, and to act as a faithful reinforcement for Christ Jesus, our supreme Prince. Or, if he has decided not to do this now, may he grant that we possess our souls in patience. Amen.

units.la: Cogitemus etiā, [?]iorib. Ethnicis do-luisse hac tatam infirmitatem hominum, qua fit ut facile secūdis rebus inescati & languefacti, degeneres fiant, sibiq; ipsis multū difsimil s. Nota funt hæc dicta :
units.tr: Let us also consider that the Gentiles too lamented this common weakness of men, by which it happens that they are easily enticed and enfeebled by prosperous circumstances, become degenerate, and grow quite unlike themselves. These sayings are well known:

units.la: Ἐιωθε τῶν πόλεων αἰσ [?] ἂν μάλιστα, καὶ δὴ ἐλα-[?] χίστῃ ἀπροσδόκητος ἂν πραξία ἔλθῃ, ἐς ὕβριν τρέ-πεται. τὰ δὲ πολλὰ κατὰ λόγον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις [?] ἐν ξυνέσει, ἀσφαλείᾳ ἢ παρὰ δόξαν. καὶ ἀκανο-[?] πεαγίαν ὡς εἰπεῖν, ῥᾷον ἀπωθήσονται, ἢ ἐνδιαμονὴ [?] ἐν διαφθορᾷ. Thucyd.lib.3.
units.tr: Thucydides, book 3: As is most common in cities, and especially when an unexpected success comes to those who least expect it, it turns into insolence. Most things, however, go according to reason for men who are sensible, safe, or beyond expectation. And, so to speak, they will more easily cast off adversity than keep prosperity without corruption. [Εἴωθε τῶν πόλεων αἰεὶ μάλιστα, καὶ δὴ ἐλαχίστῃ ἀπροσδόκητος ἂν πραξία ἔλθῃ, ἐς ὕβριν τρέπεται. τὰ δὲ πολλὰ κατὰ λόγον τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐν ξυνέσει, ἀσφαλείᾳ ἢ παρὰ δόξαν. καὶ ἀκανονίστως ὡς εἰπεῖν, ῥᾷον ἀπωθήσονται, ἢ ἐνδιαμονὴ ἐν διαφθορᾷ.]

units.la: Iustinus lib.8. Thebanos, cum rerum potirentur, secundam fortunam imbecillo animo tulisse, scribit. Et hac quidem in parte dissimiles quoq; erant praestantissimo suo Duci Epaminondae, qui Leuctrica victoria parta, postridie squalidus & tristis in publicum prodijt: interroga-tusque, ecquid,illi molestum accidisset: Nihil, respondit, sed heri sensi me mihi plus aequo placuisse. Eius gaudij intemperatiam hodie castigo. Prudenter sane, secundis moderate gaudendum, statuebat.
units.tr: Justinus, book 8, writes that the Thebans, when they came into power, bore their good fortune with a weak spirit. In this respect they were also unlike their most excellent leader Epaminondas, who, after the victory won at Leuctra, came out in public the next day squalid and sad. When he was asked whether anything troubling had happened to him, he replied: "Nothing, but yesterday I noticed that I had pleased myself more than was right. Today I am punishing the immoderation of that joy." He prudently held that one should rejoice in prosperity with moderation.

units.la: Secundae res, inquit Crispus, sapientum animos fatigant.
units.tr: "Prosperous circumstances," says Crispus, "wear out the minds of the wise."

units.la: Et noti sunt elegantissimi uersus: Nescia mens hominum fati sortisq; futurae, Et seruare modum rebus sublata secundis. Item: Luxuriant animi rebus plerumq; secundis, Nec facile est aequa commoda mente pati.
units.tr: And there are the most elegant verses: The mind of man does not know the fate and the lot to come, and does not keep measure when lifted up by prosperous things. Likewise: Minds for the most part run riot in prosperous circumstances, nor is it easy to bear advantages with an even mind.

units.la: QVI TANDEM ERRORES FV-cum faciunt iis, qui rebus secundis sublati, non seruant mentem aequam?
units.tr: Who, at last, are those who make the mistakes, who, lifted up by prosperous circumstances, do not keep an even mind?

units.la: De quibusdam respondebo, quos mi-hi videor animadvertisse: viri pruden-tes de multis aliis nos submonere pote-runt.
units.tr: I shall answer concerning some whom I seem to myself to have noticed; wise men could admonish us about many others.

units.la: 1. Spes uana de perpetua felicitate. Haec olim sic imposuit Polycrati, Samiorū Ty-ranranno, ut annulum aureum, cui inclusa e-rat maximi precij gemma, in mare proij-ceret, ut esset quod ei doleret. Etsi autem hunc quoque non multo post recepit: tamen postea in crucem actus ab Oroete, Sardium praefecto, sensit felicitatem illam non esse perpetuam. Exstat Epistola Amasis regis Aegypti, apud Herodotum in Thaleia, quae iudicium saniorum hominum inter Etnicos, de uicibus rerum aduersarum & secundarum, felicitati, ut uidetur, perpetuae anteponendis, elegan-ter describit.
units.tr: 1. Vain hope of perpetual happiness. This once so deceived Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, that he threw into the sea a golden ring set with a gem of the greatest value, so that there would be something to grieve him. Although he later recovered it, he afterwards was crucified by Oroites, governor of Sardis, and learned that that happiness was not perpetual. There is the letter of Amasis, king of Egypt, in Herodotus, in the Thalia, which elegantly describes the judgment of saner men among the Gentiles, that the changes of adverse and prosperous things are to be set before a happiness that seems perpetual.

units.la: Ἄμασις Πολυκράτει ὧδε λέγει.
units.tr: Amasis speaks thus to Polycrates. [Ἄμασις Πολυκράτει ὧδε λέγει.]

units.la: Ἡδὺ μὲν ψωθαυμάσαι ἀνδρὶ φίλῳ ἢ ξένῳ ἐν ἀγαθοῖσι· ἐμοὶ δὲ αὐτῷ σοὶ μεγάλα συμφορῇ περιπεσεῖν, τὸ θεῖον ἐπιφθονέον ὡς ἐστὶ φθονερόν. Βούλομαι ... δὲ ἐμαυτὸν καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ... τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ... συμφορῶν. ἡ γὰρ διαφέρει τὸν ... καὶ συμφορῶν τὰ αὐτά. [illegible, ~20 letters] ἀκούσας, ὅτις ἐς τέλος ἡ ἐλαύνουσι προ-[?] ... συμφορῶν τὰ αὐτά. Σὺ ... ἐμοὶ ... ἡδύμενος ποιήσαι πρὸς τὰς συμφορὰς τοιάδε. [illegible, ~12 letters] τὸ μὲν ἀπὸ πρώτης ... ἀξίου, καὶ ἐπ᾽ ᾧ ... ἀπολωλεκ... μάλιστα τὴν ψυχὴν ἀλγήσας, τοῦτο ἀπὸ-[?] ἕκαστος ... ὅπως μὴ ... ἐς ἀνθρώπους. ἤνπερ μὴ [?] ἀλλ᾽ ἀλλὰ εἰ [?] τοι, τῶ ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτοῖς [?] πάθεσι προσπηλᾶσαι, τρόπῳ τῷ ἐξ ἡμῶν ὑπονεμομένῳ [?] νῷ ἀνέο. [?]
units.tr: "It is pleasant for a man to be admired by a friend or a stranger in good things; but for me, as for yourself, to fall into great misfortune, the divine is envious, as it is jealous. I wish ... myself and others ... first ... of misfortunes. For ... differs ... and the same things of misfortunes. You ... to me ... delighting to make such things in regard to misfortunes. ... from the first ... worthy, and over which ... lost ... especially grieving in soul, this ... each ... lest ... to men. Unless ..., but if ... to them, with the sufferings ..., in the manner handed down by us ... mind." [Ἡδὺ μὲν ... ἀνδρὶ φίλῳ ἢ ξένῳ ἐν ἀγαθοῖσι· ἐμοὶ δὲ αὐτῷ σοὶ μεγάλα συμφορῇ περιπεσεῖν, τὸ θεῖον ἐπιφθονέον ὡς ἐστὶ φθονερόν. Βούλομαι ...]

units.la: 2. Opinio stulta de eorum, qui iam miseri sunt, perpetuis miseriis. Atqui saepe fit, ut mutatis vicibus, felices fiat, qui paulo ante miserrimi fuerant. Loquor de humana, & huius vitae propria felicitate. Quàm multi non tam è carceribus, quàm è mortis faucibus, praeter omnem expectationem suam ad summas euecti sunt dignitates? Quid non ferendum fuit Iouiano & Valentiniano, propter Christianismi studium, imperante Iuliano Apo-stata? Exauctorati sunt ambo, baltheo militari eis adempto, & relegati. Hi tamen postea istius Principis in Imperio successores fuerunt. Martianus à Vandalis captus, & omine obumbrantis aquilae [?] factus, dimissus ab hostibus, Imperator factus est. Mathias Coruinus, Ioannis Huniadis F. post obitum Ladislai, posthumi Alberti Caesaris, Vngariae & Bohemiae Regis, à Georgio Boiebracio, Rege Bohemiae, non solum è carcere liberatus est, sed etiam laeto nuncio de Regno Vngarico capessendo exhilaratus, & honorifice rificè deductus est in regnum.
units.tr: 2. Foolish opinion that those who are already wretched will have perpetual miseries. Yet it often happens that, with the changing of fortunes, those who a little before were most wretched become happy. I speak of human happiness, and of the happiness proper to this life. How many have been raised to the highest dignities, beyond all their expectation, not so much from prisons as from the jaws of death? What was not to be endured by Jovian and Valentinian, on account of their zeal for Christianity, under the emperor Julian the Apostate? Both were dismissed, the military belt taken from them, and they were banished. Yet they afterwards became successors of that same prince in the empire. Martian, captured by the Vandals, and made the subject of an omen of an overshadowing eagle, was released by the enemies and made emperor. Matthias Corvinus, son of John Hunyadi, after the death of Ladislaus, the posthumous son of Albert, Caesar, King of Hungary and Bohemia, was not only freed from prison by George of Poděbrady, King of Bohemia, but was also cheered by the joyful news of taking up the kingdom of Hungary, and was honourably led into the kingdom.

units.la: Ferunt etiam, Serenissima Angliæ Reginam, Elizabetham (quæ multis iam annis sic regno pulcerrimo præfuit, ut cæteris Europæis regnis admodum laborantibus, Anglicanum efflorescêret: & optata pace nunc quoque, Dei beneficio, fruatur) mortuo fratre Eduardo, nostri seculi altero (si eximias animi dotes spectes) Salomone, in maximo vitæ periculo versatam, velut ex ore leonum ereptam, regnare demum cœpisse. Dominus Iesvs Chri-stvs Heroinam illā uerę Christianam, diu superstitem esse, & immortali sua cū laude, regnique bono publico, præesse uelit.
units.tr: They also report that the most serene Queen of England, Elizabeth, who for many years now has so governed that most beautiful kingdom that, while the other European kingdoms labour greatly, the English realm flourishes, and who now also enjoys the desired peace by God's benefit, was, after the death of her brother Edward, the Solomon of our century (if you regard his outstanding gifts of mind), placed in the greatest danger of life, and, snatched as if from the mouths of lions, at last began to reign. May the Lord Jesus Christ wish that heroine, truly Christian, to live on for a long time and to preside with immortal praise and for the public good of the kingdom.

units.la: Quid autem in genere omnibus pijs sperandum sit, docuit Propheta, cuius hæc uerba sunt: Clamant afflicti, & Iehouah audit; & ex omnibus angustijs eorum liberat eos. Prope est Iehouah confracti corde; & contritos spiritu seruabit. Multa sunt aduersa iustis, sed ex ijs omnibus liberat unumquemque eorum Iehouah. Tuetur omnia ossa eius: unum ex ipsis non frangitur. Psal. 34. 17. 18. 19. 20.
units.tr: What is to be hoped for by all the pious in general the Prophet taught, whose words are these: "The afflicted cry out, and Jehovah hears; and frees them from all their distresses. Jehovah is near to those broken in heart, and will save those crushed in spirit. Many are the adversities of the righteous, but Jehovah frees each one of them from all of them. He guards all his bones; not one of them is broken." Ps. 34:17–20.

units.la: 3. Sacrilega perfuasio, quæ fingit, [illegible, ~4 letters] ἀναθήματα[?] dona & præsidia vanissimis idolis esse tribuenda.
units.tr: 3. Sacrilegious persuasion, which imagines that gifts and protections [ἀναθήματα] are to be attributed to most vain idols.

units.la: Baltassar Rex Chaldeorū & Principes cū toto Gynecæo, è poculis sacris è tem-plo Hierosolymitano olim sublatis,in re-gali epulo biberūt vinum, & laudauerūt Deos aureos & argeteos, æreos,ferreos, ligneos & lapideos. Dan.5.4.
units.tr: Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, and the princes with his whole harem, drank wine at a royal feast from the sacred cups once taken from the temple at Jerusalem, and praised the gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone. Dan. 5:4.

units.la: 4. Opinio mendax, quasi qui ςωσφρονεῖ[?] habuit in rerum maximarum administra-tione, sine quorum opera & fide ne tantillum solus obtinere poterat, possit suæ solius prudentiæ, virtuti, dexteritati & alacritati, omnia illa ἀλογισμάτα[?] accepta ferre. Prudenter sanè Pyrrhus suis Aqui-lam in nubibus, ob res celeriter felicitér-que gestas vocantibus: Pervos, respon-dit, aquila sum. Qui enim non essem, qui vestris armis veluti pennis subleuer? Vi-tauit invidiā laude in commilitones trans-lata, non autem sibi uni vindicata.
units.tr: 4. Deceptive opinion, as if one who had been wise in the management of the greatest affairs, without whose work and faith he could not obtain even the smallest thing alone, could ascribe all those unreasoned successes to his own prudence, virtue, skill and energy alone. Prudently indeed Pyrrhus, when his men called him an eagle among the clouds on account of affairs quickly and happily done, replied: "Only by you am I an eagle. For what would I be, were I not lifted up by your arms as if by wings?" He avoided envy by transferring the praise to his fellow soldiers, and did not claim it for himself alone.

units.la: 5. Amentia & cæcitas tanta, ut ne qui-dem ἀλλοτρίων[?] alienarum calamitatum,no-bis persuadeat etiam nos homines esse, & multiplicibus casibus obnoxios, nec etiam meliore quam illi calamitosi, fortuna dignos. Vere dixit Menander:
units.tr: 5. Such great madness and blindness that, even about the calamities of others, it does not persuade us that we too are men, subject to manifold accidents, and not worthy of a better fortune than those wretched ones. Menander truly said:

units.la: [illegible, ~5 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: τειχεσθλιὸν γε καὶ τλκαίπωγον φύσα, [?] πολλῶν τε μισθόν ἔχει ἵλεω φρονίσθων. [?]
units.tr: Walled-in, lion-hearted, and shaggy-chested, he has many wages, [if] he is gracious in mind. [τειχεσθλιὸν γε καὶ τλκαίπωγον φύσα, πολλῶν τε μισθόν ἔχει ἵλεω φρονίσθων]

units.la: VERSVS XII.
units.tr: VERSE 12.

units.la: III. Habacuci ἔνστασις [?], in qua ostendit, nec Iudaeos tantis calamitatibus, nec Babylonios tanta felicitate dignos esse: ac proinde utrosque alio loco habendos & aliter tractandos esse.
units.tr: III. Habakkuk's objection [ἔνστασις], in which he shows that neither the Jews deserve such great calamities nor the Babylonians such great prosperity, and that therefore both peoples should be placed in a different category and treated differently.

units.la: Nonne fuisti ab initio Iehovah Deus meus, Sancte meus? non moriemur, o Iehovah: ut iudicium facias, posuisti illum: & fortem ut increpares, fundasti eum.
units.tr: Art thou not from everlasting, O Jehovah my God, my Holy One? We shall not die, O Jehovah: thou hast appointed them for judgement, and thou hast established them as a rock to chastise.

units.la: In hoc versu Enthymemata duo occurrunt: quorum alterum ducitur à sanctificatione & segregatione populi Israelitici, alterum à destinato Dei in Chaldaeis excitandis. Nos Syllogismis integris utemur, ut omnia sint planiora.
units.tr: Two enthymemes occur in this verse. One is drawn from the sanctification and separation of the Israelite people; the other from God's purpose to raise up the Chaldeans. We shall use complete syllogisms, so that everything may be clearer.

units.la: I. ARGUMENTUM HABACUCI, DUCTUM à segregatione Israelitarum à caeteris Gentibus idololatricis.
units.tr: I. THE ARGUMENT OF HABAKKUK, DRAWN FROM THE SEPARATION OF THE ISRAELITES FROM THE OTHER IDOLATROUS NATIONS.

units.la: Reuocauerat Dominus Deus Seruum suum ad aliarum Gentium fata consideranda: & quidem eo consilio, ut disceret, non Iudæorum tantùm, sed etiam aliarum Gentium calamitates, sibi esse commiseratione prosequendas: ut est uidere vers.5. Videre in gentibus, &c.
units.tr: The Lord God had called his servant to consider the fates of the other nations, and indeed with this purpose: that he might learn that the calamities not only of the Jews but also of the other nations were to be met with compassion, as is seen in verse 5, "Behold among the nations, etc."

units.la: Etsi autem ex hac oratione Domini Dei sui colligere poterat Habacuc Propheta, Gentium, quæ versarentur in tenebris ignorantiæ & in umbra mortis, ac destituerentur omni solatio, tristissimam sortem potius esse miserandam, quàm Iudæorum, qui cum haberent legem & Prophetas, nihilominus peccaverunt, & suis delictis tanta mala sibi accersiverant: tamen doloris sensus, quem amor erga populum Dei acuebat, eò perpulit hominem, ut in hunc modum argumentaretur:
units.tr: Although Habakkuk the Prophet could from this speech of the Lord his God gather that the nations, which lived in the darkness of ignorance and in the shadow of death and were deprived of all comfort, were rather the more wretched and deserved more pity in their most miserable lot than the Jews, who, though they had the law and the Prophets, nevertheless sinned and had brought such evils upon themselves by their own offences, yet the feeling of grief, which his love for the people of God sharpened, drove the man to argue in this way:

units.la: Non est eum ad modum duriter tracta da gens sancta, quemadmodum profanæ & idololatricæ gentes. Ratio 1. Nam alioquin nihil interesse uidebitur inter populum quem sibi ut peculiarem acqui siuit Deus, & inter ἀθέοις[?] in mundo. Plurimùm autem inter illos interest. 2. Et uiderentur inanes esse promissiones pijs factæ, Leuitici 26. Deuteron. 28. quarum summam complexi sunt, Paulus hoc dulcissimo dicto: Pietas ad omnia utilis est, ut quæ promissionem habeat vitæ præ-sentis & futuræ: 1 Tim.4.8. & Dauid toto Psalmo 112.
units.tr: A holy nation ought not to be treated as harshly as the profane and idolatrous nations. Reason 1: for otherwise there would seem to be no difference between the people whom God acquired for himself as his peculiar people and the atheists [ἀθέοις] in the world. Yet there is very much difference between them. 2: And the promises made to the godly would seem to be empty, Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28, the sum of which Paul embraced in that sweetest saying: "Godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come," 1 Timothy 4:8, and David in the whole of Psalm 112.

units.la: Atqui Iudæi sunt gens illa sancta, seu segregata à colluuie cæterarum gentium idola colentium.
units.tr: But the Jews are that holy nation, that is, set apart from the filth of the other nations that worship idols.

units.la: Quare non ita duriter tractandi erant Iudæi, ut aliæ gentes impiæ & idololatricæ.
units.tr: Therefore the Jews were not to be treated as harshly as the other impious and idolatrous nations.

units.la: Minorem probat ipsius Dei testimonio, quod ardente zelo, hoc erotemate re quirit: Nonne tu fuisti ab initio Iehouah Deus meus, & Sancte meus? non moriemur. Sententia est:
units.tr: He proves the minor premise by the testimony of God himself, whom he questions with burning zeal: "Art thou not from the beginning Jehovah my God, and my Holy One? We shall not die." The sense is this:

units.la: Quorum Deus & sanctus est ipsemet Iehouah, illi certè sunt gens sancta. Iuxta illud: Beatus populus, cuius Iehouah est Deus. Psal.144.15.
units.tr: Those whose God and Holy One is Jehovah himself are certainly a holy nation, according to that saying: "Blessed is the people whose God is Jehovah," Psalm 144:15.

units.la: Atqui Iudæorum Deus & sanctus est Iehouah. Secundum hæc dicta: Quando hæreditates distribuit Excelsus Gentibus, quando separauit filios hominum, statuit terminos populorum secundum numerum filiorum Israëlis. Portio enim Iehouæ est populus eius, Iacob sors hæreditatis eius. Deut.32.8.9. Item: Agnoscitur in Iudæa Deus, in Israel magnum est nomen eius. Conditum est in Salem tabernaculū eius,& habitatio eius in Sion. Psal.76.1.2. Item: Annunciauit uerbum suum Iacobo, staruta sua & iudicia sua Israeli. Non fecit ita cuilibet genti: & iudicia eius alij nō nouerunt. Psal.47.19.20.
units.tr: But Jehovah is the God and the Holy One of the Jews. According to these words: "When the Most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of men, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel. For Jehovah's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance," Deuteronomy 32:8, 9. Likewise: "God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. His tabernacle also is in Salem, and his dwelling place in Zion," Psalm 76:1, 2. Likewise: "He declared his word to Jacob, his statutes and his judgements to Israel. He has not dealt so with any nation; and as for his judgements, they have not known them," Psalm 147:19, 20.

units.la: Iudaei itaque sunt gens sancta.
units.tr: Therefore the Jews are a holy nation.

units.la: Responsio:
units.tr: Answer:

units.la: Ad Maiorem prosyllogismi: Est paralogismus à dicto secundū quid, ad simpliciter dictum. Populus Dei non ita duriter tractandus est ut cæteræ profanæ gentes, [illegible, ~6 letters] si uidelicet officium in timore Dei faciat, nō autem si propter eius scelera nomē Dei inter gentes male audiat. Licebit autē κατὰ βλασφημίαν[?] retorquere, in hūc modum: Immò si populus Dei peccet, durius est tractandus quàm cæteri populi, qui sunt expertes Dei, & ignari uoluntatis illius. Etenim seruus qui nouit uoluntatem Domini sui, nec se comparauit, nec fecit ex uoluntate eius, cædetur plagis multis. Qui uerò non nouit, & fecit digna plagis, cædetur plagis paucis. Lucæ 12.47.48.
units.tr: To the major premise of the prosyllogism: there is a paralogism from a statement qualified in a certain respect to a statement taken absolutely. The people of God is not to be treated as harshly as the other profane nations, [illegible], namely if it performs its duty in the fear of God, but not if on account of its wickedness the name of God is ill spoken of among the nations. It will nevertheless be allowed to turn the argument back by way of reproach [κατὰ βλασφημίαν] in this manner: indeed, if the people of God sins, it is to be treated more severely than the other peoples who are strangers to God and ignorant of his will. For the servant who knows the will of his lord, and neither prepares himself nor acts according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who does not know it, and does things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. Luke 12:47, 48.

units.la: Ad rationem primam respondetur, q̄ in ea sit fallacia secundum non causam ut caussam. Non enim civilia & temporaria bona & commoda, sunt praecipua nota, populum Dei à filiis huius seculi discernes: sed adoptio, & eius arrhabo Spiritus sanctus, ac huius χαρίσματα[?].
units.tr: To the first reason it is answered that there is in it a fallacy of non-cause taken as cause. For civil and temporal goods and advantages are not the chief marks by which you distinguish the people of God from the sons of this age; rather it is adoption, and the Holy Spirit as its pledge, and his gifts [χαρίσματα].

units.la: Ad rationem secundam respondetur, ꝙ[?] pietas habeat amplissimas promissiones, sed cum exceptione de cruce, quae conformes Christo facit, seu quę nostrae cum Christo capite συμμορφώσεως[?] pars quaedam est.
units.tr: To the second reason it is answered that piety has very ample promises, but with the exception of the cross, which makes us conformed to Christ, or which is a certain part of our conformity [συμμορφώσεως] with Christ our head.

units.la: Ad Minorem respondetur, quòd ea vera sit de Judaeis iis qui sunt in spiritu tales, & in occulto, & quorum laus ex Deo est, non ex hominibus: Roman. 2. 29. non aut in genere de omnibus Judaeis, quorum multi in manifesto solùm Judei erant, ob carnis circumcisionem: qui cum legis essent transgressores, circumcisio eorum facta est praeputium: Rom. 2. 25. id est, pro incircumcisis merito sunt habiti. Quis autem intelligens dicat, hosce veros Abrahae filios & promissionum cohortes esse?
units.tr: To the minor premise it is answered that it is true of those Jews who are such in spirit and in secret, and whose praise is from God, not from men, Romans 2:29; not however as a statement about all Jews in general, many of whom were Jews only outwardly, by the circumcision of the flesh; who, since they were transgressors of the law, their circumcision was made uncircumcision, Romans 2:25, that is, they were rightly regarded as uncircumcised. But who that understands would say that these are the true sons of Abraham and heirs of the promises?

units.la: Praxis.
units.tr: Practice.

units.la: Quatus sit huius argumenti rectè perpensi usus, ex eo colligi potest, quòd illud nobis quoq; cum Habacuco Propheta commune est. Quotus enim quisque nostrûm est, qui Ecclesiæ & totius & singulorū piorū calamitates intuens, nō ita argumentetur:
units.tr: How far this argument is rightly weighed and applied can be gathered from the fact that it is shared by us too, along with the Prophet Habakkuk. For how few of us are there who, looking at the calamities of the whole Church and of each of the godly, do not reason in this way:

units.la: Non æquū est, sic tractari homines fi-deles, luce Euangelij illustratos, & eius propagandi studiosos, ut Pontificios aliósue osores doctrinæ Euangelicæ.
units.tr: It is not right that faithful men, enlightened by the light of the Gospel and eager to spread it, should be treated as the Papists and other enemies of the Evangelical doctrine treat them.

units.la: Nos uero sideles sumus, luce Euange-lij illustrati, ac doctrinæ lampadem per manus tradere posteris constitutum ha-bemus.
units.tr: Yet we are faithful, enlightened by the light of the Gospel, and we are resolved to hand down the lamp of doctrine to posterity.

units.la: Quare non æquum esse uidetur, ut cō-munibus malis, publicè grassantibus, & quæ idolomania meretur & accersit, ipsi quoque inuoluamur.
units.tr: Therefore it seems unjust that we should also be caught up in the common evils that rage publicly, and that idolatry deserves and brings upon us.

units.la: Atqui, si rem rectè reputauerimus, idē ferè de nobis dici posse animaduertemus, quod de Iudæis Paulus pronuncia-uit, Rom.2.v.17. & sequentibus. Quor-sum autem attinet de Euangelio, de fide, de excusso Antichristi iugo gloriari, cum interim fructus pœnitentia dignos non proferentes, Deum turpi nostra uita dedecoremus? Proderit quidem nobis E-uangelium, proderunt & Sacramenta, si fide per charitatem agete, Dei nomé san-ctificauerimus: at si Deum nos sci[?]pro-fesi[?] fessi fuerimus, factis autem (quod absit) negauerimus, reuera ἀνόμοι[?] habebimur, abominandi, rebelles, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi. Rom.1.25. Tit.1.16.
units.tr: But if we weigh the matter rightly, we will notice that much the same can be said of us as Paul said of the Jews, Rom. 2.17 and following. For what does it profit us to boast of the Gospel, of faith, and of having shaken off the yoke of Antichrist, while we do not bear fruits worthy of repentance and dishonour God by our shameful lives? The Gospel will indeed profit us, and the sacraments too, if we sanctify the name of God by faith working through love. But if we profess God with our lips and deny him by our deeds (which God forbid), we shall in truth be counted [ἀνόμοι] lawless, abominable, rebellious, and reprobate for every good work. Rom. 1.25; Tit. 1.16.

units.la: Porrò, quòd fideles sumus, quòd incorruptam Euangelij doctrinam profitemur, quòd è Babylone occidentali egressi, ex cufsimus Antichristi iugum: id uerò non ut meritum nostrum, sed ut gratuitum Dei donum nobis allegare licet. Actum abest ut donorum caussa, immunitatem à miseriis, quas nostris peccatis perinde accersiuimus, ut Cæcias accersere solet nubes, requirere debeamus: ut etiam multò maiores poenas promeritos nos esse, quàm alios Dei ignaros, fateri nos oporteat. Nisi forte putare conuenit, æquum esse, ut Deus nihil reliquum faciat nobis ornandis & exhilarandis, qualescunq; tandem ipsi interim simus: & etiamsi non Spiritu duci, sed secundum carnem ambulare malimus.
units.tr: Moreover, the fact that we are faithful, that we profess the uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel, and that we have gone out of western Babylon and cast off the yoke of Antichrist, these we may indeed plead, but not as our merit; they are the free gift of God to us. Far be it that, on account of these gifts, we should demand immunity from the miseries which we bring upon ourselves by our sins, just as a cloud brings on the darkness. Indeed we must confess that we have deserved far greater punishments than others who are ignorant of God. Unless perhaps it is fitting to think it right that God should do nothing more than adorn and gladden us, whatever we ourselves are meanwhile, even if we would rather not be led by the Spirit but walk according to the flesh.

units.la: Vt semel huic errori occurramus, fate-amur id quod res est, nos multò grauio-res poenas promeritos esse: & cum Dauì-de, Deo soli gloriā dantes, dicamus: Non secundum peccata nostra fecit nobis: ne-que quæ secundum iniquitates nostras repe-dit super nos. Psal.103.10.
units.tr: So that we may once for all meet this error, let us confess what is the truth: that we have deserved far heavier punishments. And with David, giving glory to God alone, let us say: He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. Psalm 103.10.

units.la: 2. ARGVMENTVM HABACVCI, à destinato Iehouæ excitantis Chaldæos.
units.tr: 2. THE ARGUMENT OF HABAKKUK: concerning the Chaldeans, raised up by the appointed purpose of Jehovah.

units.la: Est in uerbis Prophetæ primùm προλογία[?]: Tu uerò, ô Iehouah, posuisti & fundasti hostes Chaldæos, & eorum Monarcham Nebucadnezarem. Hoc est: Tu potentiæ & successuum quibus fruuntur Babylonij, auctor es. deinde, ἀντιστροφὴ[?]: Sed tamen ad iudicium posuisti Nebucadnezarem, & ut increpares multos Reges & populos superbos, fundasti eum: nō autem ut sit nostræ internecionis administer.
units.tr: In the words of the Prophet there is first the [προλογία] preface: But you, O Jehovah, have appointed and established the Chaldean enemies and their king Nebuchadnezzar. That is: you are the author of the power and the successes which the Babylonians enjoy. Then comes the [ἀντιστροφὴ] reply: Yet you have appointed Nebuchadnezzar for judgment, and you have established him to rebuke many kings and proud peoples; but not so that he may be the minister of our destruction.

units.la: Sic autē argumentatur Habacuc Pro-pheta:
units.tr: Habakkuk the Prophet argues as follows:

units.la: Aliud est seruire Deo ad iudicium, aliud non seruare inculpatæ animaduersionis moderamen, sed sæuire & grassari, belluæ in morem, in uictos ac prostratos. Hæc Maior probatur ab exemplo Dei, cui insistere eius συμφυΐς[?] decet. 1.Cor.11. 31. Etenim si nosipsos dijudicaremus, nō puniremur. 32. Sed cum punimur, à Domino erudimur,ne cum mundo cõdem-nemur.
units.tr: To serve God for judgment is one thing; not to keep within the bounds of blameless correction, but to rage and rampage like a beast against the conquered and the prostrate, is another. The major premise is proved from the example of God, whose [συμφυΐς] nature it is right to imitate. 1 Cor. 11.31: For if we judged ourselves, we would not be punished. 32: But when we are punished, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we are not condemned with the world.

units.la: Atqui Deus suo iudicio castigationem nostram respondere, non autem nos mori vult.
units.tr: But God wills that our chastisement answer to his judgment, and not that we perish.

units.la: Itaque cum Chaldaei in eo sint ut nos perdant, nō Dei iudicio seruiunt, sed suae ipsorum sæuitiæ & immanitati indulgēt. Et per consequens, commiseratione dignisimus, qui pro paterna castigatione grauisimas pœnas luimus.
units.tr: Therefore, since the Chaldeans are intent on destroying us, they do not serve the judgment of God, but indulge their own savagery and cruelty. And consequently, we who pay the most grievous penalties for a fatherly chastisement are most worthy of pity.

units.la: Minorem [illegible, ~8 letters] Propheta expo-suit, eo Dei nomine usurpato, quod monet nos per ipsum esse, viuere & moveri: Act.17.28. Non moriemur, ô Iehouah: ut iudicium facias, posuisti illum: & fortem ut increpares, fundasti eum.
units.tr: The Prophet set out the minor premise, using the name of God by which he warns us that we live, move and have our being in him: Acts 17.28. We shall not die, O Jehovah. That you might execute judgment, you have appointed him; and that he might rebuke, you have established him as strong. [illegible]

units.la: Quid in hoc argumento nobis cen-ses observandum?
units.tr: What do you think we should observe in this argument?

units.la: Non uno modo etiam pios, in afflictionum phrontisterio sudates & laborates, errare, cum suis imaginationibus, quas doloris sensus acuit, nimium indulgent: & quidem Dei, suisipsorum & hostium respectu.
units.tr: Not only in one way, even the godly, labouring and toiling in the school of afflictions, go astray, indulging too much in their own imaginations, which the sense of pain sharpens; and indeed they do so with regard to God, to themselves and to their enemies.

units.la: Primum enim, quid magis erroneum, quàm fingere, Deo conniuente fieri; ut
units.tr: For first, what is more mistaken than to imagine that things happen with God's connivance,

units.la: ea etiam, quæ ipse fieri simpliciter nolit, euenant: sicut, cum ipse ἀδικούμενος suos explorare constitutum habeat, eius administri τιμωρίαν infligant?
units.tr: so that even those things which he does not simply wish to happen come about; as when, although he himself, being wronged, intends to test his people, his ministers inflict vengeance?

units.la: Secundò, errant & sibijpsis nimium blandiuntur, cum qualem animaduersionem peccata postulent, sese rectissimè intelligere putant, ac speciem afflictionum leuissimam sibijpsis decernunt: indignè interim ferentes, si secus quàm sitipsi ui sum, tractentur.
units.tr: Secondly, they go wrong, and flatter themselves too much, when they think they understand most rightly what kind of punishment their sins deserve, and decree for themselves a very light form of affliction; meanwhile they bear it with indignation if they are treated otherwise than they themselves wish.

units.la: Postremò, nimium tribuunt potentiæ & licentiæ humanæ, cùm nullis metis diuinitùs eam coherceri, stultè opinantur. Item, cùm administris castigationis diuinæ sic irascuntur, ac si abillis solis animaduersio profecta, & in ipsorum arbitrio posita esset.
units.tr: Lastly, they foolishly suppose that human power and licence are too great, when they are restrained by no limits from God. Likewise, when they grow angry at the ministers of divine chastisement, as if the punishment came from them alone and lay in their power.

units.la: Vt ex istorum errorum labyrinthis euadamus, firmiter nobis persuadeamus, nihil sine Patre cœlesti nobis euenire: minus, quàm pro malis nostris meritis, nobiscum agi: hostes piorum nihil nisi determinante & permittente Deo, efficere posse: denique, cùm Domino uiuamus & moriamur, nihil triste nobis accidere, etiamsi ad Domini gloriam, à scelestissimis mis hostibus circumuentis perinde fit oc cumbendum in carcere, ut olim Ioanni Baptistae: Matth.14.10.
units.tr: So that we may escape the labyrinths of these errors, let us firmly persuade ourselves that nothing happens to us without our heavenly Father; that we are dealt with less than our evil deserts; that the enemies of the godly can accomplish nothing except by God's determination and permission; and finally, that since we live and die to the Lord, nothing sad befalls us, even if, for the Lord's glory, we must die in prison, surrounded by the most wicked enemies, as once happened to John the Baptist: Matt. 14.10.

units.la: Porro, nimium sane nobis placemus, cum vexari ab ijs nolumus, qui ingenio, eruditione, usu rerum, meritis in Rempub. & Ecclesiam, nobis & multis aliis inferiores videntur. Non tam enim, quales & q̄ multi sint, qui nos affligunt: quam quis nos in eorum manus tradiderit, spectemus: praestolantes interim εὐδοκίαν diuinitus determinatam.
units.tr: Moreover, we surely please ourselves too much when we are unwilling to be troubled by those who seem to us inferior to us in talent, learning, experience in affairs, and services to the commonwealth and the Church. For we should look not so much at how great and how many are those who afflict us, as at who has handed us into their hands, waiting meanwhile for the good pleasure [εὐδοκίαν] divinely determined.

units.la: Consideremus etiam, quid olim ferendum fuerit summis viris, qui cum diversis extremis luctati sunt: & quid hac ętate multis sanctis & doctissimis viris perferendum sit. Mihi sane nunquam non in recenti memoria est Eusebij narratio de Iustino Martyre & Philosopho, qui quod saepius Crescenti Cynico, φιλονόμῳ[?], non Philosopho, os obturaret, pro veritatis patrocinio martyrij munus tandem recepit. Exstant Iustini verba μαρτυρία[?] de morte, apud Eusebium Ecclesiast. historiae libro 4. cap. 16. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐν προσάπῳ[?] ὑπό τινος τῶν ὀνομασμένων[?] ἐπιβαλόντων, καὶ ξύλῳ συντεταγμένη[?] ἡ ὑπὸ Κρησκεντῆ[?] τῆς φιλοσόφου ἡ φιλονει[?]
units.tr: Let us also consider what was once to be endured by the greatest men, who struggled with various extremes, and what must be endured now by many holy and most learned men. For me, the account in Eusebius of Justin Martyr, the philosopher, is always fresh in memory: because Crescens the Cynic, a lover of gain and no philosopher, kept trying to silence him, he at last received the reward of martyrdom in defence of the truth. Justin's own words about his death survive in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 16. (The Greek of the passage is too corrupt in the scan to be reproduced reliably here.)

units.la: πν. ὁ γὰρ φιλόσοφος εἰπεῖν ἄξιον τὸν ἀνδρα, ὃς ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ ἐπιγαμεῖν ἀνυποσίᾳ λακτα̣μαρτυρεῖ, ὡς ἀ-ξίων λαὶ ἀσεβῶν χρυσίων οὔσων, πρὸς χαρὶν λαὶ κλοβλῶν τῶν πολλῶν τῶν μεπηλαρνηλαλίων τὸ ἀ-ρατ-τομ,&c. Habet enim haec aetas nimis multos Crescentes ἀθεοκόγες, qui p hierophantis sycophantas agunt, quorum umbra bonis obest. Horum alij Monarcharum crudelitate & authoritate abutuntur, ad opinionum suarum monstra asserenda & orbi obtrudenda: alij sinonio artificio idem moliuntur, bonum malum, malum bonum dicunt, prout ipsis commodum uidetur: utrique acerbissime inuehuntur in ueritatis amantes. Sed uidet & iudicat haec omnia Dominus, cui soli Ecclesiae defensionem, & assertionem incorruptae doctrinae Euangelij, & mirandas Seruorum Dei defensiones & liberationes, acceptas feremus.
units.tr: For the man deserves to be called a philosopher who, because he would not be silenced by the ... of Crescens, bore witness to the truth... [the remainder of the Greek quotation is too corrupt in the scan to render]. For this age has far too many Crescenses, godless contrivers who play the sycophant in the guise of hierophants, and whose shadow harms the good. Some of them abuse the cruelty and authority of rulers to assert the monsters of their own opinions and to thrust them upon the world; others, by a sly art, attempt the same, calling good evil and evil good, as suits them. Both attack with the greatest bitterness those who love the truth. But the Lord sees and judges all these things, to whom alone we shall ascribe the defence of the Church, the assertion of the uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel, and the wonderful defences and deliverances of the servants of God.

units.la: VERSVS XIII.
units.tr: VERSE 13.

units.la: Tu, cum sis mundus oculis, ut non cernas malum, & aspicere prauitatem non possis: ut quid respicis contemtores, & taces, disperdente impio iustiorem se?
units.tr: Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look upon iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon them that deal treacherously, and holdest thy tongue when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?

units.la: Initiô, epitheta Dei & phrafes expo-nam : deinde fubiungâ Syllogismos 3 & 4. ut τρόπος ϖαῤῥήσιας à nobis obseruetur.
units.tr: First I will explain the epithets of God and the phrases, and then add syllogisms 3 and 4, so that the manner of bold speech [tropos parrhēsias] may be observed by us.

units.la: 1. Mudus oculis,Deus hoc loco dicitur, qῒ sit ufqueadeo καθαρός, & alienus ab omni labe & impuritate, ut ne quidē ferat in conspectu suo scelerum sordes. Talis etiā esse dicitur noster Pontifex Christus Iesus, ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν. Heb.7.26. Nos mundo corde esse decet, ut Deum uidere possimus. Matth.5.8.
units.tr: 1. God is called "pure of eyes" here, because he is so utterly pure [katharos] and free from every stain and impurity that he cannot even bear the filth of sins in his sight. Our High Priest, Christ Jesus, is also said to be such: "holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners" [hosios, akakos, amiantos, kechōrismenos apo tōn hamartōlōn]. Heb. 7.26. We ought to be pure in heart, that we may be able to see God. Matt. 5.8.

units.la: 2. Deus dicitur non cernere malum,id est,non adprobare, non ad illud προσωπολημψίας conniuere: sic ut in alijs ferat, in alijs autē ulciscatur malitiam, & eius esse stus. Omniscientiam autē diuinam nec bona, nec mala fugere, extra controuersiam est. Phrasi Hebraea cernere dicitur Deus bona,quæ probat: nō cernere mala,quæ odio habet. Zach.8.17.Et quisque m『alum proximi sui ne cogitetis in cordibus uestris, atque iuramentum mendax ne diligatis: omnia enim ista sunt quæ odi, dixit Iehouah.
units.tr: 2. God is said not to behold evil, that is, not to approve it, nor to connive at it through partiality [prosōpolēmpsia], so that he tolerates it in some but avenges wickedness and judges it in others. That divine omniscience escapes neither good nor evil is beyond dispute. In Hebrew idiom God is said to "behold" the good, which he approves, and not to "behold" the evil, which he hates. Zech. 8.17: "And let none of you imagine evil against his neighbour in your hearts, and love no false oath: for all these are things that I hate, saith Jehovah."

units.la: 3. De Deo dicitur,quòd nō possit aspicere prauitates. Id non intelligatur de ἀ- k 3 Ἰωαἀνομίας[?], quæ nullo modo locum habet in Deo: sed de ἀδοξίας[?]. Iuxta illud: Quoniam non es Deus, qui delectetur impietate: non morabitur apud te malus. Non consistent gloriabundi coram oculis tuis: odisti omnes operantes iniquitatem. Perdes loquentes mendacium. Virum sanguinū & doli abominatur Iehouah. Psal-mo 5.4.5.6.
units.tr: 3. It is said of God that he cannot look upon wickedness. This is not to be understood of lawlessness [anomia], which has no place in God, but of dishonour [adoxia]. In line with that: "For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee. The foolish shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity. Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man." Psalm 5.4-6.

units.la: 4. Idem dicitur respicere contemtores & tacere, cum nō statim sua fulmina mittit, sed differt pœnas. Intelligatur itaque hæc phrasis nō de re ipsa, sed de sensu humano. Neque enim Deus contemtores respicit, & ipsorum lingua perambulante terram, semper tacet: sed suo tempore contemtores punit, & impura eorum ora obstruit. Tandem enim exsurgit Iehouah in ira sua, & exaltatur contra furorem eorum qui sunt inimici piorū hominum: & evigilat ad iudicium quodipse mandavit. Psal.7.6.
units.tr: 4. The same is said of looking upon contemners and keeping silence, when he does not at once send forth his thunderbolts but defers punishment. This phrase, therefore, is to be understood not of the thing itself but of human perception. For God does not look upon contemners with approval, nor is he always silent while their tongues walk through the earth. Rather, in his own time he punishes the contemners and stops their impure mouths. For at last the LORD arises in his anger and is exalted against the fury of those who are enemies of godly men, and he awakes to the judgment he himself has commanded. Psalm 7.6.

units.la: 5. Impius iustiorem se perdere dicitur, non respectu παραλείψεως[?]: neque enim tantum improbis permittit Dominus: sed respectu finis, cuius gratia adversus probos insurgunt. Concipiunt enim iniquitatem,& pregnantes sunt dolore, sed pariunt reminanem: Puteum fodiut,& effodiunt eum: & caduntin foueam quam fecerunt. Reuertitur molestia eorum in capita eorum. Psal.7.14.15.16.
units.tr: 5. The wicked is said to destroy one more righteous than himself, not with respect to passing over [paraleipsis], for the Lord does not merely permit this to the wicked, but with respect to the end for which they rise against the upright. For they conceive iniquity and are pregnant with trouble, but they bring forth falsehood. They dig a pit and dig it out, and fall into the ditch they have made. Their mischief returns upon their own heads. Psalm 7.14-16.

units.la: 3. ARGVMENTVM HABACVCI, à natura Dei summè munda & iusta.
units.tr: 3. ARGUMENT OF HABAKKUK, from the nature of God, supremely pure and just.

units.la: Quicunque est summè purus ab omni contagione mali, is non potest ferre con spectum eius quod malum est, & impro-borum hominum. Sunt enim ei ἐν ἀλλαμέ-τρῳ[?] repugnantia ἐχθρώματα[?]: quæ ut ille non probat, ita quoque non fert, cum sit omnipotens & sanctissimus.
units.tr: Whoever is supremely pure from every contagion of evil cannot bear the sight of what is evil, or of wicked men. For there are to him enmities [echthrōmata] that are repugnant beyond all measure: as he does not approve them, so he does not endure them, since he is almighty and most holy.

units.la: Iehouah autem Deus ille noster est pu-rus ab omni contagione & labe mali: ac vult nos quoq; sanctos esse, quemadmo-dum ipse quoq; sanctus est.
units.tr: But Jehovah, that God of ours, is pure from every contagion and stain of evil, and he wills that we too be holy, just as he himself is holy.

units.la: Non igitur ferre potest tu id quod est malum, tum malignos homines.
units.tr: Therefore he cannot bear what is evil, nor wicked men.

units.la: Et per consequens, quiddam à natura sua alienum facit, cum improbos istos Ba-bylonios impune grassari, & in nos sæui-re patitur.
units.tr: And consequently he does something foreign to his own nature when he allows those wicked Babylonians to rage with impunity and suffers them to rage against us.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Etsi totum argumentum uerum est,ta-men in consequente subsumto paralo-gismus gismus est παρὰ τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον. Neq; enim à natura Dei, qui summè iustus & purus est, alienum censeri debet, si differat poenas fontium, & mala fieri permittat: cum idem sit longanimis, & summè sapiens, ut qui malis bene nouerit uti ad probandos pios & plectendos impios, ac cum est opportunum, suos liberare, & impios perdere possit.
units.tr: Although the whole argument is true, the minor premise contains a paralogism: "treating what is not the cause as if it were the cause" [para to mē aition hōs aition]. For it ought not to be judged foreign to the nature of God, who is most just and pure, if he defers the punishments of the wicked and permits evils to happen; since he is at once long-suffering and most wise, knowing well how to use evils to prove the godly and to punish the impious, and when it is fitting he can free his own people and destroy the ungodly.

units.la: Neque uero, quia copia benignitatis, tolerantiae, lenitatis & benignitatis suae Deus ad refipiscentiam deducit, Roman.2.4. & differt poenas in id usq; tempus, quod praestituit executioni iudiciorum suorum: ideo minus iustu & purum sese praestat. Est enim ἀρμονία [?] iusticiae & sanctitatis & longanimitatis diuinae tanta, ut non pugnent inter se haec Dei attributa.
units.tr: Nor, because God by the riches of his goodness, forbearance, gentleness and kindness leads men to repentance (Rom. 2.4), and defers punishment until the very time he has appointed for the execution of his judgments, does he thereby show himself less just and pure. For the harmony of justice, holiness and divine long-suffering is so great that these attributes of God do not contend with one another.

units.la: Nec etiam sic erga improbos iustum se esse declarat, erga pios autem misericordem, ut ad horum grauia παραπτώματα cq [?] niueat. Multis sanè modis, tota sua uita, Dauid Rex Dei sui benignitatem est expertus: sed idem grauiter delinquens, eundem iustum esse sensit. Idem de caeteris Sanctis statuendum est.
units.tr: Nor does he show himself just towards the wicked, and merciful towards the godly, in such a way that he winks at their grave transgressions. Indeed, David the king of God had many experiences of his God's kindness throughout his whole life; yet when he sinned grievously, he felt that the same God was just. The same must be held concerning the other saints.

units.la: ARGVMENTVM HABACVCI, AB ἀντιθέσι[?] hominum iustorum & iniustorum.
units.tr: THE ARGUMENT OF HABAKKUK, FROM THE ANTITHESIS OF RIGHTEOUS AND UNRIGHTEOUS MEN [ἀντιθέσεως].

units.la: Argumenti sedes in his uerbis posita est: Vt quid respicis contemtores, & taces, disperdente impio iustiorem se?
units.tr: The seat of the argument is laid down in these words: "Why do you look upon the scorners and keep silent, while the wicked man destroys one more righteous than himself?"

units.la: παραφολογία[?]: Fateor Iudaeos graviter & saepius deliquisse, quàm par esset Dei populum peccare.
units.tr: Paralogy [παραφολογία]: I admit that the Jews sinned grievously and often, more than was fitting for the people of God.

units.la: ἀναγωγὴ[?]: Sed tamen, quis nō statuat, iustiores & meliores esse Iudaeos profanis cōtemtoribus istis Babylonijs, qui cū impietate & horribili idolomania coniū xerunt immanem sæuitiam, eamq; belluino more exercent?
units.tr: Anagogy [ἀναγωγή]: Yet who would not judge that the Jews were more righteous and better than these profane scorners, the Babylonians, who joined immense savagery to impiety and horrible idolatry and practised it in a beastly manner?

units.la: Res est indigna & iniqua, iustiores opprimi ab impijs.
units.tr: It is an unworthy and unjust thing for the more righteous to be oppressed by the wicked.

units.la: Sed Iudæi iustiores sunt impijs Chaldæis.
units.tr: But the Jews are more righteous than the wicked Chaldeans.

units.la: Quare indigna & iniqua est illorum sors.
units.tr: Therefore their lot is unworthy and unjust.

units.la: Responsio κατὰ βίωμ[?].
units.tr: Response, against force [κατὰ βίαν].

units.la: Iustum & æquum est, durius eos tractari seruos, qui sciunt Domini uoluntatem, nec tamen eam faciunt: Luc.12.42. & propter quos male audit nomen Dei inter Gentes: Rom.2.24. quàm eos, qui ignari & expertes sunt Dei in mundo: Eph.2.12.
units.tr: It is right and fair that those servants who know the Lord's will and yet do not do it should be treated more severely (Luke 12:42), and those on whose account the name of God is ill spoken of among the nations (Rom. 2:24), than those who are ignorant of God and have no share in him in the world (Eph. 2:12).

units.la: Vos autem Iudæi[?],Dei voluntatem vos scire, Chaldaeos vero eius ignaros esse, gloriamini.
units.tr: But you Jews boast that you know the will of God and that the Chaldeans are ignorant of it.

units.la: Quare gravi ore poena vos afficiendos esse, certissimum est.
units.tr: Therefore it is most certain that you must be punished with a heavy hand.

units.la: Quis est huius quarti Argumenti usus?
units.tr: What is the use of this fourth argument?

units.la: Usus argumenti istius, si illud recte dis-soluatur, positus est in vera cognitione i-storum axiomatum.
units.tr: The use of this argument, if it is rightly resolved, lies in a true knowledge of the following axioms.

units.la: 1. Omne bonum, quia nobis confertur divinitus, est gratuitum. Rom.ii.35. Quis prior dedit illi, & reddetur ei?
units.tr: 1. Every good, since it is conferred on us by God, is a gift of grace. Rom. 11:35: "Who has first given to him, that it should be repaid to him?"

units.la: 2. Mala, quibus interdum laboramus, meritis nostris debentur. Hoc elegante inductione probat totus Psal.107.
units.tr: 2. The evils with which we are sometimes afflicted are owed to our merits. The whole of Psalm 107 proves this by an elegant induction.

units.la: 3. Sic tamen haec moderatur Deus, ut mala poenae nobis multo leniora sint, quam mala culpae. Psal.103.10. Non secundum peccata nostra fecit nobis, neque secundum iniquitates nostras retribuit nobis.
units.tr: 3. Yet God so moderates these things that the evils of punishment are far lighter for us than the evils of guilt. Psalm 103:10: "He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor rewarded us according to our iniquities."

units.la: 4. Praestat quenq; nostrum culpam sua agnoscere, quam odiosa cum nequioribus hominibus comparatione, venari nescio quam bonitatis umbram.
units.tr: 4. It is better for each of us to acknowledge his own fault than, by a hateful comparison with more wicked men, to hunt out I know not what shadow of goodness.

units.la: 5. Quomodocunq; autem Deus iustos & iniustos videatur tractare: nostrum tamen fuerit, eius iudicia adorare, & ab omni utilitigatione cum Deo abstinere. Nemo enim nostrūm Deo est à consilijs: Roman.11.34.
units.tr: 5. However God may seem to treat the righteous and the unrighteous, it is for us to adore his judgements and to abstain from all dispute with God. For none of us is a counsellor of God (Rom. 11:34).

units.la: VERSUS XIIII.
units.tr: VERSE 14.

units.la: Facisq; homines similes piscibus maris: similes reptili, cui non est dominator.
units.tr: And you make men like the fishes of the sea, like the creeping thing that has no ruler over it.

units.la: 5. ARGUMENTUM, à disparatis.
units.tr: 5. ARGUMENT, from dissimilar things.

units.la: Non eo modo agendum est cum hominibus, quo cum piscibus & reptilibus: nec concedendum, ut homines prępote-tes in cęteros ita posint sæuire, ut solent pisces maiores in minores grassari. Nam, ut præclarè apud Cedrenum Iustinus 2. Imperator loquitur: Si me à Deo putatis Imperatorem factum, eius auxilio imperare, parete iustis meis mandatis, & iniuria afficere pauperes definite. Solis namq; piscibus moris est, ut validior & maior devoret minorem. Quòd si meis præceptis non parere, sed in rapiędo ali-ena uestris obsequi uultis cupiditatibus, alium uobis uestro arbitratu deligite Im-peratorem. Ego enim contumacibus, in-iustis, ac aliena inuolantibus imperare nolo. Pagina Annalium 319.
units.tr: We ought not to act toward men as we do toward fishes and creeping things, nor should we allow powerful men to rage against others as larger fishes usually prey upon smaller ones. For, as Justin the Second, emperor, speaks well in Cedrenus: "If you think that I have been made emperor by God, to rule with his help, obey my just commands and cease to wrong the poor. For only fishes have the custom that the stronger and larger devours the smaller. But if you do not wish to obey my precepts, and rather wish to serve your desires by snatching what belongs to others, choose for yourselves another emperor according to your own judgement. For I do not wish to rule over the stubborn, the unjust, and those who rush upon what is another's." Page 319 of the Annals.

units.la: Ergo nō debebat Deus permittere, ut Chaldæi suam <bl>Θεομότητα</bl> ita erga nos exercerent, ac si essemus pisces, aut alia animantia bruta. Non enim homo homini lupus esse debet: nec etiam Dominus universorum improbis & immanibus hominibus, ueluti quibusdam <bl>Λυκανθρώποις</bl>, saeuiendi in pios licentiā concedere debet.
units.tr: Therefore God ought not to have permitted the Chaldeans to exercise their brutality [θηριότητα] against us as if we were fishes or other brute animals. For man ought not to be a wolf to man, and the Lord of all ought not to grant to wicked and savage men, as if they were werewolves [Λυκανθρώποις], licence to rage against the godly.

units.la: Censura istius Argumenti.
units.tr: Criticism of this argument.

units.la: Primùm obseruarii in eo debet scopus, cuius cōsideratio docebit esse Paralogismum <bl>παρὰ τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον.</bl> Non enim, quia iusto iudicio Deus populum suum, multiplicis transgressionis legis reū, tradit in manus Gentium idololatricarum castigandum & puniendum, ideo homines piscibus similes facit: sed potius iusta animaduersione suam seueritatē declarat, & quid <bl>ἀθέοις</bl> & Epicureis exspectā dum fit, docet. Etenim si Dei iudicium incipit à domo Dei, quis erit finis eorū qui non parent Euangelio Dei? 1.Pet.4.17.
units.tr: First, one must observe its aim, the consideration of which will show that it is a paralogism, a false cause treated as a true cause [παρὰ τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον]. For it is not because God, by a righteous judgement, hands over his people, guilty of many transgressions of the law, into the hands of idolatrous Gentiles to be chastised and punished, that he makes men like fishes. Rather, by just correction he declares his severity, and teaches what awaits atheists [ἀθέοις] and Epicureans. For if judgement begins at the house of God, what will be the end of those who do not obey the gospel of God? 1 Pet. 4:17.

units.la: Deinde, Sancti, cum sic argutantur, reuerentiæ Deo debitæ, & suæ conditionis, non satis sunt memores. Etenim nō ideo Deo ex aduerso respondendum erat, cum durius sibi tractari uidentur, car-nis nis inquam,non autem spiritus, iudicio. Illa enim tantum sua decora respicit: hic autem ad calculos revocat vitam anteactam, iubet agnoscere offensas & errata multiplicia. Ideo illa impatieter fert manum Domini: hic autem illud repetit: Iram Domini portabo, quia peccavi ei. Mich.7.9.
units.tr: Next, the saints, when they argue in this way, are not sufficiently mindful of the reverence owed to God and of their own condition. For they ought not to answer God back because they seem to be treated more harshly, I mean by the judgement of the flesh and not of the spirit. For the flesh looks only to its own honour; the spirit, on the other hand, calls the past life back to account and bids us acknowledge our offences and many errors. Therefore the one bears the hand of the Lord impatiently; the other repeats this: "I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him" (Mic. 7:9).

units.la: Abstineamus itaque ab omni indigna-tione ἡ μεμψιμοιρίας[?]: & fateamur, nos graviora meritos: nec in administros miseriarum nostrarum, sed in Deum nos castigatem respicientes, submittamus nos sub eius potenti manu. i.Pet.5.6.
units.tr: Let us therefore refrain from all indignation and complaint [μεμψιμοιρίας], and let us confess that we deserve worse; and, looking not to the ministers of our miseries but to God who chastens us, let us humble ourselves under his mighty hand (1 Pet. 5:6).

units.la: VERSUS XV.
units.tr: VERSE 15.

units.la: Omnes hamo suo extrahet, congregabit illos sagena sua, & cōgregabit eos reti suo: ob id lætabitur exultabitq;[?]
units.tr: He will draw them all up with his hook; he will gather them in his net, and collect them in his drag; therefore he will rejoice and exult.

units.la: Perstat in eadem imagine Propheta noster, ac prædicit, Nebucadnezarem, pis-catoris instar, armis velut hamo, & exer-cituum robore velut sagena, in potesta-tem suam redacturum piscium, id est gen-tium, incredibilem copiam: ac eundem nihil alienas miserias curantem, magno afficiendum gaudio, propter tantos successus &c uictorias. Utitur autem eadem similitudine Spiritus sanctus. Hierem.16. versu 16.
units.tr: Our Prophet keeps to the same image and foretells that Nebuchadnezzar, like a fisherman, will bring under his power, with his weapons as with a hook and with the strength of his armies as with a drag-net, an incredible multitude of fish, that is, of nations. He will also be filled with great joy, caring nothing for the miseries of others, because of such great successes and victories. The Holy Spirit uses the same comparison at Jeremiah 16:16.

units.la: 6. ARGVMENTVM, A NOCENDI cupiditate & ἐπιχαιρεκακίας[?] Chaldaeorum.
units.tr: 6. ARGUMENT: ON THE DESIRE TO HARM AND THE MALICIOUS JOY OF THE CHALDEANS.

units.la: Non debebat Deus laxare frena illis, qui nocendi cupidine impulsi, alios in nassam suam illicere, & modis omnibus ἐπιχαιρεκακίαι[?] esse solent.
units.tr: God ought not to have loosed the reins for those who, driven by the lust to harm, are wont to lure others into their snare and in every way to take malicious delight in them.

units.la: Tales autem sunt Chaldaei isti: quibus nihil magis placet, quàm Brenni uox thrasonica: Quid nisi uictis dolor? Non sunt suis contenti, sed alienis auidissimè inhiant, & ex alienis miserijs summa capiunt uoluptatem.
units.tr: Such are these Chaldeans. Nothing pleases them more than the boastful cry of Brennus: "What is there for the conquered but grief?" They are not content with their own things but greedily gape after the goods of others, and they take the greatest pleasure from the miseries of others.

units.la: Quare non debebat Deus frena ferocibus istis Chaldaeis laxare, sed potius retrahere & constringere. Hoc, scilicet, reliquum est, ut quid facto opus sit, Sancti Deo significent. Atqui nemo ei à consiliis fuit: nemo mentem eius cognouit. Rom.11.34.
units.tr: Therefore God ought not to loosen the reins for these fierce Chaldeans, but rather to hold them back and restrain them. This, of course, is what remains: that the saints should tell God what needs to be done. Yet no one was his counsellor; no one has known his mind. Rom. 11:34.

units.la: Quot modis pij sic argumentantes peccant?
units.tr: How many ways do the godly err in reasoning in this way?

units.la: Primùm in eo peccant, quòd ueluti futurorum praescij, quid sit euenturum, nimis audacter & scrupulosè colligunt. Secundò, quòd ex particularibus paucis τὸ καθόλου[?] colligunt. Nebucadnezarin manus suas traditos inhumaniter tractabit. Nemo igitur uim & seuitiam illius e-vitare poterit. Quasi verò Deus suorum fidelium reliquias non possit mirabili-ter seruare.
units.tr: First, they err in that, as if they were foreknowing what is to come, they conclude too boldly and minutely what is going to happen. Second, they draw a universal conclusion from a few particulars: "Those delivered into Nebuchadnezzar's hands he will treat inhumanly; therefore no one will be able to escape his violence and cruelty." As if God could not wondrously preserve the remnants of his faithful ones.

units.la: Tertiò, quòd seruitutis & captiuitatis malafic amplificant, ut interim spiritua-lium bonorum, quæ hostis eripere nequit, usufructu sibi non gratulentur. Vt si ueritatis testis, loco motus, exilij & pau-pertatis incommoda sic deploret, ut non interea cogitet, quantum sit ueritatis decus, & quàm sit honorificum, Christi causa contumelia affici, multari terrenis commodis.
units.tr: Third, they magnify the evils of servitude and captivity, so that in the meantime they do not rejoice in the use of spiritual goods, which the enemy cannot snatch away. For example, if a witness of the truth should so lament the inconveniences of removal, exile and poverty that he does not meanwhile consider how great is the glory of the truth, and how honourable it is to suffer disgrace and be deprived of earthly advantages for Christ's sake.

units.la: Quartò, quòd non satis perpendunt, sibi in uitæ huius militia spe gaudendū, & afflictiones tolerandas esse: Roman. 12.12. Nam si hoc semper cogitarent, non tantopere quererentur de ijs, quorum opera seruos suos tētare[?] & explorare Deo est visum.
units.tr: Fourth, they do not sufficiently weigh that in the warfare of this life they must rejoice in hope and bear afflictions: Rom. 12:12. For if they always thought of this, they would not complain so much about those by whose works God has seen fit to test and examine his servants.

units.la: Quintò, nō satis cogitant, præstare ἀλλὰ [illegible, ~12 letters]: atq; ideo commiseratione profequedos eos, qui sæuitia & scelerib. suis iram Dei & poenas æternas sibiipsis accersunt. Quid enim? An non miserrimi sunt, non qui Christi causa persecutionem sustinent, sed qui persequuntur pios, & revera pyraustæ gaudiu gaudent, afficiendi non multo post gehennæ tormentis?
units.tr: Fifth, they do not sufficiently consider that it is better [illegible]; and therefore one should pity with compassion those who by their cruelty and crimes bring upon themselves God's wrath and eternal punishments. For are not those most wretched who suffer persecution not for Christ's sake but who persecute the godly, and who, like the pyrausta, truly rejoice in their own gladness, soon to be consigned to the torments of hell?

units.la: ἘΠΙΧΑΙΡΕΚΑΚΙ᾽ΑΝ[?] HOSTIVM FOR-TITER piis esse ferendam, hæ causæ monent.
units.tr: THE MALICIOUS JOY OF ENEMIES IS TO BE BORNE BRAVELY BY THE PIOUS; these reasons advise it.

units.la: i. Quia nec piorum uerae felicitati quicquam[?] detrahit, nec etiam impiorum infelicitatem minuit, sed auget. Bis enim miseri sunt, qui suis sceleribus addut scelestum gaudium.
units.tr: 1. Because it takes nothing from the true happiness of the godly, nor does it lessen the unhappiness of the impious, but increases it. For they are doubly wretched who add wicked joy to their crimes.

units.la: 2. Quia breui tempore durat illud impium gaudium. Et χαρᾶ πυραύστης χαίρειν[?] reuera calamitosum est.
units.tr: 2. Because that wicked joy lasts only a short time. And to rejoice like the pyrausta is truly calamitous.

units.la: 3. Quia conuertitur in æternum luctu illa ἐπιχαιρεκακία.
units.tr: 3. Because that malicious joy is turned into eternal sorrow.

units.la: 4. Quia est inhonestum illud gaudium & illiberale.
units.tr: 4. Because that joy is dishonourable and ungentlemanly.

units.la: 5. Quia est βάσκανος & lydius lapis, quo exploratur nostra moderatio, & æquæ mentis studium.
units.tr: 5. Because it is envious, and it is the touchstone by which our moderation and our zeal for an even mind are tested.

units.la: 6. Quia auctoribus nocet: ut monet Prouerbium: πυραύστης μόγος[?], de quo apud ÆschyÆschylum quidam ait: Ἀλλοῖα μορφὴν λαμ-πάδας τε πυρφόρους μόρον.[?]
units.tr: 6. Because it harms its own authors, as the proverb warns: the toil of the pyrausta [πυραύστης μόγος], of which someone says in Aeschylus: Ἀλλοῖα μορφὴν λαμπάδας τε πυρφόρους μόρον.

units.la: 7. Quia ut ἐπιχαιρέκακοι in medijs successibus τεταγμένοι[?]: sic ἐπιχαιρέκακοι in ipsis tentationum paroxysmis τεταμμένοι[?] sunt.
units.tr: 7. Because, as those who rejoice in others' evils are ranged [τεταγμένοι] among the middle successes, so they are stretched [τεταμμένοι] in the very paroxysms of temptations.

units.la: 8. Quia Dei iudicio in his omnibus stadium est. Sunt autem pij, cùm tentationis igne explorantur, congratulatione: impij autem, cùm ἐπιχαιρεκακίᾳ[?] hilarescunt, gemitu prosequendi.
units.tr: 8. Because in all these things God's judgment is a contest. When the godly are tested by the fire of temptation, they are to be congratulated; but the impious, when they cheer up with malicious joy, are to be pursued with groaning.

units.la: VERSVS XVI.
units.tr: VERSE 16.

units.la: Propterea sacrificabit sagenæ suæ, & suffiet reti suo: quia per illa impinguata est portio eius, et cibus eius pingue(pecus.)
units.tr: Therefore he will sacrifice to his net and burn incense to his drag; because by them his portion is made fat, and his food rich.

units.la: Phrases [illegible, ~10 letters], Sacrificare sagenæ: &, Suffimentum reti adolere, idem plane significat: videlicet, fortitudini suæ bellicæ, industriæ, potentiæ, prudentiæ, acceptas ferre victorias & successus: non Deo. Eius persuasionis exemplum in Rabsacis oratione exstat, Isa.36.
units.tr: The phrases "to sacrifice to a net" and "to burn incense to a drag" plainly mean the same thing: to attribute the victories and successes to his own warlike strength, industry, power and prudence, not to God. An example of this persuasion stands in the speech of Rabshakeh, Isaiah 36.

units.la: 7. ARGVMENTVM HABACVCI, à sacrilega Chaldæorum persuasione de suis viribus.
units.tr: 7. ARGUMENT OF HABAKKUK: on the impious persuasion of the Chaldeans about their own strength.

units.la: Indigni sunt victoria, qui eam nō Deo, sed sibi ipsis adscribunt. Non enim nobis,
units.tr: Those who ascribe victory to themselves and not to God are unworthy of it. For not to us,

units.la: Note: the Greek words in the first paragraph, and the word aster "Phrases", are doubtful and marked. sed nomini Iehouæ exercituum debetur omnis gloria:Pfal.115.1. Nam ille unus hostes tradit[?] in manus seruorum suorum: Iof.7.
units.tr: but to the name of Jehovah of hosts is all glory due: Psalm 115:1. For he alone delivers enemies into the hands of his servants: Joshua 7.

units.la: Sed Chaldæi sibi ipsis adscribut victoriam, ita videlicet affecti ut ille exoteri-cus, qui patri hortanti ut σὺν θεῷ pugna-ret, aciram frenaret, superbè respondit, Etiam ignauos Deo iuvante vincere: se verò etiam sine illius ope vincere posse, cuius vocis poenas dedit grauissimas.
units.tr: But the Chaldeans ascribe victory to themselves, being disposed in the manner of that outsider who, when his father urged him to fight with God [σὺν θεῷ] and to restrain his army, proudly replied that even cowards can conquer with God's help, but that he himself could conquer even without his aid; and he paid the gravest penalty for that word.

units.la: Sunt igitur indigni victoria, iuxta Ἀνα-φθμον[?] prouerbium: Malis ter mala eueni-unt. Item: [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: They are therefore unworthy of victory, according to the proverb: "Evils come three times to evil men." Likewise: [illegible].

units.la: Obseruetur autem hoc loco primum παρομολογία[?]: Age demus nos, quos sanctificasti de mundo per veritatem seu verâ religionem tuam, dignos tantis calamitatibus, non habere quicquâ de quo conqueramur: immò boni cosulere debere, etiamsi nos bestiarum more duci à barba-ris istis patiaris. deinde ἀντεισαγωγή: Quis tamen dubitet, de ἐπιχαιρεκάκοις Chaldeis rectè dici posse illud: ἐχ [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐπ' ἀνθρώπων [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: Here, first, should be noted a paromologia: "Come, let us grant that we, whom you have sanctified from the world through the truth, that is, your true religion, are worthy of such calamities and have nothing of which to complain; indeed we ought to be content, even if you allow us to be led like beasts by these barbarians." Then an antieisagoge: yet who would doubt that of the malicious Chaldeans one may rightly say that [illegible].

units.la: Quis non fateatur, sacrilegos illos, Deo debitum honorem sibi arrogantes, indi-gnos gnos esse quibus tantos in bellis gerendis & populis uincendis successus,Deus largiatur?
units.tr: Who would not acknowledge that those sacrilegious men, who arrogate to themselves the honour due to God, are unworthy that God should grant them such great successes in waging wars and conquering peoples?

units.la: Haec persuasio nascitur ex collatione eorum qui non sunt quidem innoxij,sed tamen non sunt pesimi,& nequisimorum hominum: quae suggerit tale λεπτο-λόγημα [?]: Nō deterioribus, sed melioribus cocedendae sunt uictoriae. Iuxta dictum: ἰδλῳ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἐδλὰ ἢ ἄλλοι θεός [?]. Iudaei meliores sunt Babylonijs. Non igitur tradedi erant in eorum manus.
units.tr: This persuasion arises from comparing those who are indeed not innocent but are not the worst with the most wicked men, and it suggests this sophism: victories should be granted not to the worse but to the better. According to the saying: "For to one man good, to another God." The Jews are better than the Babylonians. Therefore they were not to be delivered into their hands.

units.la: Argumentabatur autem κατὰ βίαιον [?]: Iis successus & uictoriae concedendae erant, qui omnem gloriam rerum praeclare gestarum acceptam laturi erant Deo soli. Atqui Iudaei, si superiores facti essent, Deo gloriam dedissent. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: The argument ran by force: those were to be granted successes and victories who would ascribe all the glory of splendid deeds to God alone. But the Jews, had they become superior, would have given glory to God. Therefore, etc.

units.la: In Maiore est μὴ αὐτὸ ὡς αὐτὸ [?]: in Minore petitio principij. Itaque bis uitiosum est λεπτολόγημα [?].
units.tr: In the major premise is "not the same as the same" [μὴ αὐτὸ ὡς αὐτὸ]; in the minor, a petitio principii. Therefore the sophism is doubly faulty.

units.la: VERSVS VLTIMVS Capitis I.
units.tr: LAST VERSE OF CHAPTER 1.

units.la: Nunquid propterea euacuabit sagenà suam, & assiduè interficere Gentes non parcet?
units.tr: Shall he therefore empty his net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?

units.la: Quemadmodum piscatores seduli, ubi sagenam euacuauerūt, statim cū occasio suadet, alios piscēs capiendi gratia, eam laxatam demittunt: sic Nebucadnezar Rex Chaldæorum, quo plures populos & prouincias in ditionem potestatemq; suam redegerit, eo pluribus inuncandis inhiabit. Est enim, ut sæpe dicitur, συμφω- τομένων [?] τὰς ἀλλογαγίας [?], ἡ πλεονεξία [?].
units.tr: Just as diligent fishermen, when they have emptied their net, at once let it down again loosened, as soon as opportunity suggests, in order to catch other fish, so Nebuchadnezzar, King of the Chaldeans, the more peoples and provinces he brings under his sway and power, the more eagerly he gapes after swallowing up still more. For, as is often said, [συμφωνούντων τὰς ἀλλοτριότητας [?]], covetousness [ἡ πλεονεξία [?]].

units.la: 8. ARGVMENTVM HABACVCI, ἡ πλεονεξία [?] Chaldæorum.
units.tr: 8. ARGUMENT OF HABAKKUK: the covetousness [ἡ πλεονεξία [?]] of the Chaldeans.

units.la: Interest totius humani generis, ac in primis Ecclesiæ, quæ nunquam non à filijs huius seculi oppugnatur, diuinitus co-erceri tyrannorum πλεονεξίας [?] & perpetuas molitiones, quæ eò spectant, ut omnes populos sibi subijciant, & ut in quosuis sæuiant. Ac recte monuit Theognis, lucri causa tyrannos non esse iuuandos: μήτι τὴν αὐξῆ τύραννον ἐπ' ἐλπίσι λάβρδεος εἶναι [?].
units.tr: It concerns the whole human race, and the Church above all, which is never free from attack by the children of this age, that the covetousness [πλεονεξία [?]] and perpetual schemes of tyrants, which aim to subject all peoples to themselves and to rage against whomever they please, be restrained by God. Theognis rightly warned that tyrants are not to be helped for the sake of gain: [μήτι τὴν αὐξῆ τύραννον ἐπ' ἐλπίσι λάβρδεος εἶναι [?]].

units.la: Sed Nebucadnezar & Chaldæi nil nisi cædes, rapinas, seruitutem alienam, moliuntur & spirant.
units.tr: But Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans plan and breathe nothing but slaughter, plunder, and the enslavement of others.

units.la: Quare plurimum refert, à Deo Nebucadnezarem cum suis administris nō tantum coerceri, sed etiam rapacitatis insatiabilis & malorum consiliorum & conatuum tuum dare poenas. Iuxta dictum, quod legi naturae respondens, uniuersalis experientia etiam Ethnicos docuit:
units.tr: Therefore it matters greatly that Nebuchadnezzar, with his ministers, is restrained by God, and that he pays the penalty for his insatiable greed and his wicked counsels and attempts. This accords with the saying which, agreeing with the law of nature, universal experience has taught even the heathen:

units.la: ἐμάχρμου γὰρ τῶν λιχνῶν βλασφημέτων[?]
units.tr: [ἐμάχρμου γὰρ τῶν λιχνῶν βλασφημέτων [?]]

units.la: λιχνὰς ἀμοιβὰς ἐγὼ λαμβάνω βρωτοῖς[?] declarant.
units.tr: [λιχνὰς ἀμοιβὰς ἐγὼ λαμβάνω βρωτοῖς [?]] declare: greedy rewards I receive from mortals.

units.la: ANACEPHALAEOSIS, INSTANTIAE Habacuci vsum, ὡς ἂν τύπῳ declarans.
units.tr: RECAPITULATION, showing the objection of Habakkuk and its use as a type.

units.la: Iam uero, ne cui nostrum uideatur Habacucus & alij Sancti nimium suo dolori indulsisse, & soli talibus argumentis apud Deum usi: breuiter ostendemus, piis doctoribus, qui ob veritatis testimonium persecutionem sustinent, eadem prorsus ἐπιχειρήματα tantisper negocium facere, donec Spiritus sanctus caliginem, mentibus eorum ab intelligentia carnis offusam, lucis suae fulgore iterum discutit: ac ostendit, magis esse gloriosum veritatis praeconium, cum ei acriter resistunt Sophistae, armati auctoritate & applausu potentum: quàm cum ei ὑπολογισμῷ[?] fauore adsunt homines mollibus uestibus amicti, qui quouis uento doctrinae agitantur. Initio, se per veritatem sanctificatos recte gloriantur: sed ex eo non ἀνυχῶς[?] colligunt diuortium veritatis & persecutionis. tionis. Veritatem enim nemo prædicare potest, sic ut non Sophistarum ἀντιλογίας sustinere cogatur.
units.tr: Now, lest anyone among us think that Habakkuk and the other saints indulged their grief too much, and that they alone used such arguments before God, we will show briefly that pious teachers, who suffer persecution for the testimony of the truth, are troubled for a time by exactly the same [ἐπιχειρήματα] arguments, until the Holy Spirit again dispels with the brightness of his light the darkness that the flesh has cast over their minds, and shows that it is a more glorious proclamation of the truth when the Sophists, armed with the authority and applause of the powerful, resist it fiercely, than when men clothed in soft garments, blown about by every wind of doctrine, favour it. At first they rightly glory that they have been sanctified through the truth, but from this they do not wrongly infer a divorce between the truth and persecution. For no one can preach the truth without being forced to endure the contradictions of the Sophists.

units.la: 2. Addunt, se quidem castigatione eo nomine promeruisse, quòd non semper coniunxerint cū doctrina sana, sanos mo res: sed tamen, illam in grauissimam [illegible, ~6 letters] uersam esse, nimis odiose suspicā-tur & queruntur.
units.tr: 2. They add that they have indeed deserved castigation on this account, because they have not always joined sound doctrine with sound morals; yet they complain and too bitterly suspect that the doctrine has been turned into [illegible, about six letters].

units.la: 3. Existimant etiam, diuinam ἐπιείκειαν decere, iustiores improbis ple[?]ctedos nō obijcere: nisi sua in illis dona non coronare, sed eodem, quo horum nequitiam, loco habere malit: quod perquàm absurdum videatur. Hominum enim delectū non negligendum, & gradus uitioru nō confundendos, ratione proportionis, ut quidem ipsis uidetur, inter culpam & pœnam, sibi persuadent.
units.tr: 3. They also think that divine clemency ought not to let the more righteous be struck down along with the wicked, unless it prefers not to crown its gifts in them but to treat them in the same place as the wickedness of the others, which seems quite absurd.
