In hac significatione, cum fi-delitatem significat, & homini tribuitur, ϖίστις qualitas est primæ speciei, de qua dicitur in uersibus Manilij: Ipsa fides operi faciet pondusq; fidemq;.
units.tr: 1. Taken in a saving sense [σωτηρικῶς], faith signifies truthfulness and constancy in words, deeds, agreements and undertakings. In this sense it is most rightly ascribed to God, Rom. 3.3: "Will their unbelief make the faith of God without effect? God forbid." Likewise it is ascribed to regenerate men, Tit. 2.10: "Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity, that they may adorn the doctrine of our Saviour in all things." In this sense, when it means fidelity and is ascribed to a man, faith [πίστις] is a quality of the first kind, of which Manilius says in his verses: "Faith itself will give weight and trust to the work."

units.la: 2. Significat etiam plenam reuelatio-nem eorum, quæ typicè in ueteris Testa-menti liturgia adumbrata erant. Gal.3.23. Antequam autem uenisset fides, sub le-gis præsidio tenebamur, conclusi in eam fidem, quæ erat reuelanda. Etsi una est fi-des des omnium saluandorum in utroq; Testamento, tamen olim obscurè varijs ceremonijs adumbrata, tempore autè plenitudinis plenius illustrata est.
units.tr: 2. It also signifies the full revelation of those things which were foreshadowed in the types of the Old Testament worship. Gal. 3.23: "But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed." Although there is one faith of all who are saved in both Testaments, yet it was formerly foreshadowed obscurely by various ceremonies, but in the time of the fullness it was more fully illuminated.

units.la: 3. Fidei vocabulum θαυματουργίας[?] donū quandoque denotat. Matth.17.20. Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis monti huic, Demigra hinc illuc, & demigrabit: & nihil impossibile erit vobis. Eadem significatione Apostolus noster Fidei vocabulum usurpauit, 1. Cor. 12. 9. Alij vero fides, per eundem Spiritum. & sequenti capite v.2. Etsi habeam totam fidem, adeo ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.
units.tr: 3. The word faith sometimes denotes the gift of working miracles [θαυματουργίας]. Matth. 17.20: "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place, and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you." In the same sense our Apostle used the word faith, 1 Cor. 12.9: "To another faith by the same Spirit." And in the following chapter, v. 2: "Though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing."

units.la: 4. Interdum religionis nostræ δόγματα[?], quorum συμβόλου[?] exstat in Symbolo Apostolico, Fides denotat. Rom.12.6. Habentes autè diversa dona pro gratia quæ nobis data est, sive prophetiam, prophetemus pro proportione fidei: hoc est, articulorum fidei, quæ in Symbolo Apostolico habentur.
units.tr: 4. Sometimes faith denotes the doctrines [δόγματα] of our religion, a summary [σύμβολον] of which exists in the Apostles' Creed. Rom. 12.6: "Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith": that is, according to the articles of faith which are contained in the Apostles' Creed.

units.la: 5. Nonnunquam totam Euangelij doctrinam Fides significat. Act.6.7. Itaq; sermo Dei crescebat, & valde multiplicaba-tur numerus discipulorum in Hierusalem: multaq; turba sacerdotum obediebat fidei. Act.14.27. Cum autē uenissent & coegissent Ecclesiā, retulerūt quanta Deus peripsos effecisset, eumq; aperuisse gentibus ostium fidei. De Paulo couerso dictum fuit: Qui persequebatur nos aliquādo, nunc annunciat fidem (id est, doctrinam fidei) quam olim uastabat: Gal.1.23.
units.tr: 5. Sometimes faith signifies the whole doctrine of the Gospel. Acts 6.7: "And the word of God increased, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem; and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith." Acts 14.27: "And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles." Of Paul after his conversion it was said: "He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith [that is, the doctrine of the faith] which he once laid waste," Gal. 1.23.

units.la: 6. Nonnunquam historiae noticiam, citra omnem fiduciam gratiae Dei, significat: ut cùm daemonijs tribuitur. Iac.2.19. Tu credis Deum unum esse: rectè facis: & daemonia credunt, & horrescunt.
units.tr: 6. Sometimes faith signifies a knowledge of history without any trust in the grace of God, as when it is ascribed to demons. James 2.19: "Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble."

units.la: 7. Cùm ijs qui ad tempus credunt, fides tribuitur, præter historicā noticiam, κατάληψιν[?] καὶ ἐπίγνωσιν[?], fiduciam non diu durantem, significat: ut haec dicta ostendunt: Qui verò super petram, ij sunt qui cum audierint, cum gaudio excipiunt sermonem: sed isti radices non habent, qui ad tempus credunt, & tempore tentationis abscedunt. Luc.8.13. Item: Nam fieri nō potest, ut qui semel fuerint illuminati, &c.
units.tr: 7. When faith is ascribed to those who believe for a time, it signifies, besides a historical knowledge, comprehension [κατάληψιν] and knowledge [ἐπίγνωσιν], a trust that does not last long, as these words show: "But they on the rock are those who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no root, who believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away," Luke 8.13. Likewise: "For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened..." (Heb. 6.4).

units.la: 8. Fides deniq; significat πληροφορίαν[?] de gratia Dei: ac de hac propositum nobis est differere. Porrò etymologia Ciceronis nō malè quadrat huic significationi: Credamus, ait ille, quia fiat quod dictum est, appellatam fidem.
units.tr: 8. Finally, faith signifies full assurance [πληροφορίαν] of the grace of God, and it is of this that we intend to speak. Moreover, Cicero's etymology fits this meaning well: "Let us believe," he says, "because what has been said is done; hence faith is so named."

units.la: 2. An sit?
units.tr: 2. Whether it exists

units.la: Esse eximium quoddam Spiritus sancti χαρισμα, quo filij Dei a filijs huius mundi discernatur, quod Fidem uocamus, res ipsa testatur. Cū dicit Paulus, 2.Cor.13.5. Vos ipsos tentate, an non fitis in fide, uos ipsos probate. an nō agnoscitis uosmetipsos, uidelicet Iesum Christum in uobis esse? nisi reprobi estis. fidem electis, incredulitatem uerò reprobis tribuit: ac fidei hoc proprium esse docet, Christum in fidelibus suis habitantem agnoscere: infidelitatis autem, eudem aspernari, ac nihil cum eodem commune habere.
units.tr: That there is a certain outstanding gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the children of God are distinguished from the children of this world, and which we call faith, the thing itself bears witness. When Paul says, 2 Cor. 13.5: "Examine yourselves whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" he ascribes faith to the elect and unbelief to the reprobate, and he teaches that it is the property of faith to recognise Christ dwelling in his faithful, while it is the property of unbelief to reject him and to have nothing in common with him.

units.la: Filius Dei, fidei & incredulitatis respe ctu, totum genus humanum distinguit in Saluandos & Damnandos, Marci 16.16. Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, seruabitur: qui uerò non crediderit, condemnabitur. Vnde colligimus, eos quibus id datum est, credere: cæteros quibus illud non est datum, non credere: nisi forte fateri oportet, quosdam credere, quibus tamen id diuinitus nō sit datum: quod nemo fanus facile dabit.
units.tr: God, with respect to faith and unbelief, divides the whole human race into the saved and the damned. Mark 16.16: "He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned." From this we gather that those to whom it has been given believe, and the rest, to whom it has not been given, do not believe; unless perhaps one must admit that some believe to whom this has not been given from heaven, which no sane person will readily grant.

units.la: 3. Quid sit?
units.tr: 3. What is it?

units.la: Fides est donum πληροφορίας[?] de gratia Dei annunciata per Euangelium: quod Deus Pater per Spiritum sanctum in nobis efficit, cooperante auditu verbi Dei: ut iustificationi seruiat, & per charitatem agat.
units.tr: Faith is a gift of full assurance [πληροφορίας] concerning the grace of God, proclaimed through the Gospel. God the Father works it in us through the Holy Spirit, with the hearing of the word of God cooperating, so that it serves justification and is active through love.

units.la: Ac pie quidam monent, Fidem esse vocabulum relativum secundum dici. Etenim eius fundamentum est qualitas, non nobiscum nata, nec exercitio nostro comparata: sed à Patre luminum infusa, quae vera agnitione & fiducia gratiae Dei Patris, in Christo promissae & praestitae, constat. Terminus autem eius est, obiectum fidei, hoc est, veritas Euangelij de Iesu Christo, nostra causa tradito in mortem, & resuscitato. Caeterum definitionem fidei à nobis traditam, esse causalem, sequentia testabuntur.
units.tr: Some pious writers also advise that faith is, so to speak, a relative term. Its foundation is a quality that is not born with us, nor acquired by our own exercise, but poured into us by the Father of lights. It consists in true knowledge of, and trust in, the grace of God the Father, promised and bestowed in Christ. Its term, however, is the object of faith, namely the truth of the Gospel concerning Jesus Christ, delivered up to death for our sake and raised again. That the definition of faith given by us is causal, the following will show.

units.la: Genus est, Donum, videlicet Dei, secundum haec testimonia: Gratias ago Deo meo per Iesum Christum pro omnib. vo-bis, quia fides vestra annunciatur in toto mundo: Roman. 1.8. Deo ut auctori fidei, gratias agit Paulus, nimirum agnoscens gratis id donum conferri à Domino. Item: VoVobis datum est in Christi negocio, non solum in eum credere, sed etiam pro eo affligi: Phil.1.29. Item: Simeon Petrus et Apostolus Iesu Christi, iis qui æquè pretiosam fidem nobis cum sortiti sunt: ἰσότιμον ἡμῖν λαχοῦσι πίστιν [?]. 2. Pet.1.1.
units.tr: The genus is gift, namely of God, according to these testimonies: "I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world" (Rom. 1.8). Paul gives thanks to God as the author of faith, plainly acknowledging that this gift is bestowed freely by the Lord. Likewise: "It has been given to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him" (Phil. 1.29). Likewise: "Simon Peter, apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith of equal value with ours" [ἰσότιμον ἡμῖν λαχοῦσι πίστιν] (2 Pet. 1.1).

units.la: Ex his testimoniis συμμαρτυρῶ [?] colligo, fidem à gratia esse, nō à natura, aut ab eius uiribus.
units.tr: From these testimonies I conclude that faith comes from grace, not from nature or its own powers.

units.la: Differetia est, πληροφορίας [?] de gratia Dei. Qui uere credit, certò persuasum habet, Deum sibi esse propitium & reconciliatum per & propter Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum. Ac nihil magis fidei e diametro repugnat, quam ἀπιστία [?] & sibi indulgens hæsitatio, quæ cum ueritatis laude Deo subtrahat, est in eum summe contumeliosa, ac proinde piis omnibus exsecrabilis & abominanda.
units.tr: The difference is full assurance concerning the grace of God. He who truly believes is firmly persuaded that God is favourable and reconciled to him through and for the sake of Christ Jesus our Lord. Nothing is more directly opposed to faith than unbelief [ἀπιστία] and self-indulgent hesitation, which, while it robs God of the praise of truth, is most insulting to him, and therefore to all the godly is accursed and abominable.

units.la: 4. Quæ causæ?
units.tr: 4. What are the causes?

units.la: Internæ causæ sunt, Materia & Forma fidei: de quibus primò agemus.
units.tr: The internal causes are the matter and form of faith, which we shall treat first.

units.la: 1. Materia in qua, est Cor hominis electi. Iuxta dictū: Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem: Rom.10.10. Ideo Dominus dicitur aperire corda, ut attendat iis quæ dicuntur à Seruis Dei: ut Lydiæ exemplo demon-stratur, Act.16.14. & nos semen verbi,cor de honesto & bono excipere & retinere, & fructum adferre per patientiam, dicimur, Lucæ 8.15. Cordis autem voce, intelligentiæ & fiduciæ veluti quoddam in homine domicilium, Scriptura sancta designat.
units.tr: 1. The matter in which is the heart of the chosen man, according to the saying: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom. 10.10). Therefore the Lord is said to open hearts, so that they attend to what is said by the servants of God, as the example of Lydia shows (Acts 16.14). And we are said to receive the seed of the word in an honest and good heart, to hold it fast, and to bring forth fruit with patience (Luke 8.15). By the word "heart" Holy Scripture designates a kind of dwelling-place in man for understanding and trust.

units.la: Quod autem electorum propriam cum Paulo (Tit.1.1.) fidem facimus, istis testi-monijs nos quidem adduci & conuinci, fatemur.
units.tr: That we make faith the proper possession of the elect, with Paul (Tit. 1.1), we admit that we are led and convinced by these testimonies.

units.la: Ioan.6.65. Nemo potest venire ad me, (id est, credere) nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo. Datur autem electis filijs, non autem alienis ἀλλοτρίοις[?]: ut fit hæreditatis illorum in cœlis repositæ testimonium.
units.tr: John 6.65: "No one can come to me (that is, believe) unless it has been given him by my Father." It is given to the elect sons, not to strangers [ἀλλοτρίοις], so that it becomes a witness of their inheritance laid up in heaven.

units.la: Ioan.10.26. Sed vos non creditis: non enim estis ex meis ovibus. Ergo per contrapositionem argumentando, qui sunt omnes Christi, credunt in eum.
units.tr: John 10.26: "But you do not believe, for you are not of my sheep." Therefore, arguing by the contrapositive, all who belong to Christ believe in him.

units.la: Ioan.12.39.40. Propterea non poterat credere, quia iterum dixit Esaias: Excæ-cauit oculos eorum, & obdurauit corda eorum: ne videant oculis, & intelligant corde, & convertantur, & sanem eos. Er-go ij solùm credunt, quorum ab æterno ase[?] electorum oculos Deus illuminat, corda carnea seu mollia facit, mentes intelli-gentiæ luce illustrat.
units.tr: John 12.39-40: "For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, lest they see with their eyes and understand with their heart, and turn, and I heal them." Therefore only those believe whose eyes God illumines from eternity, whose fleshy or soft hearts he makes, and whose minds he lights with the light of understanding.

units.la: Act.14.48. Gentes autem hæc audien-tes gauisæ sunt, & glorificabant sermonem Domini: & crediderunt quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Non igitur crediderunt ad vitam non præordinati, ut iterum per Contrapositionem ratiocinemur.
units.tr: Acts 14.48: "The Gentiles, hearing this, rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed." Therefore those who were not predestined did not believe unto eternal life, as we reason again by contraposition.

units.la: 2. Materia circa quam, seu obiectum fidei, est Euangelium Dei (quod antea per Prophetas suos in Scripturis sanctis) de Filio suo (facto ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem, declarato Filio Dei potenter secundum Spiritum sanctificationis, per resurrectionem a mortuis) nempe Iesu Christo Domino nostro. Rom.i.v i.2.3.
units.tr: 2. The matter about which, or the object of faith, is the Gospel of God (which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures) concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification by the resurrection from the dead, namely Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 1.1-3).

units.la: Versatur itaque fides, qua iustificamur & viuimus, circa agnitionem & fiduciam Dei Redemptoris, Iesu Christi Immanuelis nostri, ac statuit eum esse nostram sapientiam, iusticiam, sanctificationem & redemptionem, &c. 1.Cor.1.30.
units.tr: Faith, by which we are justified and live, is therefore concerned with the knowledge of and trust in God the Redeemer, Jesus Christ our Immanuel, and holds him to be our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, etc. (1 Cor. 1.30).

units.la: Porrò, fides non habet materiam ex qua: quia non est substantia, sed accides, seu qualitas infusa, & efficax forma, &c a-
units.tr: Moreover, faith has no matter out of which, because it is not a substance but an accident, or an infused quality, and an efficacious form, etc., of the

units.la: stionum hominis fidelis instrumentum.
units.tr: actions of the faithful man, an instrument.

units.la: 3. Forma huius fidei est, non solum [illegible, ~12 letters] historiam de Christo Redemtore comprehendere: nec tantum [illegible, ~10 letters] thesi, de salute per ipsum fidelibus parta, assentiri: sed etiam [illegible, ~12 letters] per Spiritum sanctum accensa, [illegible, ~8 letters] de nostra ipsorum salute sic statuere, ut nullus planè locus sit Academicae [illegible, ~6 letters], aut haesitationi dubium aliquod in promissione gratiae, hoc est, in scyrpo nodu quaerenti.
units.tr: 3. The form of this faith is not only to comprehend the history concerning Christ the Redeemer, nor merely to assent to the proposition about the salvation won for believers through him. It is also, kindled by the Holy Spirit, to determine about one's own salvation in such a way that there is absolutely no place for academic suspension of judgment, nor any doubt or hesitation about the promise of grace, which would be like seeking a knot in a rush.

units.la: Externae causae sunt, Efficiens & Finis.
units.tr: The external causes are the efficient and the final cause.

units.la: 4. [illegible, ~10 letters] est Deus, qui per Spiritum sanctum accedit fidem in cordibus filiorum Dei. Iuxta dicta: 2.Cor.4.13. Et quia habemus eundem Spiritum fidei: hoc est, fidem a Spiritu sancto in mentibus nostris accensam. Gal.5.22. inter fructus Spiritus recensetur fides.
units.tr: 4. The efficient cause is God, who through the Holy Spirit kindles faith in the hearts of the sons of God. According to the sayings: "And since we have the same spirit of faith" (2 Cor. 4.13), that is, faith kindled in our minds by the Holy Spirit. Among the fruits of the Spirit faith is numbered (Gal. 5.22).

units.la: Pie Augustinus in epistola ad Sixtum, quae est numero cv. Restat igitur, inquit, ut ipsam fidem, unde omnis iustitia sumit initium, propter quam dicitur ad Ecclesiam in Canticorum, Venies & pertransfibis ab initio fidei: non humano, quo isti extolluntur, tribuamus arbitrio,nec ullis præcedetibus meritis:quoniam inde incipiunt bona quæcunque sunt merita: sed gratuitum Dei donum esse fateamur, si gratiam veram,id est,sine meritis,cogitamus.
units.tr: Augustine rightly, in his letter to Sixtus, which is number cv: "It remains, he says, that we ascribe faith itself, from which all righteousness takes its beginning, on account of which it is said to the Church in the Song of Songs, 'You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith', not to human choice, by which such men are exalted, nor to any preceding merits, since from it all good merits begin; but we should confess it to be a free gift of God, if we think of grace as true, that is, without merits."

units.la: 5. Συνάκτιον[?] est, uerbum Dei. Hebr.4.2[?] Etenim nobis euangelizatum est sicut illis: at non profuit illis auditus sermo, ut qui fidei mixtus non fuerit ipsis qui audierant. Ergo,cum Euangelio,mira ueraq; [illegible, ~6 letters], fides miscetur,sic ut eo nitatur, & illud [illegible, ~8 letters] esse statuat, fides accenditur & alitur.
units.tr: 5. The co-agent of faith is the word of God (Heb. 4.2). For the Gospel was preached to us just as to them, but the word heard did not profit them, since it was not mixed with faith in those who had heard. Therefore, when faith is mixed with the Gospel, with a wonderful and true promise, so that it rests on it and holds that it is true, faith is kindled and nourished.

units.la: Et cum hæc duo,Verbum inquam promissionis & Fides, sint correlatiua: posito uno, necesse est poni & alterum. Vt ergo qui ignari sunt promissionis gratiæ, ἀπιστοῖς[?] fideles, uniuoce infideles uocantur,etiamsi in externo coetu Ecclesiæ uersentur: ita qui uera πληροφορίας[?] sibi applicant gratiæ promissionem, fideles reuera sunt, etiamsi inter Mahometistas tristissimam seruitutem seruire cogantur.
units.tr: And since these two, I mean the word of promise and faith, are correlatives, when one is posited the other must be posited too. Thus, just as those who are ignorant of the promise of grace are called unfaithful [ἀπιστοῖς] and unbelievers, univocally, even if they live within the external assembly of the Church, so those who apply to themselves the promise of grace with true full assurance [πληροφορίας] are truly believers, even if they are forced to serve in most wretched slavery among the Mahometans.

units.la: 6. Συνέργια[?] sunt, Verbi & Sacramentorum administratio. Verbi prædicatio facit ut intelligamus: Sacramenta,cum sint σφραγίδες[?], faciunt ut ne dubitemus. Etsi autem uerbum θεόπνευστος[?], & ab eo profectum qui est αὐτόπιστος[?], per se fidem facere potest: tamen ut infirmitati nostrae consulere-tur, sigilla uerbo addita sunt. De credendi autem modo erudite dixit Augustinus: Ratio subsequatur fidem, ut intelligat fidelis quid credat. Hoc utinam ij quoq; perpendant, qui in fidei negocio adeo ra tionem auersantur, ut rectae rationis per-duelles &λόγως[?] sese esse prodant. Sic enim illi in Rationem, qua bestiam (honoris opinor caussa) uocant, ex alto desto-machantur, ac fi lumen diuinitus in mente humana accensum, a corruptelis quae post lapsum irrepserunt, discernere, infci-tia foret: & perinde ac fi Christus fidei luce nunquam eam illustraret, & ab errorum caligine liberaret. Nos uero neunquam contemserimus & naturae & gratiae dotes amice conspirantes.
units.tr: 6. The helpers [συνέργια] are the administration of the Word and the Sacraments. The preaching of the Word makes us understand; the Sacraments, since they are seals [σφραγίδες], make us not doubt. Although the Word, divinely inspired [θεόπνευστος], and proceeding from him who is self-faithful [αὐτόπιστος], can of itself produce faith, nevertheless, to provide for our weakness, seals have been added to the word. Augustine spoke learnedly about the manner of believing: "Let reason follow faith, so that the believer may understand what he believes." Would that those also would weigh this who so shun reason in matters of faith that they reveal themselves to be irrational [ἀλόγως], deprived of right reason. For they rage so vehemently from on high against Reason, which they call a beast (out of honour, I suppose), as if it were folly to distinguish the light kindled by God in the human mind from the corruptions that crept in after the fall, and as if Christ had never illumined it with the light of faith and freed it from the darkness of errors. But we shall never despise the gifts of nature and grace, which agree together in friendship.

units.la: 7. Finis est, a uerbo uitae persuasum, in Christi κοινωνίαν uenire, & ab eo salutem impetrare. Huius communionis sacra tessera est Coena Domini: 1.Cor.10.16. item Baptismus, de quo dicitur: Etenim per unum Spiritum nos omnes in unum corpus baptizati fumus, &c. 1.Cor.12.13.
units.tr: 7. The end is that, having been persuaded by the word of life, one comes into fellowship [κοινωνίαν] with Christ and obtains salvation from him. The sacred token of this communion is the Lord's Supper: 1 Cor. 10:16. Likewise baptism, of which it is said: "For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," etc., 1 Cor. 12:13.

units.la: §. Quid effectus?
units.tr: §. What is its effect?

units.la: Iustificatio & Sanctificatio fidei ut causæ organicæ, κατὰ τι[?] tribuuntur. Pulcerrimè sanè Basilius Magnus: Credere, inquit, intelligere & facere sese consequuntur.
units.tr: Justification and sanctification are ascribed to faith as its organic cause, in a certain respect [κατὰ τι]. Basil the Great put it very beautifully: "Believing," he says, "is followed by understanding and doing."

units.la: Iustificamur fide, absque operibus legis: per remissionem peccatorum, & imputationem iustitiæ Christi. Rom.3.4.5. Gal.2.3.
units.tr: We are justified by faith, without the works of the law, through the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. Rom. 3:4, 5; Gal. 2:3.

units.la: Fides etiam per charitatem agens, sanctificationi nostræ, quæ in depositione veteris hominis & assumtione novi hominis posita est, seruit.
units.tr: Faith also, working through love, serves our sanctification, which consists in putting off the old man and putting on the new man.

units.la: §. Quæ propria?
units.tr: §. What are its properties?

units.la: Initium, incrementa, & finem habet fides.
units.tr: Faith has a beginning, growth and an end.

units.la: Definitio fidei illud pie statuendum est, vocationis efficacis tempori illud respondere. Neq; enim actu fides præcedit vocationem: nec hæc expers est fidei. Loquor de ea vocatione, quæ Tractus Patris vocatur, Ioan.6.44.
units.tr: It must be piously affirmed that faith corresponds in time to effectual calling. For faith does not in fact precede the calling, nor is the calling without faith. I speak of that calling which is called the drawing of the Father, John 6:44.

units.la: Incrementa sua habere fidem, argumento est Apostolorum precatio: Adde nobis fidem. Luc.17.5.
units.tr: That faith has its increases is shown by the apostles' prayer: "Increase our faith," Luke 17:5.

units.la: De fidei fine pronunciat Apostolus, 1. Corinth.13.10. Postquam autem adueneritquod perfeaö[?] est,tunc quod ex parte est abolebitur. Sedenim præstat Augusti ni uerbis,quæ exstant lib.4. de Trinitate, cap.18.sententia nostram exponere: Nunc ergo adhibemus fidem rebus temporaliter gestis propter nos, & per ipsam mundamur, & cum ad speciem uenerimus, quemadmodu succedit fidei ueritas, ita mortalitati succedet æternitas. Quapropter quoniam fides nostra fiet ueritas,cū ad id quod nobis credentibus promittitur, peruenerimus: promittitur aut nobis uita æterna: & dixit Veritas,non quæ fiet, sicut futura est fides nostra, sed quæ semper est ueritas, quia ibi est æternitas. Dixit autem Veritas: Hæc est autem uita æterna, ut cognoscant te unum uerum Deum, & quem misisti IESVM CHRISTVM. Cum fides nostra uidendo fiet ueritas, tunc mortalitatem nostram commutatam tenebit æternitas.
units.tr: The Apostle declares the end of faith, 1 Cor. 13:10: "But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part will be done away." But it is better to set out our view in the words of Augustine, which are found in book 4 of On the Trinity, chapter 18: "Now, then, we use faith in things done temporally on our behalf, and through it we are cleansed; and when we come to sight, just as truth succeeds faith, so eternity will succeed mortality. Therefore, since our faith will become truth when we arrive at what is promised to us as believers, and eternal life is promised to us, and Truth has said, not 'which will become' as our faith will be, but 'which always is the truth, because there is eternity,' and Truth has said: 'And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.' When our faith becomes truth by seeing, then eternity will hold our mortality, changed."

units.la: Idem in Ioannem tractatu 68. Qui e-nim,inqt,à Domino peregrinantur,opus habent ex fide uiuere: quia per hanc ad speciem contemplanda parantur. Beati enim mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum uidebunt. Et fide mundat corda eorum. Illud in Evangelio, hoc in Apostolorum Actibus legitur. Fides autem, quia eorum qui Deum visuri sunt, quandiu peregri-nantur, corda mundantur: quod non vi-det, credit. Nam si vides, non est fides. Credenti colligitur meritum, videnti reddit praemium.
units.tr: The same in Augustine's Tractate 68 on John: "For those who are away from the Lord, he says, need to live by faith, because through faith they are prepared to contemplate him in sight. For 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.' And by faith he cleanses their hearts. The former is read in the Gospel, the latter in the Acts of the Apostles. Now faith, because the hearts of those who are to see God are cleansed while they are away: 'what one does not see, one believes.' For if you see, it is not faith. To the believer merit is credited; to the one who sees, the reward is paid."

units.la: 7. Quae pugnantia?
units.tr: 7. What things are contrary?

units.la: Cum noticia fidei pugnat, ignorantia Dei & voluntatis eius: cum eiusdem fiducia e diametro pugnant, dubitatio, desperatio, & similia mala.
units.tr: Ignorance of God and of his will is contrary to the knowledge of faith; doubt, despair and similar evils are directly opposed to its trust.

units.la: VERSUS V.
units.tr: VERSE 5.

units.la: Et quanto magis vino deditus praenari-catur[?], & homo superbus, nec permanebit in habitaculo suo? qui dilatavit sicut infernus animam suam, estq[?] velut mors, nec satiatur: sed congregavit ad se omnes Gentes, & coacervavit ad se omnes populos.
units.tr: "And how much more, since he is a man given to wine, a proud man, will he not remain in his house? He who has enlarged his soul like hell, and is like death, and is never satisfied; but he has gathered unto himself all nations, and heaped up unto himself all peoples."

units.la: Prius membrum propositionis versu 4. traditae, de infidelibus sese attollentibus, breviq; tempore, instar cuiusdam bullae, florentibus, Iehovah Deus noster, [illegible, ~7 letters] Nebucadnezaris exemplo in medium adducto, [illegible, ~10 letters] persequitur in hoc versu & sequentibus.
units.tr: The first member of the proposition, set out in verse 4, concerns unbelievers who lift themselves up and for a short time flourish like a bubble. The Lord, our God Iehovah, [illegible] brings forward the example of Nebuchadnezzar and [illegible] pursues it in this verse and those that follow.

units.la: Sicautem declarari Syllogismo fente-tia poterit:
units.tr: The sentence can be set out in a syllogism as follows:

units.la: Certissimæ sunt comminationes diui næ de impiorum, Epicureorum, superbo-rum, dolosorum & sanguinariorum exitio. 2.Sam.23.6. Impij autem erunt tanquam spinæ, quæ propelluntur, uniuersi: quia non manu capient: 7. & quicunq; uolet tangere eas, replebitur ferro, aut hastili lanceæ, & igne comburendo comburentur in loco suo.
units.tr: The divine threats against the destruction of the wicked, Epicureans, proud, deceitful and bloodthirsty men are most certain. 2 Sam. 23:6, 7: "But the ungodly shall be all of them as thorns that are thrown away, because they cannot be taken with hands; and whoever touches them must be armed with iron and the staff of a spear, and they shall be utterly burned with fire in the same place."

units.la: Prouerb. 16. 18. Ante contritionem est superbia, & ante ruinam elatio spiritus.
units.tr: Prov. 16:18: "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall."

units.la: Psal. 55. 24. Viri sanguinarij & dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos.
units.tr: Ps. 55:24: "Bloodthirsty and deceitful men shall not live out half their days."

units.la: Atqui Nebucadnezar prævaricator, ebrius magnitudine rerum à se gestarum, crudelissimè persequetur hostes suos, & Gentes sibi subiectas seruire uolet suis cupiditatibus. Hanc Minorem expolitione rhetorica, de inferno, deq; Gentium congregatione, ut unius Monarchæ libidini morem gerant, Dominus illustrat. Exemplum autem simile si quis requirit, legat Herodoti historiam de expeditione Xerxis in Græciam, in qua inter multa alia, mentio fit maximi & diuturni apparatus, & ingentis exercitus, qui è diversis Gentibus erat conscriptus. Liquet autem ex historiae illius multis patribus, Arra-banum & alios proceres frustra dissuasisse bellum illud ingens & periculosum.
units.tr: But Nebuchadnezzar is a transgressor, drunk with the greatness of the deeds he has done, who will most cruelly persecute his enemies and will want the nations subject to him to serve his lusts. The Lord illustrates this minor premise by a rhetorical figure, concerning hell and the gathering of the nations so that they may obey the desire of one monarch. If anyone seeks a similar example, let him read Herodotus' history of Xerxes' expedition into Greece, in which, among many other things, mention is made of a very great and lasting preparation and a huge army enlisted from various nations. It is clear from that history that Artabanus and other nobles in vain dissuaded that great and dangerous war.

units.la: Quare certissimum est, Nebucadnezarem non permansurum in loco suo. Iuxta illud ὀμοιωθ[illegible, ~9 letters] dictum: Sed homo iste in splendore suo non permanebit, & similis fit brutis quae intereunt. Haec via ipsorum stultitia ipsis est (id est noxia:) posteri tamen eorum ore suo approbant. Tanquam oues in sepulcro ponuntur, mors depascit eos, & dominabuntur eis recti mane: roburipsorum est fovea, quae veterascere ipsos faciat à domicilijs suis. Psalmo 49. v. 12. 13. 14.
units.tr: Therefore it is most certain that Nebuchadnezzar will not remain in his place. Like the saying [ὀμοιωθ...]: "But this man, in his splendor, will not remain, and is like the beasts that perish." This is their way, their folly is to them (that is, harmful); yet their posterity approve their words. Like sheep they are laid in the grave, death feeds on them, and the upright shall have dominion over them in the morning; their strength is a pit which will make them wear away from their dwellings. Ps. 49:12-14.

units.la: Noti sunt & Senecae versus, in Herculé Oetaeo, de tyrannorum tragico interitu:
units.tr: The verses of Seneca in the Hercules Oetaeus about the tragic end of tyrants are also well known:

units.la: Quota pars moritur tempore fati? Quos felices Cynthia vidit, Vidit miseros abitura dies. Rarum est felix idemque senex.
units.tr: How small a part die when their fated time comes! Those whom Cynthia saw as happy, the departing day has seen wretched. Rare is the man who is both happy and old.

units.la: DE IMPIORUM, QUOS EXTREMUM FATUM URGET, INTEMPERIE ET πεο-ἀγωνίοις[?] TUMULTIBUS,
units.tr: ON THE INTEMPERANCE AND TUMULTS OF THE IMPIOUS, WHOM THEIR LAST FATE PRESSES

units.la: Quod iis, qui per ludum & iocum exi-tium tiam sibi accersunt, & in ipso præcipitij uertice ludunt παίγνιον ἐπιτάφιον[?], accidere solet: id impijs, rerum successu elatis, & perpetuâ ἀνωμαλίαν[?] uana spe sibi despon-dentibus, ac ubi iam in acie nouaculæ cõ-stituti sunt ludentibus, euenire, omnium temporum historiæ testatur. Lusit Tho-mas Morus (magnus quidem, si legum Britannicarum peritiam, & si auctoritate spectes, uir: sed acerbus Euangelij & fi-delium hostis) cum amico, qui ipsum mo-nuerat, ne Regi refractarium se præbe-ret, scommate de μεταμέλειαν[?], cum diceret, Mutasse sese sententiam: & id nõ de Re-gis auctoritate in Ecclesia Anglicana, & de diuortio Reginæ, sed de barba abraden-da interpretaretur: negans tondendam ei, cui caput esset præcidendum.
units.tr: What usually happens to those who, for sport and jest, bring destruction upon themselves and play at the very edge of the precipice, playing a funeral game, is what history shows always befalls the impious, who are puffed up by their success and promise themselves uninterrupted good fortune by vain hope, and who, when they are already standing at the razor's edge, go on joking. Thomas More (certainly a great man, if you look at his knowledge of British law and at his authority, but a bitter enemy of the Gospel and of the faithful) once joked with a friend who had warned him not to show himself obstinate toward the King. He said that he had changed his mind [μεταμέλειαν], and he meant this not about the King's authority over the Church of England or the divorce of the Queen, but about shaving his beard. He added that the man to whom the head was to be cut off should not be shaved.

units.la: Nos, priusquam ad alia exempla acce-damus, Dauidis testimonium θεόπνευστον præmittemus. Exstat illud Psalmo 73.17. Donec sum ingressus in sanctuaria Dei, & intellexi nouissima eorum. 18. Certè in lubricis ponis eos: deijcis eos in præ-cipitia. 19. Quomodo fuerunt in uasta-tionem tanquam momento? cessárunt, confumti sunt ab horroribus? 20. Quasi somsomnium sunt ab euigilando: Domine, cū expergefacis eos, imaginationes eorum contemtibiles reddis.
units.tr: Before we come to other examples, we will set out the divinely inspired testimony of David. It is found in Psalm 73:17-20: "Until I went into the sanctuary of God, and understood their latter end. Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors. As a dream when one awaketh; so, O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image."

units.la: Omisis autem Principum summorum exemplis, eorum qui ausi sunt ora blas-phema in coelum ponere, &c [illegible, ~10 letters] λίαν in Ecclesiam Dei inuehere, tragicos exitus, quos precesit eorū [illegible, ~12 letters] μεγαλοφωνταξίαι, annotabimus exempla.
units.tr: Leaving aside the examples of the highest princes, and of those who dared to set their blasphemous mouths against heaven, and ... to rail against the Church of God, we will note examples of the tragic ends that followed their boasting.

units.la: Achab & Sedecias, pseudoprophetae, qui Iudaicum populum seduxerat, & Ieremiae & alijs Dei seruis impiè contradixerat, tādem supplicio ignis affecti sunt, mandatu Nebucadnezaris Regis Babyloniorum. Ier.29.v.21.22.
units.tr: Ahab and Zedekiah, the false prophets who had led the Jewish people astray and had impiously opposed Jeremiah and the other servants of God, were at last put to death by fire, by the command of Nebuchadnezzar, King of the Babylonians. Jer. 29:21-22.

units.la: Ferunt, Simonem Magum, cum uarijs & mirabilibus praestigijs, diuersis in locis multos obstupefecisset & dementas-set, tandem Deo ad supplicia eum retrahente, & diabolo excarnificandum tradente, cū Petro Apostolo de Ascensione Christi cōtendere coepisse, ac dixisse: Tu Chri-stum Deum tuum in coelum fuisse sub-latum di-cis. En ipse quoque in coelum attollor. Atque his dictis daemonum ministerio in altum sub-latus, spectatores attonitos reddidit & obstupefecit. Sed Petrus precib, ad Deum fusi[?] fuğis obtinuit, ut dæmones histrionem suum, quem sustulerat, in terram deturbarent. Itaq; impostorille, comminutis eo casu membris, miserè interijt.
units.tr: They say that Simon Magus, who had astonished and driven mad many people in various places with his manifold and wonderful tricks, was at last drawn by God to punishment and handed over to the devil to be torn to pieces. He began to dispute with the Apostle Peter about the ascension of Christ, and said: "You say that your Christ, your God, was taken up into heaven. Behold, I too am lifted up into heaven." With these words he was raised aloft by the ministry of demons, and he astonished and amazed the onlookers. But Peter, by prayers poured out to God, obtained that the demons should cast down to the earth their actor whom they had lifted up. And so that impostor, his limbs broken in the fall, perished miserably.

units.la: Manes ἀμβρόντητος uetus Testamentum reiecit: Mundum & hominum genus à Deo non bono conditum, impiè finxit: Nouum Testamentum sic admisit, ut tamen illud sceleratè corrumperet, affirmans κατὰ φαντασίαν καὶ ἀνθρώπων Christum apparuisse ac spectrū fuisse. Cętera illius tetra deliramenta omitto. Dedit tamen & ipse pœnas, cùm se Medicum mentitus, Persarum Regis filium necasset, detracta ei cute. Ita enim habet historia Græca: ὁ βασιλεὺς Περσῶν ἐξέλειπε ζῶντα, ὡς ἂν
units.tr: Manes, thunderstruck [ἀμβρόντητος], rejected the Old Testament. He impiously invented that the world and the human race were created by a God who was not good. He admitted the New Testament, but corrupted it wickedly, asserting that Christ appeared in appearance only [κατὰ φαντασίαν] and was a phantom. I omit his other foul ravings. Yet he too paid the penalty, when, having falsely claimed to be a physician, he caused the death of the son of the King of the Persians by having his skin stripped off. For the Greek history says: the King of the Persians ordered him to be flayed alive, as [ὁ βασιλεὺς Περσῶν ἐξέλειπε ζῶντα, ὡς ἂν].

units.la: Arius, cum & hęresin, quia impiè negabat λόγον ὑφιστάμενον, Patri coessentialem & coæternum esse, diu sparsisset: & tandem in aulam sese per miros cuniculos insinuasset, ac Constantino Imperatori periurio imposuisset, cum ut uel ab inuito Alexandro Episcopo Constantinopolitano in Ecclesiam reciperetur, multis ad templum deducentibus, ἀπροσδοκήτως, è uia digressus ad cloacam, tragicè perijt. Digna sunt memoria uerba Cedreni, quę subijciam: ὁ ἀνόσιος μετὰ φαυλότητος καὶ γαυ-ριάματος[?] εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν προσερχόμενος, ἐπει-δὴ δὲ[?] τῷ φόβῳ, πλησίον τῆς λεγομένης Ἐλνάτης[?] ἐγέ-νετο, τῆς γαστρὸς νυξάσης[?] αὐτὸν τοῖς ἐπέισι[?] ἀφιδρῶ-σιν[?] ἀπονεχωρήσας, ἀγγέλῳ[?] κατα-φαίνεται[?] χειρὶ τῆς τε λοιπίας αὐτῆς ἀλλὰ τῶν ἀσκάγχνων αὐτῷ τῇ ψυχῇ φαγόντων, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς ἀφθαρσίαν κατακλυσθέντων[?].
units.tr: Arius, after he had long spread his heresy, because he impiously denied that the Word, subsisting [λόγον ὑφιστάμενον], was co-essential and co-eternal with the Father, and at last had insinuated himself into the court through remarkable underground passages and had deceived the Emperor Constantine by perjury, was about to be received back into the Church even against the will of Alexander, Bishop of Constantinople, while many were leading him to the church. Unexpectedly, he turned aside from the road to a latrine and died a tragic death. The words of Cedrenus, which I will add, are worth remembering: the impious man, approaching the church with insolence and boastfulness, when in his fear he came near the place called Elnata, his belly, which had been stirred by the ..., withdrew and was taken away; his bowels were eaten by worms, and his soul was overwhelmed with... into corruption.

units.la: Nestorij (qui Christi personam in duas diuidens, non ἄλλο ἢ ἄλλο, sed Christum alium & alium finxit) in exilium relegati Oasin, putrefactio omnia eius membra inuasit, maximè linguam eius scelestam, qua identidem protulerat hanc uocem: Hactenus nobis non est persuasum, Mariam esse Dei genitricem.
units.tr: Nestorius, who divided the person of Christ into two and fashioned not one thing or another, but a Christ who was one and another, was banished to Oasis. Putrefaction invaded all his members, most of all his wicked tongue, with which he had repeatedly uttered this saying: "Hitherto we have not been persuaded that Mary is the Mother of God."

units.la: Vidit etiam hæc nostra ætas eiusdem rei multa & tristia exempla: de quibus iam nihil dicam.
units.tr: Our own age has also seen many sad examples of the same thing, of which I shall now say nothing.

units.la: Sedenim minus mira Dei seruis esse uidetur θεομαχίᾳ, quam palàm Antichristiani ἀλάζονες exercent, dum odio, inuidiæ & aliis cæcis affectibus indulgent. Illud potius mirantur, non raro eos, qui uideri uolùt Ecclesiæ columnæ, & triarij in bello aduersus Antichristianos, sic sibi placere, ut adulatorum partim imperito-rum rum, partim factiosorum plausu exhilia rati, suffragatione◊ inflati, no modo suae infirmitatis & donorum, quibus etiam aliij quidam a Deo inftrufti sunt, obliuifca tur, nullam◊ rationem habeant: sed etia omissis fidei hostibus, in fidos [illegible, ~12 letters] , qui in eadem acie stant, venenatae linguae & dentatae chartae spicula contor queat, Antichriftianis interim in sinu ue-hementer gaudetibus. Tolerabilius hoc malum foret, fi per contentionem, Chri-ftum tamen solum praedicarent. Illud au-tem modis omnibus intolerabile est, cũ sub praetextu veritatis sua figmenta magno hiatu & conatu spargunt. Dominu eos, quos ipsi revocare in veritatis viam est uisum, cooertat, ac eis det idem nobiscum in Domino sentire: caeteros, qui spu to coelu, medacijs veritatem oppugnare pergunt, cofuridat: ut cognoscat omnes, esse Deu qui omnia uideat & iudicet.
units.tr: Yet it seems less wonderful to God's servants that the impostors of the Antichrist openly wage war against God, while they indulge in hatred, envy and other blind passions. What is more astonishing is that those who wish to appear as the pillars of the Church and the front-line warriors in the war against the Antichristians often take such pleasure in themselves that, puffed up by the applause of flatterers, partly inexperienced and partly factious, and inflated by their own support, they forget not only their own weakness and the gifts with which God has also endowed others, and take no account of them. Rather, leaving aside the enemies of the faith, they hurl the darts of a venomous tongue and a biting pen against the faithful who stand in the same battle line, while the Antichristians rejoice greatly in their bosom. This evil would be more tolerable if they preached Christ alone, even in controversy. But it is utterly intolerable that under the pretext of truth they spread their own inventions with great gaping and effort. May the Lord cover those whom they have thought fit to call back to the way of truth, and give them to think the same as we do in the Lord; and may He confound the others, who, against the heavens, continue to oppose the truth with lies, so that all may know that there is a God who sees and judges all things.

units.la: VERSVS VI.
units.tr: VERSE 6.

units.la: Nonne omnes isti populi super eum parabolam sumet, & sermonem aenigmatiu de eo, dicent: Va multiplicanti nō sua: & quousque id faciet, & aggravabit super se (opes tanquam) lutum densum?
units.tr: Shall not all these peoples take up a parable against him, and a taunting riddle about him, and say: Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own! How long will he do so, and load himself with thick clay?

units.la: Apud omnes Gentes decantatam iri Nebucadnezaris [illegible, ~20 letters] hac oratione Dominus indicat.
units.tr: By this utterance the Lord indicates that the name of Nebuchadnezzar would be sung among all the nations [illegible, ~20 letters].

units.la: Quemadmodum autem cupiditas di-vitiarum in infinitum vadit, ut in Politi-cis monet Aristoteles: ita regnadi & imperij pomœria longè lateque proferendi cupidinis nullus est modus in eorū Prin-cipum animis, qui non quam bene, sed quam multis praesint, spectare solent. Exemplo sunt Nebucadnezar, & Alexander Magnus lacrymas profundens, cùm fabula de pluribus Mundis audita, quaereretur, Nondum se unius Mundi imperio exasse potitum esse: ut nihil iam de aliis dicam.
units.tr: As covetousness for riches knows no bounds, as Aristotle observes in the Politics, so in the minds of those princes who look not to how well but to how many they rule, there is no limit to the desire to extend the boundaries of rule and empire far and wide. Nebuchadnezzar is an example, and Alexander the Great, who wept when, on hearing the tale of many worlds, he was asked whether he had not yet mastered even one world. I need say nothing more of others.

units.la: Monet autem hæc oratio, nō esse Principibus vilipendenda subiectorum iudicia, iustos gemitus, amorem & alia, de quibus aliquid addam.
units.tr: This utterance warns that rulers should not despise the judgments of their subjects, their just groans, their love, and other things of which I shall add something.

units.la: 1. Etsi hoc laudi ducitur Seuero Imperatori, quòd fuit [illegible, ~25 letters] & Augusto, quòd Timagenem historicum, qui multa petulater in Caesarem eiusq; familia dixerat, initiò quidè monuit, ut moderatius lingua uteretur:
units.tr: 1. Although it is counted to the praise of the Emperor Severus that [illegible, ~25 letters], and to Augustus that, when the historian Timagenes had said many insolent things against Caesar and his family, he at first warned him to use his tongue more moderately.

units.la: [Greek words in the text above are not legible on the scan.] deinde cum perseueraret male loqui, do[?] mo illi sua interdixit: nec Pollioni amico, maledicum domi suæ alenti, aliud dixit, quàm: ἀνεψιοτρεφὴς[?] tamen nihil est dubium, etiam summis Principibus non esse nihili plane facienda iudicia inferiorum, quæ sunt documenta uel amoris & gratitudinis erga Principes bene meritos: uel odij erga tyrannos & Promeri canes, qui illis mutuas operas tradunt: uel leuitatis in desertione legitimi Magistratus.
units.tr: [Greek words in the text above are not legible on the scan.] Then, when he persisted in speaking ill, Augustus forbade him his house; and to his friend Pollio, who was harbouring a slanderer in his home, he said nothing but [Greek words, not legible]. Yet there is no doubt that even the greatest princes ought not to make light of the judgments of their inferiors, which are evidence either of love and gratitude towards princes who have deserved well, or of hatred towards tyrants and their Promethean dogs who lend them mutual services, or of fickleness in deserting a lawful magistrate.

units.la: 2. Liberale subiectorum de Principe bono iudicium, non solum accendit amorem & reuerentiam erga eum, sed etiam fouet & alit. Econtra illiberale iudicium accendit & auget odium. Verè enim dictum est à Diodoro Siculo: οὐ τῶν ἡγεμόνων ὑπεροχὰς[?], τὰς μὲν ἐπαινουντας, ἐκ δὲ μίσους τῶν ὑποτεταγμένων[?]. Itaque ut amorem aut odium subditorum, ita etiam eorum iudicium cordatus Princeps non facile contemnet.
units.tr: 2. A generous judgment of subjects concerning a good prince not only kindles love and reverence towards him, but also cherishes and nourishes them. On the contrary, an ungenerous judgment kindles and increases hatred. Diodorus Siculus rightly said that the rulers' superiority, praised by those who are subject to them, produces love, but hatred arises from those who are under them [Greek words]. Therefore, just as a prudent prince will not easily disregard the love or hatred of his subjects, so neither will he easily disregard their judgment.

units.la: 3. Neque uerò Principe bono indignà φιλοτιμίᾳ censeri debet, delectari uera gloria, id est, approbatione rectè factorum, præsertim si sit uerus consensus conscietiæ ipsius,recte iudicantis, & aliorum recte iudicantium. Sicut necillius fuerit, iustam non recte ab eo tum dictorum tum factorum reprehensionem, uilipendere: aut iniusta uituperatione frangi animo, & sibi etiam in recte factis displicere:hoc enim pusillanimitatis foret, à qua alienum esse Principem opus est & oportet.
units.tr: 3. Nor indeed ought a good prince to be thought to be moved by unworthy ambition, but to take delight in true glory, that is, in the approval of right actions, especially if there is a true agreement of his own conscience, which judges rightly, and of others who judge rightly. Nor is it fitting for him to make light of a just rebuke of his words and deeds, or to be broken in spirit by an unjust censure, and to be displeased with himself even for right actions; for this would be a sign of pusillanimity, from which a prince must and should be free.

units.la: Id ergo ei statuendum de uirtutibus animi & eorum ἀποτελεσματικῶν[?], quod de contrariis Poeta cecinit:
units.tr: Therefore, concerning the virtues of the mind and their [Greek word], he should hold to what the poet sang about their opposites:

units.la: Omne animi uitium tanto conspectius in seCrimen habet, quanto maior qui peccat habetur.
units.tr: Every fault of the mind has the more conspicuous guilt, the greater the man who is thought to commit it.

units.la: Fridericum 3. Imperatorem cuidam dicenti, Multos esse qui ipsi maledicerent: respondisse accepimus, Summos Principes scopi instar esse, ad quem omnes fe-rè linguarum tela collimant: ac cum hominibus μεμψιμοίροις seu querulis satisfa-cere nequeant, dandam operam, ut quo-ad eius fieri potest, conscientiam ferunt puram coram Deo.
units.tr: We are told that the Emperor Frederick III, when someone said to him that many people spoke ill of him, replied that great princes are like a target at which almost all the arrows of tongues are aimed; and since they cannot satisfy men who are grumblers or complainers, they should take care, as far as possible, to keep their conscience pure before God.

units.la: 4. Nec sic ἐξ[?] τῶν ἀνθρώπων Princeps sibi positus uideri debet, ut se ἀνυπεύθυνον[?] esse somniet. Est enim Principi administratæ Reipub. ratio Deo olim reddenda. Iuxta illud Iosaphati Regis dictum ad Iudices:
units.tr: 4. Nor should a prince placed over men so regard himself as to dream that he is answerable to no one. For the prince must one day render to God an account of the government he has administered. In accordance with that saying of King Jehoshaphat to the judges:

units.la: Videte quid vos faciatis: non enim ho-mini iudicabitis, sed Iehouae: & erituo-bifcum in negocio iudicij.2.Chron.19.6.
units.tr: "Take heed what you do; for you judge not for man but for Jehovah, and he will be with you in the matter of judgment." 2 Chron. 19:6.

units.la: 5. Sic tamen fit animatus, ut nec recte iudicantium applausu, ceu vento fecun-do sublatus, nimium sibi placeat: nec eo destitutus, sibi nimium displiceat: nec iu-stam reprehensionem oderit: nec iniu-stam, plane sibi infrugiferam ducat: nec denique assentatorum fumos sibi caligi-nem in iudicando offundere, & impone-re patiatur.
units.tr: 5. Yet he should be so disposed that he is not lifted up, as if by a favourable wind, by the applause of those who judge rightly, and so takes too much pleasure in himself; nor, when deprived of it, does he displease himself too much; nor does he hate a just rebuke, nor think an unjust one wholly unprofitable to himself; and finally, he does not allow flatterers' smoke to cloud his judgment and impose upon him.

units.la: Nihil dubium est, Dauidi non medio-cri in rebus afflictis solatio fuisse illud e-logium: Certò facturus est Iehouah Do-mino meo domum stabilem, quia praelia Iehouae Dominus meus praeliatus est, & malicia nō inuēta fuit in te à diebus tuis. 1.Sam.25.28.
units.tr: There is no doubt that the eulogy was no small comfort to David in his afflicted circumstances: "Jehovah will surely make my lord a sure house, because my lord fights the battles of Jehovah, and no evil has been found in you from your days." 1 Sam. 25:28.

units.la: Idem bene sibi conscius, praeiudicijs ꝓ-mulorum, in gratiam Saulis sub quodam iuris praetextu ipsum condemnantium, opposuit ἀπολογίαν [?]: Num vere, & congregatio, iusticiam loquimini, aequitates iu-dicatis filij hominum? Psal.58.1. Nec erat cur sibi licet calamitoso displiceret, qui hominum praeiudicio circumuentus, bo-na conba[?] conscientia ad Dei tribunal & iudicium prouocare poterat.
units.tr: Conscious of his own integrity, he set against the prejudices of many, who under some pretext of law condemned him in order to win Saul's favour, his [apologia]: "Do you indeed speak justice, you assembly, and judge equity, you sons of men?" Ps. 58:1. Nor was there any reason why he who was surrounded by the prejudice of men, but had a good conscience, should be displeased with his calamity, since he could appeal to God's tribunal and judgment.

units.la: Iustam autem reprehensionem, siue ea ab amico, siue ab inimico profecta esset, Principes boni & cordati nunquam sibi aspernandam censuerunt.
units.tr: Good and wise princes have never thought that a just rebuke, whether it came from a friend or an enemy, should be spurned.

units.la: Dauid à Nathane obiurgatus, nõ ei cõ tradixit: sed ingenuè se peccauisse, fassus est. 2.Sam.12.13.
units.tr: David, rebuked by Nathan, did not spurn him, but freely confessed that he had sinned. 2 Sam. 12:13.

units.la: Philippus Rex Macedonum, cum post uictoriâ Cheronesem epulo ἐπινικίῳ[?] suos duces excepisset, largiusq; bibisset, spectatibus captiuis Athenien-sibus, inter quos erat Demades Orator, choreas immode-ste ducere coepit, choragum agens. Cum autem Demades exclamasset: Miror, ô Philippe, te, cum tibi fortuna Agamemnonis personam dederit, Therfitae opera agere: Rex non modò illa obiurgatione non fuit offensus: sed etiam ferro in terram proiecto, & neglecta muliercula, ad regiam grauitatem euestigiò se composuit: & ut remuneraretur tempestiuam admonitionem, libertate donauit Atticos ciues, quos uictor coeperat.
units.tr: Philip, King of the Macedonians, after his victory at Chersonesus, had entertained his commanders at a victory feast and drunk rather freely. When Athenian captives were brought in, among whom was the orator Demades, he began to lead dances immodestly, playing the chorus-leader. But when Demades cried out, "I am amazed, O Philip, that when fortune has given you the role of Agamemnon, you act the part of Thersites," the king was not only not offended by that rebuke; he threw down his sword on the ground, set aside the neglected little dancing girl, and at once composed himself to royal dignity. And in return for the timely admonition, he granted freedom to the Athenian citizens whom as victor he had taken captive.

units.la: Iniustam autem & calumniosam reprehesionem[?] qui omni fructu carere putatnō satis uidet,eam cum à sycophantis proficiscatur (à quibus uituperari,quàm laudari bonos,plurimum ipsorum interest) laudi ducendam. Vt enim à laudatis laudari, sic ab illaudatis uituperari, laus uera est. Prudenter sane Antisthenes,qui cum ab improbis quibusdam se laudatū accepisset: Vereor,inquit,ne quid imprudens fecerim mali.
units.tr: As for an unjust and slanderous rebuke, whoever thinks it yields no fruit does not see well enough; since it comes from sycophants (and it matters greatly to them that good men be blamed rather than praised), it should be counted as praise. For just as being praised by the praised is true praise, so being blamed by the unpraised is true praise too. Antisthenes wisely said, when he had been told that certain wicked men had praised him: "I fear, he said, that I have done something foolish and wrong."

units.la: Patienter Dauid,qui in maledicū contumacia non regesit, sed:Sinite,ait,illum ut maledicat:quia dixit ei Iehouah. Forsitā respiciet Iehouah ad afflictionem meam, & reddet mihi Iehouah bonum pro maledictione eius hodie. 2.Sam.16.v.11.12.
units.tr: David bore it patiently, who did not answer the reviler with stubbornness, but said: "Let him alone, to curse, because Jehovah has said to him. Perhaps Jehovah will look upon my affliction, and Jehovah will repay me good for his cursing this day." 2 Sam. 16:11–12.

units.la: Exitiosam autem esse Regibus, patulas aures habentibus,assentatorum ψιλολογικῶ[?] & συνοφαντικῷ[?], uel Ioæ Regis Iudæ exemplū docet, 2.Chron.24.17. Postquam autem mortuus est Ioiadas, uenerunt Principes Iehudah, & incuruauerūt se Regi: tunc obtemperauit eis Rex. 18. Et dereliquerunt domū Iehouæ Dei Patrum, &c.
units.tr: That it is destructive for kings who lend open ears to flatterers, whether of idle talk [Greek word] or of calumny [Greek word], the example of Joash, King of Judah, teaches: 2 Chron. 24:17. "But after Jehoiada died, the princes of Judah came and bowed down to the king; then the king listened to them. And they forsook the house of Jehovah, the God of their fathers," etc.

units.la: Vt autem finem faciam, cum,quæ sint de Nebucadnezaris φιλαρχίᾳ[?], uiolentia,rapacitate,gentium iudicia futura: & quid de eius interitu parabolice dicendum sit, praenunciat Hab.2.6. & toto fere 13.capite Isaiae: satis ostendit,non esse Principibus iudicia, uota, gemitus subiectorum suorum plane negligenda, & pro nihilo habenda: id quod monere uisum erat.
units.tr: To bring this to an end: Habakkuk 2:6 and almost the whole of the thirteenth chapter of Isaiah foretell what judgments of the nations would follow the violence, rapacity and [Greek word] of Nebuchadnezzar, and what must be said parabolically of his downfall. This sufficiently shows that the judgments, wishes and groans of subjects must not be wholly neglected or regarded as worthless by princes; which is what I thought it needful to warn of.

units.la: Homini cordato non esse contemnenda aliorum de se iudicia.
units.tr: That a sensible person should not despise the judgments others make of him.

units.la: 1. Ab efficiente principe. Quicquid à Deo auctore non sine eius singulari consilio proficiscitur,illud omne non est contemnendum homini sano. Atqui, tam ἀδοξία[?] & honesta existimatio apud homines, à Deo benedicente: quàm contemtus, ab eodem puniente proficiscuntur. Iuxta dicta: Gratiam & gloriam dat Iehouah: Psal.84.11. Item: Effundit contemtum in Principes: & errare facit eos in inanitate sine uia: Psal.107.40. Item; Aufer à me opprobrium & contemtum: quia testimonia tua exquisiui: Psal.119.
units.tr: 1. From the efficient cause. Whatever proceeds from God as author, and not without his particular counsel, is not to be despised by a sound man. But both honour and good esteem among men, when God blesses, and contempt, when God punishes, proceed from him. Thus the sayings: "Iehovah gives grace and glory," Ps. 84:11. Likewise: "He pours contempt upon princes and makes them wander in a trackless waste," Ps. 107:40. Likewise: "Take away from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought out your testimonies," Ps. 119.

units.la: 22. Igitur non sunt homini cordato uili-pendenda.
units.tr: 22. Therefore they are not to be held cheap by a sensible person.

units.la: 2. A' fine. Id quod plurimum facit ad agnitionem nostri, (quae posita est in bonorum quibus instructi sumus & gaude-mus, & malorum quibus laboramus,uera noticia) non parui ducendum est hominibus [illegible, ~6 letters] praeditis. Sed aliena de nobis tam iudicia, quàm praeiudicia, eò plurimùm conducunt, ut nosipsos agnoscamus. Sunt igitur nobis accuratè tum cognoscenda tum etiam perpendenda.
units.tr: 2. From the end. What contributes most to our knowledge of ourselves (which consists in true knowledge of the good things with which we are endowed and in which we rejoice, and of the evils with which we struggle) should not be thought a small matter by men [illegible] endowed with such things. But other people's judgments about us, and their prejudices alike, greatly help us to recognise ourselves. They must therefore be carefully both recognised and weighed.

units.la: Minorem δεικτικῶς[?] declarare & probare libet, hoc pacto:
units.tr: I wish to state and prove the minor premise by demonstration, in this way.

units.la: 1. Prima hominis cura esse debet, ut talis reuera fit, qualis alijs uult uideri: τετράγωνος ἀνὴρ[?] : nec instar Chamaeleontis mutabilis: ut rectè Aristoteles censuit. Finis enim praecepti, cui hominem Deus συμμορφῶσαι uult, est caritas ex puro corde, & conscientia bona, & fide non simulata. 1.Tim.1.5.
units.tr: 1. A man's first care should be to be truly such as he wishes to appear to others: a square man [τετράγωνος ἀνήρ], and not changeable like a chameleon, as Aristotle rightly judged. For the end of the command to which God wills to conform man is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned. 1 Tim. 1:5.

units.la: 2. Dei enim, qui καρδιογνώστης est: & piorum, qui cum scientia rectam rerum & personarum δοκιμασίαν coniunxerunt, iudicia: caeterorum praeiudicia, omnibus certò subeunda sunt.
units.tr: 2. The judgments of God, who knows the heart, and of the godly, who have joined right knowledge of things and persons with discernment, must certainly be undergone by all, as must the prejudices of the rest.

units.la: 3. Diuino iudicio per gratiam, propter Christum, probamur. Vt enim Christus est dilectus ille Filius, in quo Pater acquiescit: Matt.3.17. sic nos gratis facti sumus gratiin illo dilecto; Eph.1.6.
units.tr: 3. We are approved by divine judgment, through grace, on account of Christ. For as Christ is that beloved Son in whom the Father rests, Matt. 3:17, so we have been made freely accepted in that Beloved, Eph. 1:6.

units.la: 4. Iudicio humano iure iniuriáue uel laudamur, uel uituperamur.
units.tr: 4. By human judgment, rightly or wrongly, we are either praised or blamed.

units.la: 5. Nec mirum nobis uideri debet, si unus & idem laudetur ab his, culpetur ab illis. Vt olim Athanasium magnum laudauerunt Orthodoxi, uituperauerunt Ariani. Nam alij in iudicando adhibentue-ram donorum Spiritus sancti aestimationem & candorem, &[illegible, ~8 letters] aczelum ad-uersus turpitudinem manifestam & errores: alij rerum & personarum ignari, adhibent maleuolentiam, inuidiam & a-lias pestes, ceu pesimas consultrices.
units.tr: 5. Nor should it seem strange to us if one and the same man is praised by some and blamed by others. Thus the Orthodox once praised the great Athanasius, and the Arians blamed him. For some, in judging, bring to bear an esteem for the gifts of the Holy Spirit, candour, and zeal against manifest baseness and errors; others, ignorant of things and persons, bring malevolence, envy and other plagues, as the worst counsellors.

units.la: 6. Iam uero idem χάρισμα[?], aut κατόρθωμα[?], saepe aliis placet, aliis displicet. Linguarum donum, quod die Pentecostes Apostolis datum est a Spiritu sancto, ipsis quidem ornamento, praesidio & solatio fuit: illusoribus autem ludibrio. Heroi-cum facinus Phinees, trucidantis scorta-torem Israelitam una cum Midianitide mu-lierculā, hypocritis quibusdam adeo ui-sum est indignū Sacerdote,ut etiā Deum sententiam suam interponere, & facinus illud heroici & ardentis spiritus comprobare, necesse esset. Psal.106.30.31.
units.tr: 6. Indeed the same gift [χάρισμα] or achievement [κατόρθωμα] often pleases some and displeases others. The gift of tongues, which the Holy Spirit gave to the apostles on the day of Pentecost, was indeed an ornament, a protection and a comfort to them, but a mockery to scoffers. The heroic deed of Phinehas, who slew an Israelite fornicator together with the Midianite woman, seemed to certain hypocrites so unworthy of a priest that God himself had to interpose his judgment and approve that deed of a heroic and fervent spirit. Ps. 106:30–31.

units.la: 7. Enimuero, cum quidam Chamæleponte mutabiliores sint, & cum iudicio uago & sententia affectum quoq; mutent, sit interdum, utidem homo eundem hominem, idem eius factum, eandem illius doctrinam, nunc probet ametq;, nunc damnet odioq; habeat. Quàm multi sunt hoc nostro tempore, qui cum [illegible, ~8 letters] Philippi Melanchthonis, uirtutum, meritorum doctrinæq;, non ita pridem uideri uoluerint: nunc in ista [illegible, ~6 letters] Ecclesiæ, Philippo uelut de plaustro conuiciantur? Vtinam det illis Deus, ut [illegible, ~8 letters] malint, quàm [illegible, ~4 letters], extra ueritatis & charitatis orbitam, [illegible, ~5 letters].
units.tr: 7. Indeed, since some are more changeable than a chameleon, and change their affection along with their wandering judgment and opinion, it sometimes happens that the same man now approves and loves, now condemns and hates, the same man, the same deed of his, the same doctrine of that one. How many there are in our own time who, not long ago, were willing to be seen as admirers of Philip Melanchthon's virtues, merits and doctrine, and who now rail at Philip as if from a cart, in [illegible] of the Church! Would that God might grant them to prefer [illegible] to [illegible], outside the orbit of truth and charity [illegible].

units.la: 8. Homo Dei ex [illegible, ~7 letters] conscientiæ suæ, recte iudicantis & probantis opus suum, Gal.6.4. & aliorum recte iudicantium, eam uoluptatem percipiat, quæ nihil diluat mœrorem, & seruiat gloriæ Dei. Non enim seipsum admirari debet, cum fit [illegible, ~6 letters]: sed Dei erga se bonitatem agnoscere, & recte factorum laudem in solidum ei uni tribuere.
units.tr: 8. The man of God should receive, from the witness of his own conscience rightly judging and approving his work (Gal. 6:4), and from others judging rightly, that joy which dilutes no sorrow and serves the glory of God. For he ought not to admire himself when [illegible], but to acknowledge God's goodness toward him, and to ascribe the praise of right deeds wholly and solely to him.

units.la: 9. Et cum redundans in aliis charitas, iudicijs piorum aliquam offundat caligi-nem, prudentis est, dotes quæ ei attribuuntur discernere. Etenim alias uere tribui[?] deprehendet, alias charitatis quoda amabili errore. Vt autem ueras dotes i-deo agnoscere debet, ne sit erga Deu in-gratus, & erga proximos inofficiosus: sic dotes quas ὑπὸ μέτρον[?] charitatis plenitu do affingit, modesta humilitq; confessio-ne & uoto optandas esse, non autem per errorem tribuendas, testabitur.
units.tr: 9. And since charity, overflowing in others, casts some mist over the judgments of the godly, it is the part of prudence to discern the gifts that are attributed to him. For he will find some truly ascribed and others ascribed through a kindly error of charity. Just as he ought to acknowledge the true gifts, lest he be ungrateful to God and undutiful to his neighbours, so he will show that the gifts which the fullness of charity ascribes to him moderately [ὑπὸ μέτρον] are to be wished for with modest humility and confession, and not attributed through error.

units.la: 10. Sic autem laudanda laudari patia-tur, ut non laudanda uere uituperari ma-lit, quàm falsò laudari. Est enim periculosum φιλαυτίας fascinum, uitia pro uirtu-tibus habere: & dissimulatis morbis & ijs quae desunt alicui, τὸ ὑγιὲς ἡ [illegible, ~9 letters]pov, seu per errorem, seu ἐν προσωπείῳ[?] alicui affingere. Nisi forte mediocre decus, ad quod obtinendum uoris pijs & exercitijs aspirandum sit, alicui sic tribuas, ut non tam eo instructum esse & iam excellere, quàm eo illi opus esse, & ad id obtinendum omni studio coṭendendum esse, significes.
units.tr: 10. Let him, however, allow things worthy of praise to be praised in such a way that he would rather be truly blamed for what is not worthy of praise than falsely praised. For it is a dangerous charm of self-love [φιλαυτίας] to hold vices for virtues, and, through error or pretence, to ascribe to someone diseases that are concealed, or what he lacks, [illegible] [τὸ ὑγιὲς ...]. Unless perhaps you ascribe to someone a moderate distinction, which must be aspired to by pious labours and exercises, in such a way that you signify not that he is already furnished with it and excels, but that he has need of it and must strive with every effort to obtain it.

units.la: 11. Quemadmodum uerò etiam hostiu (quorum laus praeclara reputatur, auctore Ariftotele) uituperanda in nobis uitu-perantium, reprehensio grata esse debet: sic fratrum uituperanda laudantium, aut laulaudanda vituperantium, præiudicium ingratum esse debet. Non tam enim quis de nobis pronūciet, quàm quomodo, & quàm vere, utiliter & appositè pronunciet, nobis est considerandum.
units.tr: 11. Just as the reproof of enemies (whose praise is reckoned distinguished, according to Aristotle) ought to be welcome to us in respect of the faults in us that they censure, so the censure of brothers who praise what should be censured, or who censure what should be praised, ought to be an unwelcome prejudice. For it is not so much what someone pronounces about us that we must consider, as how, and how truly, usefully and fittingly he pronounces it.

units.la: II. Iniusta autè præiudicia, calumnias, vellicationes, æquis feramus animis: ac memores simus dicti Prophetæ de viro beato: Ab auditu malo non trepidabit: firmum est cor eius cōfidens in Iehouah. Psal.112.7.
units.tr: II. Unjust prejudices, calumnies and jibes we should bear with an even mind, and remember the Prophet's words about the blessed man: "He will not be startled by evil tidings; his heart is firm, trusting in Iehovah." Ps. 112:7.

units.la: Hæc de alienis iudicijs, de nobisipsis & vita nostra, paucis licuit ἐπιαγχαφάν[?]. Vos pro vestra diligentia & pietate, addetis quæ huc facere videbuntur.
units.tr: Briefly, it has been permitted to touch upon these matters: the judgments of others, and ourselves and our life. You, in your diligence and piety, will add whatever seems to pertain to this.

units.la: ALTERA PARS VERSVS
units.tr: THE SECOND PART OF THE VERSE

units.la: 6. de πλεονεξίᾳ[?] Nebucadnezaris, & opibus male partis.
units.tr: 6. On the covetousness of Nebuchadnezzar, and wealth ill-gotten.

units.la: Væ multiplicanti non sua: & quousque id faciet, & aggravabit super se lutum de-sum? id est, opes terrenas, οἵτινες βυθίζωσι[?] τὰς ἀνθρώπως εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ[?] ἀπώλειαν. 1. Timoth.6.9.
units.tr: Woe to him who multiplies what is not his! And how long will he do so, and load himself with thick clay? That is, earthly riches, which "plunge men into destruction and perdition" [ὅτινες βυθίζουσι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν]. 1 Timothy 6:9.

units.la: Hac exclamatione Dominus ostedit, Nebucadnezaris insatiabilem esse φιλαρ-χίαν χἰκμ̄ ἡ [?]πλεονεξίᾳ, eamq; tanto minus exple ri posse, quo plures prouinciæ & opes in potestatem illius venirent.
units.tr: By this exclamation the Lord shows that the ambition [φιλαρχία] and covetousness [πλεονεξία] of Nebuchadnezzar were insatiable, and that the more provinces and riches came into his power, the less he could be satisfied.

units.la: De seniore Dionysio memoriæ proditum est, eum, cum circa initium tyranni-dis, in regia, à Syracusanis συγομαχῆσαι [?] obsessus, in summo vitæ discrimine versaretur: & amici hortarentur, ut deposito imperio vitam redimeret: conspicientem bouem à lanione uno ictu prostratum, dixisse: Quum mors adeò breuis sit, an'nō absurdum fuerit, mortis metu tale regnū deponere?
units.tr: It is recorded of the elder Dionysius that, near the beginning of his tyranny, while he was in the citadel and besieged by the Syracusans, he was in the greatest danger of his life. His friends urged him to lay down his power and redeem his life. But seeing an ox struck down by a butcher with one blow, he said: "Since death is so brief, would it not be absurd to lay down such a kingdom out of fear of death?"

units.la: Jam vero, si quidam vel mortis periculo regnum sibi esse redimendum existimant: quid animi Principibus ambitiosis & regnandi cupidis esse dicemus, qui magnos habent successus: & quorum conatibus vix quisquam dehortatione modesta ἀντοφθαλμῷ [?], nedum omni conatu resistere audet? Nihil dubium est, eos magis magisq; & plura habendi, & pluribus imperandi libidine exardescere. Crescit enim regnandi amor, cum accessione ignorum: ut σύμφυτον νόσημα [?].
units.tr: Now, if some think that they must buy back a kingdom for themselves even at the risk of death, what shall we say of the disposition of ambitious princes who desire to rule, who enjoy great successes, and against whose undertakings hardly anyone dares to oppose even a modest dissuasion face to face [ἀντοφθαλμῷ], much less to resist with every effort? There is no doubt that they burn ever more and more with the lust of having more and of ruling over more. For the love of ruling grows with the addition of what feeds it, like an innate disease [σύμφυτον νόσημα].

units.la: DE AVARITIA.
units.tr: ON COVETOUSNESS.

units.la: Ex hoc loco & definitionem Avaritiæ, &c. & eius illustrem ὑποτύπωσιν, petere licebit.
units.tr: From this passage it will be permissible to take both the definition of covetousness, and its distinguished portrait [ὑποτύπωσις].

units.la: I. Definitio haec est: Auaritia est insatiabilis multiplicatio non suorum, seu alienorum. Auarus enim is est, qui aliena cogerit sine modo. Ex hac finitione colligimus:
units.tr: I. The definition is this: covetousness is the insatiable multiplying of what is not one's own, or of what belongs to others. For the covetous man is one who seizes others' goods without measure. From this definition we gather:

units.la: 1. Auaritiam opponi τῇ αὐτάρκεια, de qua dicitur: Est autem quaestus magnus pietas cum animo sua sorte contento. Nihil enim intulimus in mundum, uidelicet nec efferre quicquam possumus. Sed habentes alimenta, & quibus tegamur, his contenti erimus. 1. Tim. 6. v. 6. 7. 8.
units.tr: 1. Covetousness is opposed to self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια], of which it is said: "Godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and clearly we can carry nothing out. But having food and clothing, with these we shall be content." 1 Timothy 6:6–8.

units.la: 2. Diuini iuris esse distinctionem domi niorum & facultatum: eamque scelerate uiolari abijs, qui suis non contenti, alienis inhiant, & ea inuncare conantur. Notum est illud eiusdem Apostoli dictum: Sint mores alieni ab auaritia: fitis contenti praesentibus. dixit enim ipse: Non te deferam, neq; te derelinquâ. Heb. 13. 5. 6.
units.tr: 2. The distinction of dominions and property is of divine law, and it is wickedly violated by those who, not content with their own, gape after others' goods and try to lay hands on them. That saying of the same Apostle is well known: "Let your manners be free from covetousness; be content with what you have. For he himself has said: I will not leave you, nor forsake you." Hebrews 13:5–6.

units.la: 3. Non redundantem copiam, sed eorum quae praestò sunt usum, homini pio requirendum. Luc. 12. 15. Dixit Dominus Iesus eis: Videte & cauete ab auaritia. neque enim cum bona cuipiam redundant, uita ipsi constat ex bonis suis. Scite autè de auaro dicitur, deesse ei tam ea quae habet, bet,quàm etiam illa quæ nō habet. Neu-tris enim uti & frui potest. Econtrà ὁ αὐ-[?]τάρκης nouit deprimi & abundare: ubiqʒ & in omnibus initiatus est,&c. Phil.4.12. Recte Ambrosius: Illud,ait,possidemus, quo utimur. & Augustinus: Possidet ma-le,qui malè utitur.
units.tr: 3. A godly man should seek not an overflowing abundance but the use of what is at hand. Luke 12:15: the Lord Jesus said to them, "Take heed and beware of covetousness." For when goods overflow for someone, his life does not consist in his possessions. Rightly is it said of the covetous man that he lacks both what he has and what he does not have, for he can use and enjoy neither. The self-sufficient man, on the other hand, knows both how to be brought low and how to abound; in all things and in every respect he is initiated. Philippians 4:12. Rightly Ambrose: "We possess that," he says, "which we use." And Augustine: "He possesses badly who uses badly."

units.la: II. ὑποτύπωσις[?] hominis rapacis & fordi-di est, Aggrauat fuperfe lutum densum. Quemadmodum is,qui seipsum luto nō conspurcat & inuoluit solùm, sed etiam eius magno pondere congesto aggrauat, tantò minus elustari & emergere potest, quò maius luti pondus sibi ipse imponit: ita quò homo auarus maiores facultates opum corradit,tantò magis id experitur quod est apud Paulū, 1.Timoth.6.9. Qui autem uolunt ditescere, incidunt in tentationem & laqueum,& cupiditates multas amentes & damnosas, quæ demergunt homines in exitium & interitum.
units.tr: II. The portrait of the rapacious and filthy man is: "He loads himself with thick clay."
