Just as one who not only soils himself with mud and wraps himself in it, but also weighs himself down with a great mass of it heaped on, is the less able to cleanse himself and rise up, the greater the weight of mud he lays on himself; so the more the covetous man piles up greater means of wealth, the more he experiences what Paul says, 1 Timothy 6:9: "But those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires, which drown men in ruin and destruction."

units.la: Mirum autè est, quòd Lutum densum uocat Dominus aurum,argentum,gem-mas,denique quicquid preciosum uidetur. Sed meminerimus, bonas & utiles Dei creaturas non uocari per contumeliam Lutum, sed κατὰ συγχρησιν[?]. Vt enim cœlecœlestia bona in cœlis reponenda sunt, ne nobis eripi aut corrumpi possint: & ut corda quoq; nostra in cœlis sint: Matt. 6.20.21. Sic terrestria bona mentem huius mundi sordibus obruunt & sepeliunt, & humo affigunt, sic ut extra terræ ster-quilinium non possit emergere.
units.tr: It is remarkable that the Lord calls gold, silver, gems, in short whatever seems precious, "thick clay." But let us remember that the good and useful creatures of God are not called clay by way of insult, but by a figure of speech [κατὰ συγχρησιν]. For just as heavenly goods are to be laid up in heaven, so that they cannot be taken from us or corrupted, and so that our hearts too may be in heaven (Matthew 6:20–21), so earthly goods bury and entomb the mind under the filth of this world and fasten it to the ground, so that it cannot rise out of the dunghill of the earth.

units.la: Nobis placeat illud Cypriani: Patrimonium Deo creditum in tuto est. & hoc Hieronymi dictum: Qui diuitiarum seruus est, diuitias custodit ut seruus: qui autem seruitutis discusseritiugum[?], distribuet eas ut dominus.
units.tr: Let us take pleasure in that saying of Cyprian: "A patrimony entrusted to God is safe." And in this saying of Jerome: "He who is a slave to riches guards them as a slave; but he who has shaken off the yoke of servitude will distribute them as a master."

units.la: Laboremus ergo de spiritualibus opi-bus parandis & augendis, ut & nobis & alijs plurimum prosimus.
units.tr: Let us therefore labour to acquire and increase spiritual riches, so that we may be of the greatest benefit both to ourselves and to others.

units.la: VERSVS VII.
units.tr: VERSE VII.

units.la: Nonne repente consurgent qui morde-ant te, & expergiscentur qui commoueant te, erisq; in rapinam illis?
units.tr: Shall not they rise up suddenly that shall bite you, and awake that shall vex you, and you shall be booty for them? (Habakkuk 2:7.)

units.la: τὸ ὅτι,
units.tr: That [τὸ ὅτι],

units.la: Talionis poenam Chaldaeis minatur Dominus, adhibita imagine ducta à leonibus, aut molosis. Vt enim hi ouem aut aliud animal subito adoriuntur, mordi-cus cùs prehendunt, concutiunt & lacerant: ita,inquit Dominus,Persæ & Medi inua-dent Chaldæos, & mordebunt ac concu tient eos, pro sua libidine ἀγοντες[?] ἡ φαύρον[?] τις ā se deuictos.
units.tr: The Lord threatens the Chaldeans with retribution in kind, using the image of lions or mastiffs. As these animals suddenly fall upon a sheep or some other beast, seize it in their jaws, and shake and tear it, so, says the Lord, the Persians and Medes will invade the Chaldeans, and will bite and shake them and carry them off as they please, having conquered them.

units.la: Illustrior erit hæc prophetia, si quia-nimo perpenderit Danielis uerba de prima Monarchia, quæ Babyloniorum & Assyriorum fuit, & de secunda, quæ Persarum fuit: Dan.7.4.5.
units.tr: This prophecy will be clearer if one carefully weighs Daniel's words about the first monarchy, which was that of the Babylonians and Assyrians, and about the second, which was that of the Persians: Dan. 7:4, 5.

units.la: Prima erat sicut leo, & alæ aquilæ e-rant ei: spectabam uero donec euulsæ sunt alæ eius, & ablata est è terra: atque in pedes more hominis stetit, cor̄ hominis datum est ei. Cor hominū datur, cum τὰ ψαθήματα[?] fiunt μαθήματα.
units.tr: The first was like a lion, and it had the wings of an eagle; I watched until its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted from the earth and made to stand on its feet like a man, and a man's heart was given to it. A man's heart is given when sufferings [pathēmata] become lessons [mathēmata].

units.la: Ecce autem alia bestia secunda similis erat urso, & ad latus unum stetit, tres quoq; costæ erant in ore eius inter dentes ipsius, ficq; dicebant ei: Surge & uora carnes multas.
units.tr: And behold another beast, a second, like a bear; it was raised up on one side, and it had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and they said to it, "Arise, devour much flesh."

units.la: Ex his & similibus dictis colligimus, sæpenumero homines hominibus lupo-rum instar esse, nulla habita humanitatis ratione: ut hac pulcerrima ὑπαρτυπωσις[?] Dauid Propheta docet: Sed & in insidijs uicorum, in latebris occidit innocentem: oculi eius in pauperem intenti sunt. Insidiatur in abscondito, sicut leo in spelunca: insidiatur ad abripiendum pauperem: discerpit pauperem attrahens eum in rete suum. Deijcit & deprimit se, & cadit in vites eius turba pauperum. Psal. 10. 8. 9. 10.
units.tr: From these and similar sayings we gather that men are often like wolves to men, with no regard for humanity at all, as the prophet David teaches in this most beautiful picture: "He lies in wait in the villages, in hiding places he kills the innocent; his eyes are fixed upon the poor. He lies in wait in secret, as a lion in its den; he lies in wait to seize the poor; he catches the poor man, drawing him into his net. He crouches and bows down, and the multitude of the poor falls into his claws." Ps. 10:8, 9, 10.

units.la: Amplificationis autem, à circumstantiis ductae, haec sunt capita:
units.tr: The points that amplify this, drawn from the circumstances, are these:

units.la: 1. Quod repente, seu ἀπροσδοκήτως, Chaldaei ab hostibus Persis sint opprimendi.
units.tr: (1) That the Chaldeans are to be overwhelmed suddenly, or unexpectedly, by the Persian enemy.

units.la: 2. Quod ab iis qui iam sopiti, & sub iugum Babylonium missi videantur, sint inuadendi.
units.tr: (2) That they are to be attacked by those who seem already lulled to sleep and sent under the Babylonian yoke.

units.la: 3. Quod velut humi iacentes hostes insurrecturi sint, leonum praedae inhiantium instar.
units.tr: (3) That the enemies, lying as if on the ground, will rise up like lions eager for prey.

units.la: 4. Quod Chaldaeos, qui sibi ἀνίκητοι ἢ ἀνίκητοι videantur, vehementer sint commoturi.
units.tr: (4) That they will greatly shake the Chaldeans, who seem to themselves invincible.

units.la: 5. Quod horribili morsu laniaturi sint Babylonios.
units.tr: (5) That they will tear the Babylonians with a dreadful bite.

units.la: 6. Quod ut lupi agnos, sic Persae Babylonios, praedae loco sint habituri.
units.tr: (6) That the Persians will treat the Babylonians as the wolf treats lambs, as booty.

units.la: Noti sunt versus Rhadamanti apud Aristotelem:
units.tr: The verses of Rhadamanthus are well known, as quoted by Aristotle:

units.la: Iusta malis haec admissio pro crimine poena est, Si quae fecerunt aliis, patiantur & ipsi. Sed Babylonij repentè alias atq; aliàs gentes hostiliter invaserunt & oppresserunt. Ergo idem erit eorum quoque fatum. Utitur autem Dominus ἐρωτήματι[?] ut torporem excutiat ijs, qui ista absurda & impossibilia esse putabant.
units.tr: The admission is a just penalty for evil deeds: if they have done these things to others, let them suffer them too. But the Babylonians have suddenly attacked and oppressed nation after nation in hostile fashion. Therefore their fate will be the same. The Lord uses a rhetorical question to shake out the torpor of those who thought these things absurd and impossible.

units.la: In subitis rerum conuersionibus, infelices esse seculi huius filios, contra vero felices Dei filios.
units.tr: In sudden reversals of affairs, the sons of this age are unhappy, but on the contrary the sons of God are happy.

units.la: Multum dissimiles esse fideles & infideles, cum subitae rerum conuersiones, tempestatis cuiusdam instar, ingruunt, o-ratio Domini Dei nostri docet, etsi in ea tantum huius seculi hominum mentio fiat.
units.tr: That the faithful and the unfaithful are very unlike one another when sudden reversals of affairs break in like a storm is taught by the word of the Lord our God, although in that passage only men of this age are mentioned.

units.la: Infelices sunt infideles, sive in magnis illis rerum humanarum mutationibus e-mergant, sive mergantur: ut ex hisce colligi potest.
units.tr: The unfaithful are unhappy, whether they emerge from or are submerged by those great changes in human affairs, as can be gathered from the following:

units.la: 1. Quòd neutrum providentia Dei eve-nire, vere statuunt.
units.tr: (1) Because they truly maintain that neither happens by the providence of God.

units.la: 2. Quòd in rebus secundis vehementer luxuriant eorum animi.
units.tr: (2) Because in prosperity their minds grow exceedingly wanton.

units.la: 3. Quòd in rebus adversis non habent quò se conuertant. De numinis enim benevolentia ἀλλὰ τῇ φιλανθρωπίᾳ[?] ipsis non constat: hominum autem illis est suspesta fides & ficulnum subsidium.
units.tr: (3) Because in adversity they have nowhere to turn. For they are not sure of the goodwill of the divinity toward them, but have only a doubtful trust in men and a fig-leaf of help.

units.la: 4. Quòd consilia ponunt in anima, dolorem in corde, nec tamen quicquá proficiunt.
units.tr: (4) Because they make plans in their soul, and pain in their heart, yet accomplish nothing.

units.la: 5. Quòd licet per auia feratur, & se iam sibijpsis & alijs obfuisse & damna inferre sentiant: tamen adeò sunt [illegible, ~7 letters] ut ne cuiquam errasse uideantur, malint [illegible, ~12 letters] : ut habet uetus Proverbium.
units.tr: (5) Because, although they are carried astray by devious ways, and already perceive that they have harmed themselves and others and are inflicting loss, yet they are so [illegible] that they seem to have erred toward no one, and prefer [illegible], as the old proverb has it.

units.la: Econtrà uerò filij Dei felices sunt, etiā cùm cæteris infelices esse uidentur: ut ex hisce colligi potest.
units.tr: On the other hand, the sons of God are happy, even when they seem unhappy compared with others, as can be gathered from the following:

units.la: 1. Intelligunt enim, bona & mala diui-nitùs dispensari.
units.tr: (1) For they understand that good and evil are dispensed by divine decree.

units.la: 2. Res secundas (quas norunt esse inferiora bona) euanidas esse rectè statuunt: eoq; ijs non confidunt. ut de opibus dicitur: Diuitiæ si proueniant, ne apponatis cor: Psal.62.10.
units.tr: (2) They rightly hold that prosperous things (which they know to be lesser goods) are fleeting, and therefore they do not trust in them. As is said of riches: "If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them." Ps. 62:10.

units.la: 3. In rebus aduersis lætantur se habere Deum opitulatorem, qui dixit: Inuoca me in die tribulationis, & eruam te, & glorificabis me: Psal.50.15.
units.tr: (3) In adversity they rejoice that they have God as their helper, who said: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." Ps. 50:15.

units.la: 4. Consilium Dei dudumq; sequuntur, & successus habent exoptatissimos. Idèo repetunt assiduè dulcissimam Dei promissionem:Erudiam te,&docebo te qua via ambules: dirigam te oculo meo:Psal. 32.8. Item: Et est vir ille tanquam arbor plantata secundum fluenta aquarū, quae fructum suum dabit in tempore suo: & folium eius non marcescit: & quicquid facit, prosperum est. Psal.i.3.
units.tr: (4) They follow God's counsel long since given, and have the most desired success. Therefore they repeat constantly God's most sweet promise: "I will instruct you and teach you the way you should walk; I will guide you with my eye." Ps. 32:8. Likewise: "That man is like a tree planted by streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season; its leaf does not wither, and whatever he does prospers." Ps. 1:3.

units.la: 5. Deum ὁδηγὸν[?] sequuntur: & sicubi cat[?]nis intemperie abrepti deflexerunt, in viam se reduci petunt, & cū Dauide precantur: Errores quis intelligat? ab occultis munda me: Psal.19.12. Item: Vias tuas, Jehouah, fac me scire: semitas tuas doce me. Dirige me in veritate tua,& doce mei[?]: quoniam tu es Deus liberator meus: te expecto toto die: Psal.25.4.5. Caetera dissimilitudinis fidelium & infidelium capita consulto nunc praetereo.
units.tr: (5) They follow God as their guide; and if at any time they have swerved, carried away by the storm of their passions, they ask to be brought back onto the way, and pray with David: "Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from hidden faults." Ps. 19:12. Likewise: "Show me your ways, O Jehovah; teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God who delivers me; I wait for you all day long." Ps. 25:4, 5. I deliberately pass over the other points of difference between the faithful and the unfaithful for now.

units.la: VERSUS VIII.
units.tr: VERSE 8.

units.la: Quia tu spoliasti gentes multas, spolia-bunt te omnes reliqui populi,propter san-guinem hominum,& violentiam terræ & ciuitatis, omnium habitantium in ea. Αἰτιολογία[?] est. Prædixerat Jehouah, Chaldæorū opes diripiendas esse à Gentibus: quæ oratio non minus mira videri poterat ea aetate, quàm si quis hac nostra tristissima tempestate dicat, futurum ut Imperium & opes Turcarū nō multo pòst à Persis, aut à Germanis diripiantur.
units.tr: "Because you have plundered many nations, all the remaining peoples shall plunder you, because of the blood of men and the violence done to the land and the city and all who dwell in it." This is an aetiology [αἰτιολογία]. Jehovah had foretold that the wealth of the Chaldeans would be plundered by the Gentiles. This saying could have seemed no less strange in that age than if someone said in our own most sorrowful times that the empire and wealth of the Turks would soon be plundered by the Persians or the Germans.

units.la: Ducitur autem argumentum à iusto.
units.tr: The argument is drawn from justice.

units.la: Iustum est, par pari referri, non solùm priuatis hominibus, sed etiam totis gentibus. Iuxta dictum: Qua mensura metimini, uicissim metietur uobis:Matth.7.2. Luc.6.38. Item: Cum consummaueris esse prædator, prædationem patieris: cum consummaueris præuaricari, alij præuaricabuntur in te: Isa.33.v.1. Ac de malè factis eorumq; poenis, uniuersalis experientia suggesit Ethnicis has uoces: ὁ ἀνὴρ ῥέξει[?] τοῖον τέλος αὐτοῦ ἀκαίρια[?]. Item: τῶν μεγάλων ἀδικημάτων[?], μεγάλαι δὲ καὶ τιμωρίαι[?] παρὰ τῆς θεοῦ.
units.tr: It is just that like be repaid with like, not only to private persons but also to whole nations. According to the saying: "With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again" (Matt. 7.2; Luke 6.38). Likewise: "When you have ceased to be a plunderer, you will be plundered; when you have ceased to act treacherously, others will act treacherously against you" (Isa. 33.1). Universal experience also taught the heathen these words about evil deeds and their punishments: "A man's end will be such as his deeds" [ὁ ἀνὴρ ῥέξει τοῖον τέλος αὐτοῦ ἀκαίρια]; and again: "Great wrongs bring great punishments from the god" [τῶν μεγάλων ἀδικημάτων, μεγάλαι δὲ καὶ τιμωρίαι παρὰ τῆς θεοῦ].

units.la: Sed Babylonij omnibus belli incommodis gentes multas affecerunt. Hanc Minorem enumeratione sufficiente probat & illustrat Dominus. Meminit autem Dominus quinque maximorum malorum, quæ bellum inuehere solet: ac testatur, Chaldæos bella gerentes, tum Iudæos, tum alias gentes ijs affecisse. Catalogus θετικῶς[?] sic potest ex uerbis Domini colligi.
units.tr: But the Babylonians inflicted on many nations all the disadvantages of war. The Lord proves and illustrates this minor premise by an enumeration. He recalls five great evils which war is wont to bring, and testifies that the Chaldeans, waging war, inflicted these on the Jews as well as on other nations. A positive catalogue can be gathered from the Lord's words in this way.

units.la: 1. Direptio facultatum. Hostes enim sacra & profana pro sua libidine ἀγῶσι ἀλλὰ φόβοι[?]. Expugnatis Sardibus à Cyro, Irus & est subito, qui modo Croesus erat. Quàm sit hoc malum honestis hominibus graue, ex Menandri monosticho liquet: ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡδὺ ἀνὴρ ἀτιμίαν [illegible, ~6 letters] ποιεῖ, & ex illo versu Euripidis: ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡδὺ ἀνὴρ ἀνδρὸς ἀνυβρὶς [?] ἀνήρ.
units.tr: 1. Plundering of goods. For enemies seize sacred and profane things at their pleasure. When Sardis was taken by Cyrus, Croesus, who had just been a king, suddenly became a beggar like Irus. How grievous this evil is to honourable men is clear from the monostich of Menander, "for just as it is sweet..." [ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡδὺ ἀνὴρ ἀτιμίαν ... ποιεῖ], and from that verse of Euripides [ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡδὺ ἀνὴρ ἀνδρὸς ἀνυβρὶς ἀνήρ].

units.la: 2. Promiscuae cædes. Trucidantur omnium ordinum homines, ac inprimis iij qui patriae praesidio & ornamento ef-se[?] videntur.
units.tr: 2. Indiscriminate slaughter. Men of every rank are killed, and especially those who seem to be the defence and ornament of their country.

units.la: 3. Provinciarum occupatio. Vt Cam byses victo Psammeticho, & interfecto eius filio, Ægyptum Perfarū imperio subij-cit. Paulus Æmilius, debellato captoq; Perseo, Macedoniæ regnum in provin-ciam populi Romani convertit.
units.tr: 3. Occupation of provinces. Thus Cambyses, having defeated Psammetichus and killed his son, subjected Egypt to the empire of the Persians. Paulus Aemilius, having crushed and captured Perseus, turned the kingdom of Macedonia into a province of the Roman people.

units.la: 4. Vrbium expugnatio. Sæpe urbes κατὰ κράτος expugnatæ & captæ, funditus euertuntur: ut Hierosolyma à Tito, Vespasiani Imp. F. solo æquata est, sicut Dominus IESVS futurum prædixerat. Eadem urbs sancta iam antea à Babylonijs, usu Nebucadnezaris, incesa fuit & deleta.
units.tr: 4. Storming of cities. Often cities taken by storm and captured are utterly overthrown, as Jerusalem was razed to the ground by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, just as the Lord Jesus had foretold. That same holy city had earlier been burned and destroyed by the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar.

units.la: 5. Seruitus & mutatio Reipub. Reliquiæ enim ciuium & prouincialium, amissa αὐτονομίας & libertate, coguntur parere nouo domino. Vt urbs Attica à Lysandro expugnata, Tyrannis 30. coacta est seruire.
units.tr: 5. Servitude and change of government. For the remnant of citizens and provincials, having lost autonomy [αὐτονομία] and liberty, are compelled to obey a new master. Thus the Attic city taken by Lysander was forced to serve the Thirty Tyrants.

units.la: Ex his concludit Dominus, futurum ut Babylonij, qui tot tantorumque malorum auctores alijs exstitissent, iuxta talionis legem eadem aliquando perferre cogantur.
units.tr: From these things the Lord concludes that the Babylonians, who had been the authors of so many and so great evils for others, would at some time be compelled by the law of retaliation to suffer the same things.

units.la: Quis autem fructus ex huius argumenti consideratione ad nos redit?
units.tr: What fruit, then, does the consideration of this argument bring back to us?

units.la: Amplissimus sane. Etenim si hocunice optamus, ne qua iniuria seu dictis, seu factis afficiamur: demus etiam operam, ne in ullum mortalium scientes & prudentes simus iniurij. Neque tamen satis esse putemus, ab inferenda iniuria abstinere: nam illud quoque a nobis requirit Dominus, ut non modo bene uelimus proximis, sed etiam eisdem bene faciamus. Ac si Ethnicus ille Demosthenes recte persuasum habuit, hominem Deo similem fieri τὸ [illegible, ~10 letters] καὶ τὸ ἀληθὲς: multò magis nobis fide Christi illustra-tis id certò persuasum esse debet. Caeterum caueda nobis elt προσωπολημψία. Nō enim ij solum,qui nos diligunt, & qui opibus pollentes beneficentiam benefice-tia pensare possunt: sed etiam ij qui nos oderunt, aut qui par pari referre nō pos-sunt,nobis diligendi,& beneficijs(cū da-tur occasio)ornandi &iuuandi sunt. Vt autem est, cur nobis & alijs gratulemur, si quos nostra ἀνθρωπίᾳ[?] nos lucri fecisse animaduertamus: ita si quorum inuinci-bilem ergā nos inhumanitatem experia-mur, non est cur religiosi propositi & of-ficij unquam nos poeniteat: cum & Dei exemplo deceat nos τροπο-φορὰν[?]. Notum enim est illud Apostoli: Caritas omnia suffert: πάντα στέγει. 1.Cor.13.7.
units.tr: A very ample one indeed. For if we desire only this, that we be harmed by no injury, whether in words or in deeds, let us also take care not to be knowingly and deliberately unjust to any mortal. Nor should we think it enough to refrain from inflicting injury, for the Lord also requires of us that we not only wish well to our neighbours but also do them good. And if that heathen Demosthenes rightly held it to be persuaded that man becomes like God through [...] and the truth, then much more ought this to be firmly persuaded in us, who have been enlightened by the faith of Christ. Moreover we must beware of partiality [προσωπολημψία]. For not only those who love us, and who are able to repay kindness with kindness because of their wealth, but also those who hate us, or who cannot return like for like, are to be loved by us and adorned and helped with benefits whenever occasion is given. Just as there is cause to rejoice, both for ourselves and for others, when we see that we have gained some by our humanity, so if we experience the invincible inhumanity of some towards us, there is no cause ever to repent of our religious purpose and duty, since it becomes us to imitate God's example of forbearance [τροποφορά]. For that saying of the Apostle is well known: "Love bears all things" [πάντα στέγει] (1 Cor. 13.7).

units.la: Hæc ut ad usum transferre discamus, exemplo familiari utar.
units.tr: To learn to put these things into practice, I shall use a familiar example.

units.la: Propter φιλαλληλίαν[?] & cōfefsionem ingenuam sincerae doctrinae Euagelij, multi pij doctores & eorū ἀπολογίᾳ[?] hoc tempore deformatur calumnijs, premuntur Sinonio artificio, remouentur ab officio docendi tanquam ἐπιβουλαῖς[?], iniurijs denique multis & magnis afficiutur. Quid his faciundum censes? Respondeo [illegible, ~9 letters]:
units.tr: On account of brotherly love and the open confession of the pure doctrine of the gospel, many godly teachers and their defence [ἀπολογία] are at this time disfigured by calumnies, pressed by Sinonian trickery, removed from the office of teaching as if by plots [ἐπιβουλαί], and finally subjected to many great injuries. What do you think should be done about these things? I answer:

units.la: 1. Ne mutent sanctum propositum de veritate & eius confessione ingenua, & ab omni fuco aliena.
units.tr: 1. That they not alter the holy purpose concerning the truth and its open confession, a purpose free from all pretence.

units.la: 2. Dent operam, ut bonam causam bene agant, οὐ λαμπρῷ[?], cum spiritu lenitatis & mansuetudinis, sic ut re ipsa testentur, studio veri, non contendendi libidine sese duci.
units.tr: 2. That they take care to conduct the good cause well, with a spirit of gentleness and meekness, so that by their conduct they show themselves led by a zeal for the truth and not by a desire to quarrel.

units.la: 3. Ne unquam convicijs aut malefactis certent cum antagonistis, cum horum aliquos converti posse ad meliorem mentem, spes Christiana: ἀμετανοήτως[?] autem mensuram suam implere, fides, doceant.
units.tr: 3. That they never contend with their opponents by reproaches or wrongdoing, since the Christian hope is that some of them may be converted to a better mind, while faith teaches that the others fill up their measure without repentance [ἀμετανοήτως].

units.la: 4. Iniurias omnes magno animo ferre, auctorum miserari, ab eo quod malū est non vinci, sed bonitate maliciam vincere, discant. Haec & alia cum non sint in nostra potestate posita, oremus Filium Dei, ut ille robore sui sancti Spiritus nos omnes fulciat & confirmet.
units.tr: 4. That they learn to bear all injuries with a great mind, to pity those who inflict them, and not to be conquered by what is evil but to overcome evil with goodness. Since these and other things are not placed in our power, let us pray the Son of God that by the strength of his Holy Spirit he may uphold and confirm us all.

units.la: VERSVS IX.
units.tr: VERSE IX.

units.la: Va avarè sectanti avaritiam malam, ut domum suam aedificet, ut ponat in excelso nidum suum, ut liberetur e manu mali.
units.tr: Woe to him who greedily pursues evil gain for his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the hand of harm.

units.la: Est ὑποφορά, qua respondetur ad hoc προλόγισμα[?] Nebucadnezaris & Chaldeorum: Non est cur sibi suisque ab ullo hoste metuat, qui instructi sunt praecipuis prę-sidijs uitae cum dignitate transigendae, ut delicet, facultatibus opum, magnificis & munitissimis palatijs & arcibus, regnis deniq; & prouincijs florentissimis. Quibus enim haec suppetunt, ijs nec administri, uelut potentiae conseruandae & exercendae instrumenta, nec alia praesidia desunt. Econtrà, ἀν[?]ὴρ χρημάτων ἰδί[?]ου ἐστὶ γιγνώσκειν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων[?], ut dicebat Demosthenes: & qui sunt ἀνίατοι καὶ ἀπόλεις, miseri sunt, & ubique iacent, uidelicet expositi omnium iniurijs & ludibrio.
units.tr: This is a hypophora, by which the objection of Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans is answered. They have no cause to fear any enemy, since they are equipped with the chief safeguards of a life lived with dignity: abundant wealth, magnificent and very strongly fortified palaces and citadels, and finally kingdoms and most flourishing provinces. Those who have these things lack neither servants, as instruments for keeping and exercising power, nor other protections. On the contrary, "a man of wealth is one who knows how to recognise what belongs to others" [ἀνὴρ χρημάτων ἰδίου ἐστὶ γιγνώσκειν τῶν ἀλλοτρίων], as Demosthenes used to say; and those who are [ἀνίατοι καὶ ἀπόλεις] are wretched and lie everywhere, exposed, of course, to the injuries and mockery of all.

units.la: At Nebucadnezar & Chaldaei opes multarum Gentium cogefferunt & possident, arces & urbes plurimas munitissimasq; obtinent, florentissimas prouincias colunt & subiectas habent.
units.tr: But Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans have heaped together and possess the wealth of many nations; they hold very many citadels and most strongly fortified cities, cultivate the most flourishing provinces and have them under their rule.

units.la: Non igitur est cur, inferiorum Regum & populorum exemplo, sibi metuant.
units.tr: There is therefore no reason for them to fear, following the example of lesser kings and peoples.

units.la: Respondet Dominus: Non solùm qd quisq; nunc obtineat, sed etiam quo iure possideat, spectandum est. Male enim parta dilabuntur: & secundum Paræmiam, lucrum malum æquale est dispedio. Iam uerò Nebucadnezar & Chaldaei ex spolijs & rapinis tantas opes congesse-runt. Proinde non est cur opinentur su-turum, ut de iis tertius hæres gaudeat.
units.tr: The Lord replies: one must consider not only what anyone now holds, but also by what right he possesses it. For things wrongly gained slip away, and according to the proverb, ill-gotten gain is equal to loss. Indeed Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans gathered such great wealth from spoils and plunder. Therefore there is no reason for them to suppose that it will come about that a third heir rejoices over them.

units.la: Lex naturæ & experientia universalis docuerunt Sophoclem id quod eius versus monent:
units.tr: Natural law and universal experience have taught what the verses of Sophocles admonish:

units.la: Οὐκ ἐξ ἁπάντων[?] ἀλλὰ τὸ λῷστον φιλεῖν[?], ἐν γὰρ τῶν[?] [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀτυμωτάτοις[?] ἰδίοις αὐτ' ἀ σιγωμένοις[?].
units.tr: Not of all things, but to love the best [Οὐκ ἐξ ἁπάντων, ἀλλὰ τὸ λῷστον φιλεῖν], for ... [illegible in the scan] most unreal and most one's own, but silenced [ἀτυμωτάτοις ἰδίοις αὐτ' ἀ σιγωμένοις].

units.la: Quomodo autem etiam summi homines, non tam interres ipsas, quàm earum simulacra, anxij oberrent, hæc Domini Dei nostri oratio ostendit: Studio illis est, primùm ut per fas & nefas ingentes opes corradant, quasi in earum copia potius quàm usu, hominis uita felix posita foret: deinde, ut sibi suisq; eiusmodi palatia ædificent, quæ inhabitantibus magno usui, & aduersus uim hostilem præsidio esse possint, & quæ perpetua sint potentiæ, opulentiæ, καὶ τῆς ἀνδραγαθίας[?] monumenta. Sed quid profuit nepoti Nebucadnezaris, opum affluentia, & Babylonicæ urbis magnitudo & munitiones, cum Cyrus eam metropolin Monarchiæ Babylonicæ occuparet?
units.tr: How even the greatest men wander anxiously, not so much among the things themselves as among their images, this utterance of the Lord our God shows. They are eager, first, to amass vast wealth by right or wrong, as if a happy human life lay in the abundance of such things rather than in their use. Then they build for themselves and their families palaces of such a kind as may be of great use to the inhabitants and a defence against hostile force, and which may be lasting monuments of power, wealth and [καὶ τῆς ἀνδραγαθίας] manliness. But what did the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar gain from the abundance of his riches, the greatness and fortifications of the city of Babylon, when Cyrus captured that metropolis of the Babylonian monarchy?

units.la: Quid hoc loco piam mentem discere oportere censes?
units.tr: What do you think a godly mind ought to learn from this place?

units.la: Cùm tanto tamq; peruerso zelo & af- fectu dućti improbi, mala perpetrent, bo-na temporalia corradant, ad exitium & ruinam suam totis uiribus contendant: multò maiore studio bona nobis faciẹn-da, mala fugienda, spiritualia bona peten-da & suscitanda, & ad instaurationem sa-lutemq; nobis esse, Christo Iesu duce, properandum. Multò enim maiore zelo & amore boni nos affici par est, quàm fi-lij huius seculi mali aut boni [illegible, ~8 letters] af-fici possint.
units.tr: Since wicked men, led by so great and so perverse a zeal and passion, commit evils, gather temporal goods, and strive with all their strength towards their own destruction and ruin, we ought with much greater eagerness to do good, flee evil, seek and stir up spiritual goods, and hasten, with Christ Jesus as our leader, towards our own restoration and salvation. For we ought to be moved by a much greater zeal and love of the good than the sons of this age, whether evil or good, are able to be moved.

units.la: Ne igitur simus tepidi, sed spiritu fer-uentes, Domino seruientes: Rom.12.11.
units.tr: Let us therefore not be lukewarm, but fervent in spirit, serving the Lord: Rom. 12.11.

units.la: Non enim nos fugit illud Spiritus sancti oraculum: Noui opera tua, nempe te ne-que frigidum esse, neque feruidum: utinam frigidus esses aut feruidus. Itaque quoniam tepidus es, nec frigidus, nec feruidus, futurum est ut te euomam ex ore meo. Apoc.4.15.16.
units.tr: For that oracle of the Holy Spirit does not escape us: "I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot; I would that you were cold or hot. So because you are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, it will come about that I shall spew you out of my mouth." Apoc. 4.15.16.

units.la: Quoties improbos συνυφαντίζω[?] conspi-rare uidemus, charitatis ardor & paro-xysmus in nobis magis magisq; inflam-mari & augeri debet. Iuxta dictum: Et observemus alii alios, ut nos acuamus ad charitatem & bona opera. Hebr.10.24.
units.tr: Whenever we see the wicked conspiring together [συνυφαντίζω], the ardour and fervour of charity ought to be kindled and increased in us more and more, according to the saying: "And let us consider one another, to provoke one another to love and good works." Heb. 10.24.

units.la: Cum illos Dei nomen blasphamare audimus: maiore studio & ζήλῳ[?] illud sanctificemus tum dictis, tum factis.
units.tr: When we hear them blaspheming the name of God, let us sanctify it all the more with zeal [ζήλῳ], both by our words and by our deeds.

units.la: Cùm terrena illos cogerere videmus: thesaurizemus ipsi in cœlis, quęrentes eas quæ sursum sunt, non quæ in terris sunt, &c. Colos.3.1.
units.tr: When we see them heaping up earthly things, let us ourselves store up treasures in heaven, seeking those things which are above, not those which are on the earth, etc. Col. 3.1.

units.la: Det nobis Dominus IESUS, ut toto pectore per omnem vitam hoc unum agamus, ut mala fugientes, bona faciamus, ad ipsius laudem. Amen.
units.tr: May the Lord Jesus grant us that with our whole heart, throughout all our life, we do this one thing: fleeing evil, we do good, to his praise. Amen.

units.la: VERSUS X.
units.tr: VERSE X.

units.la: Consilium inivisti ad ignominiam domus tuae, excidisti populos multos, & peccasti in animam tuam.
units.tr: You have taken counsel to the shame of your house, you have cut off many peoples, and you have sinned against your own soul.

units.la: Ἐπιτίμησις est, qua Iehouah Deus noster gravissimè perstringit Regem Babylonicum, occulta cordis illius consilia in lucem proferens. Tria autem hoc loco illi tribuit.
units.tr: It is a rebuke, by which Jehovah our God severely censures the Babylonian king, bringing to light the hidden counsels of his heart. He attributes three things to him in this place.

units.la: 1. Quòd consilium inierit ad ignominiam domus suae. Istud vero hauddubiè παράδοξον[?] videbatur, quòd qua ratione honori & commodis domus seu familiae suae totiusq; posteritatis consulere fata-gebat, ea ipsa ratione ignominiam & ⸗ πολισθέμιν eidem accersere diceretur. Certum autem est, iusticia stabiliri thronum, iniusticia subuerti. Itaque Rex iniuste a-gens, pessime sibi suisq; consulebat.
units.tr: 1. That he took counsel to the shame of his house. This indeed seemed undoubtedly paradoxical: that by the very means by which he strove to provide for the honour and advantage of his house or family and all his posterity, by those same means he is said to bring upon it shame and [πολισθέμιν]. It is certain, however, that a throne is established by justice and overturned by injustice. Therefore the king, acting unjustly, was consulting worst for himself and his own.

units.la: 2. Quòd excidisset populos multos. Reuocat Dominus Tyranno in memo-riam crudelitatem, quâ erga multas gen-tes, quas bellis deuicerat, declarârat. Etsi autem hoc genus hominum adeò asperi esse solent monitoribus suis, ut nemo liberè eos obiurgare audet: Deus tamen ἀκριβῶς nouit, qua ratione exsuscitanda sit conscientia, sic ut mille testium instar sit, & ut Tyrannos horribiliter excarnificet: ut testatur exempla Neronis, qui sibi terra dehiscente absorberi & exstingui uisus est, & multorum aliorum.
units.tr: 2. That he had cut off many peoples. The Lord recalls to the tyrant's memory the cruelty by which he had shown himself towards many nations whom he had conquered in war. Although men of this sort are usually so harsh towards their admonishers that no one dares to rebuke them freely, God nevertheless knows exactly by what means conscience is to be roused, so that it is the equal of a thousand witnesses, and so that it horribly tortures tyrants. The examples of Nero testify to this, who seemed to himself to be swallowed up and extinguished by the opening earth, and of many others.

units.la: 3. Quòd in animam suam peccasset. Vt qui scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat: 1. Cor. 6. 18. sic qui in Deum & homines iniurius est, in suam ipsius animam peccat: ei enim exitiû & poenas aeternas ac-cersit.
units.tr: 3. That he had sinned against his own soul. As one who fornicates sins against his own body (1 Cor. 6.18), so one who is unjust towards God and men sins against his own soul, for he brings on himself destruction and eternal punishments.

units.la: Iam vero, ut ad usum nostrum ista transfe-ramus, tria nobis summo studio cauen-da sunt.
units.tr: Now, to transfer these things to our own use, we must guard against three things with the greatest care.

units.la: 1. Ne consilium ineamus ad ignominiâ domus nostræ. Est enim uia quæ uidetur homini bona, sed exitus eius ducunt ad mortem, ut ait Salomon. Itaq; ne ponamus consilia in anima nostra: sed à Spiritu sancto nos regi petamus: & Spiritu incedetes, carnis desideria ne impleamus.
units.tr: 1. Let us not take counsel to the shame of our house. For there is a way which seems good to a man, but its ends lead to death, as Solomon says. Therefore let us not put counsels in our soul, but ask to be ruled by the Holy Spirit; and walking in the Spirit, let us not fulfil the desires of the flesh.

units.la: 2. Ne simus scientes & prudentes iniuriji in quenquam mortalium: ac si quos per intemperiem aut imprudentiam nos læsisse animaduertimus, malû bono com pensare, & si qua fieri possit, condupli-care studeamus.
units.tr: 2. Let us not knowingly and prudently be unjust to anyone at all. And if we notice that we have harmed anyone through intemperance or imprudence, let us strive to make amends with good, and, if it can be done, to repay twofold.

units.la: 3. Ne ἐν προσκαιρίως peccatum faciamus; sed Deo obedire studeamus per omnem uitam.
units.tr: 3. Let us not commit sin for a temporary time [ἐν προσκαιρίως]; but let us strive to obey God throughout all our life.

units.la: Dominus Iesus det nobis, ut prodesse omnibus, obesse nulli mortalium studetes, μετ᾽ ἀναστ[?] uitæ nostræ ψυχ[?] defungamur, ad Dei gloriam, & nostram & aliorum emendationem. Amen.
units.tr: May the Lord Jesus grant us, striving to benefit all and to harm no mortal, that we may be discharged from the life of our soul [μετὰ ἀναστ... ψυχῆς], to the glory of God and to the amendment of ourselves and others. Amen.

units.la: VERSVS XI.
units.tr: VERSE XI.

units.la: Nam lapides è muris clamabunt contra te, & tigna è structuris ligneis respondebunt tibi. Ethopœia est, qua rebus inanimatis clamor & sermo tribuitur.
units.tr: For the stones shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it. This is an ethopoeia, by which a cry and speech are attributed to inanimate things.

units.la: Non est cur etiam summi homines voluptatem aliquam ex iis rebus captent, quae ipsorum πλεονεξίαν[?] & inhumanitatem plena uoce contestantur & accusant.
units.tr: There is no reason why even great men should take pleasure in those things which plainly testify to and accuse their greed and inhumanity.

units.la: Atqui magnifica Regum & Principū, eorum inquam, qui exercuerunt tyrannidem, palatia, sudore & sanguine subiectorum exstructa, illos reos peragunt, & cum superstites sunt, & cum fatis co-cesserunt.
units.tr: Yet the magnificent palaces of kings and princes, I mean of those who have practised tyranny, built with the sweat and blood of their subjects, convict them as guilty, both while they are alive and after they have met their fate.

units.la: Haec Minor illustratur & confirmatur ἀδικίᾳ[?], in qua per ἀνθρωποπαθείαν[?], clamor lapidibus parietum, & sermo tignis tribuitur.
units.tr: This minor premise is illustrated and confirmed by injustice, in which, through anthropopathy, a cry is attributed to the stones of the walls and speech to the beams.

units.la: Quare non est cur eiusmodi Principes delicias sibi faciant ex magnificis aedificijs & arcibus, quas quotiescunque aspiciunt, caeco conscientiæ vulnere afficiuntur, cum intelligant constitisse sanguine subditorum.
units.tr: Therefore there is no reason why such princes should take delight in their magnificent buildings and citadels, for whenever they look upon them they are struck by a blind wound of conscience, since they understand that they were built with the blood of their subjects.

units.la: Hoc loco monendi mihi estis de mira quadam specie iusti iudicij Dei adversus eos, qui dum ex scelerum illiberali usufructu delicias sibi faciunt, pro vo-luptasluptate tormentu sibi præter opinionem suam accersunt.
units.tr: Here I must warn you of a certain remarkable form of the just judgment of God against those who, while they make themselves delights out of the ungenerous enjoyment of their crimes, bring upon themselves torment instead of pleasure, beyond their own expectation.

units.la: 1. Quàm multi sunt Dynastæ & Topar-chæ, qui non contenti domicilijs maiorū fuorū, illis destructis alia aedificant. Fer-ri quidem id poterat, si suo sumtu palatia noua aedificarent, si subditis laboratibus & eorum iumentis alimenta non denegarent, denique si non cogerent miseros agricolas, suis oeconomijs & occupationibus omisis, seruire unius domini desiderijs. Debent equidè subditi Magistratibus officia & fidem egregiè probare, & quidem in aduersis & secundis. Sed & Principes meminerint, nihil differre sese à bonis Patribus, ut Ethnicus ille Xeno-phon dicebat. Atqui hi non abutuntur fi-liorum opera, non denegant illis alimen-ta. Quare nec Principes abuti decet infe-riorum ministerio, nec æquū est illos ci-vibus laboratibus demensum diurnum denegare. Vidimus munitissimas arces destructas hac ætate. Sed quis tandem, cogitans sanguine provincialium aedifi-catas, miretur destructas esse?
units.tr: 1. How many dynasts and toparchs there are who, not content with the homes of their ancestors, pull them down and build new ones! This could be borne if they built their new palaces at their own expense, if they did not deny food to labouring subjects and their beasts of burden, and finally if they did not compel poor farmers, setting aside their own households and occupations, to serve the desires of one lord. Subjects indeed ought to show their duty and loyalty to the magistrates admirably, both in adversity and in prosperity. But princes too should remember that they differ in nothing from good fathers, as that heathen Xenophon used to say. Yet good fathers do not abuse their children's labour, nor deny them food. Therefore it is not fitting for princes to abuse the service of their inferiors, nor is it right to deny citizens who labour their daily wage. We have seen the most strongly fortified citadels destroyed in our own age. But who, reflecting that they were built with the blood of the provincials, would wonder that they were destroyed?

units.la: 2. Idem euenire solet hominibus ava-ris, qui ubi congestis undiq; gazis indor-mire mire cupiunt, primùm magno dolore af-ficiuntur, cum non omnibus quibus inhiant, potiri possunt: deinde miseri sunt, quòd cùm ijs quæ adsunt, uti non audeant, tam ea quæ adsunt, quàm quæ non adsunt, sibi deesse experiùtur: postremò, quæcunque per nefas à se parta uel uident, uel contrectant, conscientiæ uulnus exa-sperare sentiunt. Sic Deus delicias illorum felle tinctas amaras reddit.
units.tr: 2. The same usually happens to greedy men, who, when they wish to sleep soundly amid treasures heaped up from every side, are first struck with great grief, since they cannot possess all they covet; then they are wretched, because although they dare not use what they have, they experience a lack both of what they have and of what they do not have; finally, whatever they have acquired by wrongdoing and see or handle, they feel it aggravating the wound of their conscience. So God makes their delights, steeped in gall, bitter.

units.la: 3. Qui maledictis alios insectantur[?], ut uel alienæ, uel suæ iracundiæ satisfaciat: cæcum uulnus suis cordibus infligunt. Non enim obscurè uident, primùm Deum se offendere: deinde, scelerati affectus ma-cipia sese esse: tertiò, non eum cui fit co-uicium, sed illum qui facit, esse miserum.
units.tr: 3. Those who assail others with abuse, to satisfy either another's anger or their own, inflict a blind wound on their own hearts. For they clearly see, first, that they offend God; second, that they are slaves of wicked passions; third, that it is not the one who suffers the wrong but the one who does it who is wretched.

units.la: 4. Qui sic in unius alicuius Magistri (Christum Dominum, qui unicus noster Doctor est, excipio) uerba & opinionem iurârunt, ut neminem alium, quantum-uis pie docetem, audiant, & ut posterio-ribus curis locum nullum relinquant: dum sibi placent & gaudent, ueritatis luce fe-ipsos[?] priuant. Recte Augustinus: Duo, inquit, sunt, quæ in errore hominum dif-ficilime tolerantur: Præsumtio priufquam veritas pateat, & cum jam pa-tuerit, præfumtæ defensio falsitatis.
units.tr: 4. Those who have sworn to the words and opinion of a single teacher (excepting Christ the Lord, who is our only Teacher), so that they will hear no one else, however piously he teaches, and leave no room for later concerns, while they please and gratify themselves, deprive themselves of the light of truth. Augustine rightly says: "There are two things which are most intolerably borne in the error of men: presumption before the truth is revealed, and, once it has been revealed, the defence of a presumed falsehood."

units.la: Faxit Deus, ne in peccatis evanidam voluptatem, cum conscientiæ tormentis coniunctam, unquam feſtemur[?].
units.tr: May God grant that we never take pleasure in a fading delight in sins, joined with the torments of conscience.

units.la: VERSVS XII.
units.tr: VERSE XII.

units.la: Va ædificanti urbem sanguine, & ei qui stabilit civitatem iniquitate.
units.tr: Woe to him who builds a city with blood, and establishes a town by iniquity.

units.la: Exclamatio est, qua amplificatur rei indignitas.
units.tr: This is an exclamation by which the indignity of the matter is amplified.

units.la: Quæ res ad destruendas urbes potissimum faciunt, eæ non citra summum me-tis errorem ad eas exstruendas adhibentur: ut ex repugnantium rerum natura liquet.
units.tr: Those things which most tend to destroy cities are not, without the greatest error of mind, employed to build them up; as is clear from the nature of contrary things.

units.la: Sanguinis autem iniuste fusi, & sudoris pauperum servientium alienæ magnificentiæ, copia & effusio facit ad destruendas urbes: Ezech.24.9. Nah.3.1.[?] Econtrà iustitia & æquitate superiorum erga inferiores, & horum erga illos egregia fide & officijs, ædificantur palatia bonorum Principum & urbes.
units.tr: Yet an abundance and outpouring of unjustly shed blood, and of the sweat of poor men serving another's magnificence, tends to destroy cities: Ezek. 24:9; Nah. 3:1. On the contrary, the palaces of good princes and their cities are built up by the justice and equity of superiors towards inferiors, and by the excellent fidelity and services of the latter towards the former.

units.la: Itaque res ipsa docet, Nebucadneza-rem & Chaldæos toto cœlo errare, cum urbes præclaras sanguine, sudore ac la-boriboribus[?] pauperum sese aedificare posse opinantur.
units.tr: Therefore the thing itself teaches that Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans are wholly mistaken when they suppose that they can build famous cities with the blood, sweat and toil of the poor.

units.la: Exemplo est Rex Ægypti Pharao, qui abusus Israelitarum opera, aedificauit urbes thesaurorum Pithom & Raamses,E-xodi i.ii.[?] sed non multo post decem plagis affectus, perijt cū exercitu suo in mari rubro: Exod.14.
units.tr: The example is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who, abusing the labour of the Israelites, built the treasure cities Pithom and Raamses (Exod. 1:11); but not long after, struck by ten plagues, he perished with his army in the Red Sea: Exod. 14.

units.la: πρᾶξις[?] de errore mentis circa rerum delectum.
units.tr: On the error of the mind concerning the choice of things.

units.la: Inter cæteras formas pœnarum est & mentis cæcitas, quæ facit, ut improbi no-xia pro salutaribus habeant & expetant, & salutaria tanquam noxia refugiant, ἀνυ-φιλίας[?] perniciosa laborantes.
units.tr: Among the other forms of punishment is also blindness of mind, which causes the wicked to hold and seek harmful things as if they were salutary, and to shun salutary things as if they were harmful, suffering from a perverse aversion [ἀνυφιλίας].

units.la: Pharao, spreto Domini Dei imperio, fuumq; consilium secutus, se fuosq; perdidit.
units.tr: Pharaoh, scorning the command of the Lord God and following his own counsel, destroyed himself and his own.

units.la: Saul, iracundiæ indulgens, mala accumulat, Dauidem persequitur hostiliter, filium Ionathanem recta monentem contumeliosè tractat, Sacerdotes innoxios trucidat, Doegum impium quadruplatorem in precio habet, rerum suarum desperatione ductus Pythonissam consulit, & sibi ipsi auctor est exitij.
units.tr: Saul, indulging his anger, heaps up evils: he persecutes David as an enemy, treats his son Jonathan, who gave sound advice, with contempt, slaughters innocent priests, holds the impious informer Doeg in high esteem, and, driven to despair of his affairs, consults a sorceress and becomes the author of his own ruin.

units.la: Nebucadnezar sanguine ædificans urbem, & multa iniuste agens, thronum suum, quem stabilire cupiebat, ipsemet per imprudentiam subuertit.
units.tr: Nebuchadnezzar, building a city with blood and acting unjustly in many things, through his own folly overthrew the throne he was eager to make secure.

units.la: Hoc reuera est [illegible, ~12 letters]: ut habet uetus prouerbium. Nos itaque precemur Deum Patrem per nomen unigeniti eius filij Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ne nos tradat in reprobam omnisq; iudicij expertem mentem: sed Spiritu suo sancto in omnem ueritatem ducat, regat, & ab omni fanatico errore & ἐνθυσιασμῷ [?] custodiat. Scimus enim fieri interdum, ut etiam Sancti in consilijs errent, & moueant non necessarias res, quae ipsis & aliis magna mala accersunt: ut est uidere in exemplo Iosiae bellum inferentis Ægyptio Regi.
units.tr: This is indeed [illegible], as the old proverb has it. Let us therefore pray God the Father, through the name of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, that he not deliver us over to a reprobate mind, devoid of all judgment, but that by his Holy Spirit he lead and guide us into all truth, and keep us from every fanatical error and enthusiasm [ἐνθουσιασμῷ]. For we know that it sometimes happens that even saints err in their counsels and set in motion matters that are not necessary, which bring great evils upon themselves and others: as can be seen in the example of Josiah making war on the Egyptian king.

units.la: VERSVS XIII.
units.tr: Verse 13.

units.la: Nonne ecce[?] à Iehouah exercituum? (veniet ultio) laborabunt itaque populi igne, & gentes frustra fatigabuntur.
units.tr: Is it not from Jehovah of hosts? (Vengeance will come.) So the peoples will labour for the fire, and the nations will weary themselves in vain.

units.la: Tria gratia docendi in hoc versu obser uabimus: λέξιν, ἀπόδειξιν, καὶ τὴν χρῆσιν: id est, Genus orationis, Demonstrationem, & Vsum.
units.tr: In this verse we shall note three things for teaching purposes: λέξις, ἀπόδειξις, καὶ χρῆσις [λέξιν, ἀπόδειξιν, καὶ τὴν χρῆσιν]: that is, the kind of expression, the demonstration, and the use.

units.la: 1. GENUS ORATIONIS.
units.tr: 1. The Kind of Expression.

units.la: Oratio ecliptica est, quæ complebitur, si quis addat illa verba ωαχρευθέος[?] inclusa. Sententia enim est: Etsi Chaldæi nulla humana iudicia, nullam vim seu potentiam verentur, ac totis viribus res suas cō stabilire satagunt: tamen ultionem Dei iudicis (ἐνδίκου ὄμμα[?] habentis) effugere nequaquam poterunt.
units.tr: The expression is elliptical, and it is completed if one supplies the words enclosed in brackets. The sense is this: although the Chaldeans fear no human judgements and no force or power, and strive with all their might to make their affairs secure, yet they will by no means be able to escape the vengeance of God as judge, who has a just eye.

units.la: Idem ϑεῖνως[?], de impijs loquens David Propheta, his verbis monet: Interius eorum (hoc est, cogitatio eorum est, quòd) domus suæ (stabunt) in perpetuū: & habitationes suæ in generationem & generationem: ut vocentur nominibus suis super terram. Sed homo iste in splendore nō perdurabit, & similis fit brutis quæ intereunt: Psal.49.11.12. Illud autem dignum est obseruatu, quod idem sequente versu monet, Ut maximè istud perver-sum vitæ genus, & illa agendi ratio exi-tio fit sectatoribus: posteros tamen ijsde[?] maiorum suorum vestigijs insistere, ni-mirum eorum malis minimè doctos sic, ut in parentibus isti sapiant. Hæc, inquit, via ipsorum stulticia ipsis, & tamen posteri eorum ore suo approbant. Caeterum παροιμιωδῶς[?], in igne laborare dicuntur, qui ἐν ἀνομωτι[?] ἢ ἀνιδρώτι[?] quidem laborant, frustra tamen defatigantur. Notum est illud Persae cuiusdam dictum, quod apud Herodotum exstat: ἐξ ἰξ-ῆς[illegible, ~3 letters] δὲ ὁδὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων[?], πολλὰ φρονέοντα μηδὲν ἐπιτυχέειν[?]. Occurrunt autem in Scripturis sanctis & exotericis idem fere significantes formulae: ἀσφὰ ἀσφάλῃ[?], εἰς ὑψηλὸν τρίχειν[?], τὰ πνεύματα ἀπὸ[?] ἀνέμων[?]: pascere uentos: concipere iniquitatem, praegnatem esse dolore, & parere rem inanem, & aliae similes.
units.tr: David the Prophet, speaking of the wicked, warns of the same thing in these words: "Their inward thought is that their houses will last for ever, and their dwellings for all generations, and that they will call the lands after their own names. But man in honour does not remain; he is like the beasts that perish" (Ps. 49:11, 12). It is worth noting what the same psalm adds in the following verse: this most perverse way of life and this manner of acting prove fatal to their followers, yet their posterity, not taught by their elders' misfortunes, walk in the footsteps of their forefathers and approve of them. "This," it says, "is their way, their folly; and yet their posterity approve with their mouth." Moreover, proverbially, those are said to labour in the fire who toil without sweat or skill and yet wear themselves out in vain. Well known is the saying of a certain Persian recorded in Herodotus: [ἐξ ἴσης δὲ ὁδὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων, πολλὰ φρονέοντα μηδὲν ἐπιτυχέειν]. In the Holy Scriptures and in profane writers there occur also formulas meaning much the same: [ἀσφὰ ἀσφάλῃ], [εἰς ὑψηλὸν τρίχειν], [τὰ πνεύματα ἀπὸ ἀνέμων]: to feed on the winds; to conceive iniquity, to be pregnant with mischief, and to bring forth emptiness; and others like them.

units.la: 2. DEMONSTRATIO.
units.tr: 2. Demonstration.

units.la: Id quod Deus omnipotes efficere decreuit, nulla ratione praepediri potest. Iuxta haec dicta:
units.tr: What Almighty God has decided to bring about cannot be hindered by any means. In accordance with these sayings:

units.la: Prouerb.21.30. Non est sapientia, neq; intelligentia, neq; consilium contra Iehouam. 31. Equus paratus est ad diem belli: sed Iehouae est ipsa salus.
units.tr: Prov. 21:30, 31. There is no wisdom, nor understanding, nor counsel against the LORD. The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but safety belongs to the LORD.

units.la: Isai.46.10. Consilium meum stabit, & omnem voluntatem meam faciam.
units.tr: Isa. 46:10. My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.

units.la: Luc.1.37. Apud Deum non erit impos-sibile ullum verbum.
units.tr: Luke 1:37. With God no word shall be impossible.

units.la: Luc.18.27. Quae impossibilia sunt apud homines, possibilia sunt apud Deum.
units.tr: Luke 18:27. The things which are impossible with men are possible with God.

units.la: Ex his liquet, Deo, cuius infinita est sapientia & potentia, nullis uiribus humanis, nullis consilijs, quenquam posse reniti, sic ut ea non fiant, quae seu mediate, seu immediate Deus facere decreuit.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that no human strength and no counsels can resist God, whose wisdom and power are infinite, so that those things which God has decided to do, whether mediately or immediately, are not done by anyone.

units.la: Decreuit autem Deus Babylonios poenis promeritis afficere, & quidem iuxta talionis legem. Haec Minor ideo in du-bium uocari non poterat, quòd esset denunciata uoce Dei, qui est ἀψευδὴς[?]: Tit.1.1. & qui non minus omnipotentia quàm ueritas ipsa est.
units.tr: God has decided to visit the Babylonians with the punishments they have earned, and indeed according to the law of retaliation. This minor premise could not be called in doubt, because it was declared by the voice of God, who cannot lie (Tit. 1:1), and who is no less omnipotence than truth itself.

units.la: Ex his ἀντιρρήτως[?] consequitur, Chaldaeos cum suo Monarcha Nebucadnezare ac huius posteris, grauissimas poenas esse daturos crudelitatis, auaritiae & aliorum scelerum.
units.tr: From this it follows beyond contradiction that the Chaldeans, together with their monarch Nebuchadnezzar and his descendants, will pay the gravest penalties for cruelty, avarice and their other crimes.

units.la: 3. USUS.
units.tr: 3. Use.

units.la: Etsi in hac tanta infirmitate & pusillanimitate nostra, nō mediocriter animos nostros percellit μεγάλῃ φαντασίᾳ[?] & potentia filiorum huius saeculi & Antichristia-norum, qui omni contentione hoc unum agunt, ut res suas constabiliant, & ut Ecclesiam & singulos etiam fideles, si minus delere & exstirpare, saltem premere & in metu continere queant: est tamen cur eleuatis capitibus cum Dauide canta/mus : Deus nobis Tutamen & Robur,in quo auxilium in afflictionibus inuenimus abunde. Propterea non timebimus cum mouebitur terra,& concident montes in medio mari. Psal.46.1.2.
units.tr: Although in this great weakness and faintheartedness of ours, the great show [μεγάλῃ φαντασίᾳ] and power of the children of this age and of the Antichrists sorely shake our spirits, who strive with all their effort toward this one end, that they may make their affairs secure, and that they may be able, if not to destroy and root out the Church and even individual believers, at least to oppress them and keep them in fear, still there is reason for us to lift up our heads and sing with David: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." Therefore we will not fear when the earth is moved and the mountains are carried into the midst of the sea (Ps. 46:1, 2).

units.la: Non tam enim quid Ecclesiæ & singulorum piorum hostes moliantur, quàm quid boni publici caussa, Deo uniuersa moderante, futurum sit, spectare conue-nit. Semper autem sint in conspectu hęc dicta, quæ monent, nihil fieri sine Dei cō filio, & Deo neminem resistere posse.
units.tr: For we ought to consider not so much what the enemies of the Church and of each godly person are plotting, as what will come about for the common good under God's governance of all things. And let these sayings always be before our eyes, which teach that nothing happens without God's counsel, and that no one can resist God.

units.la: Act.4.28. Vt facerent quæcunque manus tua & consilium tuum prius definierat facienda.
units.tr: Acts 4:28. To do whatever your hand and your counsel had decided beforehand should be done.

units.la: Act.5.38. Sin ex Deo est, non poteritis dissoluere, & nescio an etiam cum Deo pugnare comperiamini.
units.tr: Acts 5:38, 39. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you may find that you are even fighting against God.

units.la: VERSVS XIIII.
units.tr: Verse 14.

units.la: Replebitur enim terra ipsa (cognitione ultionis Iehouæ,) ut agnoscant gloriam Iehouæ: (eritq; ultio illa) instar aquarum quæ operiunt mare.
units.tr: For the earth shall be filled (with the knowledge of the vengeance of the LORD), that they may acknowledge the glory of the LORD: (and that vengeance shall be) like the waters that cover the sea.

units.la: Αἰτιολογία est, quæ ducitur à destinato diuidiuinæ uindistæ[?], uidelicet à cognitione & adprobatione ultionis diuinæ, declaratæ erga Babylonios, qui inhumanissimè tractauerant & populum Dei,& multas alias gentes. Obseruabimus autem ordine,
units.tr: Aetiologia is the figure drawn from the purpose of divine vengeance, namely from the knowledge and approval of the divine vengeance declared against the Babylonians, who had treated most inhumanely both the people of God and many other nations. We shall observe in order

units.la: 1. ARGVMENTVM A CAVSA FINALI.
units.tr: 1. ARGUMENT FROM THE FINAL CAUSE.

units.la: Quod ad agnitionem & celebratione iusti iudicij Dei summè iusti facit, id nequaquam Deus prætermissurus est. Habet enim ille eam quam oportet, nominis & honoris sui rationem.
units.tr: God will by no means pass over that which makes for the recognition and celebration of his most just judgment. For he has regard to his own name and honour, as he ought.

units.la: Sed de Chaldæis sumtæ pœnæ plurimū eò facturæ sunt, ut agnoscatur Deus mundi iudex, zelotes, & ignis consumes.
units.tr: But the punishments inflicted on the Chaldeans will greatly serve to make God known as the judge of the world, a jealous God and a consuming fire.

units.la: Quare nihil dubium est, suo tempore Deum in Babylonios sic animaduersurū, ut nemo non sit intellecturus, singulari consilio iudicioq; Dei, pœnas crudelitatis & aliorum sceleru dedisse Chaldæos.
units.tr: Therefore there is no doubt that in due time God will take such vengeance on the Babylonians that everyone will understand that the Chaldeans were punished for their cruelty and the crimes of others, by the singular counsel and judgment of God.

units.la: 2. SIMILE.
units.tr: 2. SIMILE.

units.la: Quemadmodū incredibilis illa aquarum copia, quæ in Oceano conspicitur, mare eiusq; alueum operit: sic animaduersio Dei in Chaldæos, & horum pœnæ,terram,id est,generis humani partem maximaximam operiet,ac redundabit in glo-riam Dei iudicis. Iuxta illud : Cessarefa-cit bella usque ad extremum terrae : arcum conterit, & concidit hastam, plau-stra comburit igni. Cessate, & scitote ego sum Deus: exaltabor in gentibus, exaltabor,inquam,in terra. Psal.46.10.11.
units.tr: Just as that incredible abundance of water which is seen in the ocean covers the sea and its bed, so the vengeance of God upon the Chaldeans, and their punishments, will cover the earth, that is, the greater part of mankind, and will redound to the glory of God the judge. To this corresponds the saying: "He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear, and burns the chariots with fire. Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth." Ps. 46.10, 11.

units.la: 3. USUS HUIUS LOCI.
units.tr: 3. THE USE OF THIS PASSAGE.

units.la: De iudiciis Dei observentur hæc capita:
units.tr: Concerning the judgments of God, the following heads should be observed:

units.la: 1. Dum occulta sunt, curiosè non esse scrutanda. Rectè Gregorius: Iudicia,inquit,divina dum nesciuntur, non audaci sermone discutienda sunt, sed formido-loso silentio veneranda.
units.tr: 1. While they are hidden, they are not to be searched into with curiosity. Gregory rightly says: "The divine judgments, while they are unknown, are not to be discussed in bold speech, but to be revered with fearful silence."

units.la: 2. Cum manifesta sunt, nō sunt improbanda. Nam, ut idem Gregorius docet, quia homo de humo sumtus est, iudicia Dei discutere dignus non est.
units.tr: 2. When they are manifest, they are not to be condemned. For, as the same Gregory teaches, since man was taken from the dust, he is not worthy to call the judgments of God into question.

units.la: 3. Referri autè debent ad Domini gloriam. Quia, ut ex Davidis sententia in agone suo dicebat Mauricius Imperator, Iustus est Dominus, & iusta sunt eius iudicia.
units.tr: 3. They ought to be referred to the glory of the Lord. For, in accordance with the saying of David, the Emperor Maurice said in his agony: "The Lord is just, and his judgments are right."

units.la: Coronidis vice addo nobile dictum Bernardi: Ira Dei tunc metuenda est, cū peccata non punit. Neigitur ferulæ divinæ sensu perturbemur: castigat enim Deus filios γνησίως[?], quos videlicet unicè diligit.
units.tr: By way of a garland, I add a noble saying of Bernard: "The wrath of God is to be feared when he does not punish sins." Therefore let us not be disturbed by the sense of God's rod: for God chastises his sons [γνησίως], whom indeed he loves alone.

units.la: VERSVS XV.
units.tr: VERSE 15.

units.la: Va potanti socios suos(nimio vino,)ad-moventi utrem suum (plenum vini,) atq; inebrianti eos, ut aspiciat nuditates eorū.
units.tr: Woe to him who gives drink to his neighbours (with excess of wine), who brings near his skin bottle (full of wine) and makes them drunk, so that he may look upon their nakedness.

units.la: Prophetica comminatio est, qua Chaldæis denunciat, futurum ut calicem iræ Dei, ab eis propinatum multis gentibus, ipsi quoq; exorbere unà cum fecibus cogantur.
units.tr: This is a prophetic threat, by which the Chaldeans are warned that the cup of God's wrath, which they have poured out to many nations, shall itself be forced down by them, dregs and all.

units.la: Digni enim sunt,qui iisdem pœnis afficiantur, quicunque sociis seu æqualibus auctores fuerunt maximarum calamitatum, cum nihilo illis essent meliores. Aciusticia est, æqualia æqualibus evenire: & eos quoque puniri, qui in pœnis exequendis nullo inculpatæ animadversionis moderamine usi, sævierunt in eos quos in illorū manus Deus tradidit.
units.tr: For those who have been the authors of the greatest calamities to their companions or equals are worthy to suffer the same punishments, since they were no better than those they harmed. And it is just that equals should fare alike; and that those too should be punished who, in carrying out punishments, have raged against those whom God has delivered into their hands, without any restraint of blameless moderation.

units.la: Atqui Chaldæi ἐπιχαιρέκακοι horribiliter sæuierunt in alias gentes,quæ ipsis revera nihilo erant deteriores. Excessit medicina modum omnem.
units.tr: Yet the Chaldeans, from a [ἐπιχαιρέκακοι] malicious delight, raged horribly against other nations, which in truth were no worse than they were. Their remedy exceeded all measure.

units.la: Quapropter futurū est,ut ipsi quoq; bibant è calice irae diuinae, & dent poenas sæuitiæ, erga Gentes & erga Ecclesiam populi Judaici declaratæ.
units.tr: Wherefore it will come to pass that they too will drink from the cup of the divine wrath, and will pay the penalty for the savagery shown towards the nations and towards the Church of the Jewish people.

units.la: Hæc autē illustriora erunt, si quis [illegible, ~3 letters]-[illegible, ~7 letters] dicta adhibeat, quæ monent, fatale esse improbis, ut ipsi quoq; dent poenas improbitatis & sæuitiæ. Psalmo 11.6. Pluet super impios, laqueos & ignem & sulfur: & spiritus procellarum erit pars calicis eorum. Psal.75.9. Quoniam calix est in manu Jehouæ: & vinum quod in eo rubet: & plenus est misto, & effundit ex hoc: utiq; fæces eius fugent & bibent omnes impii terræ.
units.tr: These things will be clearer if one applies the sayings which warn that it is fated for the wicked to pay the penalty of their wickedness and savagery as well. Psalm 11.6: "Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and a horrible tempest; this shall be the portion of their cup." Psalm 75.9: "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture, and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out and drink them." [...]

units.la: Instantia: Atqui iniquum est, vindictæ divinæ administros & instrumenta, eò quòd iudiciis Dei inseruierint, dare poenas. Nihil enim aliud agunt, quam quod manus & consilium Dei decreuit ut fieret: Actorum 4.28. Ac ne quidem Satan plura efficere potest, quam Deus non solùm permittit, sed etiam decernit, cùm eo inuito nihil possit fieri: ut ex historia Jobi liquet. Fuerunt autem Chaldæi vasa iræ Dei, quibus usus est ad puniendam Getium impietatem & iniusticiam. Non igitur propterea erant eodem modo trastandi, quo cæteræ gentes.
units.tr: Objection: Yet it is unjust that the ministers and instruments of divine vengeance should pay the penalty, because they served the judgments of God. For they do nothing other than what the hand and counsel of God decreed should be done: Acts 4.28. Nor can even Satan accomplish more than God not only permits but also decrees, since nothing can be done against his will, as the story of Job makes plain. The Chaldeans, moreover, were vessels of God's wrath, which he used to punish the impiety and injustice of the Jews. Therefore they were not to be treated in the same way as the other nations.

units.la: Respondeo, esse paralogismum secundum non causam ut causam. Etenim Chaldæi nō ob id pœnas dederūt, quòd instrumenta uindictæ diuinæ fuissent, & q; nihil nisi determinante Deo perficere potuissent: sed primùm quidé, q; non studio obediendi Deo, sed impia ἐπιχαυρτωμανίᾳ[?] ducti, ut uidelicet alienam nuditatem, id est, turpitudinem, fragilitatem & miserias uiderent & augerent, cupidissimè executi sunt Dei iudicia: deinde uerò, quòd nihilo essent cæteris gentibus meliores, & quòd mensuram peccatorum suorum repleuissent inhumanitate, immò crudelitate summa erga alias gentes.
units.tr: I answer that this is a paralogism of the non-cause taken as cause. For the Chaldeans did not suffer punishment because they were instruments of divine vengeance, and because they could accomplish nothing except as God determined. Rather, in the first place, they, driven not by zeal to obey God but by impious [ἐπιχαιρεκακομανία] mania for malicious delight, namely to see and increase the nakedness, that is the shame, frailty and miseries of others, carried out the judgments of God most eagerly; and in the second place, because they were no better than the other nations, and because they filled up the measure of their sins with inhumanity, indeed with the greatest cruelty towards other nations.

units.la: Discimus hoc loco, Vasa iræ Dei, dum seruiunt Dei iudiciis, nequaquam mereri impunitatem suorum scelerum. Enimverò quòd ad ulciscenda scelera aliena adhibentur, id argumento illis esse debebat, ne quidem ipsorummet scelera impunita fore. Nequaquam carnifici peccandi licentiá parit animadversio in son-tes, à Magistratu ipsi delegata.
units.tr: We learn from this passage that the vessels of God's wrath, while they serve the judgments of God, by no means deserve impunity for their own crimes. Indeed, the fact that they are employed to avenge the crimes of others ought to be a reason for them to know that their own crimes will not go unpunished either. The punishment of guilty men, delegated to the executioner by the magistrate, by no means gives him licence to sin.

units.la: Secundò & illud discimus, nō esse impiam uoluptatem ex alienis calamitatibus cuiquam captādam. Vult enim Deus nos esse ἐπιχ[?]ρ[?]ἀγαθὸς, misericordes, benignos. Ac uel saniores Ethnici ita rem habere intellexerunt. Nota est honestissima Thesei uox apud Euripidem:
units.tr: Secondly, we also learn that no one should seek impious pleasure from the misfortunes of others. For God wills us to be [χρηστός] kind, merciful and benevolent. Even the more sensible heathen understood matters thus. The most honourable saying of Theseus in Euripides is well known: [ἐν ἀσχαλῶσιν ἀνθρώποισιν ἀλλήλων λαχεῖν] that among men in distress it is fitting to share one another's lot.

units.la: ἐν ἀσχ[?]ν ἀνθρώποισιν ἀλλήλων λαχεῖν[?]
units.tr: [ἐν ἀσχαλῶσιν ἀνθρώποισιν ἀλλήλων λαχεῖν]

units.la: Filius Dei diserte inquit: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur: Matth.5.7.
units.tr: The Son of God plainly says: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy." Matt. 5.7.

units.la: Tertiò uidemus, Deum malorum instrumentorum ministerio bene uti, sic ut ipse sit maneatqué ἀναμάρτητος, culpa autē penes instrumenta λογικὰ remaneat. Vt Iudaeorum opera usus est Deus ad Dominum gloriae crucifigendum, citra omnem suam culpam.
units.tr: Thirdly, we see that God makes good use of the ministry of evil instruments, so that he himself remains [ἀναμάρτητος] without sin, while the guilt remains with the rational [λογικὰ] instruments. Thus God used the works of the Jews to have the Lord of glory crucified, without any fault of his own.

units.la: Quartò animaduertimus, orandū nobis esse Deum, ut nos uelit esse uasa amabilia πρὸς ἀνθρώπους [?] ἐπιτήδεια, non autem ad mala. Graue sane fuit Dei iudicium in Patriarchas, qui secundum Dei consilium, Iosephum fratrem uendiderunt, & eo facto grauissime deliquerunt. Etsi autē Deus saepe per falsos Doctores, & eorum στρόφοι διδασκαλίαι, nos excitat, ut attentiores simus in studio cognoscendae & illustrandae ueritatis, quam illi nobis eripere aut obscurare conantur: tamen triste est, fi quis illorum κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς[?] nobis falsa obtrudedo & sophistice pingendo prodesse cogatur. Vt hac ætate homines illi eruditi & exercitati, qui Iesu nomen suæ societati tribuunt, sophistica sua faciunt, ut solidæ & seueriori Theologiæ nobis incumbedum esse, re ipsa experiamur. Faxit Christus Iesus, ut dictis & factis, totaque uita nostra, seruiamus instaurationi tum nostræ, tum etiam proximorum nostrorum, in fide & conuersatione sancta, & seruiente diuini nominis sanctifica-tioni.
units.tr: Fourthly, we observe that we must pray to God that he will make us vessels fit for [πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ἐπιτήδεια] serving men and lovable, and not for evil. Truly heavy was the judgment of God upon the patriarchs, who, according to God's counsel, sold their brother Joseph, and by that deed sinned most grievously. And although God often stirs us up, through false teachers and their [στρόφοι διδασκαλίαι] perverse teachings, to be more attentive in the study of knowing and making clear the truth, which they attempt to snatch from us or obscure, yet it is sad if any of them, [κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς] by accident, is compelled to be of service to us by thrusting falsehoods upon us and painting them sophistically. Thus in this age those learned and practised men who ascribe the name of Jesus to their society make their sophistries, so that we experience in fact that we must devote ourselves to a solid and more serious theology. May Christ Jesus grant that by word and deed, and by our whole life, we may serve the restoration both of ourselves and of our neighbours, in faith and holy conduct, and in serving the sanctification of the divine name.

units.la: VERSVS XVI.
units.tr: VERSE 16.

units.la: Saturatus es (Regum) ignominia præ gloria: bibes tu quoq;, & nudaberis: vertet enim se super te calix dextera Iehoua, & vomitus ignominiosus (decidet) super gloriam tuam.
units.tr: You are sated with shame instead of glory; you also shall drink and be uncovered. The cup in the LORD's right hand shall turn against you, and shameful vomit shall fall upon your glory.

units.la: Qui adeò sunt ebrij voluptatibus & magnitudine rerum gestarum & succef-suum, ut illiberalem voluptatem perci-piant ex aliena ignominia, calamitate & ruina: ij profecto digni sunt, qui in eorū-dem malorū gurgites tandem prolaban-tur, tur, & in iis discant, quid sit insultare miseris & oppressis.
units.tr: Those who are so drunk with pleasure, with the greatness of their achievements and successes, that they draw a base pleasure from another's shame, calamity and ruin: these are certainly deserving of being swept at last into the whirlpools of those same evils, and of learning there what it means to insult the wretched and the oppressed.

units.la: Sed Nebucadnezar & Chaldaei obsaturati[?] sunt, aliena ignominia, suam nescio quam gloriam: aliena nuditate, suum ornatum: aliena denique ebrietate vomituq;, suam voluptatem redimentes. Quare, &c.
units.tr: But Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans were sated: from another's shame they gained I know not what glory of their own; from another's nakedness, their adornment; and finally from another's drunkenness and vomit, their pleasure. Wherefore, etc.

units.la: Observetur autem hoc loco, & causae tanti mali.
units.tr: Let us also observe at this place the causes of so great an evil.

units.la: 1. προκαταχρησιν[?] erat ἐπιχαιρεκακία[?] Babyloniorum, quam magnis poenis digna fuisse, nemo non intelligit.
units.tr: 1. The antecedent cause [προκαταχρησις] was the Babylonians' malicious joy at others' misfortune [ἐπιχαιρεκακία], which clearly deserved great punishments, as no one fails to understand.

units.la: 2. Efficiens, Deus. Ideo enim Calix Iehouae nūcupatur. Porrò inde colligitur inevitabilis necessitas exhauriendi calicem irae Dei. Digni sunt autē relatu versus Menādri de ἐπιχαιρεκακία, qui monet, non esse gaudendū aliorum calamitate: ταῖς ἀτυχίαις μὴ ἐπιχαίρε τῶν πέλας· πρὸς τὴν τύχην γὰρ ξυγομαχεῖν[?] ῥᾴδιον.
units.tr: 2. The efficient cause is God. For this reason it is called the cup of the LORD. From this it is further inferred that there is an inevitable necessity of drinking the cup of God's wrath. The verses of Menander on malicious joy are worth quoting here, which advise that one should not rejoice at the misfortunes of neighbours: "Do not rejoice at your neighbours' misfortunes; for it is easy to contend with fortune" [ταῖς ἀτυχίαις μὴ ἐπιχαίρε τῶν πέλας· πρὸς τὴν τύχην γὰρ ξυγομαχεῖν ῥᾴδιον].

units.la: QVID AVTEM PIAE MENTI CO-gitandum censes, cum animadvertit, quanta sit ἐπιχαιρεκακία improborum hominum?
units.tr: But what should a godly mind consider when it notices how great is the malicious joy of wicked men?

units.la: In diuersa sibi tendendum, & summo stustudio ἐπιχαραγαθίαν[?] sectandam esse: ne isti peruerso sæculo filii lucis configuren-tur. Rom.12.2.
units.tr: That one must set oneself against it, and with the utmost zeal pursue joy in the good [ἐπιχαραγαθία], lest we be conformed to this wicked age, as the children of light. Rom. 12.2.

units.la: Cum boni affliguntur, eorum miserari: cum iisdem res fecundæ sunt, gaudere oportet. i.Cor.13.
units.tr: When the good are afflicted, one should pity them; when prosperity comes to them, one should rejoice with them. 1 Cor. 13.

units.la: Cum mali affliguntur, itidem miserari decet, & cum in rebus fecundis luxuriant eorum animi. Sciunt enim, in aduersis quidem solida consolatione, in fecundis uero & stabili gaudio eos destitui.
units.tr: When the wicked are afflicted, one should likewise pity them, and also when their minds run riot in prosperity. For they know that such men are deprived of solid consolation in adversity, and of stable joy in prosperity.

units.la: Vere itaque gaudeamus cum gaudentibus: Rom.12.15. nam charitas non inuidet: 1.Corinth.13.4. & absit a nobis fucus simulationis & dissimulationis, de quo Æschylus ficticium congaudium depingens, ait:
units.tr: Let us therefore truly rejoice with those who rejoice, Rom. 12.15; for charity does not envy, 1 Cor. 13.4. Far from us be the mask of pretence and insincerity, of which Aeschylus, depicting feigned rejoicing, says:

units.la: τῷ ἀντιφαγήντι[?] δ' ἐπιφθονάχαι[?] ὡς τις ἑτοίμος[?], ἀλγμα[?] δὲ λύπης ἐν ἦμαρ[?] προσαινέτω[?]:
units.tr: "To the one who is ready to envy, as if..., and let him bring forth a pang of grief in the day..." [τῷ ἀντιφαγήντι δ' ἐπιφθονάχαι ὡς τις ἑτοίμος, ἀλγμα δὲ λύπης ἐν ἦμαρ προσαινέτω]:

units.la: ὧν νύντι δὲ χαίρει[?] ὁμοιοπρεπῆς[?] ἀγέλαστα[?] πρόσωπα[?] βιαφθέγγοι[?].
units.tr: "Of whom, now rejoicing in a fitting manner, the faces without laughter utter..." [ὧν νύντι δὲ χαίρει ὁμοιοπρεπῆς ἀγέλαστα πρόσωπα βιαφθέγγοι].

units.la: VERSVS XVII.
units.tr: VERSE 17.

units.la: Quandoquidem rapina quam fecisti in Libano, obruet te: & praeda illata a feris, conteret eas, propter sanguinem hominum, & uio & uiolentiam terra, & ciuitatis, omni-umq; habitantium in ea.
