units.tr: Because the violence done to Lebanon shall overwhelm you, and the spoil of the beasts, which terrified them, shall crush them, because of the blood of men and the violence done to the land and the city, and to all who dwell in it.

units.la: Sunt qui hæc uerba restringant ad po-pulum Iudaicum, à Babylonijs uic[?]tum & abductum in tristissimum exilium: & ad urbem Ierosolymam, quæ ab ijsdem expugnata est, & una cum templo incen-sa & solo æquata, anno mundi 3 3 5 6. ut quidam Chronographi uolunt. Sumitur autem in hac significatione Libani uocabulum, Zach.11.1. Aperi,ô Libane, portas tuas, & absumat ignis cedros tuas. 2.V-lula abies, quia cecidit cedrus, quoniam magnifici uastati sunt: ululate quercus Balan, quoniam deijcietur saltus munitus. Hæc de secunda euersione urbis sanctæ & templi, cuius ὀφγοδιῶκτης diuinitus excitatus, fuit Titus, Vespasiani Imp.F.dici, nemo intelligens dubitare porest.
units.tr: Some restrict these words to the Jewish people, conquered by the Babylonians and carried off into most miserable exile, and to the city of Jerusalem, which was taken by the same enemy and burned together with the temple and levelled to the ground, in the year of the world 3356, as some chronologers hold. The name of Lebanon is used in this sense at Zech. 11.1: "Open your doors, O Lebanon, that fire may devour your cedars." 2. "Howl, fir tree, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty are laid waste; howl, oaks of Bashan, for the fortified forest has been brought down." That this concerns the second overthrow of the holy city and temple, whose avenger divinely raised up was Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian [ὀργοδίωκτης], no one who understands the matter can doubt.

units.la: Certum autem est, Gentes illas, quæ nō tantum in socias & idololatricas gen-tes, sed etiā in Ecclesiam sæuierunt, hu-ius inhumanitatis caussa graviores luere pœnas, eò quòd pupillam oculi Dei, & Christos Domini tetigerunt.
units.tr: It is certain, however, that those nations which raged not only against allied and idolatrous peoples but also against the Church have paid heavier penalties for this inhumanity, because they touched the apple of God's eye and the anointed of the Lord.

units.la: Fatendum tamen est, Libani nomine, κατά ἐχτὰ μεταφορᾶν, alias quidem robur exercituum, & succisionis Libani φράσσω, internecionem exercitus significari. Vt Isa.10. 13. Ecce Dominator Iehouah exercituum excidet ramū cū robore, & excelsi statura succisi, & sublimes humiliabūtur. 34. Succidetq; arbores perplexas sylvæ ferro, & Lybanus ferro forti cadet. Alias uero significat uberrimas & florentisimas prouincias. Nahum.1.4. Qui increpat mare, & exiccat illud, omnia quoq; flumina siccare solet: desolatus est Basan & Charmel, & flos Libani desolatus est.
units.tr: It must be admitted, however, that by the name of Lebanon, through various metaphors, is sometimes signified the strength of armies, and by the felling of Lebanon (a figurative expression) the destruction of an army, as at Isa. 10.13: "Behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror, and the tall of stature shall be hewn down, and the lofty shall be brought low." And at 34: "He shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one." At other times it signifies very fertile and flourishing provinces, as at Nahum 1.4: "He rebukes the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers run dry; Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon fades."

units.la: DE LIBANO MONTE, ET sylua Cedrina.
units.tr: ON MOUNT LEBANON AND THE CEDAR FOREST.

units.la: Strabo lib.16. Geograph. Duo montes sunt qui Cœlesyriam includunt, æqualibus fere inter se dissiti spacijs, Libanus & Antilibanus, paulò supra mare incipientes: Libanus prope Tripolin & Dei facie: Antilibanus supra mare Sidoniū. desinunt autem ad Arabiæ montes, qui sunt ultra Damascum, & eos qui ibi Trachonitæ dicuntur, qui glebosos atq; fructiferos colles habent, &c.
units.tr: Strabo, Geography, book 16: Two mountains enclose Coele-Syria, lying at roughly equal distances from each other, Libanus and Antilibanus, beginning a little above the sea. Libanus lies near Tripolis and the Face of God; Antilibanus lies above the Sidonian sea. They end at the mountains of Arabia beyond Damascus, and at those called the Trachonitae, which have clayey and fruitful hills, and so on.

units.la: Ptolemæus Geographiæ lib 5. cap.15. in descriptione Syriæ & eius montium, s 2 memia meminit Libani &c Antilibani. Crebra autem mentio Libani pasim in vetere Testamento occurrit. Itaque non necef-fe est, me in tanta breuitate temporis de hoc monte ἀντιβολογίαν[?] &c multis agere.
units.tr: Ptolemy, Geography, book 5, chapter 15, in his description of Syria and its mountains, also mentions Libanus and Antilibanus. Mention of Libanus occurs frequently throughout the Old Testament. Therefore, in so brief a space, it is not necessary for me to go into the many controversies about this mountain.

units.la: Quòd si quis in posterioribus significationibus Libani nomen hoc loco accipere malit, erit sententia, Chaldæos, qui &c à se deuictis exercitibus spolia detraxissent, &c prouincias &c urbes opulentis-simas depræ-dati essent, &c ex manubijs i-stis opes suas prope in immensum accu-mulauissent, velut ipso pondere spoliorum oppressos, pœnas daturos, &c prædã Persis &c Medis futuros.
units.tr: But if anyone prefers to take the name Libanus here in its later senses, the meaning will be this: the Chaldeans, who had stripped spoils from the armies they had defeated, and had plundered provinces and the most wealthy cities, and had piled up their riches from this booty almost beyond measure, would, as if weighed down by the very weight of the spoils, pay the penalty and become booty for the Persians and the Medes.

units.la: Idem seculis aliquot post Macedoniæ regno evenit, in quod cum multarum gentium opes longo tempore &c magno studio essent congestæ: victo Perseo Rege ultimo, à Paulo Æmilio Romam trans-vectæ sunt: &c non ita multo post partim civilibus bellis exhaustæ, partim urbe à barbaris spoliata, translatæ &c dissipatæ sunt. Idem enim opum ex spolijs accu-mulatorum fatum esse consueuit, quod Tolosani auri, de quo vetus proverbium monet.
units.tr: The same thing happened some centuries later to the kingdom of Macedonia. Into it the wealth of many nations had been heaped over a long time and with great zeal. After King Perseus, the last of its kings, was defeated, the treasure was carried to Rome by Paulus Aemilius. Not long after, it was partly drained by civil wars and partly scattered when the city was plundered by barbarians. For it is customary that wealth accumulated from spoils meets this same fate, as the gold of Tolosa does, of which an old proverb gives warning.

units.la: VERSVS XVIII.
units.tr: VERSE 18.

units.la: Quid prodest sculptile, quod sculpserit illud fictor eius: aut conflatile, & quod docet mendacium, quod speret fictor in figmē to suo, ut faciat idola muta?
units.tr: What profit is the graven image, that the maker thereof hath graven it; or the molten image, and the teacher of lies, that the maker trusteth in his own work, to make dumb idols?

units.la: Est ὑποφορά. Etsi animalis homo æger-rime fiduciam humanorum praesidiorū sibi eximi patitur: ubi tamen eam sibi præter expectationem suam ademtam uidet, ad Numinis alicuius tanquam superioris praesidium confugere solet, ne uideatur omni patrocinio & subsidio destitui. Videre id licet in Babyloniorum exemplo. Cum enim illis uoce diuina denunciatum esset, ad illorum res constabiliendas & poenas euitandas nequaquam illis profutura arma & praesidia carnalia, ab horum fiducia, tanquam possessione deiecti, confugiendum sibi censuerunt ad numina sua, quae illi magna cum superstitione colebant.
units.tr: This is a hypophora. Although man, as a creature of flesh, is most reluctant to be deprived of his confidence in human protections, yet when he sees it taken from him beyond his expectation, he is accustomed to flee to the protection of some deity as a superior power, lest he seem to be left without any patronage or help. This can be seen in the example of the Babylonians. For when it had been declared to them by a divine voice that their arms and carnal defences would by no means avail to secure their affairs and avert their punishments, they, cast down from their trust as if from a possession, judged that they must flee to their gods, whom they worshipped with great superstition.

units.la: Huic uanissimæ persuasioni occurrit Dominus, & ἐρωτήματι utitur: Siccine tanta est uestra uecordia & stupiditas, ut in uanissimis idolis uestris aliquid bonæ spei uobis, in tanta rerum uestrarum coversione & inclinatione, reponendum putetis?
units.tr: The Lord meets this most vain persuasion and uses a rhetorical question: Is your folly and stupidity so great that, in such an overturning and collapse of your affairs, you think anything of good hope should be placed in your most vain idols?

units.la: Sic autem ratiocinatur: Ea quæ nec prodesse suis auctoribus, nec eos docere possunt vera & salutaria, præsidio in rebus adversis esse non possunt: ac proinde non est in eis acquiescendum.
units.tr: He reasons thus: those things which can neither profit their makers nor teach them what is true and salutary cannot be a protection in adverse circumstances; and therefore one should not rest in them.

units.la: Atqui turpissima Chaldæorum simulacra, sunt eiusmodi. Quare neutiquam præsidio erunt suis cultoribus, cum iam in acie novaculæ constituti, pœnas dabūt suorum delictorum.
units.tr: But the most shameful images of the Chaldeans are of this kind. Therefore they will by no means be a protection to their worshippers, since, now standing on the edge of the razor, they will pay the penalty for their sins.

units.la: Minor probatur. Impossibile est effectu præstantius esse suo efficiente, & maiorem habere agendi vim: sicut ea etiam efficere & præstare possit, quæ eius efficiens causa præstare nequeat.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved as follows. It is impossible for an effect to be more excellent than its efficient cause, or to have greater power of acting; nor can it produce or provide those things which its efficient cause cannot provide.

units.la: Sunt autem idola effecta idoloplastarum. Achi rebus adversis circumuenti, sibi ipsis nec consilio, nec auxilio, adesse poterunt.
units.tr: Now idols are made by idol-makers. Men who are overwhelmed by adverse circumstances cannot provide counsel or help even for themselves.

units.la: Quare multò minus eis prodesunt ἀ-ἰδωλα[?] seu simulacra: immò cum hæc cultores suos fallant, eòq; mendacium doceant, quis dubitet ea plurimum obesse?
units.tr: Much less, therefore, do the images, or a-eidola, profit anyone. Indeed, since these deceive their worshippers and so teach lies, who would doubt that they do great harm?

units.la: In eandem sententiâ pronunciat Dominus apud Iesaiam, cap.2.i8.Idola penitus concidet. 20.In die illa proijciet homo idola argetea sua, & idola aurea sua, quæ fecerunt sibi, ut incuruaret fe coram talpis & uespertilionibus, &c.
units.tr: The Lord pronounces to the same effect through Isaiah, chapter 2, verse 18: "The idols he shall utterly abolish." Verse 20: "In that day a man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which they made for themselves, to bow down to moles and bats," and so on.

units.la: DE IDOLIS, METHO-dus ὀ[?]γ[?]ηνή[?].
units.tr: CONCERNING IDOLS: THE METHOD OF TREATMENT.

units.la: Idolum est fictoris fui figmentum, seu sculptum, seu fusum, seu pictum: mutū, docens mendacium, in quo non sperandum est. Hæc cauffalis definitio Idoli, hoc loco ab ipso Spiritu sancto tradita est: accum non sine impietate eludi possit, nos eius [illegible, ~8 letters] subiungemus.
units.tr: An idol is the figment of its maker, whether carved, cast or painted: dumb, teaching lies, and not to be trusted. This causal definition of the idol is given here by the Holy Spirit himself. Since it cannot be mocked without impiety, we will add its [illegible] below.

units.la: 1. Definitum. Idolum, quod à forma accidentali & artificiosa materiæ industa Conflatile & Sculptile uocatur, simulacrum & spectru significat, humano errore ad alium repræsentandum pictū aut fictum. Etsi liber Sapientiæ non habetur in Canone: tamen utile fuerit eius uerba de prima idolorum origine hoc loco adducere, è cap.14.v.15.16. Nam acerbo luctu filij præmature erepti mœrens pater, effecta imagine iam antea mortuum hominem, nunc ut Deum colere cœpit, atque subditis suis sacra ceremoniasque tradidit. Deinde progressu temporis inValescens impia consuetudo pro lege servata est, mandatisque tyrannorum esse-ctum, ut sculptae imagines religiosè co-lerentur.
units.tr: 1. Definition. The idol, which from its accidental and artificial form impressed on the material is called cast or carved, signifies an image or likeness, painted or fashioned by human error to represent another. Although the Book of Wisdom is not in the Canon, it will be useful to cite its words here about the first origin of idols, from chapter 14, verses 15-16: "For a father, mourning in bitter grief over his son prematurely snatched away, made an image of the dead man, and began now to worship him as a god, and handed down to his subjects sacred rites and ceremonies. Then, as time went on, this impious custom grew strong and was kept as law, and by the commands of tyrants carved images were worshipped with religious reverence."

units.la: 2. Efficiens cuffa est fictoridoli, hoc est, seu figulus, Sap.15.v.7. seu aurifex aut faber ærarius, eod.cap.v.8. & Actor.19.23.24. seu faber lignarius, Isai.40.20. & 41.7. & 44.v.11.12.13.14.&c. seu deniq; pictor.
units.tr: 2. The efficient cause of the idol is the idol-maker: either the potter (Wisdom 15:7), or the goldsmith or bronze-worker (ibid. 8; Acts 19:23-24), or the carpenter (Isaiah 40:20; 41:7; 44:11-14, etc.), or finally the painter.

units.la: Quanta verò fit insania, rebus inanimatis id tribuere, quod ne quidem idolopœo conuenit, videlicet, esse Deum, Iesaias sapienter monet cap.44.10. Quis formauit Deum, & sculptile quod non pro-fit? Dei proprium est, prodesse suis cultoribus. Idola nō prosunt cultoribus, nec obsunt cotemtoribus. Igitur Dij nō sunt.
units.tr: How great is the madness of attributing to inanimate things what does not even suit the idolater, namely, to be God! Isaiah wisely warns of this in chapter 44, verse 10: "Who has formed a god, or cast a graven image that profits nothing?" It belongs to God to profit his worshippers. Idols do not profit their worshippers, nor do they harm those who despise them. Therefore they are not gods.

units.la: 3. Genus, est figmentum. Fingitur enim id esse quod non est, cū materiæ noua forma artificialis inducitur, quæ perinde ei conuenit, ut igni frigus, & aquæ siccitas. Deum fingere & repræsentare velle simulacro ex argilla, ligno, lapide aut metallo confecto: essentiam spiritualem, infinitam, omnipotentem, re mini-ma, corporea, inanimata, bruta, inerte, quanta est dementia?
units.tr: 3. The genus is figment. For a thing is feigned to be what it is not when an artificial form is newly imposed on matter, a form that fits it just as cold fits fire or dryness fits water. To wish to feign and represent God by an image made of clay, wood, stone or metal, to represent a spiritual, infinite, omnipotent essence by a very small, corporeal, lifeless, brute and inert thing: how great is the folly!

units.la: 4. Varietas. Idola, quæ mens reproba excogitat, manus improba efficit, pro materiæ diuersitate, varia sunt. Sunt sculptilia, sunt conflatilia, sunt picturæ: quo-rum nullæ in hoc genere minus habent impietatis, quàm aliæ: etiam inuitis Græcis posterioribus, qui, ut perhibet, in templis Christianorum pictis idolis locum esse uolunt, non autem sculptis aut fusis, aut alio modo fictis.
units.tr: 4. Variety. The idols which a reprobate mind devises and a wicked hand makes are various, according to the diversity of their material. There are carved idols, cast idols and paintings. Of these, none in this class has less impiety than the others, even though, as is reported, the later Greeks, though unwillingly, want painted idols to have a place in Christian temples, but not carved, cast, or otherwise fashioned ones.

units.la: 5. Mutum idolum esse, notum est. Etsi autem cacodæmones, ut idololatris imponerent, interdum apud idola vocem edidisse concedamus: cum Propheta tamen nostro, & cum Paulo Apostolo, per se ἄφωνα esse idola, credimus: 1.Cor.12.2. Recte Dauid Rex & Propheta: Sed idola istorū sunt argentum & aurum: opus manuum hominum. Os illis, & non loquuntur: oculi illis, & non vident. Psal-mo 115.4 & 5.
units.tr: That an idol is mute is well known. Although we grant that evil demons sometimes uttered a voice near idols in order to deceive idolaters, yet we believe, with our Prophet and with the Apostle Paul, that idols are in themselves speechless (aphōna): 1 Corinthians 12:2. King David and prophet rightly says: "But their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands. They have mouths, but they speak not; eyes have they, but they see not" (Psalm 115:4-5).

units.la: 6. Proprium est, docere mendacium. Docent mendacium, qui spem cultorum suorum frustrantur. Ridicula est apud Aristophanem irrisio Deorum Ethnicorum, quos ait supinas & explicitas manus habere, ut moneant, ad accipiendum, non ad dandum paratos esse. Iam si idola do-cent mendacium, quis credat esse laico-rum libros? Vtinam hoc cogitent, qui in templis nostris, idolis, modo non ado-rentur, locum esse posse, garriunt?
units.tr: 6. It is proper to idols to teach lies. Those who frustrate the hope of their worshippers teach lies. Aristophanes' mockery of the heathen gods is ridiculous: he says they have hands turned up and outstretched, to signal that they are ready to receive, not to give. Now if idols teach lies, who would believe that they are books for the unlettered? Would that those who chatter that they may be allowed a place in our temples, provided they are not worshipped, would think on this!

units.la: 7. In idolis spes non reponenda est: cū nec sibi, nec aliis prodesse possint, ut multis in locis Scriptura docet.
units.tr: 7. No hope is to be placed in idols, since they can profit neither themselves nor others, as Scripture teaches in many places.

units.la: Sed haec de Ethnicorum idolis, non de Christianorum imaginibus & statuis sunt dicta: quae si non ado-rentur, videntur in templis ideo ferri posse, quod hi statuam Christi & Sanctorum in memoriam revocantes, erudiunt Eccle-siam.
units.tr: But these things have been said of the idols of the heathen, not of the images and statues of Christians. If these are not worshipped, they seem to be tolerated in temples on the ground that they recall the statue of Christ and of the saints to memory, and so instruct the Church.

units.la: Pudeat hac stolida ἀτοπολογία[?] in Ecclesia ex praescripto verbi Dei reformata u-ti: & quidem in unius hominis gratiam, qui irae suae nimium indulgens, a collega cum aliquo tumultu sublata e templis i-dola, pessimo & posteris nocentissimo exemplo reposuit, revera malum malo medicans. Sed ad rem.
units.tr: Shame on this foolish absurdity [ἀτοπολογία], that in a Church reformed according to the prescription of God's Word anyone should use such an argument, and that for the sake of one man, who, indulging his anger too much, had idols removed from the temples with some uproar by his colleague, and so set down an example that is very bad and very harmful to posterity: in fact, he cured evil with evil. But to the matter.

units.la: Siccine Eccianum Sophisma, de Chri-stianorum imaginibus cum Ethnicorum idolis non confundendis: & de his prohibitis, illis autem cōcessis[?], velut Cram-ben ben bis costam repetere,tibi non est religio? Proba vel unico dicto. è novo Testamento petito, Christianis istarum imaginum & laivarum[?] diabolicarum usum es-se concessum.
units.tr: Is this how you harp on the Eckian sophism, that Christian images must not be confused with the idols of the heathen, and that the one are forbidden while the other are allowed, like rehashing cabbage that has already been cooked twice? Do you feel no scruple? Prove it by a single saying taken from the New Testament, that the use of these images and diabolical snares was permitted to Christians.

units.la: Verbi sui sacrosanẽti & Sacramentorū usum nobis commendavit Dominus, ac docuit servire Spiritus sanẽti magisterio & institutioni internæ: non autem idola intueri, & ea pro libris habere, voluit.
units.tr: The Lord has commended to us the use of his most holy Word and of the Sacraments, and he taught us to serve the teaching and inner instruction of the Holy Spirit. He did not, however, will that we should gaze at idols and treat them as books.

units.la: Sacrificulorum Pontificiorum est, infci-tiæ nimirum conscientia dućtorum, non piorum & doćtorum Ministrorum Verbi, docendi in Ecclesia partes aliquas idolis deferre, quibus videlicet ipsi defungi nequeant.
units.tr: It is the business of the Papist priests, clearly, who are led by a guilty conscience and not by pious and learned ministers of the Word, to offer idols as some part of the teaching office in the Church, since they themselves cannot perform that office.

units.la: Si imagines in templis, ut laicorum libri, locum habere debent, cur primitiæ Ecclesiæ, Apostoli & eorum successores, hac in parte defuerunt? Cur libros istos, verè mutos magistros, erudiędo Dei populo non commendaverunt? Constat enim, abominandas idolorum sordes, seculis quæ proxima fuerūt Apostolorum temporibus, in templis Christianorum non habuisse locum.
units.tr: If images ought to have a place in the temples as the books of the laity, why did the first Church, the Apostles and their successors, fall short in this respect? Why did they not commend those books, truly mute teachers, for instructing the people of God? For it is established that in the centuries nearest to the times of the Apostles, the abominable filth of idols had no place in the temples of Christians.

units.la: Qui elusione utuntur,nō quidem cultum aliquem imaginibus & statuis præ-standum, in templis tamen relinquen-das memoriæ & institutionis gratia: illi primùm quidem in Ministerium uerbi contumeliosi sunt, quo nos erudiri, non brutorum & inanimatorum idolorum ma-gisterio uti, Deus uoluit: deinde, uel i-gnaros se esse historiæ Ecclesiasticæ, uel certè sine omni iudicio in ea uersari, testā-tur. Velim enim mihi dicant egregij isti idolorum patroni, quamdiu, uerbi gra-tia, Ecclesia Græca posterior, ubi semel in templa irrepsissent idola, ab eorum cul-tu abstinuerit? Iam cum constet, cultum & adorationem, prostitutionis idolorum comitem indiuiduum fuisse, ánne est ho-minis pij, idololatriæ adminicula magi-sterij & institutionis commentitio præ-textu Ecclesiæ obtrudere?
units.tr: Those who use the evasion that images and statues are not to be given any worship, but are to be left in the temples for the sake of remembrance and instruction, are first of all insulting to the ministry of the Word, by which God willed that we be taught, and not to be instructed by the teaching of brute and lifeless idols. Then they bear witness either that they are ignorant of ecclesiastical history, or at least that they move in it without any judgment. For I would like those distinguished defenders of idols to tell me how long, for instance, the later Greek Church abstained from their worship, once idols had crept into its temples. Since it is established that worship and adoration were the companion of the prostitution of idols, is it the mark of a pious man to thrust upon the Church, under the pretext of teaching and instruction, aids to idolatry?

units.la: Sunt qui teneras Ecclesias καινοτομίας[?] non esse offendendas, speciosè conten-dant. Sed alia est eorum ratio, qui recès Euangelium audire cœperunt, alia eorū, qui totos sexaginta annos illud se suosq; maiores professos esse, gloriantur.
units.tr: There are those who plausibly contend that tender Churches should not be offended by innovations [καινοτομίας]. But the reasoning is one thing for those who have only just begun to hear the Gospel, and another for those who boast that they and their forebears have professed it for sixty whole years.

units.la: Equidem illud in Domino persuasum habeo, in Ecclesia infirmorum habedam esse rationem summam, nihil per tumultum, omnia autem ordine & decenter agenda esse. Ac initio, praedicatione verbi Dei e cordibus exstirpanda esse: postea vero, idola picta & fiͤta, a pio Magistratu e templis tollenda esse, iuxta divinae legis praescriptum, & piorum Principum exempla, nequaquam dubito.
units.tr: I am indeed firmly persuaded in the Lord that the greatest consideration must be shown to the weak in the Church, that nothing should be done by tumult, but that all things should be done in order and decently. And I have no doubt that at first the preaching of God's Word must root out idols from the hearts of men, and afterwards that painted and feigned idols must be removed from the temples by a pious magistrate, according to the prescription of divine law and the examples of pious princes.

units.la: Seipsos autem graviter accusant ij docto-res, qui in Ecclesijs iam pridem reformatis, infirmos negant amotione idolorum scandalizandos. Quid enim? An’ne auditores eorum semper infirmi censeri debent, quorum multi tempore repurgatae a Papatu Ecclesiae nati & educati sunt? An’ne illi sine fructu audierunt oracula Dei de Deo in spiritu colendo, & de idolis fugiendis? Sic ita res habet, tum pastores & doctores officium suum non fecerunt docendo fugiendam esse idololatriam, & per consequens, eiusdem administrationis.
units.tr: Those teachers, however, bring grave charges against themselves, who in Churches long since reformed deny that the weak are to be scandalized by the removal of idols. For what? Ought their hearers always to be counted weak, when many of them have been born and brought up in a Church purged of Papacy? Did they hear the oracles of God in vain, concerning worship of God in spirit and concerning the shunning of idols? So the matter stands: the pastors and teachers have failed in their duty, by not teaching that idolatry must be shunned, and consequently in the administration of that same duty.

units.la: Vitio vertitur quibusdam Ecclesijs, quod non sine aliquo tumultu, qui tamen άδακτος πόλεμος fuit, sublatae e templis statuae fuerunt, cum offendiculo paucorum & superstitiosorum hominum. Sed cur non cogitant Critici illi, maiore iure offendi multarum Gentium Ecclesias,quæ uidet eò,proh dolor, illorū res redijse,ut propter unius hominis præiudicium, impia consuetudo ferendi in templis idola,anteponatur expressæ legi Dei de illis tollendis & abolendis: & eò rem redire,ut nemo propemodū mutire audeat de sor dibus illis e templis eliminandis? Quid est culicem colare,& deglutire camelū,si hoc non est?
units.tr: Some Churches are blamed because idols were removed from the temples, not without some uproar, which was nonetheless a bloodless war [ἄδακτος πόλεμος], and with offence to a few superstitious people. But why do those critics not consider that the Churches of many nations have far greater right to be offended, since, alas, matters have come to such a pass that, on account of the prejudice of one man, the impure custom of keeping idols in the temples is preferred to the express law of God, which commands that they be removed and abolished; and matters have come to the point where almost no one dares to murmur about removing those filthy things from the temples? What is it to strain out a gnat and swallow a camel, if this is not so?

units.la: VERSVS XIX.
units.tr: VERSE XIX.

units.la: Va dicenti ligno, Expergiscere: & lapidi silenti, Excitare. num ipse docet? En copertus est auro & argento, nec ullus spiritus est in eo.
units.tr: Woe to him who says to the wood, Awake; to the silent stone, Arise. Can it teach? Behold, it is covered with gold and silver, and there is no spirit in it at all.

units.la: Ἐπιτίμησις est, seu reprehensio superstitionis idololatrarum, qui ibi consilium & auxilium quærunt, ubi nullum plane est, uidelicet apud idola sua.
units.tr: This is a rebuke [ἐπιτίμησις], or a reproof, of the superstition of idolaters, who seek counsel and help where there is plainly none, namely from their own idols.

units.la: Maledicti & omnium hominum infelicissimi sunt, qui non solum cum inani-matis[?] rebus loqui conantur, sed etiam ab iis flagitant ea, quæ propria sunt beneficia naturæ uiuentis, intelligentis & omnipotentis: ut sunt, excitari & expergisci (hæc per ἀνθρωποπαθίαν[?] passim Deo in Scripturis tribuuntur) ad ferendam laborantibus opem: docere eos, consulendo & erudiendo.
units.tr: They are cursed and the most wretched of all men who try to speak not only to lifeless things, but also to ask of them those things that are the proper benefits of a living, intelligent and almighty nature: such as to be roused and to awake (which are attributed to God throughout the Scriptures by way of anthropopathy [ἀνθρωποπάθεια]), in order to bring help to those in trouble, and to teach them by giving counsel and instruction.

units.la: Atqui Chaldæi in rerum aduersarum & fatalium pœnarum labyrinthis hærentes, è pumice aquam postulabunt: id est, confugient ad sua idola, & magnis clamoribus ea expergefacere ad opem re consilioq; miseris cultoribus ferendam, conabuntur.
units.tr: Yet the Chaldeans, caught in the labyrinths of adverse affairs and fatal punishments, will demand water from pumice stone. That is, they will flee to their idols, and with loud cries they will try to rouse them, so that they may bring help and counsel to their wretched worshippers.

units.la: Igitur reuera maledicti & exsecrabiles erunt.
units.tr: Therefore they will truly be cursed and accursed.

units.la: Maior probatur, primum à materia, deinde à forma.
units.tr: The major premise is proved first from the matter, then from the form.

units.la: Si materiam, è qua idola formari solent, spectes, etsi non est eadem omnium, tamen omnis quæ adhiberi solet, stupida & inanimata est. Ex ligno enim, & lapidibus ac metallis sculpendo & fundēdo[?] idola effici, quis tandem ignorat?
units.tr: If you look at the matter out of which idols are usually made, although it is not the same in all cases, yet all that is commonly used is stupid and lifeless. For who indeed does not know that idols are produced by carving and casting wood, stones and metals?

units.la: Rursus, si consideres formam, etsi idola forma artificiosa ἔξωθεν[?] ornantur, videlicet auro, argento, aut coloribus: tamen destituuntur forma substantiali, videlicet spiritu vivifico & intelligente: ut hoc loco diserte affirmat Deus noster.
units.tr: Again, if you consider the form, although idols are adorned from outside [ἔξωθεν] with skilful artistry, namely with gold, silver or colours, yet they lack a substantial form, namely a living and intelligent spirit, as our God expressly affirms in this passage.

units.la: Iam uerò, cùm spiritu intelligente,ui-ta, & huius certisimis indicijs motu & sensu,idola careant: quis homo fanus du-bitet, ea nec sibijpsis,nec alijs,quicquam praestare posse? Rectè itaque Dominus apud Iesaiam inquit: Fictores sculptilis omnes ipsi uanitas,& concupiscibilia eo-rum non proderunt: & testes eorum ipsi, quòd non uident, neque cognoscunt, ut pudore afficiantur. Cap.44.9.
units.tr: Now, since idols lack an intelligent spirit, life, and its most certain signs, motion and sensation, what sane man would doubt that they can accomplish nothing, either for themselves or for others? Rightly therefore the Lord says through Isaiah: All the makers of graven images are vanity themselves, and their precious things will not profit; and their own witnesses, because they neither see nor know, so that they may be put to shame. Isa. 44.9.

units.la: VERSVS XX.
units.tr: Verse 20

units.la: Iehouah autem est in templo sancto suo: sileat ergo à facie eius uniuersa terra.
units.tr: But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.

units.la: Enthymema est, quo finem responsioni imponens Iehouah,in sua iudicia nobis non esse scrupulosè inquirendum, o-stendit. Sententia est:
units.tr: This is an enthymeme, by which Jehovah, bringing the answer to a close, shows that we are not to inquire anxiously into his judgments. The sense is this:

units.la: Iehouah Deus noster sic inhabitat lucem inaccessam, ut tamen coelum illi sit sedes, terra scabellum pedum,& ut rebus conditis assit, eas sapienter moderetur: deniq; ut ipsi in eo uno uiuamus, simus & moueamur. 1.Tim.6.16. Isa.66.1. Act.7.49. & 17.27.28.
units.tr: Jehovah our God so dwells in unapproachable light that heaven is nonetheless his throne and the earth his footstool; and although he is present with created things, he governs them wisely; and finally, it is in him alone that we live, move and have our being. 1 Tim. 6.16; Isa. 66.1; Acts 7.49; Acts 17.27-28.

units.la: Ergo sileat à facie eius omnis terra: id est, omnes homines Dei iudicia adorent, necin ea curiose inquirat, nedum ut ad-versus ea vitilitigatione aliqua instituat.
units.tr: Therefore let all the earth be silent before him: that is, all men should adore God's judgments and not inquire curiously into them, much less bring some quarrelsome dispute against them.

units.la: Huius modestiae & reuerentiae Deo debitae exemplum laude dignum occur-rit in Psal.39.9. Obmutui, nō aperiam os meum: nam tu fecisti.
units.tr: An example of this modesty and reverence due to God, worthy of praise, occurs in Psalm 39.9: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth, because thou didst it."

units.la: Ergo siue emergant & floreant impij, ac multis magnis calamitatibus pios af-ficiant: siue hi in caussa optima laborare & deseri, siue numerus piorum ad ma-gnā paucitatem redigi, siue facta & profana misceri uideantur: nobis tamen non[?] est obloquendum Deo, nec eius iudicia accusanda: sed illud Propheticum repe-tendum: Cum sedero in tenebris, Iehouah erit illuminatio mea. Item: Iram Ie-houae portabo, quia peccaui ei. Sunt e-nim profundae diuitiae tum sapientiae, tū cognitionis Dei: inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia, & viae eius imperuestigabiles. Quis enim cognouit mentem Domini, aut quis ei fuit a consilijs? Rom.11. 33.34. Haec de cap.2. paucis dicere licuit.
units.tr: Therefore, whether the wicked rise up and flourish and afflict the godly with many great calamities; or whether the godly seem to labour and be forsaken in the best of causes; or whether the number of the pious is reduced to a very small handful; or whether good and profane things seem to be mixed together: yet we must not speak against God, nor accuse his judgments. Rather we must repeat that prophetic word: "When I sit in darkness, Jehovah will be my light." Likewise: "I will bear the wrath of Jehovah, because I have sinned against him." For the riches of both the wisdom and the knowledge of God are deep: his judgments are unsearchable and his ways past finding out. "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?" Rom. 11.33-34. It has been permitted to say these few things on chapter 2.

units.la: CAPVT TERTIVM.
units.tr: CHAPTER 3.

units.la: FIlum & feriem orationis Prophetæ Habacuc in hoc capite ultimo, pridé tradidimus in Prolegomenis. Istud autē satis fuerit initiò monere, Prophetā nostrum suo exemplo nos docere, non esse nobis intuentibus tristia Ecclesiæ & singulorum piorum fata, nimium indulgendum dolori, nec immorandum disquisitioni curiosæ iudiciorum Dei, quæ longè uincunt captum nostrum: sed potius nostram ignorantiam & infirmitatem agnoscendam, & præclara bonitatis, iustitiæ & uirtutis diuinæ specimina repetenda: ut eorum meditatio confirmandæ in nobis fidei & spei seruiat. Vtrumque enim nobis considerandū est, & quid nos deceat, & quid nos non deceat. Decet nos opera & beneficia Dei memoria repetere, ut celebretur eorum auctor Deus, qui est mirabilis in cunctis suis operibus. Non decet τὰ ἀσυγγνώμονα[?] & abstrusa, quæ Deus in sua solius potestate posuit, curiosè scrutari. Prudenter Gregorius: Rationem, inquit, de occulto Dei iuditio quærere, nihil aliud est, quàm contrà eius consilium superbire. Et Augustinus de Spiritu & litera, præclarè inquit: Operum Dei causa si lateat hominem, non sé obliuiscatur esse hominem, nec propterea Deo det insipientiam, quia non bene capit eius scientiam.
units.tr: We set out the thread and sequence of the prophet Habakkuk's discourse in this final chapter earlier, in the Prolegomena. It will be enough to remind the reader at the outset that our prophet teaches us by his example: when we look upon the sorrows of the Church and the fates of individual believers, we must not indulge our grief too much, nor linger over a curious inquiry into the judgments of God, which far exceed our understanding. Rather, we should acknowledge our ignorance and weakness and recall the outstanding displays of God's goodness, justice and power, so that meditating on them may serve to strengthen faith and hope in us. For we must consider both what befits us and what does not. It befits us to recall the works and benefits of God, so that God, the author of them, who is wonderful in all his works, may be celebrated. It does not befit us to pry curiously into the unpardonable and hidden things [τὰ ἀσυγγνώμονα] which God has placed in his own sole power. Gregory wisely says: "To seek a reason for God's hidden judgment is nothing other than to rebel against his counsel." And Augustine, in his book On the Spirit and the Letter, says admirably: "If the cause of God's works is hidden from a man, let him not forget that he is a man, nor on that account ascribe folly to God because he does not grasp his knowledge well."

units.la: VERSVS 1.
units.tr: VERSE 1.

units.la: Oratio Habacuc Prophetæ pro ignorantiâ[?].
units.tr: The prayer of the prophet Habakkuk on ignorance.

units.la: Hæc est inscriptio Psalmi Habacuc Prophetæ, quæ monet, inscitiam & infirmitatem nostram nobis potius esse confitendam, quàm cum Deo litigandum de eius operibus & iudiciis.
units.tr: This is the title of the psalm of the prophet Habakkuk, which warns that we ought rather to confess our ignorance and weakness than to contend with God over his works and judgments.

units.la: Rabi Salomon existimat, Prophetam voce Dei in hac disceptatione convictum erubuisse: & ut Deo debitam gloriam deferret, ignorantiam suam confessum esse.
units.tr: Rabbi Solomon thinks that the prophet, convicted in this dispute by the voice of God, blushed and, in order to give to God the glory due to him, confessed his ignorance.

units.la: Quod si vir tantus, patriæ excidium, hostium insolentiam, & alia mala publicè & privatim grassantia ingenti cum dolo re expertus & intues, cum primum à Domino admonitus, sese repressit, ac Deo gloriam dedit: meminerimus, idem nobis quoq; faciendum : rerum omnium[?] initia, media & fines, cū uera ἀθυμίας[?], seu mentis tranquillitate, Deo relinquenda: nec fremitu & indignatione peccādum, cum fors aspera nos premit.
units.tr: But if a man so great, who had experienced and seen with great grief the destruction of his country, the insolence of enemies, and other evils raging publicly and privately, restrained himself as soon as he was admonished by the Lord and gave glory to God, let us remember that we too must do the same. The beginnings, middles and ends of all things must be left to God, along with a true freedom from dejection [ἀθυμίας], that is, tranquillity of mind. Nor should we sin by fretting and indignation when harsh fortune presses upon us.

units.la: DE IGNORANTIA HVMANA,distinctiones aliquot.
units.tr: ON HUMAN IGNORANCE, several distinctions.

units.la: Fons omnium errorum in cogitationibus, uotis & desideriis, dictis & factis, est ignorantia: quae alias scientiae alicuius fucosae, alias contraria specie, imponit homini, sic ut uel secus quàm oportebat agendo aut omittendo, uel omittendo quae agenda erat, aut agendo quae omittenda fuerat, delinquat. Nos, ut hæc doctrina illustretur, distinctiones aliquot in gratiam Iuniorum recitabimus, & locis opportunis dicta quaedam ueterum aspergemus, ut sint condimenti uice.
units.tr: The source of all errors, in thoughts, wishes and desires, in words and deeds, is ignorance, which imposes on a man now one counterfeit kind of knowledge, now another of contrary appearance, so that he goes wrong either by acting or omitting otherwise than he ought, or by omitting what should have been done, or by doing what should have been left undone. To illustrate this teaching, we shall set out some distinctions for the sake of younger students, and at suitable places we shall sprinkle in some sayings of the ancients, so that they may serve as a seasoning.

units.la: 1. Ignorantia uel est affectata, uel non affectata, si causam efficientem spectes.
units.tr: 1. Ignorance is either wilful or not wilful, if you look at its efficient cause.

units.la: Nam si mens & uoluntas, respuentes scientiae lucem, tenebras ignorantiae retinere malint, quàm radios ueritatis admittere, affectata dicitur ignorantia: cuius quae causa fit, docet hoc Christi dictū de Pseudoiudaeis: Hæc autem est condemnatio, quòd Lux uenit in mūdum, sed dilexerunt homines potius tenebras q Lucem: quia sunt eorū opera mala: Ioan.3.19. Recte Augustinus contra Academicos: Indoctum esse, inquit, minus malum est, quàm esse indocibilem: id est, auersantem institutionem, & contemtorem τῆς ψυχῆς.
units.tr: For if the mind and will, rejecting the light of knowledge, prefer to hold on to the darkness of ignorance rather than admit the rays of truth, the ignorance is called wilful. The saying of Christ about the false Jews teaches what causes it: "This is the condemnation, that light has come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than light, because their works were evil" (John 3:19). Augustine rightly says against the Academics: "To be untaught is less evil than to be unteachable, that is, to shun instruction and to despise the soul [τῆς ψυχῆς]."

units.la: 2. Si subiecta, hoc est, eos de quib. praedicatur quòd sint ignari, spectes, occurrut primum οἱ ἐξω, hoc est, ij qui extra Ecclesiam uersantur, & sunt Dei expertes in mundo: deinde & ij qui in Ecclesiae militantis externa societate uersantur, & aliquandiu hoc malo laborant.
units.tr: 2. If you look at the subjects, that is, the people of whom it is said that they are ignorant, there first come those who are outside [οἱ ἐξω], that is, those who live outside the Church and are strangers to God in the world. Then come those who live within the outward fellowship of the militant Church and for some time suffer from this evil.

units.la: De illis exstat dictum Act.17.30. Temporibus igitur istius ignorantiae (qua uidelicet profanae gentes in mundo, multis seculis orbatae luce gratiae, laboraue-runt) disimulatis, Deus nunc denunciat omnibus ubiq; hominibus ut resipiscat.
units.tr: A saying about the former stands in Acts 17:30. Therefore, passing over the times of that ignorance (in which, of course, the profane nations of the world, for many centuries deprived of the light of grace, laboured), God now declares to all men everywhere that they should repent.

units.la: Si autem hos respicias, ut iam de Pseu dochristianis, qui non sunt uiua Christi membra, non loquamur: fatendum est, miram esse etiam piorum hominum dissimilitudinem. Alij enim cito ueritatis lu ce illustrantur, alij autem seri ūs: ut monet exemplum Apostolorum Christi, qu i paulatim profecerūt in cognitione Christi: utipsimet fatentur. Paulus autem [?] Christo, eodem fere momento, didicit Evangelium per miràdam reuelationem: quòd ita ei opus esset.
units.tr: But if you consider the latter, not to speak now of the pseudo-Christians, who are not living members of Christ, it must be admitted that there is a remarkable dissimilarity even among pious men. For some are quickly illuminated by the light of truth, others more slowly, as the example of Christ's apostles shows, who progressed little by little in the knowledge of Christ, as they themselves confess. Paul, however, learned the Gospel almost in the same moment as he came to Christ, through a wonderful revelation, because it was necessary for him to be so.

units.la: Nos, cum necesse sit legendo sacras literas, & exercitijs veræ pietatis & tolerantiæ, Dei dona suscitare, per gradus [illegible, ~6 letters] proficimus. Vtinam autem, quantū quidem in nobis est, demus operam, ut profectus noster aliquando manifestus sit in omnibus: & ut dissimilimi simus illis mulierculis, quas semper discere, nunquam autem ad veritatis cognitionem peruenire, Apostolus noster queritur.
units.tr: We, since it is necessary that by reading the holy letters and by the exercises of true piety and patience we stir up the gifts of God, make progress by degrees [illegible]. Would that, so far as lies in us, we might give our effort so that our progress may at some time be manifest in all, and that we may be most unlike those little women whom our Apostle complains are always learning and never come to the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: 3. Obiectorum respectu distingui potest ignorantia, in Rerum & Personarum, Factorum & Iuris ignorantiam.
units.tr: 3. With respect to the objects, ignorance can be distinguished into ignorance of things, of persons, of deeds, and of law.

units.la: I. Rerum aliæ nobis notæ esse debent, aliæ contra ignotæ.
units.tr: I. Some things ought to be known to us, others on the contrary are unknown.

units.la: Rectè Aristoteles in Rhetoricis: Turpe, inquit, est ignorare, quod universos scire convenit. Vt Dei sanctam voluntatem nos omnes scire & præstare decet: cum ideò simus conditi, ut Deum agnoscamus, & ei obediamus. Idem iudicium est & de uniuscuiusque officio in societate humana, & de uirtutum exercitijs.
units.tr: Aristotle rightly says in the Rhetoric: "It is shameful to be ignorant of what all men ought to know." Thus we all ought to know and perform God's holy will, since we were created for this purpose, that we should acknowledge God and obey him. The same judgment holds concerning each person's duty in human society and concerning the exercise of the virtues.

units.la: Quae uerò turpia sunt, aut certo consilio Dei nobis abscondita, ea ignorare laus est. Aristoteles in Metaphysicis ait, ignorare turpia multò melius esse, quàm ea scire. Et uox diuina de iis, quae cum sibi seruarit Deus, nos curiosè perquisitigare non decet, testatur: Non est uestrum nos-se tempora siue opportunitates, quas Pa-ter in sua ipsius auctoritate posuit. Act.1.7.
units.tr: But those things which are shameful, or which by God's settled counsel are hidden from us, it is praiseworthy to be ignorant of. Aristotle, in the Metaphysics, says that it is far better to be ignorant of shameful things than to know them. And the divine voice testifies concerning those things which God has kept to himself, that we ought not to inquire into them curiously: "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father has placed in his own authority" (Acts 1:7).

units.la: De Personis, quarum noticia requiri-tur, digna sunt memoria haec dicta:
units.tr: Concerning persons whose acquaintance is required, the following sayings are worth remembering:

units.la: Ignorantia sui, ut ait Bernardus, initium omnis peccati: ignorantia Dei, consummatio omnis peccati.
units.tr: Ignorance of oneself, as Bernard says, is the beginning of all sin; ignorance of God is the completion of all sin.

units.la: Et subscribens Lactantius: Prauitatis, ait, causa ignoratio sui.
units.tr: And Lactantius, agreeing, says: "The cause of wickedness is ignorance of oneself."

units.la: Et Gregorius ii. Moral. A luce ueritatis in tantas ignorantiae tenebras corruimus, ut nos ipsos ignoremus.
units.tr: And Gregory, in the second book of the Moralia: "We have fallen from the light of truth into such darkness of ignorance that we do not know ourselves."

units.la: De Iuris ignorantia, uidetur pronunciasse beatus Augustinus, in his duob. dictis:
units.tr: Concerning ignorance of law, the blessed Augustine seems to have pronounced in these two sayings:

units.la: Non omnis ignorans immunis est, sed is solum, qui non habuit unde disceret. In quaest. utriusq; Testamenti, q.67.
units.tr: "Not every ignorant person is immune, but only the one who had no means by which he might learn." In Questions on Both Testaments, q. 67.

units.la: Ignorantia infidelitatis, peccatum non excusat. De Gratia & lib.arb. Exemplū ignorantiæ, cui Deus ignovit, habetur 1.Timoth.1.13. Qui prius eram blasphemus, & persecutor, & iniuriosus: sed mei misertus est. nam ignorans id fa-ciebam, fidei expers.
units.tr: "Ignorance of unbelief does not excuse sin." On Grace and Free Will. An example of ignorance which God pardoned is found in 1 Timothy 1:13: "I who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious; but I obtained mercy, for I did it ignorantly, in unbelief."

units.la: Cum autem etiam Sancti homines se-pe errent in consiliis & actionibus: ut Abraham, dicens Saram sororem suam ef-se: David, numerans populum: Josias, bellum inferes Ægyptio: Petrus aliquā-do non recto pede in Euangelio Christi incedens, cum Antiochiæ esset: agnoscamus ignorantiam & infirmitatem perinde nobis incumbere, ut sici oculis incum-bunt: ac deplorantes nostra mala, cum Da-vide precemur: Errores quis intelligat? Ab occultis munda me Domine: Psal.19. 12. Petamus etiam, ut Deus dispulsa ca-ligine mentium nostrarum, lucis suae radios spargat in corda nostra, eaq; san-ctificet ad gloriam nominis sui. Amen.
units.tr: Since, however, even holy men often err in their counsels and actions, as Abraham did in saying that Sarah was his sister, David in numbering the people, Josiah in making war on the Egyptian, and Peter at times not walking uprightly in the Gospel of Christ when he was at Antioch, let us acknowledge that ignorance and weakness press upon us just as dimness presses upon our eyes. And, lamenting our evils, let us pray with David: "Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from hidden faults, O Lord" (Psalm 19:12). Let us also pray that God, having dispelled the darkness of our minds, may scatter the rays of his light into our hearts and sanctify them to the glory of his name. Amen.

units.la: VERSVS II.
units.tr: VERSE 2.

units.la: O Jehovah, audi famam tuam, & timui: Jehovah opus manuum tuarum in medio annorum viuifica, in medio (in-quam) quam) annorum notum fac(illud:) in ira misericordiæ recorderis.
units.tr: O Jehovah, I have heard your fame, and I was afraid. O Jehovah, quicken your work in the midst of the years; in the midst of the years (I say) make it known; in wrath remember mercy.

units.la: I. VOCVM CONIVNCTARVM ET simplicium expositio.
units.tr: I. Explanation of the conjoined and simple words.

units.la: 1. Audire famam Iehouæ, hoc loco significat, sententiam Iehouæ de populi Iudaici castigatione, & de pœnis hostium, utiustam, sanctam & certissimam cognoscere. Hanc cognitionem timor, natus ex consideratione & admiratione iudiciorum Dei, perinde ut corpus umbra, subsequitur.
units.tr: 1. To hear the fame of Jehovah here means to learn, as just, holy and most certain, his judgment concerning the chastisement of the Jewish people and the punishments of their enemies. This knowledge is followed by fear, born from the consideration and wonder at God's judgments, just as a body is followed by its shadow.

units.la: 2. Populus Iudaicus autē hoc loco vocatur opus manuum Iehouæ, non solùm creationis, sed etiā segregationis in Dei peculium, nomine. Ita enim dicitur Ifa. 64. 8. Nunc igitur Iehouah Pater noster es: nos lutum, & tu fictor noster es, opúsque manus tuæ omnes nos. 9. Ne irascaris Iehouah ufq; ualde, & ne in seculum memineris iniquitatis: en respice, quæso, populus tuus omnes nos.
units.tr: 2. The Jewish people is called here the work of Jehovah's hands, by the name not only of creation but also of separation into God's own possession. For Isaiah 64:8 says: "But now, O Jehovah, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter, and we are all the work of your hand. 9. Be not angry, O Jehovah, very sore, and remember not iniquity for ever. Behold, I beg you, look upon us, all of us your people."

units.la: 3. Medium annorum, id tempus appellat, quod maximè opportunum, & liberationi diuinitùs præstitutum est. Dauid id, gratuitæ Dei beneuolentiæ tempus, t nuncupat, Psal.69.13. Ac ex professo de eo tempore agitur Psal.102.13. de quo non ster Propheta: Itaque tu exurgens miseraberis Sion: quia tempus miserendi eius: quia venit statutum tempus.
units.tr: 3. "The midst of the years" names that time which is most opportune and which God has appointed for deliverance. David calls it the time of God's free goodwill, Psalm 69:13. And the matter is treated expressly of this time in Psalm 102:13, of which the Prophet speaks thus: "So you, rising up, will have mercy on Zion, for the time to have mercy on her has come, for the appointed time has come."

units.la: 4. Deliberatione autem a malis, & bonorum corporalium & spiritualium communicatione, accipi debent voces illae: Viuificare: Notam facere clementiam: In ira recordari misericordiae.
units.tr: 4. But these words, "to quicken," "to make mercy known," and "to remember mercy in wrath," must be understood as a turning away from evils and a sharing of bodily and spiritual goods.

units.la: 2. SENTENTIA.
units.tr: 2. The sense.

units.la: Psalmi istius πρόθεσιν[?], supplici precatione enunciatam, hic uersiculus tradit:
units.tr: The purpose [πρόθεσιν] of this psalm, expressed in a suppliant prayer, is set forth in this little verse:

units.la: O' Iehouah, etsi uehementer afficior triftisima denunciatione de populi tui castigatione, quam uideo ineuitabilem esse: tamen fiducia misericordiae tuae confirmatus, te supplex oro, ut populum tuum, quem tanto studio & tot iam seculis formasti & conseruasti, ut esset peculium tuum, in medijs afflictionibus uiuificare, inq; iusta tua ira misericordiae tuae meminisse uelis.
units.tr: O Jehovah, although I am greatly troubled by the most sorrowful announcement of the chastisement of your people, which I see to be unavoidable, yet, strengthened by confidence in your mercy, I beg you as a suppliant: quicken your people, whom you have formed and preserved with such great zeal and through so many ages, so that it might be your own possession, in the midst of afflictions; and in your just wrath, be pleased to remember your mercy.

units.la: Hic habetis pij hominis, expauescentis ob conscientiam publicorum & priuatorum peccatorum & malorum, ac eorū acerbisimum sensum, & tamen fide sese erigenerigentis,ac è tentationis gurgite elustatis,commemorabile exemplum.
units.tr: Here you have a memorable example of a godly man, alarmed by the awareness of public and private sins and evils and by their most bitter sense, yet raising himself up by faith and struggling out of the whirlpool of temptation.

units.la: Monet autem hoc exemplum,nō tam de nostris commodis,incōmodis & periculis nos solicitos esse, & ea quæ nostra sunt quærere: sed de Ecclesia,de alijs pijs laborantibus, & publicis calamitatibus, nos ferió solicitos esse debere. Laudat eo nomine Imperatorem Theodosium Ambrosius,quòd de Ecclesia in agone solicitè cogitaret.
units.tr: This example warns us not to be so anxious about our own advantages, disadvantages and dangers, and to seek what is ours; rather, we ought to be earnestly anxious about the Church, about other pious people who labour, and about public calamities. Ambrose praises the Emperor Theodosius on this very account, because he thought anxiously about the Church in its struggle.

units.la: 3. DEMONSTRATIO.
units.tr: 3. Demonstration.

units.la: A' sanctificatione & segregatione populi Dei, sic ἀναλυτικῶς[?] argumentatur Propheta:
units.tr: The Prophet argues analytically from the sanctification and separation of the people of God:

units.la: Non est consentaneum,Deum summè bonum ὡς φιλάνθρωπον[?], Architectum & Conseruatorem uniuersorum, nō habere rationem præstantissimi sui operis, in quo formando & elaborando,summam suam sapientiam, bonitatem, iusticiam, clementiam,potetiam toties declarauit.
units.tr: It is not consistent that God, supremely good, as a lover of humankind [ὡς φιλάνθρωπον], the architect and preserver of all things, should have no regard for his most excellent work, in forming and fashioning which he has so often displayed his supreme wisdom, goodness, justice, mercy and power.

units.la: Hæc Maior probatur à natura Dei,qui cum sit Iehouah, nihil aggreditur, nihil etiam præstat & efficit, nisi quod est ἀμε-ταμέλητος[?] : Rom.11.29. Nam dona Dei & vocatio eiusmodi sunt, ut eorum nō possit eum poenitere. Neque id mirum est, cum omnium rerum initia, media & fines in sua potestate habeat, & omnia ipsius gloriae seruire oporteat.
units.tr: This major premise is proved from the nature of God, who, since he is Jehovah, undertakes nothing and accomplishes or effects nothing except what is irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητος]: Romans 11:29. For the gifts and the calling of God are such that he cannot repent of them. Nor is this surprising, since he has the beginnings, means and ends of all things in his power, and all things must serve his glory.

units.la: Eadem Maior probatur & à comparatis: Qui ne quidem inferiorum graduum opera negligit, multò minus negligit summa sua opera, quæq; maximè faciunt ad Opificis gloriam. Atqui Deus inferiora sua opera non negligit. Matth. 10. 29. Nónne duo passerculi assario veneunt, & unus ex illis non cadet humi sine Patre vestro? 30. Vestri verò etiam capilli capitis omnes numerati sunt. 31. Ne igitur timete: vos multis passerculis præ-statis.
units.tr: The same major premise is proved also from comparison: whoever does not neglect even the works of lower rank will much less neglect his greatest works, which contribute most to the glory of the Maker. But God does not neglect his lesser works. Matthew 10:29-31: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore: you are of more value than many sparrows."

units.la: Atqui populus Israël eximium Dei opus est: ut hoc loco Habacuc testatur. Et ὁμόψυχον[?] testimonium occurrit Isaiae 64. 8. Ac in huius populi gratiam Deus μεγάλα plurima præstitit, & beneficijs suis eum accumulauit, & multis seculis benignè conseruauit.
units.tr: Yet the people of Israel is an outstanding work of God, as Habakkuk bears witness in this place. And a unanimous testimony occurs in Isaiah 64:8. For the sake of this people God has done many great things [μεγάλα], has loaded it with his benefits, and has kindly preserved it through many ages.

units.la: Hanc Minorem in sequentibus uersib. ἀλληλουϊὰς[?] persequitur Propheta, instituta enumeratione magnificorum Dei operum, & beneficiorum huic populo præstitorum. Quare consentaneum est,Deum habiturum esse rationem populi Iudaici, nec permissurum,ut malorum gurgite absorbeatur & plane intereat.
units.tr: The Prophet pursues this minor premise in the following verses, setting out an enumeration of the magnificent works of God and of the benefits bestowed upon this people. Therefore it is consistent that God will have regard for the Jewish people, and will not allow it to be swallowed up by the whirlpool of evils and utterly perish.

units.la: Suntautem illustria praesentiae gratiae Dei & reconciliationis documenta,uiui-ficatio: declaratio clementiae & miseri-cordiae in ira, id est, in media castigatio-ne,aut in poenis publicis & priuatis.
units.tr: There are, moreover, clear proofs of the presence of God's grace and of reconciliation: quickening; and the declaration of clemency and mercy in wrath, that is, in the midst of chastisement, or in public and private punishments.

units.la: Viuificatio opponitur mortificationi: ac de utroq; Dei opere Hanna mater Samuelis Prophetae cecinit: Iehouah occidit & uiuificat: descendere facit ad sepulcrum,& ascendere facit e sepulcro. Iehouah pauperem facit & ditat,deijcit & attollit. 1.Sam.2.6.7.
units.tr: Quickening is set against mortification, and Hannah, the mother of the prophet Samuel, sang of both works of God: "Jehovah kills and makes alive; he brings down to the grave and brings up again. Jehovah makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and he lifts up." 1 Samuel 2:6-7.

units.la: Notum facit opus fuu Iehouah,& quidem in medio annorum, cum opportuno tempore Ecclesiae laborantri,& singulis fidelibus oppressis, dexter adest: & eos subleuat e luto coeni & cisterna perftrepente, & iudicia sua exercet: sic ut etiam hostes piorum animaduertant, Dei manum, pijs auxiliatricem, & scelerum uindicem, nunquam deesse.
units.tr: Jehovah makes known his work, indeed in the midst of the years, when at the opportune time he stands at the right hand of the labouring Church and of each oppressed faithful person, and lifts them out of the mire of mud and the roaring pit, and executes his judgments; so that even the enemies of the pious perceive that the hand of God, helpful to the pious and avenger of wickedness, never fails.

units.la: In ira aute meminit misericordiae suae Dominus, cum efficit, ut ferui ipsius re ipsa experiantur, & plurimùm profuisse ipsis Domini ac Patris optimi ferulam,& eundem pro immensa sua bonitate eam sustulisse. Itaq; canunt: Misericors & clemens Iehouah: tardus ira, & multus bonitate. Non in perpetuum rixari solitus, nec in seculum (iram) custodire. Non secundum peccata nostra fecit nobis, &c. Psal.103.8.9.10. & sequentibus.
units.tr: But the Lord remembers his mercy in wrath when he brings it about that his servants actually experience how greatly the rod of the Lord and of the best Father has profited them, and how, in his immense goodness, he has lifted it up again. So they sing: "Merciful and gracious is Jehovah, slow to anger and abundant in goodness. He is not wont to quarrel for ever, nor to keep his anger to eternity. He has not dealt with us according to our sins," etc. Psalm 103:8-10 and following.

units.la: In ira Deum misericordiæ suæ meminisse, unde tandem certò colligam?
units.tr: How, finally, can I surely gather that God remembers his mercy in wrath?

units.la: Ex his quæ subiungâ, & aliis similibus:
units.tr: From what I subjoin, and from others like them:

units.la: 1. Cum suos ideò castigat, ut peccare de sinant, & ut peccatū odio habere discant, quorum utrumque fieri, ipsorum plurimum interest.
units.tr: 1. Because he chastises his own in order that they may be kept from sinning and learn to hate sin; and it is very much in their interest that both of these should happen.

units.la: 2. Cum amorem studiumq; boni illis dulce reddit.
units.tr: 2. Because he makes the love and eagerness for what is good sweet to them.

units.la: 3. Cum eos seiunctos à filijs huius mundi, sanctificat ad obedientiæ cultum sibi præstandum.
units.tr: 3. Because, separating them from the children of this world, he sanctifies them to render him the worship of obedience.

units.la: 4. Cum nō patitur exemplo alienæ vanitatis, veluti torrete abreptos, in eadem cum illis præcipitia progredi & perire.
units.tr: 4. Because he does not allow them, by the example of another's vanity, to be carried away like a torrent and to advance and perish with those headlong into the same precipices.

units.la: 5. Cùm conscientijs eorum medetur, ne sibi permisisi, & alieno exemplo inducti, seipsos lædant.
units.tr: 5. Because he heals their consciences, lest, having been given licence, and led on by another's example, they harm themselves.

units.la: 6. Cum patientiæ & inuocationis ma-teriam & exercitia iisdem subministrat.
units.tr: 6. Because he supplies them with the matter and exercises of patience and of prayer.

units.la: 7. Cum in mediis ærumnis piis se ad-esse testatur.
units.tr: 7. Because in the midst of troubles he declares that he is present with the pious.

units.la: 8. Cùm subtractis inferioribus seu corporalibus bonis, superiora seu spiritualia illis largitur, χρυσᾶ χαλκείων[?] permutando.
units.tr: 8. Because, taking away lesser or bodily goods, he bestows upon them higher or spiritual goods, exchanging gold for bronze [χρυσᾶ χαλκείων].

units.la: 9. Cum eos facit conformes Iesu Chri-sto filio suo.
units.tr: 9. Because he makes them conformed to Jesus Christ his Son.

units.la: 10. Cum inter media contraria opus suum sic agit, ut per carceres liberet, per infamiam glorificet, per oppressiones extol-lat, per mortem vivificet, &c.
units.tr: 10. Because, amid contrary circumstances, he so carries on his work that through prisons he frees, through infamy he glorifies, through oppressions he exalts, through death he quickens, and so on.

units.la: 11. Cum efficit ut intelligant, mala hæc carni molesta,non esse αὐτῶν τινὸς αἰχμαλωσίας[?] bona autem caduca, quæ ipsis adimutur, non esse perfecta nec præcipua bona.
units.tr: 11. Because he brings it about that they understand these evils, troublesome to the flesh, are not some sort of captivity [αὐτῶν τινὸς αἰχμαλωσίας], and that the perishable goods taken from them are not perfect or chief goods.

units.la: 12. Cum deniq; docet nos Deo gratias agere, nō solum cum ea eueniunt nobis, quæ carni grata sunt: sed etiā cum eidem tristia & molesta accidunt. Sed hæc usus docebit.
units.tr: 12. Because, finally, he teaches us to give thanks to God not only when things happen to us that are pleasing to the flesh, but also when things sad and troublesome befall us. But experience will teach these things.

units.la: VERSVS III.
units.tr: VERSVS III.

units.la: Deus à Theman venit, & Sanctus è monte Paran: operiebat cœlos gloria eius, & laude illius plena erat terra.
units.tr: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran: his glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.

units.la: Minorem demonstrationis supra traditæ probat argumento àstupendis Dei operibus,in gratiâ populi Ifraëlitici præstitis, cum peruaftam illâ eremum, quæ Ægyptum inter terramq; Canaan media interiacet,is transiret. Meminit eiusdem peregrinationis & Moses, Deut.1.vers.31. Et ut in ipso deferto,ubi uidisti quòd pot tauit te Iehouah Deus tuus,quemadmodum portare solet homo filium suum, & hoc per totam uiam per quam ambulastis, donec ueniretis ad locum istum. 32. Et tamen per hoc non credidistis Iehouæ Deo uestro: 33. Qui præcedebat uos per uiam ad explorandum uobis locum, in quo castra figeretis, per ignem in nocte, ut ostenderet uobis uiam per quam ambularetis, & per nubem in die.
units.tr: He proves the minor premise of the demonstration stated above from the wonderful works of God performed for the Israelite people, when he passed through that vast desert which lies between Egypt and the land of Canaan. Moses also recalls this journey, Deut. 1, verses 31–33: "And in the wilderness, where you saw how the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all along the way that you walked until you came to this place. Yet for all this you did not believe the LORD your God, who went before you on the way to search out a place for you to pitch your camp, by fire in the night to show you the way you should walk, and by cloud in the day."

units.la: Pharan mons Sinai contiguus hoc loco designatur, ut ex Deut.33.2.liquet: Iehouah in Sinai venit, & ortus est è Seir eis:illuxit è monte Pharan,& venit cum decem millibus sanctitatis: à dextera illius erat Lex ignis.
units.tr: Paran, a mountain adjoining Sinai, is meant in this place, as is clear from Deut. 33:2: "The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir to them; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of holiness: at his right hand was a fiery law."

units.la: Theman, Australis, nomen civitatis Idumeæ, à Theman filio Eliphaz. Gen.36. 15. Ierem.49.20.
units.tr: Teman, the south, the name of a city of Edom, from Teman the son of Eliphaz. Gen. 36:15. Jer. 49:20.

units.la: Primum autè Dei opus hoc loco proponiponitur, Νομοθεσία, seu solennis illa legis diuinæ promulgatio & repetitio facta in monte Sina, multis milibus hominum audientibus & spectantibus. Exod. 19. & 20.
units.tr: The first work of God set forth in this place is the Nomothesia [νομοθεσία], that is, the solemn promulgation and repetition of the divine law made on Mount Sinai, with many thousands of men hearing and watching. Exod. 19 and 20.

units.la: Sic autem ratiocinatur: Quis homo intelligens dubitet, eum populum, Dei opus, & quidem κατ' ἐξοχὴν uocare, cui ne deesset ueri cultus Dei & officiorum certissima regula, Legem suam Dominus Deus publice & ingentibus cum miraculis & prodigijs dignatus est promulgare & inculcare?
units.tr: Now he reasons thus: what intelligent person could doubt that the people to whom the Lord God deigned to publish and impress his law, with great miracles and wonders, so that the true worship of God and the most certain rule of duties should not be lacking, should be called his work, and indeed preeminently [κατ' ἐξοχήν]?

units.la: Atqui in gratia populi Israelitici istud præstitit Iehouah.
units.tr: But the Lord did this for the Israelite people.

units.la: Quare certum est, hunc populum recte dici Opus Dei.
units.tr: Therefore it is certain that this people is rightly called the work of God.

units.la: Quæ tibi in hoc argumento obseruanda uidentur?
units.tr: What seems to you to be observed in this argument?

units.la: Circumstantiæ promulgatæ Legis in monte Sina, de quibus ordine & breuiter hæc annotare libet.
units.tr: The circumstances of the law's promulgation on Mount Sinai, which I am pleased to note briefly and in order.

units.la: 1. Νομοθέτης fuit Iehouah, qui hoc loco uocatur Elohah & Sanctus. Tribuitur autem ei, qui σοφωδῶς ubique est, aduentus κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν: eo quòd in illa Legis promulgatione præsentiam suā illustribus testimonijs fecit, testatam.
units.tr: 1. The lawgiver was the LORD, who is here called Elohah and the Holy One. But his coming is ascribed to him, who is wisely [σοφωδῶς] everywhere, after the manner of men [κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν], because in that promulgation of the law he attested his presence by clear signs.

units.la: 2. Forma externa promulgationis Le-gis. Quod fulgura crebra & ingens ignis conspiceretur, ac exaudirentur tonitrua, & fumaret mons Sinai, Cœli gloria eius operti, & laude eius terra repleta dicitur.
units.tr: 2. The outward form of the promulgation of the law: it is said that frequent flashes of lightning were seen, and a great fire, and that thunders were heard, and Mount Sinai smoked; the heavens were covered with his glory, and the earth was filled with his praise.

units.la: 3. Finis istius tempestatis fuit, ut Legis-lator suis cultoribus reuerendum se esse demonstraret. Etsi enim paterni amoris argumentum erat, filijs praescribere regulam internarum & externarum actionum: tamen & auctoritatem suo numini sacro-sanctam esse voluit.
units.tr: 3. The purpose of that storm was that the lawgiver should show his worshippers that he was to be revered. For although it was a sign of fatherly love to prescribe to his sons a rule for inward and outward actions, he also wished his authority to be held as sacrosanct as his divine majesty.

units.la: 4. Locus, de quo in Exodo & alibi agitur.
units.tr: 4. The place, which is treated in Exodus and elsewhere.

units.la: De usu versiculi istius hoc tantum breuiter monebo, Ut olim veros Israelitas, gratis mentibus, cum caetera Dei beneficia, tum inprimis Legis promulgationem & repetitionem, veterisque Testamenti sanctionem, repetiuisse: & Deo, tantorum beneficiorum auctori, gratias egisse uidemus: ita nostrum esse, nunquam non Deo gratias agere, quod e tristi seruitute & tenebris regni Antichristiani liberatos, luce doctrinae Euangelicae illustrauit: quod in nobis quoq; fidei lucem accendit & fouet: quod alienos esse voluit ab omni ψευδοδιδασκαλίας[?], & à fermeto impurorum & commentitiorum dogmatum.
units.tr: On the use of this verse I will say only this briefly. As of old we see true Israelites, with grateful minds, repeating their thanks to God, the author of such great benefits, for the other blessings of God and especially for the promulgation and repetition of the law and the sanction of the Old Testament; so it is our duty never to cease giving thanks to God, who has freed us from the sad slavery and darkness of the Antichristian kingdom and illuminated us with the light of evangelical doctrine; who kindles and fosters in us the light of faith; and who has willed us to be free from every false teaching [ψευδοδιδασκαλίας] and from the leaven of impure and fabricated dogmas.

units.la: Orandus quinetiam nobis est Domi-nus, ut, quod pro infinita sua bonitate,& constantissima sua erga nos beneuolen-tia, hauddubie facturus est, feruet intec[?] nos semen sanctum, protegat & regat Ecclesias nostras, detq; ut ad ipsius gloriam donum ipsius eximium ἀπαξιωνυχείαν[?] possimus.
units.tr: We must also pray to the Lord that, as he surely will do in his infinite goodness and his most constant benevolence toward us, he keep the holy seed alive within us, protect and govern our churches, and grant that we may, to his glory, make proper use of his outstanding gift [ἀπαξιωνυχείαν].

units.la: Oremus etiā Deum, ut Ecclesias, quæ nunc miserandum in modum ματαιολογίας[?] ambitiosorum ἀλλοτριοεπισκοπῶν[?] turbatæ sunt, clementer respiciat: & eis synceri-tatis in doctrina fidei, spei & caritatis donum largiatur, ut sint nobiscum unum in Christo Iesu, qui est Deus benedictus in secula. Amen.
units.tr: Let us also pray God to look mercifully upon the churches, which are now lamentably disturbed by the empty talk [ματαιολογίας] of ambitious men who meddle in other people's affairs [ἀλλοτριοεπισκοπῶν]; and let him grant them the gift of sincerity in the doctrine of faith, hope and love, so that they may be one with us in Christ Jesus, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

units.la: VERSVS IIII.
units.tr: VERSVS IIII.

units.la: Splendor ipsius erat ut lux ipsa: cornua (id est, radij) quoq; è manu eius (erant) ei, & ibi erat absconsio roboris eius.
units.tr: His brightness was as the light itself: and horns (that is, rays) were to him from his hand, and there was the hiding of his strength.

units.la: Sententia est, Deus omnipotentiam suam testatam fecit ἐν τῇ νομοθεσίᾳ, cùm aliis multis modis, tum uerò præcipuè luce clarissima, & eius micantibus radijs: secundum illa verba Moses: Et fuit die tertia, cum factum esset mane, facta sunt tonitrua, & fulgura, & nubes densissima super montem, & clangor buccinae intè-tisimus: expauitq; universus populus, qui erat in castris. Et eduxit Mose popu-lum in occursum Dei è castris: qui stete-runt in inferiore parte montis. Mons autem Sinai fumabat totus, eo quòd defcé-diffet super eum Iehouah in igne: afcen-debatq; fumus eius sicut fumus fornacis, & commotus est universus mons vehementer. Erat praeterea clangor buccinae procedes, & invalescebat valde: Mo-se loquebatur, & Deus ei respondebat in voce. Exod.19.16.17.18, &c.
units.tr: The sense is that God made his omnipotence known in the giving of the law [ἐν τῇ νομοθεσίᾳ], in many ways but chiefly by the clearest light and its gleaming rays, according to Moses' words: "And it came to pass on the third day, when it was morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; and all the people that was in the camp trembled. And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet with God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount. And Mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly. And when the voice of the trumpet sounded long, and waxed louder and louder, Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice." Exod. 19:16–18, etc.

units.la: Quàm fuerit autem grauis populo Israelitico tum sonus ille terribilis, tum lucis fulgor, testatur Moses capite sequenti, versu 18. Omnis autem populus videbant tonitrua & lampades, & clangorem buccinae, & motem fumantem: vidit-in-quam populus, & commoti sunt, steterunt-que procul. 19. Atque dixerunt Mosi: Loquere tu nobiscum, & obsequemur: & ne loquatur nobiscum Deus, ne mo-riamur.
units.tr: How heavy that terrible sound and the brightness of the light were for the Israelite people, Moses bears witness in the following chapter, verse 18: "And all the people saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking: and when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off. And they said unto Moses, Speak thou with us, and we will hear: but let not God speak with us, lest we die."

units.la: Ac nihil aliud sibi vult hæc historia, q; nobis esse intolerabilem legis concione, nisi Christus interveniens, ei nostro nomine satisfaciat, & Euangelij concione de ἐπιεικείᾳ[?] & misericordia Dei Patris nos exhilaret & reficiat in illis terroribus.
units.tr: Indeed this history means nothing else to us than that the preaching of the law is intolerable unless Christ intervenes and satisfies it on our behalf, and unless the preaching of the gospel, of the gentleness [ἐπιεικείᾳ] and mercy of God the Father, cheers and restores us amid those terrors.

units.la: VERSVS V.
units.tr: Verse 5

units.la: Ad faciem eius (id est, ante eum) ibat pestis: & egrediebatur ultio ad pedes eius.
units.tr: Before him (that is, in front of him) went the pestilence, and the plague went forth at his feet.

units.la: Hoc secundum Dei magnificum factu erat, quòd in gratiam populi sui Cananæas Gentes immissa pestilentia extirpauit, ut earum reliquiæ vindice gladio, tanto minore cum negocio deleri, & Israelitæ in earum prouincias, tanquā novi coloni introduci possent. Sic autem argumentatur Propheta:
units.tr: This was another of God's wonderful works: by a pestilence sent among them he destroyed the Canaanite nations for the sake of his people, so that the survivors could be put to the sword with much less trouble, and the Israelites could be brought into their provinces as new settlers. The prophet argues as follows:

units.la: Recte dicitur Dei opus illa gens, cuius gratia aliæ & quidem olim floretisimæ gentes peste divinitus immissa consumtæ sunt, ut illi cederent.
units.tr: Rightly is that work called God's, the nation for whose sake other nations, indeed once very flourishing nations, were consumed by a pestilence sent from God, so that they would give way to it.

units.la: Sed ut terræ Canaan possessio Israelitis obtingeret, peste consumti sunt Cananæi. Hanc Minorem Asaph Propheta pulcerrima imagine adhibita illustrauit, Psal. 80.8. Vitem ex Ægypto transtulisti, expulisti gentes, & plantasti eam, &c.
units.tr: But in order that the land of Canaan might fall to the Israelites, the Canaanites were consumed by pestilence. The prophet Asaph illustrates this minor point with a most beautiful image, Psalm 80.8: "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt; thou hast cast out the nations and planted it," etc.

units.la: Hoc loco obseruentur externæ pestis caussæ.
units.tr: Here the external causes of the pestilence are to be noted.

units.la: 1. Si αὐτὸμ λύεσον spectes, occurrit Deus, qui cum ei uisum est, numerat homines ad gladium, Isa.65.12. liberat suos à peste noxia, sicut cadentibus ad eorum latera multis millibus, ad ipsos tamen non appropinquet: Psal.91.v.3 & 7. Idem, quos vult, peste immissa e medio tollit.
units.tr: 1. If you look at the deliverance (αὐτὸμ λύεσον), God meets us, who, when it pleases him, numbers men for the sword (Isa. 65.12); he delivers his own from the destructive pestilence, so that while many thousands fall at their side, it does not come near them (Ps. 91.3, 7).
