The same God removes from the midst whom he wills by sending a plague.

units.la: 2. Si finem consideres, ultio occurret, tanquā ultimus finis: at si illam qua Cananæi consumti sunt pestilentiam respiciamus, proximus finis erat, ut provincias quas incoluerant, Israelitæ, noui coloni, inhabitarent, prioribus illis possessoribus, ubi iniquitatum suarum mensuram compleuissent, è medio sublatis.
units.tr: 2. If you consider the end, vengeance presents itself as the final end. But if we look at the pestilence by which the Canaanites were destroyed, its nearer end was that the Israelites, as new settlers, should inhabit the provinces they had dwelt in, after those earlier possessors had been taken away from the midst once they had filled up the measure of their iniquities.

units.la: VERSVS VI.
units.tr: Verse 6

units.la: Stetit, & mensus est terram: aspexit, & trepidare fecit gentes, & diruti sunt montes perpetuitatis (id est, antiquissimi) depresserunt se colles seculi (id est, uetustissimi) itinera seculi (id est, seculis tantum superioribus nota) illius. Pulcerrima est ἀδόπολια[?], qua Deum stantem, & ueluti decempeda terram Cananaan secundum numerum tribuum Israelis in certas prouincias dimetientem & diuidentem: ac solo aspectu, Gentes perterrefacientem: & tam mœtanam & colliculosam, quàm campestrem regionem, sibi suisque subijcientem: loca denique multis seculis, ut uidebantur, inaccessa, patefacientem, Propheta introducit.
units.tr: He stood and measured the earth; he looked and made the nations tremble; and the everlasting mountains were broken, the perpetual hills bowed down (that is, the most ancient); the ways of the world (that is, known only to earlier ages) are his. The prophet introduces God standing, and as it were measuring the land of Canaan with a measuring rod, dividing it according to the number of the tribes of Israel into fixed provinces; by his mere look he terrifies the nations, and he brings under himself and his own people regions both mountainous and level alike; finally he opens up places that for many ages seemed inaccessible. It is a most beautiful description (ἀδόπολια).

units.la: Sit hoc tertium Dei μεγαλεῖον & κατροφωμα[?], quod sanè multis in locis ueteris Testamenti ualde celebratur.
units.tr: This may be called God's third great wonder (μεγαλεῖον) and κατορθωμα, which is indeed much celebrated in many places of the Old Testament.

units.la: Deus, qui transfert & stabilit reges, Dan.2.21. & qui condidit ex uno sanguine omne genus hominum, ut habitarent per uniuersam superficiem terrae, definitis tempestiuitatibus quas praestituit, & positis terminis habitationis eorum, ut quaererent Deum,&c.Act.17.26. extirpatis & deletis Cananaeis, distribuit illorū prouincias populo Israel secundum tribus XII.[?]usus ad eam rem administro Iofua & alijs praestantibus uiris.
units.tr: God, who transfers and establishes kings (Dan. 2.21), and who made of one blood every nation of men to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, appointing their seasons and the bounds of their habitation, that they should seek God (Acts 17.26), having driven out and destroyed the Canaanites, distributed their provinces to the people of Israel according to the twelve tribes, using Joshua and other eminent men as his agents in this matter.

units.la: Quare fatendum est, hunc populum, velut eximium Dei opus, peculiariter ei curae esse.
units.tr: Wherefore we must acknowledge that this people, as a singular work of God, is under his special care.

units.la: Hoc loco observabimus ista capita:
units.tr: Here we shall observe the following heads:

units.la: 1. Τὰς τῆς κατοικίας ὁροθεσίας [?], id est, terminos habitationis, divinitus praestitui & Gentibus & privatis hominibus: Hab.3. 6. Psal.107.7. Et deduxit eos in viam rectam, ut venirent in urbem habitatam. Actor.17.
units.tr: 1. The boundaries of habitation (τὰς τῆς κατοικίας ὁροθεσίας), that is, the limits of dwelling, are divinely fixed both for nations and for private persons (Hab. 3.6; Ps. 107.7: "And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation"; Acts 17).

units.la: Qui nunc propter φιλαληθείαν [?] stipendijs recens privati sunt Theologiæ studiosi, apud nos exulat, aut pauperta tis incommodis laborant, ne nimium perturbentur: sed meminerint sibi panem quotidianum non defuturum, ac sibi quoq; ὁρο-θεσίας [?] τῆς κατοικίας diuinitus praestitutam. Sint pij & φιλοπαθεῖς [?], nec dubitent Deo sese curæ esse.
units.tr: Those students of theology who have lately been deprived of their stipends for the sake of the love of truth, and who live in exile among us or suffer the hardships of poverty, should not be too greatly troubled; let them remember that their daily bread will not fail them, and that the boundaries of their habitation too have been divinely fixed. Let them be godly and compassionate, and let them not doubt that God cares for them.

units.la: 2. Etiam Gentes, nedum privatos homines, loco & dignitate moueri à Domino propter scelera. Exemplum de Sobna (ut iam de gentibus nihil dicamus) exstat Iesa.22.15.16.
units.tr: 2. Not only private persons but even nations are moved from their place and dignity by the Lord on account of their crimes, to say nothing yet of the nations. An example of Shebna is found in Isaiah 22.15-16.

units.la: 3. Nihil interesse ad amoliendam vim divinam, cui nulla potentia humana resistere poterit, sive qui montanas, sive campestres regiones obtineant.
units.tr: 3. It makes no difference, for overcoming the divine power, against which no human strength will be able to resist, whether men hold mountainous or level regions.

units.la: 4. Etiā inaccessas regiones aperire Deū hostibus, cum illarum incolas pœnis me-ritis ritis afficere decreuit. Seculis aliquot no cofpectus fuit hostilis exercitus in Laconica: sed tandem Epaminondas, post uiftoriam Leuctricam, Spartam obsedit.
units.tr: 4. God can also open to enemies regions that were inaccessible, when he has decided to punish the inhabitants of those regions as they deserve. For some centuries no hostile army had been seen in Laconia; but at last Epaminondas, after his victory at Leuctra, besieged Sparta.

units.la: Hæc omnia pertinet ad regulam: παρ-άγει τὸ σχῆμα τῆς κόσμου τούτου[?]. 1.Cor.7.13.
units.tr: All these things pertain to the rule: the form of this world passes away (παράγει τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ κόσμου τούτου; 1 Cor. 7.13).

units.la: 5. Cuiq; ea quæ diuinitus obtigerunt, non solum boni esse consulenda, sed etiā ad Dei dantis gloriam magnificienda. Psal.16.5. Iehouah est sors portionis meæ & calicis mei, tu sustentas fortem mea. 6, Funes ceciderunt mihi in locis amoenis: utique hæreditas pulcra est mihi.
units.tr: 5. Whatever has come to each one from God is not only to be taken in good part, but also to be magnified to the glory of the God who gives it: "Jehovah is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; thou maintainest my lot" (Ps. 16.5). "The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places; surely I have a goodly heritage" (Ps. 16.6).

units.la: 6. Neminem debere πλεονεκτεῖν[?]. Iuxta præceptum: Non furtum facies.
units.tr: 6. No one ought to covet or defraud (πλεονεκτεῖν), according to the precept: "Thou shalt not steal."

units.la: 7. Distinguenda esse bona spiritualia & corporalia. Illa enim sunt communia omnibus pijs: hæc autem possessione distinguuntur.
units.tr: 7. Spiritual and bodily goods are to be distinguished. For the former are common to all the godly, whereas the latter are distinguished by possession.

units.la: VERSVS VII.
units.tr: Verse 7.

units.la: Sub anxietate uidi tentoria Chusan: trepidauerunt cortinæ Midian.
units.tr: Under affliction I saw the tents of Cushan; the curtains of the land of Midian trembled.

units.la: Per προσωποποιΐαν[?], rebus inanimatis, tentorijs uidelicet & cortinis, tribuuntur affectus, anxietas & trepidatio, qui non nisi animatis conueniunt. Per Synecdochen autem continens, uidelicet Tabernacula seu Tentoria Nomadum Midianitarum & Æthiopum, pro ipsis Midianitis & Æthiopibus, sumuntur: id quod Iuniores hoc loco obseruare, utile est.
units.tr: By prosopopoeia [προσωποποιΐα], feelings, namely anxiety and trembling, are attributed to inanimate things, the tents and curtains, which belong only to living beings. By synecdoche, the container is taken for the contents: the tents or dwellings of the Midianite and Ethiopian nomads stand for the Midianites and Ethiopians themselves. Younger readers would do well to note this point.

units.la: Quartum μεγαλεῖον[?], seu magnificu Dei opus fuit, Æthiopum (qui hoc loco Chusanitæ dicuntur) & Midianitarum, gentium sanè bellicosarum, nominiq; Israe-litarum infensarum, repressionem uoco, tum coercitionem, ne in palantes & sparsos in eremo Israelitas, pro sua libidine, impetum facerent: tum clades, quibus diuersis temporibus affecti sunt, ducibus Pinehas & Gedeone. Numeri 31. & Iudic. 7. & 8.
units.tr: The fourth magnificent work [μεγαλεῖον] of God was the checking and restraint of the Ethiopians (here called Cushites) and the Midianites, warlike peoples hostile to the name of Israel. God held them back so that they could not, at their own pleasure, attack the Israelites who were scattered and wandering in the wilderness. He also inflicted the defeats they suffered at different times, under the leaders Phinehas and Gideon. Numbers 31; Judges 7 and 8.

units.la: Posteriores autem uictorias de Midia-nitis partas celebrat Asaphus Propheta, Psalm.83.9 Fac illis sicut Midianitis, sicut Sisaræ, sicut Iabin apud torrentem Kison. Extirpati sunt in Endor: facti sunt stercus terræ. 11. Pone eos, principes eorum, sicut Oreb, & sicut Zeeb: sicut Seba & sicut Salmuna, omnes principes eorum.
units.tr: The later victories won over the Midianites are celebrated by the prophet Asaph, Psalm 83:9: "Do to them as to the Midianites, as to Sisera, as to Jabin at the brook Kishon. They were destroyed at Endor; they became dung for the earth. 11. Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb; like Zebah and Zalmunna, all their princes."

units.la: Sic autem ratiocinatur Habacucus: Si in gratiam Israelitarum Deus potentissi-mos Reges & bellicosissimas gentes coercuit & repulit, exercitus eorum dele-uit, uit, & omnes eorum conatus infregit & elisit, tum nihil dubium est, Israelitas recte dici Opus & peculium Dei singulare. Atqui prius est: ut Æthiopes & Midianitæ tragicis suis exemplis testantur. Verum igitur est & consequens.
units.tr: Habakkuk reasons in this way: if God, for the sake of the Israelites, restrained and drove back the most powerful kings and the most warlike nations, destroyed their armies, and broke and crushed all their attempts, then there is no doubt that the Israelites are rightly called God's special work and peculiar possession. But the first premise is true, as the Ethiopians and Midianites attest by their tragic examples. Therefore the conclusion is true also.

units.la: USUS.
units.tr: Use.

units.la: Quemadmodū verò Deus totam gentem Israeliticam adversus hostes protexisse dicitur: ita quoq; & pias familias, & singulos etiam fideles mirabiliter protegit & gubernat: idquod consolationi nostrae plurimum servit. Juxta hæc dicta:
units.tr: Just as God is said to have protected the whole Israelite nation against its enemies, so he also wonderfully protects and governs pious households and even individual believers, and this greatly serves our comfort, according to these words:

units.la: Et pertransierunt (scilicet Patriarchæ Abraham, Isaac & Jacob) de gente in gentem, & de regno ad populum alium. Nec permisit quenquam nocere ipsis: & corripuit propter eos Reges, dicens: Nolite tangere unctos meos, & prophetis meis nolite malefacere. Psal. 105.13.14.15.
units.tr: "And they passed (namely the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob) from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people. He allowed no one to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake, saying: Touch not my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." Psalm 105:13-15.

units.la: Item: Multa sunt adversa iustis, sed ex ijs omnibus liberat unumquenq; eorum Iehouah. Tuetur omnia ossa eius: unum ex ipsis non frangitur. Occidet impium malicia: & odio habentes iustos perden-tur. Psal.34.19.20.21. &c.
units.tr: Likewise: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers each one of them from all of them. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken. Evil shall slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous shall be condemned." Psalm 34:19-21, etc.

units.la: Celebre dictum est: Late patent præ-mia mia & pœnæ. Id uerũ esse,uel ex ijs quæ ὡς ἐν τύπῳ subijciam,manifestum fit.
units.tr: There is a well-known saying: "The rewards and punishments extend widely." That this is true will be clear from the examples I shall set out below.

units.la: 1. Sæpe bonorum caussa, etiam improbis bene est. ut Soaritis pepercit Deus, Lothi hospitis caussa: Gen.19.v.20.21. Ac nihil dubium est,piorum caussa uel miti-gare Deũ,uel auferre ingentia mala: interdum & pœnas publicas differre. Ita Deus dicitur benefecisse Potipharo Ægy ptio propter Iosephum seruum eius: & pœnas publicas distulisse donec uixit pi-us Rex Iosias.
units.tr: 1. Often, for the sake of the good, even the wicked fare well. Thus God spared Zoar for the sake of Lot, his guest: Genesis 19:20-21. There is no doubt that for the sake of the pious God either softens or removes great evils, and sometimes even postpones public punishments. So God is said to have done good to Potiphar the Egyptian on account of Joseph his servant, and to have deferred public punishments as long as the godly King Josiah lived.

units.la: 2 Interdum improbis male est propter pios. Vt cum illi inuidia & odio marce-scũt,& seipsos excruciant. Iuxta dictum: Ecce iste concepit iniquitatem,prægnans est dolore,& pariet rem inanem. Puteũ fodit,& effodit eum,& cecidit in foueam quam fecit. Reuertetur molestia eius in caput eius: &supra uerticem eius iniu-ria eius descendet: Psal.7.14.15.16.
units.tr: 2. Sometimes it goes badly for the wicked because of the pious, when they wither away with envy and hatred and torment themselves. According to the saying: "Behold, he conceives iniquity, he is pregnant with mischief and brings forth falsehood. He digs a pit and hollows it out, and falls into the hole he has made. His trouble shall return upon his own head, and his violence shall come down upon his own crown." Psalm 7:14-16.

units.la: Aut cũ in operibus manuum suarũ il-laqueati, iusto Dei iudicio, tragicas sce-lerum & machinationum suarum pœnas dant. Vt Danielis accusatores, tandem, mandatu Darij Regis, præcipitati in la-cum leonum,unà cum uxoribus & libe-ris ris miserè perierunt:Dan.6.v.24. Neq;ue rò raró fit, ut homines versatiles & in religione vertumni, abusi credulitate Monarcharum & Dynastarū, præstantes virtute, sapientia meritisq; viros, qui illorū luminibus officiunt, loco moveant, pyraustæ autem gaudio exultent, cum fraude illorum cognita, bonorum virtutes & merita inclarescant, & Protei illi ad pœnas abripiantur.
units.tr: Or when, caught in the works of their own hands, they pay, by the just judgment of God, the tragic penalties of their crimes and schemes. Thus Daniel's accusers, at last, by the command of King Darius, were thrown into the lions' den together with their wives and children, and perished miserably (Daniel 6:24). Nor is it rare that fickle men, turncoats in religion, who abuse the credulity of monarchs and rulers and who excel in virtue, wisdom and merit, and who stand in the way of those men's influence, are driven from their posts. Meanwhile the moths rejoice, when the deceit is exposed, the virtues and merits of the good shine forth, and those Proteus-like men are dragged off to punishment.

units.la: 3. Sæpius autem fit, ut hominum impiorum causa, etiā pii & innocentes incidant in magnas miserias, velut communes quosdam labyrinthos. Ut Lothus una cum impiis Sodomitis captus fuit ab hostibus, & abductus: Gen.14.
units.tr: 3. More often it happens that the pious and innocent, for the sake of impious men, fall into great miseries, like common labyrinths. Thus Lot, together with the impious Sodomites, was captured by enemies and led away (Genesis 14).

units.la: 4. Interdum fit, ut pii piorum amicorum causa in discrimen veniant, nulla horum culpa, sed improborum, tyrannidem exercentiū, scelere. Ut propter Davidem innoxium, cui Rex Saul infensus erat, Sacerdotes 85, præter omne eorum malum meritum, occisi sunt. 1.Sam.22.
units.tr: 4. Sometimes it happens that the pious are put in peril for the sake of their pious friends, through no fault of their own but through the crime of wicked men who exercise tyranny. Thus, on account of the innocent David, against whom King Saul was hostile, eighty-five priests were killed, though they had done nothing to deserve it (1 Samuel 22).

units.la: 5. Non autem debet filiis Dei, in huius vitæ militia versantibus, insolens & acerbum videri, si eius gratia brevi tempore, & quidem magno suo bono, in luctu & dolore aliquo uersari eos oporteat, cuius dono æterna uita & læticia potientur, una cum omnibus beatis angelis & electis hominibus. Atqui Christi Iesu dono meritoq; uitam & læticiam ꝑternam consequentur. Itaque parati sint eius caussa dura omnia pati, cum certissima sit uictoriæ & æternæ salutis gloriæq; spes.
units.tr: 5. Nor should it seem strange or harsh to the sons of God, who are engaged in the warfare of this life, if they must for his sake endure some grief and pain for a short time, and indeed to their great good, when the eternal life and joy which they will possess by his gift, together with all the blessed angels and chosen men, are his gift. Yet they will obtain eternal life and joy through the gift and merit of Jesus Christ. Therefore let them be ready to suffer all hard things for his sake, since the hope of victory, eternal salvation and glory is most certain.

units.la: VERSVS VIII.
units.tr: VERSE 8

units.la: Num contra flumina iratus est Iehovah? num contra ipsa flumina bilis tua? num contra mare ipsum excandescentia tua, quod equitasti super equos tuos, & quadrigas tuas ad salutem?
units.tr: Was the LORD angry with the rivers? Was your wrath against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, that you rode upon your horses and your chariots of salvation?

units.la: De traductione Israelitarum per mare rubrum, & per Iordanem fluuium, loquitur Propheta. Sit hoc quintum Dei μεγαλεῖον, bis editum, & sæpe in Scripturis sanctis decantatum. Historiæ extant, Exodi 14. Iosuæ 3 & 4 cap. In Psalmo 114. 5. Quid tibi mare, quod fugisti? Iordanis, quod conuersus es retrorsum?
units.tr: The prophet speaks of the passage of the Israelites through the Red Sea and through the river Jordan. This is the fifth magnificent work of God, already related twice and often celebrated in Holy Scripture. The accounts are found in Exodus 14 and Joshua 3 and 4. In Psalm 114.5: "What ailed you, O sea, that you fled? Jordan, that you turned back?"

units.la: Iram autem, bilem & excandescentiā, metaphoricè per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν Deo tribui, manifestum est.
units.tr: It is plain that anger, wrath and indignation are attributed to God metaphorically, by way of anthropopathy.

units.la: Quòd idem equis & quadrigis uectus dicitur, nihil aliud sibi uult, quàm properasse Dominum ad salutem, id est, ad opem populo suo ferendam. Prouerbialis autem oratio est, similis istis: Ocyor Euro, Remis uelisq;, Nauibus atq; quadrigis, & similibus.
units.tr: That he is said to ride upon horses and chariots means nothing else than that the Lord hastened to salvation, that is, to bring help to his people. The expression is proverbial, like those: "swifter than the east wind," "with oars and sails," "with ships and chariots," and similar ones.

units.la: Diluit autem Propheta Paralogismum παρὰ τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον[?], cum docet, Deū non inanimatis rebus iratum fuisse, nec eorum caussa edidisse ingens hoc miraculum: sed ideo, persequentibus Israelitas Ægyptijs, illos incolumes & saluos per mare rubrum traduētos esse, vt in eodem opere luceret Dei iusticia erga hostes Ecclesiæ, & eiusdem misericordia erga Ecclesiam.
units.tr: The prophet also answers the paralogism the fallacy of taking a non-cause for a cause [παρὰ τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον], when he teaches that God was not angry with inanimate things, nor did he perform this great miracle on their account. Rather, because the Egyptians pursued the Israelites, God led them safe and unharmed through the Red Sea, so that in the same work the justice of God toward the enemies of the Church and his mercy toward the Church might shine forth.

units.la: Si Deus non dedignatus est in gratiam Israelitarum edere præclarum hoc miraculum, vt per medias aquas, tâquam per siccum, eos incolumes traduceret: hostes aut aquis immissis suffocaret: tum uerò, Israelitas Dei eximiū opus esse, quis homo pius & prudens dubitet?
units.tr: If God did not disdain, for the sake of the Israelites, to perform this remarkable miracle, of carrying them safely through the midst of the waters as though over dry land, and of drowning their enemies when the waters were let loose, who, being pious and sensible, could doubt that the Israelites were a singular work of God?

units.la: Prius est. Nam ita Deus per mare ru-brum traduxit Israelitas, vt persecutores Ægyptios suffocaret: ita per Iordanis alueum, mefsis tempore, quo fluuius ille exundare folet, Ifraëlitas duxit, ut in terram promiffam Patribus læti & alacres tranfirent. Ergo & pofterius uerum eft.
units.tr: The first part is true. For God so led the Israelites through the Red Sea that he drowned the Egyptian persecutors; so too he led the Israelites through the channel of the Jordan, at harvest time, when that river is accustomed to overflow, so that they might cross gladly and eagerly into the land promised to the fathers. Therefore the latter part is also true.

units.la: In hoc argumento notabimus [illegible, ~10 letters]?
units.tr: In this argument we shall note [illegible]?

units.la: 1. Beatam effe Dei Ecclefiam, etfi a tergo & a fronte hoftes eiimmineant. Vt enim ultricibus aquis fubmerfi funt Ægyptij perfecutores Ifraëlitarum: ita uindice gladio occifi funt Cananæi eorudem aduerfarij.
units.tr: 1. That the Church of God is blessed, even though enemies threaten from behind and from in front. For just as the Egyptian persecutors of the Israelites were overwhelmed by avenging waters, so their adversaries, the Canaanites, were slain by the avenging sword.

units.la: 2. Maledicos & infelices effe hoftes Ecclefiæ, fiue per infidias & cuniculos, fiue aperto Marte oppugnent Ecclefiam, & fingulos fideles.
units.tr: 2. That the enemies of the Church are accursed and unhappy, whether they attack the Church and its individual faithful by plots and mines or by open war.

units.la: 3. Sub umbra Dei tutos effe fanctos, etiamfi multi hoftes eis imminere & ueftigia eorum premere uideantur. Pfal.3.6. Non timebo a multis myriadibus populi, qui undique fefe opponunt mihi.
units.tr: 3. That the saints are safe under the shadow of God, even when many enemies seem to hang over them and to tread on their footsteps. Psalm 3.6: "I will not fear the many thousands of the people who set themselves against me on every side."

units.la: 4. In acie nouaculæ, quod dici folet, conftitutos effe θεομάχους[?], cum fibi uidentur iamiam ftringere enfes in ceruices feruorum Dei. Deus det, ut ista adusum noftrū transferre possimus: Amen. Deftituor ocio: itaq; manum de tabula.
units.tr: 4. That those who think they are about to strike the necks of the servants of God with their swords stand, as the saying goes, on the edge of a razor, and are fighters against God [θεομάχους]. May God grant that we can turn these things to our own use: Amen. I am lacking leisure, and so I lay down my pen.

units.la: VERSVS IX.
units.tr: VERSE 9

units.la: Denudatione fuit excitatus arcus tuus (secundum) iuramenta tribuum (id est, quae fecisti tribubus) & sermonem tuum: fluuijs scidisti terram.
units.tr: Your bow was made quite bare, according to the oaths of the tribes (that is, the things you have done for the tribes) and your word. You split the earth with rivers.

units.la: Sextum Dei μεγαλείον[?], è quo colligit Is-raelem eximium Dei opus esse, fuit eius introductio in terram Canaan, & foecunditas diuinitus eidem terrae concessa.
units.tr: The sixth magnificent work of God, from which he gathers that Israel is a singular work of God, was his bringing them into the land of Canaan and the fruitfulness divinely granted to that land.

units.la: Denudatio excitati arcus Iehouae, nihil aliud hoc loco significat, q[?] potentiae Dei armipotentis declarationem, erga Cananæos, quos deleuit & è suis sedibus submouit, & erga Israelitas, quos in illorum regiones eodem praepotete suo bra-chio introduxit.
units.tr: The bareness of the bow of the Lord, drawn out, here signifies nothing else than a display of the power of the Almighty God, against the Canaanites, whom he destroyed and removed from their dwellings, and toward the Israelites, whom he led into those regions by the same all-powerful arm.

units.la: Iuramenta tribuum & sermonem Dei, accipio de promisione diuina, iureiurando contestata, qua Patribus Deus fidem fecit, quòd eorum semini traditurus ef-set terram illam inhabitandam: ut est vi-dere Gen.12.7. & 13. v.14.15.
units.tr: I take the oaths of the tribes and the word of God to refer to the divine promise, confirmed by an oath, by which God gave assurance to the fathers that he would hand that land over to their seed to inhabit, as may be seen in Genesis 12.7 and 13.14-15.

units.la: Argumentum sextum.
units.tr: Sixth argument.

units.la: Si Deus in gratiam populi sui submouit è suis sedibus Cananæos, quos hic alioquin neutiquam debellare potuisset: ac terrae benedixit, sic ut fluviis scinderet terram, id est, multis locis irriguam redderet: tum vero certum est, populum il-lum recte dici eximium Dei opus, cuius videlicet formandi ornandiq; gratia, tan-ta μεγαλεία[?] praestare Dominus Deus para-tus fuit.
units.tr: If God, for the sake of his people, removed the Canaanites from their dwellings, whom otherwise he could by no means have subdued here, and blessed the land so that he split the earth with rivers, that is, made it well watered in many places, then it is certain that that people is rightly called a singular work of God, for whose forming and adorning the Lord God was prepared to show such great magnificence.

units.la: Atqui in gratiam Israelitarum utrumq; praestitit Deus. Ac si prius spectes, fatentur Coritę[?] Psal.44.2.3. idem, quod hoc loco noster Propheta. Tu, aiunt, manu tua expulisti gentes, & plantasti eas: contri-visti populos, & propagasti eos. Neq; e-nim gladio suo adepti sunt terram, neq; brachium ipsorum eos seruavit: sed dextera tua, & brachium tuum, & lumen vultus tui: quia benevolus fuisti erga nos.
units.tr: But God has done both for the sake of the Israelites. If you look first at the former, the sons of Korah confess the same thing that our prophet says here (Psalm 44.2-3): "You with your hand drove out the nations and planted them; you crushed the peoples and spread them abroad. For they did not get the land by their own sword, nor did their arm save them; but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, because you favoured us."

units.la: In eodem autem virtutis divinae opere, declarata fuit Dei iustitia & nemesis[?] erga gentes idololatricas, pollutas omni genere scelerum & turpitudinis: & eius-dem amor erga Israelitas, & fides in pa-stis servandis.
units.tr: In the same work of divine power, the justice of God and his retribution against idolatrous nations, polluted with every kind of wickedness and filthiness, were displayed, and likewise his love toward the Israelites and his faithfulness in keeping the promises made to the fathers.

units.la: Quod si alterum Dei beneficium respi-cias, Fluviis scidisse terram dicitur, dando pluvias & tempora frugifera : ponendo desertum in stagnum aquarum, & terram desertam in exitus aquarum : Psalmo 107.35.
units.tr: If you consider the other benefit of God, it is said that he split the earth with rivers, by giving rains and fruitful seasons, by turning the wilderness into a pool of water and the dry land into springs of water (Psalm 107.35).

units.la: Quid hoc loco piæ menti obseruan-dum censes?
units.tr: What do you think a devout mind should observe in this passage?

units.la: 1. Deum alias improbis submotis è medio, substituere pios. Habet enim pietas promissiones etiam huius uitæ. 1.Tim.4.
units.tr: 1. God sometimes removes the wicked from their place and puts the godly in their stead, for godliness has promises even for this life. (1 Tim. 4.8.)

units.la: 8.[?] Vt improbo Sobnæ Eliacim pius succesit.
units.tr: So the godly Eliakim succeeded the wicked Shebna.

units.la: 2. Eundem sæpe submotis pijs è statione locoq;[?], substituere improbos. Olim tempore Achab, partim occisis, partim pulsis ueris Prophetis, Baalitæ successerunt in publico docendi munere.
units.tr: 2. Conversely, God sometimes removes the godly from their office and station and puts the wicked in their place. In the time of Ahab, the true prophets were partly killed and partly driven out, and the Baalites succeeded them in the public office of teaching.

units.la: 3. Interdum fit, ut mercenarij aut hostes fidei regnent, submotis pijs tum doctoribus, tum discipulis. Vt tempore Christi & Apostolorum, ordinarium ministerium sibi sumebant Pontifices, Pharisæi, Saducæi, Scribæ, & alij ἑτεροδιδάσκαλοι : & à docendi munere submouebant Apostolos.
units.tr: 3. Sometimes it happens that hirelings or enemies of the faith rule, while both teachers and disciples who are godly are pushed aside. So in the time of Christ and the apostles, the high priests, Pharisees, Sadducees, scribes, and other [ἑτεροδιδάσκαλοι] (teachers of other doctrine) claimed the ordinary ministry for themselves and shut the apostles out of the office of teaching.

units.la: 4. Quomodocunque autem Deus seu pios, seu impios tractet, nunquam non lucent Dei iusticia & bonitas, piorum feli-citas, & impiorum infelicitas. Etenim, cum malos male tractat Deus, seipsum iustū esse:cum bonos bene tractat, bonum sese esse, ostendit. Rursum, pij etiam sub cruce ingemiscentes, beati sunt: nam ijs qui diligunt Deum, omnia simul conferunt ad bonum: Rom.8.28. Iidem iacturam & direptionem facultatum suarum cum gaudio accipiunt: quia sciunt se habere potiorem substantiam in coelis, & quae permaneat: Hebr.10.34. Econtrà improbi, etiam in medijs successibus, voluptatibus & opibus sunt infortunati. Iacob.5.1.2.3. Agite nunc diuites, flete, ululates super miserijs uestris superuenturis, &c.
units.tr: 4. However God treats the godly or the ungodly, the justice and goodness of God, the happiness of the godly, and the unhappiness of the wicked always shine forth. For when God treats the wicked badly, he shows himself to be just; when he treats the good well, he shows himself to be good. Again, the godly are blessed even when they groan under the cross, for God makes all things work together for good for those who love him (Rom. 8.28). They also accept the loss and plundering of their goods with joy, because they know that they have a better possession in heaven, one that endures (Heb. 10.34). On the other hand, the wicked are unhappy even in the midst of prosperity, pleasures, and riches (James 5.1–3): "Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you," and so on.

units.la: 5. Lucet enim iustum Dei iudicium adversus summorum & aliorum hominum ingratitudinem erga Deum inprimis, & erga praestantissimos ac diu multumque de se bene meritos viros. Vt enim ij, qui non uident, Medicum, qui est [?πολλῶν ἀν-] [?τάξιος ἄλλων], esse honorandum ut insigne Dei donum, tandem in Empiricorum, Agyrtarum, delirarum anicularum manus incidunt: ita, qui doctorum pie docentium & uiuetium fidelem institutionem, qui Praeceptorum orthodoxorum merita fusq; deq; faciunt, iusto Domini iudicio incidunt in [?περιπεφυκότες ἀθεολόγους], à quiquibus contumeliosè tractantur, expilatur, & in opinionum fanaticarū labyrinthos conijciuntur: quemadmodum Corinthios à Pseudapostolis tractatos esse, Paulus Apostolus testatur, 2.[?] Cor.11.20. Toleratis,inquiens,si quis uos in seruitutem adigit, si quis exedit, si quis accipit, si quis attollit sese, si quis uos in faciem caedit. O utinam huius rei nulla exstent in Europaeis quibusdam Ecclesijs exempla.
units.tr: 5. For the just judgment of God shines out against the ingratitude of the great and of other men towards God above all, and towards the most excellent men who have deserved well of them for a long time. Just as those who do not see the value of a physician [πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων] (worth many others), to be honoured as a distinguished gift of God, at last fall into the hands of quacks, charlatans and foolish old women, so those who make light of the merits of faithful teachers who teach piously and live well, and of orthodox ministers, by the just judgment of the Lord fall among [περιπεφυκότες ἀθεολόγους] (atheistic theologians), by whom they are treated with contempt, are plundered, and are cast into the labyrinths of fanatical opinions. Paul the Apostle testifies that the Corinthians were treated in this way by false apostles (2 Cor. 11.20): "You put up with it," he says, "if anyone brings you into bondage, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you in the face." Oh, that there were no examples of this thing in certain churches of Europe!

units.la: VERSVS X.
units.tr: VERSE 10.

units.la: Viderunt te, & doluerunt quasi partus cruciatu montes: inundatio aquarū transfiit, edidit vorago sonitum suum, altitudo manus suas elevauit.
units.tr: They saw you, and the mountains were in pain as in the agony of childbirth; the flood of waters passed over; the deep sent forth its voice, and lifted up its hands on high.

units.la: Etsi elegans sane est allegoria, qua quidam hoc loco tradunt, cum omnium ordinum homines in Cananaea, sub aduersum Israelitarum perturbatos & anxios fuisse, significari dicunt: etenim Montes, summos Reges: loca campestria, vulgus: inundationem aquarū, omnia mala, quae bellum & hostis victor inferre solet: altitudinem manus subleuatem, gestus Principum deuictorum ac supplicum, ευχοἀμῶς[?] alibi denotare, obscurum non est: tamen, cum præstet simplici & natiuæ sententiæ, cū datur, insistere, fateor me malle sequi eorum sententiam, qui huncversum esse iudicat poeticam, postremi lemmatis versus præcedentis, expositionem. Poeticam voco, quia constat ὑποποιΐας[?] ὡς[?] τῇ ὑπαλλαγῇ[?], velut orationis luminib.sple[?]-didisimis. Ethopœia est, quia in descriptione fontium diuersis in locis erumpe-tium, terramq; rigantium, montes partu-rientes, & voraginem maximo cum sonitu aquas ebullientem, introducit. Hypalage aut est, cum rebus inanimatis, montibus, voraginibus & aquis ea tribuit, quæ sunt animatarum quarundam creaturarum propria.
units.tr: Certainly this is an elegant allegory, by which some explain the passage: they say that it signifies the terror and anxiety of all orders of men in Canaan when the Israelites were opposed to them. For they say the mountains are the greatest kings, the plains the common people, the flood of waters all the evils that war and a victorious enemy are wont to bring, and the raising of the hands on high is the gesture of defeated princes and suppliants, which elsewhere [ἀμῶς] (in other ways) denotes. This is not obscure. Nevertheless, since it is better to keep to the plain and natural sense where one is given, I confess that I prefer to follow those who judge this verse to be a poetic explanation of the last phrase of the preceding verse. I call it poetic because it is clearly full of the most splendid ornaments of speech. It is an ethopoeia, because in describing springs breaking out in various places and watering the land, it introduces mountains in labour and an abyss boiling up waters with a great roar. It is a hypallage, because it attributes to inanimate things, mountains, abysses and waters, what belongs to certain living creatures.

units.la: Quid hoc loco observabimus?
units.tr: What shall we observe in this passage?

units.la: Primò id quod docet sensus gramma-ticus, Deū videlicet pro suo arbitrio vel cœlitus pluendo, vel fontes excitando, terram irrigare & fœcundam reddere: aut etiam cohibitis pluvijs, aut exiccatis fontibus, ἀντιθέσει[?] sterilitatem inuehere. Iuxta dicta:
units.tr: First, what the grammatical sense teaches: namely, that God, at his own pleasure, either by sending rain from heaven or by bringing forth springs, waters the land and makes it fruitful; or, conversely, by withholding the rains or drying up the springs, brings sterility, by contrast. Compare the sayings:

units.la: Deut.28.23. Erunt què cœli tui, qui sunt supra caput tuum, ærei: & terra, quæ est subter te, ferrea. 24.Dabit Iehouah pluviam terrae tuae pulverem & cineres, è coelis descendet super te, donec disperdaris.
units.tr: Deut. 28.23: "Your heavens that are above your head shall be brass, and the earth that is under you shall be iron." 24: "The LORD will make the rain of your land powder and dust; from heaven shall it come down upon you until you are destroyed."

units.la: Psalm.107.33. Redigit flumina in desertum, & scaturigines aquarum in sitim.
units.tr: Ps. 107.33: "He turns rivers into a wilderness, and springs of water into a thirsty ground."

units.la: 34.Terram fructiferā in salsuginem: propter maliciam habitantium in ea. 35.Redigit desertum in stagnū aquarum, & terram solitudinis in scaturigines aquarū.
units.tr: 34: "A fruitful land into salt marsh, for the wickedness of those who dwell in it. 35: He turns a wilderness into pools of water, and dry land into springs of water."

units.la: Nota est historia, de coelo per triennīu & sex menses ad preces Eliæ Prophetæ clauso, ne plueret, temporibus Achab Regis Israelis: & de fame, quæ siccitatem & [illegible, ~8 letters] illam est secuta: 1.Regū 17.& 18. Iac.5.17.18.
units.tr: The story is well known of heaven being shut up for three years and six months at the prayer of the prophet Elijah, so that it did not rain, in the time of Ahab, king of Israel, and of the famine that followed that drought [illegible, ~8 letters] (1 Kings 17 and 18; James 5.17, 18).

units.la: Secundò mysterium. alias enim parca manu, alias larga, verbum Dei, ceu pluvia irrigans, & potus recreans animas nostras, nobis coceditur: interdum autem iusto Dei iudicio denegatur ingratis. Iu-xta hæc dicta:
units.tr: Second, the mystery. The word of God, like rain watering and refreshing our souls, is given to us sometimes with a sparing hand and sometimes with a liberal one. But at other times, by the just judgment of God, it is denied to the ungrateful. Compare these sayings:

units.la: Ifaiæ 30.20.Dabit vobis Dominus panem angustum, & aquam oppressionis: sed nō elongabitur ultra doctor tuus, &c.
units.tr: Isa. 30.20: "The Lord will give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction; yet your teacher shall not be removed any more," and so on.

units.la: Isai.55.1. Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas: etiam vos quib.non est argentum, venite, &c.
units.tr: Isa. 55.1: "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come," and so on.

units.la: Ezech.36.25. Spargam supervos aquâ mundam, & mundabimini ab omnibus inquinamentis vestris, &c.
units.tr: Ezek. 36.25: "I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be clean from all your filthiness," and so on.

units.la: Oro Filium Dei, Dominum nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, ut propter gloriam nominis sui, lucem Euangelij sui in no-stris, & alijs ex divini verbi praescripto re formatis Ecclesiis, foveat & conservet: & ut nobis det, non modò ne unquà corruptelis impijs doctrina, quam profitemur, corrumpatur: sed etiam, ut constanter, ardenter, prudenter & elegater eam defendamus adversus hostes, sine iactantia vana, sine conviciorum sordibus. Bona enim causa bene, hoc est, placidè & solidè agenda est.
units.tr: I pray the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, that for the glory of his name he may foster and preserve the light of his gospel in our churches and in others reformed according to the prescription of the divine word; and that he may grant us not only that the doctrine we profess may never be corrupted by impious corruptions, but also that we may defend it constantly, ardently, prudently and elegantly against its enemies, without vain boasting and without the filth of insults. For a good cause must be pursued well, that is, calmly and solidly.

units.la: VERSVS XI.
units.tr: Verse 11

units.la: Sol & Luna steterunt in habitaculo suo: ad lucem sagittarum tuarum ambulaue-runt, ad splendorem fulgoris hasta tua.
units.tr: The sun and the moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, at the shining of thy glittering spear.

units.la: Pulcerrima est ἀνθρωποπάθεια[?], qua Deo, de cœlo pro Israelitis adversus Reges quinque in Gibeon pugnanti, tribuuntur sagittæ lucidæ, & hasta refulgens. Historia exstat Iosuæ 10.capite, in quo versu ii. dicitur: Dum autem fugerent (hostes) i[?] facie Jsraël,& essent in descésu Beth-ho-ron, Jehouah demisit super eos lapides magnos è cœlo,usque ad Azecha,& mortui sunt: plures autem mortui sunt lapi-dibus grandinis,quàm quos interfecerūt filij Jsraël gladio,&c.
units.tr: Very beautiful is the anthropopatheia [ἀνθρωποπάθεια] by which arrows of light and a flashing spear are attributed to God, who from heaven fought for the Israelites against the five kings at Gibeon. The story is in Joshua chapter 10, where verse 11 says: "And as they fled (the enemies) before Israel, and were going down the descent of Beth-horon, the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them, unto Azekah, and they died: there were more who died from the hailstones than those whom the sons of Israel killed with the sword, etc."

units.la: Hoc septimum numero magnificum Dei opus fuit, è quo itidem ut è superio-ribus,Habacucus Propheta colligit, quo apud Deum loco fuerit populus Jsraëliticus.
units.tr: This was the seventh magnificent work of God in number, and from it, as from the preceding ones, the prophet Habakkuk gathers what place the Israelite people held with God.

units.la: Deus olim non dedignatus est,exerci-tum,quem quinque præpotentes Reges duxerat aduersus Jsraëlitas suos, nō tam horum gladijs conficere, quàm horribili grandine & tempestate obruere & conterere : ac ut dies illa ultionis longior es-set,Solem & Lunam sistere.
units.tr: God once deigned not so much to destroy with the swords of these men the army which the five mighty kings had led against his Israelites, as to overwhelm and crush it with terrible hail and storm, and to make the sun and moon stand still so that that day of vengeance might be longer.

units.la: Quis ergo dubitet,hunc populum præ omnibus alijs gentibus Deo curæ esse,& singulare istud ac eximiū eiusdem opus haberi debere?
units.tr: Who then could doubt that this people is cared for by God above all other nations, and that this unique and remarkable work of his ought to be regarded as such?

units.la: Ex hoc argumento colligere licet,tam facile esse Deo omnem uim hostilem repellere ab Ecclesia & singulis fidelibus, cū in discrimine uersantur: quàm illi nō deest benigna erga Ecclesiam, & erga fisingulos, voluntas. Cum Dauide igitur canamus: Nō timebo à multis myriadibus populi, qui undique sese opponunt mihi. Exurge Iehouah, serua me Deus meus: Sanè percute omnes inimicos meos in maxilla, dentes eorum contere. Pfalm. 3. 6, 7.
units.tr: From this argument we may gather that it is as easy for God to drive away every hostile force from the Church and from individual believers when they are in danger, as his kindly will towards the Church and towards each of them is never lacking. Therefore let us sing with David: "I will not fear the tens of thousands of people who set themselves against me on every side. Arise, O LORD; save me, O my God: for thou hast smitten all my enemies on the cheek; thou hast broken the teeth of the ungodly." Ps. 3:6, 7.

units.la: Ne igitur opinemur, tum maximè periclitari Ecclesiam, cum tyranni θυμαχοι[?] omni genere armorum eam oppugnant: ut factum est temporibus Antiochi Epiphanis, Neronis, Diocletiani: & ut hac nostra ætate factu uidimus in uicinis quibusdam regnis. Sed tum demum in periculo esse, & graviter tentari & periclitari statuamus, cum longæ pacis incommoda sentit, & cum ij qui Ecclesiæ primarij Antistites uideri uolunt, prodigiosa dogmata in Ecclesiam inuehunt, dijudicandæ prophetiæ iuris sedentibus in Ecclesia eripiunt, & in conseruos sequiunt anathe-matismis, proscriptionibus, & alijs præ-sidijs deploratæ caussæ. Sedenim uiuit & regnat omnipotens ille & verax Ec-clesiæ suo sanguine redemptæ Defensor CHRISTVS IESVS, qui non nimium indulgebit licentiæ, quam φιλοπρωτευοντις[?] Diotrephes & pseudepiscopi exercent, suosq; seruabit incontaminatos à mundo, & ab omni maloeofdem praestabit indemnes.
units.tr: Let us not therefore suppose that the Church is then most in peril when fighting tyrants [θυμαχοι] assail her with every kind of weapon, as happened in the times of Antiochus Epiphanes, Nero and Diocletian, and as we have seen happen in our own age in certain neighbouring kingdoms. Rather let us judge that she is then truly in danger and gravely tested and imperilled when she feels the troubles of long peace, and when those who wish to be seen as the chief leaders of the Church bring monstrous doctrines into the Church, snatch from those sitting in judgment in the Church the right of testing prophecy, and pursue their fellow servants with anathemas, proscriptions and other defences of a desperate cause. For that almighty and true Defender of the Church, redeemed by his own blood, Christ Jesus, lives and reigns; he will not greatly indulge the licence which Diotrephes, who loves to be first [φιλοπρωτευοντις], and the false bishops exercise, but he will keep his own unpolluted from the world, and will grant them safety from all evil.

units.la: VERSVS XII.
units.tr: Verse 12

units.la: Cum indignatione (incesiisti Iehouah) super terram: in bile triturasti gentes, scilicet Cananaeas, &c.
units.tr: In indignation (thou didst march, O LORD) upon the earth: in anger thou didst thresh the nations, namely the Canaanites, etc.

units.la: Octauum Dei μεγαλεῖον hoc loco occurrit, πανωλεθρία Gentium, de qua & Stephanus protomartyr loquitur, Act. 7. 45.
units.tr: Here occurs the eighth magnificent work [μεγαλεῖον] of God, the total destruction of the Gentiles, of which Stephen the first martyr also speaks, Acts 7:45.

units.la: Non autem indignatione & bile (quae in Deum non cadunt: & non nisi more humano loquendo, de eo dicuntur) sed singulari iustoq; consilio ductus Dominus Deus Israelis, deleuit septem gentes, & in earum sedes & domicilia traduxit Israelitarum colonias, duodenario tribus numero distributas.
units.tr: Yet the Lord God of Israel was not moved by indignation and anger (which do not fall upon God, and are spoken of him only in human fashion), but by a singular and just counsel he destroyed the seven nations and transferred the Israelite colonies into their seats and dwellings, distributed by the number of the twelve tribes.

units.la: Caeterum Dei νέμεσις, imagine a triturantibus ducta, depingere Propheta voluit in hoc argumento:
units.tr: Moreover, the prophet wished in this argument to depict God's vengeance [νέμεσις], drawn from the image of threshers:

units.la: In quorum gratiam Deus florentissimas gentes extirpauit, illi uero Dei opus haberi debent.
units.tr: For the sake of whose favour God uprooted the most flourishing nations, to them the work of God ought indeed to be regarded.

units.la: In Israelitarum gratiam deleuit Deus, parpartim gladio, partim peste, partim ui fa‑ua tempeftatu, Gentes septe. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: For the sake of the Israelites God destroyed the seven nations, partly by the sword, partly by plague, partly by the violence of storms. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Eodem autem facto, ueracem fe esse, fiue comminationes eius, fiue promissio nes fpeftes, Deus testatus est. Minatus fuit poenas Amorrhaeis, ubi mensura fce‑lerum suorum compleuissent: & promi‑ferat patribus, fe eorum posteris traditu‑rum esse terram Canaan inhabitandam. Vtrumque ergo summa fide praestitit.
units.tr: By the same deed, moreover, God showed that he is true, whether in his threats or in his promises. He threatened punishment to the Amorites when they had filled up the measure of their wickedness, and he had promised the fathers that he would give the land of Canaan to their posterity to inhabit. He fulfilled both with the utmost faithfulness.

units.la: Quid pie menti statuendum existimas, cum Deus uidetur non animaduertere in peccantes?
units.tr: What should a godly mind judge when God seems not to notice those who sin?

units.la: Primùm id quod Bernardus super Cá‑tica Serm. 42. prudenter monet: Iram Dei tum potissimùm metuendam esse, cum peccata non punit. Est enim castigatio, paterna Dei ferula, qua nos ad refi‑pifcentiam reuocat. Quos itaq; hac non dignatur, eos ut ἀμεταμελήτως filiorum loco fe non habere, testatur. Hebr. 12. 8.
units.tr: First, what Bernard wisely advises in his sermon 42 on the Song of Songs: the wrath of God is then especially to be feared when he does not punish sins. For chastisement is the fatherly rod of God, by which he calls us back to repentance. Those whom he does not deign to chastise, he testifies that he does not regard as sons, as if they were unrepentant [ἀμεταμελήτως]. Heb. 12:8.

units.la: Secundò, illud quoque Cypriani, qui grauissimè dicit: Ex ira Dei aliquando delicta non intelligimus, ne poenitentia sequatur.
units.tr: Second, that saying of Cyprian, who speaks very weightily: "Sometimes we do not perceive our sins through the anger of God, lest repentance should follow."

units.la: Tertiò, istud Augustini: Deus iratus a‑liquanliquando petentibus concedit petita. Præstat autem, Deum propitium easo-lūm nobis largiri, quæ ipse nobis salutaria esse intelligit, quàm quæ nobis grata & utilia esse putamus.
units.tr: Third, that saying of Augustine: "God in anger sometimes grants to those who ask what they have asked for." It is better, however, that God grant us only those things which he himself knows to be salutary for us, than those which we think pleasing and useful.

units.la: Quartò, ad nostri consolationem Am-brosianum dictum repetamus: Dei indi-gnatio, non ultionis executio, sed absolutionis operatio magis est.
units.tr: Fourth, for our comfort let us repeat the saying of Ambrose: "The indignation of God is not the execution of vengeance but rather the working of absolution."

units.la: Postremò, aliter irasci Deum nobis, quos filiorū loco habere dignatur, quan-do peccato præoccupamur: aliter ijs ira-sci, à quibus alienus est, ne dubitemus.
units.tr: Last, God is angry otherwise with us, whom he deigns to hold as sons, when we are overtaken by sin; and otherwise he is angry with those from whom he is estranged. Let us not doubt this.

units.la: Deo Patri, per sanctum nomen Iesu Christi, sit gloria & laus in æternum, quòd dum nos miseri in tenebris sedemus, ipse est illuminatio[?] nostra, & quòd in ira sua memor est misericordiæ suæ.
units.tr: To God the Father, through the holy name of Jesus Christ, be glory and praise for ever, because while we wretched men sit in darkness, he is our illumination, and because in his anger he remembers his mercy.

units.la: VERSVS XIII.
units.tr: VERSE 13.

units.la: Egressus es in salutem populi tui: in salutem cum Christo tuo: transfixisti caput de domo impij, denudando fundamentum usq; ad collum.
units.tr: You went forth for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed: you pierced the head of the house of the wicked, laying bare the foundation even to the neck.

units.la: Quomodo Deus egrediatur in salute populi sui, & singulorum piorum, cum periclitantur, eleganter & copiosè docuit Psaltes, his quidem uerbis: In angustia mea inuocaui Iehouam, & ad Deū meū clamaui: audiuit ex palatio suo uocem meam: & clamor meus in conspectu eius peruenit ad aures eius. Et cōmota est & tremuit terra: & fundamenta montium nutárunt, & sese mouerunt, quia ira erat ei. Ascēdit fumus per nares eius, & ignis uorax ex ore eius: prunæ ardebant corā eo. Et inclinauit cœlos, & descendit: & caligo erat sub pedibus eius. Et ueheba-tur super Cherub, & uolabat, & agitaba-tur super alas uenti. Posuit tenebras latibulum suum circa se, & tabernaculum suum, tenebras inquam aquarum, nubes ætheris. Præ splendore coram ipso nubes eius transierūt: grando adfuit & prunæ ignitæ. Tunc intonuit ex cœlis Iehouah: & Altissimus edidit uocem suam, grandinem & prunas ignitas. Et emisit sagittas suas, & dissipauit eos: & fulgura multiplicauit, & disiecit illos. Tunc apparuerunt gurgites aquarum, & retecta sunt fundamenta orbis, ab increpatione tua Iehouah, & à flatu uenti iræ tuæ. Emisit manum ex alto, apprehendit me, & extraxit me ex aquis multis. Eripuit me abinimico meo potente, & ab odio habentibus me: quoniam praevaluerat mihi,&c. Pfal.18.v.6.usque ad 20.
units.tr: How God goes forth for the salvation of his people, and of each of the godly when they are in peril, the Psalmist has taught elegantly and at length in these words: "In my distress I called upon Jehovah, and cried to my God: he heard my voice out of his temple, and my cry came before him, into his ears. Then the earth shook and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains moved and were shaken, because he was angry. Smoke went up from his nostrils, and fire devouring from his mouth: coals burned before him. He bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet. He rode upon a cherub and flew, and was borne on the wings of the wind. He made darkness his hiding place round about him, his tabernacle, darkness of waters, thick clouds of the sky. Before the brightness of his presence his clouds passed on: hail and fiery coals came. Then Jehovah thundered from the heavens, and the Most High gave forth his voice, hail and fiery coals. He sent out his arrows and scattered them, and multiplied lightnings and routed them. Then the channels of the waters appeared, and the foundations of the world were laid bare, at your rebuke, Jehovah, and at the blast of the breath of your anger. He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters. He delivered me from my mighty enemy, and from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me," etc. Psalm 18, verses 6 to 20.

units.la: Argumentum 9.
units.tr: Argument 9.

units.la: Iehouah armipotens, ut populum suum tueretur aduersus uicinas getes ei infen-fas, non modo cum Iosua, Othoniele, E-hud, Gedeone, Iephte, Samsone egressus est: sed etiam, & quidem praecipue, cum Dauide Rege praelia Iehouae praeliante, de quo dicitur in Psal.89.20. Inueni Dauid seruum meum: oleo sancto meo unxi eum. 21. Ideo manus mea stabilietur cum ipso, utiq; brachium meum corroborabit eum. 22. Non obruent eum inimici superuenientes: nec scelerati opprimēt[?] eum. 23. Nam conteram a facie eius oppressores eius: & eos qui oderunt ipsum, percutiam. 24. Et veritas mea & clementia mea erunt cum eo, & in nomi-ne meo attolletur cornu eius.
units.tr: Jehovah of hosts, to defend his people against the neighbouring nations hostile to them, went forth not only with Joshua, Othniel, Ehud, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson, but also, and especially, with King David, when Jehovah fought the battles; of him it is said in Psalm 89:20–24: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. Therefore my hand shall be established with him, and my arm shall strengthen him. The enemies shall not overcome him, nor the wicked oppress him. For I will crush his foes before his face, and strike down those who hate him. My faithfulness and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted."

units.la: Consentaneum ergo est, praeclarum Dei opus Israelitas esse, quorum causa haec magnifica opera peregerit, sublatis domesticis piorum aemulis, & de-bellatis externis eorundem hostibus.
units.tr: It is therefore fitting that the Israelites are the illustrious work of God, for whose sake he performed these magnificent deeds, removing the domestic rivals of the godly and overcoming their external enemies.

units.la: VERSVS XIIII.
units.tr: VERSE 14.

units.la: Perfodisti baculis eius, caput uillarum (id est, subditorum) ipsius: tanquam turbo irruerant, ut dissiperent me (id est, Israelem:) exultatio eorum erat ut properantium ad devorandum afflictum in abscondito.
units.tr: You pierced with his own staves the head of his villages (that is, his subjects): they came like a whirlwind to scatter me (that is, Israel); their exultation was as of those hastening to devour the afflicted in secret.

units.la: 1. Quòd eodem omnes populi Dei hostes animo, ἀσπονδον πόλεμον[?] gereret, perinde ac si unus hostis esset, de eis loquitur.
units.tr: 1. He speaks of them as one, because all the enemies of God's people bore the same mind, waging an unending war, as though they were a single enemy.

units.la: 2. Saepe autem, panico terrore immis-so, perfecisse Dominum, ut Israelitarum hostes seipsos conficerent, testatur exempla, Midianitarum, quos uicit Gedeon: & Aethiopum aliorumque συμμάχων, qui temporibus Iosaphati pij Regis, Iudaeam invaserant.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, that the Lord, by sending a panic terror, brought it about that the enemies of the Israelites destroyed themselves, is attested by examples: the Midianites, whom Gideon defeated, and the Ethiopians and other allies who invaded Judah in the time of the godly King Jehoshaphat.

units.la: 3. Caput uillarum, de subditorum reliquijs, quorum robore θεόμαχοι illi Reges sperabant Israelitas à se uinci posse, quidam intelligendum censent.
units.tr: 3. Some think that the "head of the villages" should be understood as the remnants of the subjects, by whose strength those god-fighting kings hoped they could conquer the Israelites.

units.la: 4. Metaphora à turbine irruente & obuia disiciente[?] ducta, hostium enthusias-mum & impetum, ac eius finem, uidelicet dissipationem populi Dei, indicat Propheta.
units.tr: 4. The Prophet, by a metaphor drawn from a whirlwind rushing in and scattering whatever lies in its path, indicates the enthusiasm and onslaught of the enemies and its end, namely the dispersal of the people of God.

units.la: 5. Postremò ἐπιχαιρεκακίας[?] hostilis descriptionem, ultimo loco additam, explicare licebit verbis Dauidis, quae exstant in Psal. 10.8. Sedet in insidiis vicorum: in latebris occidit innocentem: oculi eius in pauperem intenti sunt. 9. Insidiatur in abscondito, sicut leo in spelunca: insidiatur ad abripiendum pauperem: (discerpit) pauperem attrahens eum in rete suo. 10. Deiicit & deprimit se, & cadit in vires eius congregatio pauperum.
units.tr: 5. Finally, the description of the enemy's malice, added in the last place, may be explained in the words of David in Psalm 10:8–10: "He sits in ambush in the villages; in hiding he kills the innocent; his eyes are fixed on the poor. He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in its den; he lies in wait to seize the poor; he drags the poor away in his net. He crouches and bows down, and the company of the poor falls into his power."

units.la: Decimum hoc Dei μεγαλέου[?], saepe repetitum, fuit: Hostium populi Dei φόβος ἀντιμόνιος[?], ut eum vocat Pindarus: & eorum, suisipsorum gladijs se invicem conficientium, tragica internecio. Eo enim facto demonstrauit Dominus, longè alio loco apud se esse populum selectum, & verè eximium ποίημα[?]: alio Ethnicos, idololatras, Dei in mundo expertes: ut de illis alicubi pronunciauit diuinus Apostolus.
units.tr: This tenth wonder of God, often repeated, was the terror of the enemies of God's people, which Pindar calls a fear that turns against them, and the tragic slaughter of them, as they destroy each other with their own swords. For by this deed the Lord showed that his chosen people stand in a very different place with him, and are truly a remarkable work [ποίημα, poiēma], while the heathen, idolaters, are strangers to God in the world, as the divine Apostle declares about them somewhere.

units.la: VERSVS XV.
units.tr: VERSE 15.

units.la: Incedere fecisti in mari equos tuos per introitum aquarum multarum.
units.tr: You made your horses tread the sea, the heap of great waters.

units.la: Populum Dei in mediis imperiorum confusionibus, & rerum humanarum vicibus & conuersionibus, velut in medio mari, eoq; horribiliter commoto & ç[?]ftu-ante, conseruatum esse, ad consolationem nostram Propheta, enumerationem magnificorū Dei operum hac coronide absoluens, testatur.
units.tr: The Prophet, concluding his enumeration of the great works of God with this crown, testifies, for our consolation, that the people of God was preserved in the midst of the confusions of empires and the changes and upheavals of human affairs, as though in the middle of the sea, which was dreadfully stirred and raging.

units.la: Illustrabitur autem sententia, si quis perpendet,
units.tr: The meaning will be made clearer if one considers

units.la: 1. Hostium Ecclesiae tetram imaginem.
units.tr: 1. the hideous picture of the enemies of the Church;

units.la: 2. Descriptione praesentiae gratiae Dei.
units.tr: 2. the description of the presence of the grace of God.

units.la: Imago hostium Ecclesiae illustratur hisce dictis.
units.tr: The picture of the enemies of the Church is illustrated by these sayings.

units.la: Isa.57.20.Impij autem sunt velut mare impulsum: nam quiescere non potest, propelluntq; aquae eius caenum aclutu.
units.tr: Isaiah 57:20: "But the wicked are like the troubled sea, for it cannot be still, and its waters cast up mire and dirt."

units.la: 21.Non est pax (dicit Deus) impijs. Quis igitur intelligens miretur adeo esse inquietos, polypragmonicos, & in Sisy-phio suo saxo volvendo assiduos homi-nes impios?
units.tr: Verse 21: "There is no peace, says God, for the wicked." Who, understanding this, would wonder that wicked men are so restless, meddlesome, and constantly rolling their stone like Sisyphus?

units.la: Psalmo 46.2.Non timebimus cum movebitur terra: & concident montes in medio mari.
units.tr: Psalm 46:2: "We will not fear when the earth is moved, and the mountains fall into the heart of the sea."

units.la: 3. Et personent ac turbentur aquae eius, & concutiantur montes ab eius procellis.
units.tr: 3. "Let its waters roar and be troubled, and let the mountains be shaken by its storms."

units.la: Psal.124.4. de persecutionibus diuini-tus repressis dicitur: Nisi Iehouah nobis adfuisset, aquæ inundassent nos: torrens transijsset super animam nostram: 5. Tunc transijssent super animam nostram aquæ tumidæ.
units.tr: Psalm 124:4–5, speaking of persecutions restrained by God: "If Jehovah had not been on our side, the waters would have overwhelmed us; the torrent would have gone over our soul; then the proud waters would have gone over our soul."

units.la: De præsentia gratiæ Dei.
units.tr: On the presence of God's grace.

units.la: Etsi Ecclesia, cymbæ instar in sæuissima tempestate inter medios & undique aduersos fluctus hærentis, mundi huius ei infesti caussa, in summo discrimine uersari uidetur: tamen Deus, uelut undiq; obequitans, eam tutam præstat, fouet, cõseruat, eiq; omni benedictione in cœlestibus benedicit. Iuxta dictum Deut.33.26. Non est sicut Deus, ô Israël, equitans cœlum in auxilium tui, & in magnificentia sua cœlos.
units.tr: Although the Church, like a boat caught in the most savage storm, held fast amid waves that rise on every side and oppose her, and though she seems to be in the greatest peril because of this hostile world, God, as if riding round her on every side, keeps her safe, cherishes and preserves her, and blesses her with every blessing in the heavenly places. This accords with the saying in Deut. 33.26: "There is none like God, O Israel, who rides the heavens to help you, and the skies in his majesty."

units.la: Hoc anni tempus hybernum, & halcyonij isti dies, mihi in memoriam reuocant dulcissimos uersus Philippi Melanchthonis de Ecclesia Dei, quos libenter sane uobis recitabo.
units.tr: This wintry season of the year and these halcyon days bring back to my mind the sweetest verses of Philip Melanchthon on the Church of God, which I shall gladly recite to you.

units.la: Fluctibus in medijs pariens Ecclesia, quare Halcyonum similis sit, tabula ista docet.
units.tr: Amid the waves the Church gives birth; this picture shows why she is like the halcyons.

units.la: Illa sed est aliis etiam depicta figuris: Naturæ impressit plurima signa Deus.
units.tr: Yet she is also portrayed in other figures: God has stamped many signs upon nature.

units.la: Nidus humi iacet inter saxa hypolaidos, in quem Ignauus coccyx ova souenda locat.
units.tr: The nest of the hypolaidos lies on the ground among the rocks, and there the lazy cuckoo lays eggs for another to hatch.

units.la: Cumʃ Cumq; diu pauit cuculum officiosa uoracem, Nec tamen ingluuiem iam saturare potest: Tum sibi seruatæ soluens mala præmia uitæ, Nutricem cuculus deuorat ore suam, &c.
units.tr: Although for a long time the dutiful bird has fed the greedy cuckoo, yet it cannot satisfy its gluttony. Then the cuckoo, repaying the reward of the life that was spared, devours its own nurse with its beak, etc.

units.la: Sedenim huic nostro instituto aliud eiusdem uiri Epigramma, de Naui Christi, quæ est Ecclesia Dei, pulcrè quadrat.
units.tr: But indeed, for our present purpose, another epigram by the same man, on the ship of Christ, which is the Church of God, fits beautifully.

units.la: Auricomum uellus postquam transuexit Iason In patriam, sperans debita regna sibi: Oppressit dominum nauis de culmine lapsa, Sed qua desessus iam cubat ipse domi. Non te Christe tamen tua, quam regis, opprimet Ar- Quamuis & rimis est lacerata suis. (go, Tunc quoq; cum fluctus ciet imo ex gurgite Orion, Et rapidi uenti prælia sæua mouent: Quassatam in medio pelago tua dextera seruat, Et uere es nautis anchora sacra tuis. O uiua effigies æterni luxq; Parentis, Defendas cœtus optime Christe tuos: Qui tua non ficta discunt oracula mente, Aq; tuo poscunt Numine semper opem.
units.tr: After Jason had carried the golden fleece home to his country, hoping for the kingdom owed to him, a ship fell from its height and crushed its lord, who now lies exhausted at home. But you, Christ, whom you rule, will not be crushed, though she is torn by her own cracks. Even when Orion stirs the waves from the deep depths and the fierce battles of the swift winds rage, your right hand keeps her, battered, in the middle of the sea, and truly you are the sacred anchor for your sailors. O living image of the eternal Father and his light, best of Christ, defend your assemblies, who learn your oracles with an unfeigned mind and always seek help from your divine power.

units.la: Hactenus primā Psalmi partem, prolixè traditam, persecuti sumus. Eam si quis centro & spacio breuiter circumscri bere uolet, adducat hæc uerba è Psalmo 90. v.16. Appareat erga seruos tuos opus tuum,& gloria tua filijs eorum. 17. Etsit pulcritudo Iehouæ Dei nostri super nos, & opus manuum nostrarum confirma su per nos, opus inquam manuum nostrarum confirma.
units.tr: Thus far we have followed the first part of the Psalm, set out at length. If anyone wishes to enclose it briefly within its centre and circuit, let him take these words from Psalm 90, vv. 16-17: "Let your work appear to your servants, and your glory to their children. And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us; confirm for us the work of our hands, yes, confirm the work of our hands."

units.la: ALTERA PARS PSALMI Habacuc Prophetæ, in qua ingenuè fatetur, sese mirificè commoueri iudiciorum Dei consideratione: sed addit, fide sese intelligere futurum, ut piorum reliquias seruet Dominus.
units.tr: The second part of the psalm of the prophet Habakkuk, in which he frankly confesses that he is wonderfully moved by the consideration of God's judgments, but adds that by faith he understands the Lord will preserve a remnant of the godly.

units.la: VERSVS XVI.
units.tr: VERSE 16.

units.la: Audiui(verba tua)& contremuit venter meus: ad vocem tuam palpitarunt labia mea: ingressa est putredo in ossa mea, & apud me tremui: qui (tamen) requiescam in die angustia, (quo) ascensurus in populum, disperdet eum.
units.tr: I heard (your words) and my belly trembled; at your voice my lips quivered. Rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled within myself. Yet (I will) rest in the day of trouble, when he shall go up against the people, he will destroy him.

units.la: Est παραφομολογία [?] Prophetæ & ἀντιψαλμω- [?] ῳ. Etsi fateor me consideratione iudiciorum Dei sic affici, ut horror & tremor me totum vehementer commoueat & concutiat: tamen in Domino mihi polliceor quietem, etiam ijs temporibus, quibus hoste Chaldæo ad nos in Iudæam ascen-dente, in maximis angustijs hæc tota gens uersabitur.
units.tr: This is a paraphomologia [?] of the prophet and an antipsalm [?]. Although I confess that I am so affected by the consideration of God's judgments that horror and trembling move me entirely and shake me violently, nevertheless I promise myself rest in the Lord, even in those times when, with the Chaldean enemy coming up against us into Judea, this whole nation will be in the greatest distress.

units.la: Istud uerò maximum est, quòd Christi consolatio tum potissimùm elucet,cū ingruuntineuitabiles miseriæ. Ut Baby-las Antiochenus, martyr, in principio a-gonis dicitur repetiuisse uerba Dauidis: Reuertere anima mea in requiem tuam: quia Iehouah commutatione usus est su-per te: Quia eripuisti animam meam à morte, oculum meum è lacrymis, & pe-dem meum è lapsu. Ambulabo coram facie Iehouæ in terra uiuentium. Psalmo 116,7.8.9.
units.tr: But this is most remarkable: Christ's consolation shines forth especially when unavoidable miseries press upon us. Thus Babylas of Antioch, the martyr, is said to have repeated at the beginning of his struggle the words of David: Return, my soul, to your rest, for Jehovah has dealt bountifully with you. For you have delivered my soul from death, my eye from tears, and my foot from falling. I will walk before the face of Jehovah in the land of the living. Psalm 116:7–9.

units.la: Quid tibi Spiritus sanctus hoc loco docere uidetur?
units.tr: What does the Holy Spirit seem to teach you in this place?

units.la: 1. Cum diuinis denunciationibus, tam præmiorum, quæ pijs pollicetur Deus: quàm pœnarum, quas cõtumacibus denunciat: Dei seruis & temporum signa conferenda, Matth.16.3. ut Deum ueracem, uindicemq; scelerum agnoscentes, reuereantur: & discant fugere mala, & sectari bona.
units.tr: 1. Divine threats must be set alongside the signs of the times, both of the rewards God promises to the godly and of the punishments he denounces against the obstinate (Matt. 16:3), so that God's servants, acknowledging him as truthful and the avenger of wickedness, may revere him and learn to flee evils and pursue good.

units.la: 2. Fide tamen & spe præsentiæ & auxi-lij diuini, superandam esse humanam infirmitatem: & statuendum,Deum pijs in tanta tribulatione adesse,Ecclesiam protegere & seruare,pereuntibus interim eius hostibus.
units.tr: 2. Yet human weakness must be overcome by faith and hope in God's presence and help, and it must be held that God is present with the godly in such great tribulation, protecting and preserving the Church, while its enemies meanwhile perish.

units.la: Lugendum quidem est pijs omnibus spectaculum, de quo hi uersus D.Theodori Bezæ loquuntur:
units.tr: Indeed, it is a sight that all the godly must lament, of which these verses of the venerable Theodore Beza speak:

units.la: Insanum hunc quicunq; uides sefeq; suosq;
units.tr: Whoever you see sinking this madman and his own in a leaky boat,

units.la: Rate perforata mergere:
units.tr: Ah, how true what you see! For what you behold painted

units.la: Ah,quàm uera uides? nam quod pictu aspicis,sorùs
units.tr: is a living image of the times.

units.la: Viua est imago temporum.
units.tr: (line 4 of the verse as printed)

units.la: tamen non est cur seu hostium rabiem & potentiam, seu eorum qui intestinis malis Ecclesiam afficiunt,technas &μακτυο-λογίαν,nobis qui Christo concorpores fasti sumus, salutis palmam interuertere unquam posse,opinemur. Nouit enim Deus qui sint sui: nec quisquâ ouiculas è Christi manibus eripere potest.
units.tr: Yet there is no reason to think that the rage and power of enemies, or of those who afflict the Church with internal evils, could ever, by tricks or boasting [μακτυολογία], overturn for us, who have been made fellow-members with Christ, the palm of salvation. For God knows who are his own, and no one can snatch the sheep out of Christ's hands.

units.la: VERSVS XVII.
units.tr: VERSE 17.

units.la: Ficus enim non florebit, nec erit prouentus in uitibus: mentietur opus oliuæ, & arua nö proferent cibum: abscindet se ab ouili pecus, nec erit bos in stabulis.
units.tr: For the fig tree shall not blossom, nor shall there be produce on the vines; the work of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no food; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no ox in the stalls.

units.la: Altera παραμολογία, qua ad belli mala, terræ sterilitate eiusq; comitem famem acaccessuram, tempore aduentus Babylo-niorum in Iudæam, prædicit. Vtituraút τῆ ἐπαγωγῆ, ut doceat Iudæis ob peccata non tantum cum hoste belligerandum, sed etiam cum fame confliɛtandum. Notum est autem Prouerbium : οἰκ[?]ῳ ὀμμάτων λιμῷ θανάτῳ ἡ ποτήρι ἐπιακεῖν.
units.tr: Another paramologia, by which he foretells that the evils of war, along with barrenness of the land and its companion, famine, will arrive at the time of the Babylonians' coming into Judea. He uses the figure of epagoge [ἐπαγωγή], to teach the Jews that on account of their sins they must contend not only with the enemy but also with famine. There is a well-known proverb about this [οἰκ[?]ῳ ὀμμάτων λιμῷ θανάτῳ].

units.la: Nec uites, uini copiam : nec ficus, oliuæ aut aliæ arbores, suos fructus : nec arua frumentum : nec armentorum pecorumque greges, suos fœtus subministrabunt. Fame igitur laborandū erit Iudæis. Videtur autem de ea loqui, quæ fuit tempore ultimæ obsidionis urbis Ierosolymorum, sub Sedecia Rege : de qua uide 2. Reg. 25. 3. Nona mensis prævaluit fames in ciuitate, nec erat panis populo tes ræ. Ier. 52. 6. Threm. 2. 11 & 12.
units.tr: Neither the vines will supply their abundance of wine, nor the fig trees, olives or other trees their fruits; nor will the fields supply grain, nor the herds and flocks their young. The Jews will therefore have to suffer from famine. He seems to be speaking of the famine that prevailed at the time of the last siege of the city of Jerusalem under King Zedekiah, concerning which see 2 Kings 25:3: On the ninth month the famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land. Jer. 52:6. Lam. 2:11–12.

units.la: Cæterum, cū contraria iuxta se posita magis elucescat, promissionem de terrena benedictione, & descriptionem <bl>τῆς ἀν-ποξίας</bl> omniū rerū, ex Psalmis addemus.
units.tr: Moreover, since contraries placed side by side shine more clearly, we will add from the Psalms a promise of earthly blessing and a description of the abundance of all things.

units.la: Psal. 72. 16. Erunt manipuli frumenti in terra, in capite montium, commouebitur sicut Libani fructus eius : & efflorebunt è ciuitate tanquam herba terræ.
units.tr: Psalm 72:16. There shall be handfuls of grain in the earth, on the top of the mountains; its fruit shall shake like Lebanon, and they shall flourish out of the city like the grass of the earth.

units.la: Psalmo 81. 10. Ego sum Iehouah Deus tuus,qui eduxi te ex terra Ægypti: dilata os tuum,& implebo illud.
units.tr: Psalm 81:10. I am Jehovah your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt: open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

units.la: Pfalm.67.6.Terra dabit fructum suum: benedicet nobis Deus Deus noster.
units.tr: Psalm 67:6. The earth shall yield its fruit; God, our God, shall bless us.

units.la: Pfal.144.13.Egressus nostri erunt pleni, producentes à specie in speciem : oues nostræ mille parientes,decem millia parientes in plateis nostris. 14. Boues nostri onusti : non erit irruptio (scilicet hostium in nostros fines) neq; egressus, neque clamor in plateis nostris.
units.tr: Psalm 144:13–14. Our storehouses shall be full, producing from kind to kind; our sheep bearing thousands and ten thousands in our streets. Our oxen shall be laden; there shall be no breaking in (namely of enemies into our borders), nor going out, nor cry in our streets.

units.la: VERSVS XVIII.
units.tr: VERSE 18.

units.la: Ego tamen in Iehouah exultabo : gefliam in Deo salute mea.
units.tr: Yet I will exult in Jehovah; I will rejoice in God my salvation.

units.la: Fidei ἀντεναγωγὴ est, quæ etiam summi mœroris remedium indicat.
units.tr: This is the counter-argument of faith, which also points out the remedy even for the deepest sorrow.

units.la: Qui Deum habent Saluatorem, illis bona spe discutienda est trifticia, & exultandum in Seruatore Deo.
units.tr: Those who have God as their Saviour must dispel sadness with a good hope, and exult in God the Saviour.

units.la: Ego uerò,inquit Propheta,Deũ salute, id est,salutis certissimũ auctorem habeo.
units.tr: But I, says the prophet, have God as my salvation, that is, the most certain author of salvation.

units.la: Est igitur mihi in Iehouah exultandũ præ gaudio. Idem uerò etiam aliis pijs, quorũ eadẽ fors est, faciendũ esse statuo.
units.tr: Therefore I must exult in Jehovah with joy. And I hold that the same must be done by other godly people, whose lot is the same.

units.la: Atque hoc est spe gaudere, Rom.12.12. gloriari in oppressionibus, quòd hæc pa-tientientiam,ista autem experientiam,experientia denique spem non confundentem pariat: Rom.5.3.4.5.
units.tr: And this is to rejoice in hope (Rom. 12:12), to glory in tribulations, since these produce patience, patience produces experience, and experience finally produces a hope that does not disappoint (Rom. 5:3–5).

units.la: Dignum est memoratu beati Ambro-sij dictum: De divina misericordia amplius sperandum est,cum humana praesidia deficiunt. In Hexamero.
units.tr: A memorable saying of the blessed Ambrose: one must hope more in divine mercy when human help fails. In the Hexameron.

units.la: De spei autem, qua gaudemus, adminiculis pie dixit Bernardus: Tria confidero, in quibus tota spes mea consistit: caritatem adoptionis,veritatem promissionis, potestatem redditionis.
units.tr: Concerning the supports of the hope in which we rejoice, Bernard piously said: I consider three things in which my whole hope consists: the charity of adoption, the truth of the promise, and the power of restoration.

units.la: Et cum,Augustino teste,spes comes amoris sit, quis eius gaudium negare audeat? Sed de his non licet hoc tam angusto tempore ἀνεχιβολεγάμ[?].
units.tr: And since, according to Augustine's testimony, hope is the companion of love, who would dare to deny its joy? But on these matters it is not permitted, in so short a time, to speak at length.

units.la: VERSVS VLTIMVS.
units.tr: LAST VERSE.

units.la: Iehouah Dominus est Fortitudo mea, & posuit pedes meos tanquam cervarum: atq; super excelsa mea incedere me faciet magistro symphoniae fidibus meis.
units.tr: Jehovah the Lord is my strength, and he maketh my feet like hinds' feet, and will make me to walk upon mine high places, to the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
